question: A butcher breaking down a whole steer takes two prized steaks, the ribeye and the New York strip, from one long stretch of muscle. It barely works while the steer walks, so its meat stays soft. Where on the animal does that muscle run?
answer: Along the middle of the back, over the spine
choices: Along the middle of the back, over the spine
Across the lower chest, above the front legs
Down the rear leg and into the rump
Up in the front shoulder, behind the neck
context: Ribeye and strip are cut from the rib and loin primals that run along the middle of the back, right over the spine. That long back muscle (the longissimus dorsi) barely moves during the animal's life, so it stays lean and tender. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_eye_steak

question: A cook braising an American pot roast is most often working with chuck, the biggest single cut on a steer and a heavily worked one, and much of the ground beef in burgers comes from it too. Which part of the steer is the chuck?
context: The chuck is the front shoulder, running from the neck back to about the fifth rib — the largest primal, roughly a quarter of the carcass. Because the shoulder works constantly, it's full of tough connective tissue, so it's cheap and best braised or ground into burger. Source: https://butchershandbook.com/guides/primal-cuts-of-beef/

question: Sold as a cheap roast, the round turns dry and chewy if a cook rushes it over high heat. It is the second-biggest of the primals, the big sections a steer is broken into, and its hard-worked meat is lean, with almost no marbling. Which part of the steer is the round?
context: The round is the rear leg and rump, the second-largest primal at about a fifth of the animal. A steer's back legs carry and push it all day, so the round is lean but tough. Chuck (shoulder) and round (rear leg) are the two biggest, hardest-working primals — which is why they're the cheapest and need low, slow, moist cooking. Source: https://www.aol.com/articles/beef-chuck-vs-round-butcher-170000007.html

question: Butchers in New York and Kansas City named a favorite steak after their home cities, yet the New York strip and the Kansas City strip are one and the same cut. It comes off the longissimus dorsi, the same long muscle that gives the ribeye. Along that muscle, where does the strip lie compared with the ribeye?
answer: Farther back, toward the rear of the loin
choices: Farther back, toward the rear of the loin
Farther forward, right behind the shoulder
At the very center, sharing the ribeye's spot
Right up front, over the shoulder blade
context: The strip steak — New York strip or Kansas City strip — is the top-loin side of the T-bone. It's the same longissimus back muscle as the ribeye, just taken from farther back, toward the rear of the loin. Source: https://www.chefs-resources.com/types-of-meat/beef/cuts-of-beef/short-loin-t-bone-steak-porterhouse-steak/

question: A Texas pitmaster smokes a brisket over oak or mesquite for twelve or fourteen hours at low heat, until it is tender enough to fall apart under a fork. Cooked fast, the same slab of hard-working meat, streaked with fat and connective tissue, comes out as chewy as a boot. Which part of the steer does brisket come from?
context: Brisket is the breast — the lower chest — lying right over the sternum and front ribs, just above the front legs. It's one of the hardest-working muscles on a standing steer, which is why it starts out so tough. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisket

question: A diner slides the edge of a butter knife straight through a steak famous as the most tender in the world. It was cut from the tenderloin, a slim muscle that never bulges or shows on the outside of a steer. In the living animal it does almost no work, which is why the meat stays so soft. Where inside the steer does the tenderloin hide?
answer: Under the lower spine, near the kidneys
choices: Under the lower spine, near the kidneys
Inside the front shoulder, near the windpipe
Within the rear rump, near the tailbone
Behind the front ribs, near the heart
context: Filet mignon comes from the tenderloin (the psoas major), a slender muscle tucked under the spine inside the short loin, near the kidneys. It's the least-worked muscle on the animal, so it develops almost no connective tissue — making it the most tender cut on the whole carcass. Source: https://www.corewalking.com/a-filet-mignon-is-the-psoas-major/

question: Old-school butchers used to trim a thin ribbon of muscle, the spinalis dorsi, off the ribeyes bound for their customers and keep it for their own dinners. The ribbon hugs the outer curve of every ribeye, it is heavily marbled, and many cooks call it the tastiest bite of the whole steak. What nickname did the butchers give it?
context: The ribeye cap — the spinalis dorsi, also called the deckle — is the ribbon wrapping the outside of the ribeye. It's the most marbled, most flavorful bite of the steak, nicknamed 'butcher's butter.' Source: https://jesspryles.com/spinalis-dorsi-ribeye-cap/

question: A porterhouse steak, sliced from the short loin near the middle of a steer's back, has a T-shaped bone with a different muscle on each side: one broad, dark and beefy, the other narrow, pale and almost butter-soft. That is why butchers call it two steaks in one. Which two muscles share the bone?
answer: The strip loin and the tenderloin
choices: The strip loin and the tenderloin
The ribeye and the chuck eye
context: A porterhouse (and its cousin the T-bone) is really two steaks in one slice: the strip loin on one side of the T-shaped bone and the tenderloin on the other, joined right at the bone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-bone_steak

question: A T-bone and a porterhouse look like near-twins on the plate, and a butcher cuts both from the same short loin. The porterhouse, though, comes from farther back, where one of its two muscles grows noticeably bigger. A diner who orders the porterhouse gets more of which cut?
context: Both come from the short loin where the strip and tenderloin meet, but the porterhouse is cut from the rear, where the tenderloin is much larger. USDA rules even set the line — a porterhouse's tenderloin must be at least 1.25 inches wide, a T-bone's only about half an inch. So a porterhouse is essentially a T-bone with a bigger filet mignon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_loin

question: A girl turning a pineapple in her hands counts the little diamond-shaped 'eyes' spiraling over its rough skin. The fruit is really dozens of tiny fruits fused around a central stalk. Each eye marks the spot where the plant once grew a single what?
context: Every one of those diamond 'eyes' was once a separate flower. Each flower left behind a single small fruitlet, and all of them fused together side by side into one head -- which means a pineapple isn't really one fruit at all, but dozens of tiny fruits merged into a single body. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pineapple' and 'Multiple fruit.'

question: A worker on a pineapple farm in Hawaii or Costa Rica walks out with a knife to cut a ripe fruit. The plant he visits lives for several years and slowly raises just one pineapple at a time, right at its center. Where does he find that fruit growing?
answer: on a low, spiky plant near the ground
choices: on a low, spiky plant near the ground
high in the branches of a tall tree
dangling from a woody climbing vine
down in the soil among the roots
context: It grows low to the ground. A pineapple plant is a herbaceous perennial only about 1 to 1.5 m (3.5 to 5 ft) tall -- a spiky rosette of stiff, sword-shaped leaves with a single fruit rising from the center. It never grows on a tree, so the 'pineapple tree' is pure myth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pineapple.'

question: A boy finishing a fresh pineapple can grow a whole new plant without buying a single seed, because the pineapple is a bromeliad. He twists off one part of the fruit, lets it dry for a day, roots it in a glass of water and plants it. Which part does he twist off?
answer: the spiky, leafy crown on top
choices: the spiky, leafy crown on top
the hard core from the middle
a strip of the tough outer rind
context: The leafy crown. Twist or slice off the spiky top, let it root in water or soil, and it will grow into a whole new plant -- no seed required. Patience helps: a pineapple plant grows slowly, taking roughly 18 to 24 months (about two years) to flower and yield its single fruit. Source: LSU AgCenter; corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Pineapple.'

question: Suppose you eat a big bowl of fresh, raw pineapple. After a while your tongue starts to sting and prickle and feels oddly raw and sore, yet canned pineapple never does this. Something in the raw juice goes to work on the soft tissue of your mouth. What is the fresh fruit doing to it?
answer: digesting the protein in your mouth, like a stomach would
choices: digesting the protein in your mouth, like a stomach would
burning the skin in your mouth with sharp acid
scraping the skin in your mouth with tiny crystals
numbing the nerves in your mouth with hot spice
context: It's digesting you back. Fresh raw pineapple is loaded with bromelain, a protein-splitting (proteolytic) enzyme, and on your tongue it actually begins breaking down the proteins in your mouth -- that raw, prickly sting is the enzyme at work. The same enzyme makes fresh pineapple a natural meat tenderizer, breaking down the tough proteins in a steak. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bromelain.'

question: A cook stirs chunks of fresh pineapple into a bowl of Jell-O, and the dessert never sets: an enzyme in the raw fruit eats the gelatin's protein and leaves a runny liquid. Pineapple straight from a can, stirred into the same Jell-O, lets it set perfectly. What is different about the canned fruit?
answer: it was cooked with heat, which wrecked the enzyme
choices: it was cooked with heat, which wrecked the enzyme
it was soaked in sweet syrup, which cancels the enzyme
its juice was drained away, taking the enzyme with it
it was frozen solid, which locks the enzyme in place
context: Canned pineapple is heated during processing, and heat destroys bromelain -- the enzyme is heat-sensitive and goes inactive around 71 C (160 F). With its enzyme knocked out, canned or cooked pineapple can no longer attack the gelatin's protein, so the Jell-O sets perfectly. Fresh, raw pineapple still has its live enzyme, which is why it keeps the dessert a liquid. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bromelain.'

question: A shopper leaves a rock-hard banana on the kitchen counter, and within days it turns soft and sweet. She sets a slightly tart pineapple right beside the ripening bananas and waits, but the pineapple stays exactly as tart as the day she bought it. Why does a banana keep sweetening after it is picked while a pineapple never does?
answer: a banana stores starch it slowly turns to sugar; a pineapple has none to convert
choices: a banana stores starch it slowly turns to sugar; a pineapple has none to convert
a banana keeps ripening gas trapped under its peel; a pineapple's skin lets it out
a banana stays attached to its stalk longer; a pineapple is cut away too soon
a banana holds far more water inside; a pineapple just dries out on the counter
context: A pineapple is 'non-climacteric': it stores no starch reserve to convert into sugar once it leaves the plant, so its sweetness is locked in the instant it's picked -- which is why pineapples must be harvested fully ripe. A banana is the opposite, a 'climacteric' fruit that stores starch and keeps ripening and sweetening after picking. Parking a pineapple next to bananas does nothing, because it simply has no starch left to turn into sugar. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pineapple' and 'Climacteric (botany).'

question: A boy takes a first sip of his dad's black coffee and scrunches up his face. People pull the same face at a first taste of dark stout or a nibble of unsweetened baking chocolate. What harsh taste do all three share?
context: These three are the classic 'acquired tastes.' Almost nobody's first sip of black coffee or beer is 'Wow, this tastes great' — the scrunched, coughing face is nearly universal. Source: ScienceABC 'The Science Of Acquired Taste'; BeerDecoded 'Is Beer An Acquired Taste?'

question: Babies a few days old, long before anyone teaches them about food, screw up their faces and spit out anything bitter. Scientists think the reflex is a built-in alarm against one danger in nature. What danger did it evolve to guard against?
context: Most natural plant poisons taste bitter, so evolution wired the rejection in before birth — no learning required. The reflex shows up in an infant's first days of life. Source: Duke Health 'Toxins Drove Evolution of Human Taste Sense'; PMC4654709 'The sweetness and bitterness of childhood.'

question: Marcus has drunk a mug of black coffee every morning for thirty years. His ten-year-old son Leo tries one sip from the same pot, gags and spits it into the sink. The coffee is chemically identical for both and hits the same taste buds. Why does Marcus enjoy a taste his son cannot stand?
answer: The coffee still tastes just as bitter, but his brain now rates that bitterness as pleasant
choices: The coffee still tastes just as bitter, but his brain now rates that bitterness as pleasant
Years of daily coffee wore out the bitter taste buds, so his tongue barely registers it
The caffeine grew stronger over the years, enough to mask and cancel out the bitterness
His usual dark roast is a naturally mild bean, so there was little bitterness to begin with
context: As one summary of the science puts it, coffee always tastes bitter to the mouth — the brain only updates its 'hedonic value,' or how pleasant it judges the taste. The tongue didn't change its mind; the brain did. Source: ScienceABC 'The Science Of Acquired Taste.'

question: Bitter coffee never stops tasting bitter, even to someone who loves it, so the brain must have a reason to learn to enjoy it. Scientists point to one thing that coffee, beer and strong tea all quietly deliver with every sip. What teaches the brain to crave the bitter drink?
answer: A chemical reward, like caffeine's lift or beer's buzz
choices: A chemical reward, like caffeine's lift or beer's buzz
A dose of vitamins found only in bitter plants
A cleaner, fresher feeling left in the mouth
A slowly-built tolerance to natural poisons
context: The brain re-labels a bitter drink as pleasant because each sip pays off: the lift of caffeine, the buzz of alcohol. In time the payoff comes to outweigh the bitterness, and with no payoff there is no acquired liking. Source: ScienceABC on the brain's reward pathways; BeerDecoded on alcohol reward learning.

question: Tonic water, the fizzy mixer, has a sharp, bitter bite that many adults grow to love. The bitterness comes from a compound in the bark of the cinchona tree of South America, and it is not only a flavoring. What else has this bitter compound long been used as?
answer: A real medicine that fights malaria
choices: A real medicine that fights malaria
A dye for coloring cloth deep red
A preservative that keeps drinks fizzy
A polish for shining brass and copper
context: The compound is quinine — a genuine anti-malaria drug that is toxic in quantity, so the U.S. FDA caps tonic water at 83 parts per million (higher doses can cause nausea, vomiting, even kidney injury). In a tonic-sized dose, drinkers simply enjoy a real poison-flavor made safe. Source: BiologyInsights 'What Has Quinine in It?'; U.S. FDA quinine limit for tonic water.

question: Bitter taste evolved as an ancient poison alarm: a bite of something too bitter, and the tongue says spit it out. Some plants hide tiny amounts of cyanide in their cells, released when teeth crush the tissue, and a faint bitterness warns the eater not to have too much. Which ordinary kitchen foods carry these cyanide-releasing compounds?
answer: Cassava, bitter almonds, and lima beans
choices: Cassava, bitter almonds, and lima beans
context: The bitter alarm is written in deep time. Scientists estimate that one favoured bitter-receptor variant arose before humans left Africa, sharpening early humans' detection of the cyanide-releasing compounds in plants such as cassava, bitter almonds and beans; the faint bitterness warns the eater not to have too much. Sweet almonds, the kind sold for snacking, carry almost none of these compounds. Source: Duke Health 'Toxins Drove Evolution of Human Taste Sense'; Soranzo & Goldstein et al., Current Biology (July 26, 2005); https://grokipedia.com/page/Amygdalin

question: Anna Russell, Duchess of Bedford, grew faint with hunger each afternoon around 1840, since fashionable dinner waited until eight. She began inviting friends to tea at four, with thin sandwiches, little cakes and a warm baked round eaten with clotted cream and jam. What is that baked round called?
context: Anna Russell, the 7th Duchess of Bedford, had tea, bread-and-butter and cake sent up to her room to beat the late-afternoon 'sinking feeling' of hunger before a dinner that might not appear until 7:30 or 8pm. As a lady-in-waiting to Queen Victoria, she spread the habit through the court, and afternoon tea became a British institution. Source: British Museum, 'The tea-rific history of Victorian afternoon tea'; Wikipedia, Anna Russell, Duchess of Bedford / Tea (meal).

question: A posh hotel sells 'high tea': dainty finger sandwiches and little cakes. The name sounds like the grandest meal of all, and the hotel happily plays along, but the name is borrowed. What was a real high tea in 1800s Britain?
answer: A hearty hot evening meal for working families
choices: A hearty hot evening meal for working families
A dainty afternoon spread for the wealthy
A children's after-school snack of milk and cake
A late-night supper served after the theatre
context: A working family's high tea, eaten around 5-7pm, was built on bread, butter and tea but bulked out with a hot dish - fried fish or meat - plus hams, cheese, pies and cakes. Over time it simply became the evening 'dinner,' and many Britons still call that meal 'tea' today. Source: Wikipedia, Tea (meal); CNN Travel, 'British teatime... sometimes there isn't even any tea.'

question: Wealthy ladies in a Victorian parlour nibbled little cakes at a dainty afternoon spread that Britons called 'low tea', and another meal of the day was 'high tea'. The words had nothing to do with social class or how fancy the meal was. What did 'high' and 'low' describe?
answer: The kind of table it was eaten at
choices: The kind of table it was eaten at
The time of day the meal was served
The heartiness of the meal itself
The strength of the tea served
context: 'High' tea was eaten at a high dining table, while 'low' tea - another name for afternoon tea - was taken on the low parlour or drawing-room tables people lounged beside. The words mark the furniture, not the diner's rank. Source: CNN Travel, 'British teatime... sometimes there isn't even any tea'; Wikipedia, Tea (meal).

question: A Cornish cook builds a cream tea in a strict order: first the jam, spread straight onto the split warm scone, and only then a heavy spoonful of thick clotted cream on top. Cornish traditionalists say that reversing the order ruins the plate, for a very practical kitchen reason. What reason do they give?
answer: Cream underneath would melt into a soggy scone
choices: Cream underneath would melt into a soggy scone
Jam won't stick to clotted cream once it sets
The hot scone would turn the clotted cream sour
Jam on top would slide off the slippery cream
context: Devon does it the opposite way - clotted cream first, treated like a thick butter, then jam on top, with fans there calling the cream the star of the show. The order genuinely splits the West Country, and even the late Queen Elizabeth II was reported to take the Cornish side, jam first. Source: Wikipedia, Cream tea; gosouthwestengland.co.uk, 'How to eat a scone.'

question: A butcher cuts soft, floppy meat from a steer the moment it is slaughtered and leaves it alone. Back 10 to 24 hours later, he finds that, untouched and uncooked, the meat no longer bends the way it did. What does the meat do on its own?
context: The stiffening is rigor mortis: within about 10-24 hours of slaughter, the proteins actin and myosin lock together into permanent cross-bridges. Cooked in that state, beef is chewy and unpalatable — which is exactly why it must rest and age before it's any good. Source: agriculture.institute, 'Conditioning of Meat / Post-Rigor Tenderization.'

question: A whole side of beef hangs in a cold, dark room while its butcher waits, sometimes for days, sometimes for weeks. He never pounds it, cooks it or salts it, yet when he finally cuts steaks from it, meat that started out chewy has turned buttery. What is doing all that work inside the muscle?
choices: Ice crystals forming in the fibers
Salt drawing moisture from the edges
context: The muscle's own enzymes — mainly calpains, with help from cathepsins — slowly snip apart the proteins that make meat tough. The beef essentially digests its own toughness, with no cooking, marinade, or pounding involved. Source: MeatEater, 'The Science of Aging Meat.'

question: Steakhouse dry-aged beef hangs for weeks in special humidity-controlled rooms. Ordinary supermarket beef has also aged for a couple of weeks by the time it reaches the shelf, yet no one ever hung it up in a room. How did the supermarket beef age along the way?
answer: Sealed in vacuum plastic during shipping
choices: Sealed in vacuum plastic during shipping
Soaked in a saltwater tank at the plant
Hung on open racks in a cold warehouse
Packed in crushed ice inside the truck
context: This is wet-aging: beef sealed in Cryovac plastic ages in its own juices, so nothing evaporates and no weight is lost. It happens automatically over the roughly 14-21 days beef spends in shipping and distribution, which makes it the milder, cheaper, industry-standard default. Source: meatcutguide.com, 'Dry-Aged vs Wet-Aged.'

question: A dry-aged steak comes off the grill tasting like someone seasoned it, though nothing was ever rubbed or sprinkled on it. Weeks in the cold room built up one compound inside the muscle — and the exact same stuff is sold by the jar on the seasoning aisle. Which jar is it?
context: Aging enzymes break the muscle proteins down into free amino acids, especially glutamate — the exact savory ('umami') compound in monosodium glutamate, MSG. That's why aged beef tastes meatier, and dry-aged beef measures even higher in glutamate than wet-aged. Source: MeatEater, 'The Science of Aging Meat.'

question: A pricey Manhattan steakhouse lists a '45-day dry-aged' ribeye on its menu for a hundred dollars a plate. The longer beef dry-ages in a cold cellar, the further its flavor shifts away from fresh beef. By 45 days, chefs say, it tastes uncannily like one sharp, funky, aged food. Which food?
context: Dry-aged beef turns nutty and savory around 30 days, then develops an 'almost blue-cheese-like' funk by 45 days and beyond — the same aging logic that makes stinky cheese stinky. A '45-day dry-aged' menu boast is bragging about exactly that deep funk. Source: meatcutguide.com, 'Dry-Aged vs Wet-Aged.'

question: Fans blow cold, dry air night and day over a beef roast left uncovered in a chilled room for four to six weeks, pulling moisture from every surface. At the end, the butcher shaves the whole outer layer off with his knife and throws it in the bin before he cuts a single steak to sell. What has that layer become?
context: That dried outer layer is called the 'bark.' Together with roughly 15% of the roast's weight lost to evaporation by 30 days, the trimmed-away bark can push total loss to 25-40% of the starting weight — part of why dry-aged steak commonly costs 30-50% more than the same cut un-aged. Sources: PMC (PMC4872334); meatcutguide.com, 'Dry-Aged vs Wet-Aged.'

question: At a taquería in Mexico City, most taco fillings sizzle flat on a griddle called a plancha. Al pastor meat is cooked another way, one that immigrants from the Middle East brought to Mexico along with their shawarma. How is al pastor meat cooked?
answer: stacked on an upright post and shaved off as it spins
choices: stacked on an upright post and shaved off as it spins
slow-simmered in a covered clay pot until it shreds
deep-fried in bubbling lard until crisp and golden
roasted for hours buried in an underground pit
context: Al pastor is grilled on a 'trompo' (Spanish for a spinning-top toy, named for the cone shape of the stacked meat) - a tall vertical spit. The taquero shaves thin, crispy ribbons off the browning outside straight into a tortilla, exactly like a shawarma or doner kebab. Source: Wikipedia, 'Al pastor'.

question: A whole fruit sits on top of the trompo, the tall cone of al pastor meat turning slowly beside a taquería's fire. Its warm juice drips down over the meat, and a charred bit of it ends up on each taco. Which fruit crowns the stack?
context: The pineapple both flavors the meat and bastes it with sweet juice. How it ended up on the spinning spit is a genuine puzzle - chef Alex Stupak calls the pineapple's origin 'one of history's most delicious mysteries.' Source: Tasting Table, 'The history of tacos al pastor'.

question: Immigrants from the Middle East brought shawarma, seasoned lamb stacked on a spit that turns beside a flame, to Mexico. Mexican cooks tried to keep the spinning spit, but lamb was scarce and costly there, so the cooks who invented tacos al pastor swapped it for a cheaper meat that Mexicans already raised and loved. Which meat took lamb's place?
context: Pork came to rule the spit as tacos al pastor took shape in Mexico City in the 1950s and 1960s; the older Puebla versions used lamb or beef. The switch was easy partly because the immigrants who brought the spit were mostly Christians, with no religious rule against pork. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Al_pastor ; The Eye (Huatulco), 'Al pastor and the Lebanese influence on Mexican food'.

question: Newcomers from abroad cooked their homeland's lamb shawarma on an upright turning spit, and Mexican cooks watched, learned and remade the dish with local meat and dried chilies. That spit is no old Aztec invention: the immigrants who brought it first reached Mexico in the late 1800s. Where did they come from?
context: Lebanese immigrants began reaching Mexico in the late 1800s, many of them settling around Puebla; their homeland was then part of the Ottoman Empire. Their lamb shawarma was the direct model for al pastor, which took off in Mexico City in the 1950s and 1960s. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Al_pastor ; Wikipedia, 'Al pastor'.

question: A taquero carves al pastor meat that glows a deep reddish orange, nothing like ordinary pale grilled meat. Dried red chilies in the marinade give part of that color, but a small brick-red seed native to the Yucatán, ground into paste, deepens it; Mexican cooks have colored food with it since the days of the Maya. Which spice is it?
context: Achiote - also called annatto - is the seed of a small tropical tree and a classic Latin American food coloring; it gives al pastor and many dishes their warm red-orange hue. The adobo also carries garlic, cumin, clove, bay leaf, and vinegar. Source: Wikipedia, 'Al pastor'.

question: Taquerías in Puebla, in central Mexico, have served an older cousin of tacos al pastor since the 1930s. The meat is the same, roasted on a spit, but instead of a corn tortilla it comes wrapped in a soft, round wheat flatbread that the immigrants who opened those shops brought from home. What is this Puebla taco called?
context: These 'tacos arabes' are the closest surviving link back to al pastor's Middle Eastern ancestor: the same spit meat on 'pan arabe,' a wheat flatbread the immigrants brought over. Puebla's La Oriental restaurant, open since 1933, still bills itself 'la cuna del taco arabe' - the birthplace of the Arab taco. Source: Tasting Table, 'The history of tacos al pastor'; The Eye (Huatulco).

question: Diners who came to Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, after Alice Waters opened it in 1971 expected fancy French food. Instead, the restaurant that became a landmark of American farm-to-table cooking ran on a surprising rule about a perfect, ripe, in-season fruit or vegetable. What was her rule?
answer: It should be treated as the star of the plate and cooked simply, or barely at all
choices: It should be treated as the star of the plate and cooked simply, or barely at all
It should be blended into rich sauces so that no single flavor stands out
It should be saved only for holidays and special-occasion tasting menus
It should always be paired with an equally expensive imported ingredient
context: Waters built the whole restaurant around the ripe ingredient instead of fancy recipes. In her words: 'When you have the best and tastiest ingredients, you can cook very simply and the food will be extraordinary because it tastes like what it is' -- the seasoning meant only to heighten the food's virtues, never to hide its faults. Note: Waters was a pioneer and popularizer of American farm-to-table, not the lone inventor; seasonal, local cooking long predates her. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Waters; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chez_Panisse.

question: A diner sits down at Alice Waters's Chez Panisse in Berkeley and finds no long menu to choose from: one fixed meal, no choices, and it is completely different every single night. Waters built the restaurant around one rule that decides each evening's menu. What is the rule?
answer: Whatever local produce is perfectly ripe that week
choices: Whatever local produce is perfectly ripe that week
Whatever dish the chef feels like improvising that morning
Whichever rare delicacy the kitchen flew in that day
Whichever dish comes up at random from the old recipe box
context: To keep that promise, Waters built direct relationships with nearby farmers, ranchers and dairies, some of whom still supply Chez Panisse today. A fixed menu set by the week's harvest meant you simply ate what Alice was making that night -- a seasonal, local style that became known as 'California cuisine.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chez_Panisse.

question: Alice Waters carried her food ideas out of the Chez Panisse kitchen in 1995 and into Martin Luther King Junior Middle School in Berkeley. She and the students took a neglected one-acre lot behind the school, all cracked pavement, weeds and trash, and slowly turned it into the Edible Schoolyard. What did the students do there?
answer: Grew, harvested, and cooked their own food in a garden and kitchen classroom
choices: Grew, harvested, and cooked their own food in a garden and kitchen classroom
Tended garden plots that a catering company later harvested and cooked for them
Grew the vegetables while adult chefs did all the harvesting and the cooking
Grew produce that got trucked off to supply the Chez Panisse dinner menu
context: The Edible Schoolyard opened in 1995 at Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School in Berkeley: a one-acre organic garden and kitchen classroom where kids grow, harvest and cook their own food. The idea spread, and Waters' example helped inspire Michelle Obama's White House vegetable garden. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Waters.

question: English cooks of the 1600s pried open a jar of a new spice from the Caribbean, and its smell hit them at once: warm cinnamon, sweet nutmeg and sharp clove braided together in one small brown bead. Sure the seller was blending three familiar spices, they named it 'allspice'. They were wrong about the blend. What is allspice really?
answer: A single dried berry from one tree
choices: A single dried berry from one tree
A ground blend of three spices
A mix of clove and cinnamon oils
The dried bark of a spice tree
context: Allspice comes from just one plant, the tree Pimenta dioica. Its dried unripe berries taste so much like cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove combined that early English cooks assumed it was a mixture of those spices and coined the name 'allspice' around 1621 — the 'all-spice' name describes the flavor, not the ingredients. Source: Wikipedia, 'Allspice'.

question: Columbus's crews crossed the ocean hunting for pepper, and when they found small brown berries that looked just like peppercorns, they were sure they'd found a new kind of pepper. Europeans nicknamed the spice after the Caribbean island it came from. What did they call it?
context: Allspice is a New World spice — Columbus's men met it in the Caribbean in the 1490s while searching for the pepper of the Indies, and the peppercorn-looking berries earned the nickname 'Jamaica pepper.' Jamaica is still the heart of the world's allspice, and allspice is one of the very few major spices grown almost entirely in the Americas rather than Asia. Source: jamaicatimeline.com (pimento history); Wikipedia, 'Allspice'.

question: Growers shipped allspice seeds from the Caribbean to other tropical countries and watched them fail to sprout year after year; for centuries the tree would grow only at home. Then they found that the seeds wake up only after passing through the body of a certain animal. Which animal?
context: Allspice seeds germinate reliably only after passing through a bird's digestive tract — the trip through the gut is what triggers them to sprout. Because of this quirk, plantations struggled to establish allspice outside its native range for a very long time. Source: Wikipedia, 'Allspice'.

question: Before a pork roast goes into the oven, a cook scores thin crisscross lines into its fatty skin, then peels a strip of tough, silvery membrane off a beef tenderloin. Both jobs need small, precise cuts, not brute chopping. Which part of her chef's knife does that work?
context: The tip is the very point of the blade, where the spine and the edge sweep together. It's the knife's precision instrument — scoring, trimming, small controlled cuts, piercing, even nicking a bit of meat to peek inside and check if it's done. Source: Shun Cutlery knife-anatomy (shun.kaiusa.com/knife-anatomy); The Custom Chef (thecustomchef.com/blogs/care/the-complete-guide-to-knife-anatomy).

question: To smash garlic for a pan sauce, a cook lays the broad side of her blade on a peeled clove and thumps it with her palm, bursting it in one snap. With the same broad side she scoops the bits into the hot pan. Which part of the knife does both jobs?
context: The flat is the broad side of the blade. It's both a smasher and a scoop: lay it over a garlic clove or a cucumber and thump to crush it, then use it to sweep chopped food off the board into the pan. (Crush with the flat — never the sharp edge.) Source: F.N. Sharp (fnsharp.com/blogs/fns/parts-of-a-kitchen-knife); The Custom Chef (thecustomchef.com/blogs/care/the-complete-guide-to-knife-anatomy).

question: A rock-hard butternut squash waits on the cutting board, its skin like leather and its dense neck nearly as tough as wood. The cook must drive the blade straight down through that neck with real muscle; a dainty slice from the pointed end will not do. Which part of the chef's knife is built for that chop?
context: The heel is the rear of the edge, nearest the handle — the widest, thickest part of the cutting edge, so it takes the most force. Drive it down through the dense, tough jobs: hard carrots, winter squash, even bones. Source: The Custom Chef (thecustomchef.com/blogs/care/the-complete-guide-to-knife-anatomy); Shun Cutlery (shun.kaiusa.com/knife-anatomy).

question: A chef cracking a tough knob of ginger lays her free palm flat along the top of her chef's knife and bears down hard for extra power and control. Which part of the blade is her palm pressing on?
context: The spine is the blunt back of the blade, opposite the edge and much thicker than the razor-thin cutting edge. Because it is dull, it is the side a cook can safely press on with a hand for extra power and control. Source: The Custom Chef (thecustomchef.com/blogs/care/the-complete-guide-to-knife-anatomy); F.N. Sharp (fnsharp.com/blogs/fns/parts-of-a-kitchen-knife).

question: A line cook minces a pile of parsley into bright green confetti, the point of her chef's knife anchored to the board while she rocks the blade up and down in a smooth arc. A dead-flat edge would only slap the board; the rocking needs a gentle curve along the edge. Which part of the knife makes that rocking motion possible?
context: The belly is the curved section of the cutting edge, and that curve is what lets a knife rock — keep the tip on the board and rock the handle up and down to mince garlic or herbs. A dead-flat edge, like on many Japanese knives, can't rock at all. Source: Shun Cutlery (shun.kaiusa.com/knife-anatomy); Element Knife Company (elementknife.com/pages/kitchen-knife-anatomy).

question: Right where a chef's knife blade leaves its handle sits a small scooped notch called the choil. A pro cook's fingers settle into it during the grip that gives far more control than holding the handle alone. How does that grip hold the knife?
answer: Thumb and forefinger pinch the base of the blade
choices: Thumb and forefinger pinch the base of the blade
All four fingers wrap the far end of the handle
The forefinger points along the back of the blade
The whole fist clamps the handle like a hammer
context: This is the pinch grip: the thumb and the side of the forefinger squeeze the base of the blade itself, with the fingers resting in the choil, the small recessed curve where the blade leaves the handle. Pinching the blade gives far more control than gripping the handle alone. Source: Shun Cutlery (shun.kaiusa.com/knife-anatomy); Element Knife Company (elementknife.com/pages/kitchen-knife-anatomy).

question: A cook picks up a forged Western chef's knife. Where its steel blade meets the handle sits a thick collar of steel, the bolster, which adds heft and balance so the knife rocks evenly through a cut. On knives that have one, it also does a second, cleverer job that keeps a working cook safe. What is that job?
answer: It stops a wet hand sliding forward onto the edge
choices: It stops a wet hand sliding forward onto the edge
It caps the handle so the cook can pound nuts
It hones the edge a little with every cut
It keeps the steel from rusting where it is held
context: The bolster is the thick collar of steel where the blade meets the handle, and it does two jobs at once: it adds balance, and it acts as a finger guard — a raised barrier that keeps a wet, slippery hand from sliding forward off the handle onto the edge. Note: not every knife has one — many Japanese knives skip the bolster entirely. Source: F.N. Sharp (fnsharp.com/blogs/fns/parts-of-a-kitchen-knife); Element Knife Company (elementknife.com/pages/kitchen-knife-anatomy); Misen (misen.com/blogs/news/parts-of-a-knife).

question: A knifemaker builds a good Western chef's knife so that its steel runs the entire length of the handle in one solid piece. Cooks call that a full tang, and it makes the knife strong. What else does all that steel in the handle do to the way the knife sits in a cook's hand?
answer: pulls the balance point back toward the hand
choices: pulls the balance point back toward the hand
tips the balance forward toward the point
makes the blade flex enough to fillet around bones
helps the steel hold its edge and resist rust
context: A full tang runs the entire length (and width) of the handle as one solid piece: strong, and it pulls the balance point back toward the hand, so the knife feels planted, 'like an extension of the arm,' instead of tip-heavy. Source: Dalstrong (dalstrong.com/blogs/news/knife-tang-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters); Misen knife-tang guide (misen.com/blogs/news/knife-tang).

question: A cook lifts a traditional Japanese chef's knife and finds it light in the hand, its balance tipped forward toward the point, made for slicing with a smooth forward push rather than a rocking chop. Inside its wooden handle, how is the blade's steel built?
answer: it narrows to a thin spike hidden up inside the handle
choices: it narrows to a thin spike hidden up inside the handle
it runs the full width as a solid slab through the handle
it splits into two flat prongs bolted through the handle
it ends in a short stub capped by a metal collar
context: This is a hidden (concealed) tang — the traditional Japanese design. Instead of a broad slab of steel sandwiched between two riveted scales like a Western full tang, the steel narrows to a spike buried inside a wooden handle. Less steel makes the knife lighter and shifts its balance forward, which suits slicing with a forward push. Source: Element Knife Company (elementknife.com/pages/kitchen-knife-anatomy); Dalstrong (dalstrong.com/blogs/news/knife-tang-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters); Misen (misen.com/blogs/news/knife-tang).

question: A dad starts the keto diet, meant to make the body burn fat for fuel instead of carbohydrates. Bread rolls, pasta and sugary soda leave his dinner table, but cutting carbs alone does not make a meal keto. What swap does he still need to make?
answer: Replace them with plenty of fat
choices: Replace them with plenty of fat
Replace them with lean, low-fat protein
Replace them with more leafy vegetables
Replace them with a bit more of everything
context: Keto's whole trick is counterintuitive: unlike most 'diets,' it doesn't cut fat — it makes fat the main fuel, around 70-75% of calories, while carbs drop to a fraction of a normal day's intake. Fatty meat, eggs, cheese, avocado, butter, and olive oil are staples; bread, pasta, rice, sugar, and potatoes are out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketogenic_diet; carbmanager.com keto-macros guide.

question: On the keto diet, a person eats so little bread, rice or sugar that the body can no longer lean on its usual blood-sugar fuel. One organ turns into a kind of fuel factory: it breaks stored body fat apart and turns it into ketones, which the body can burn instead. Which organ does this job?
context: With carbs scarce, the liver breaks fat into three 'ketone bodies' — beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, and acetone — which the body burns for energy instead of glucose. That fat-burning state is called ketosis, the engine the whole diet is named for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketogenic_diet.

question: Doctors long taught that one organ lived on almost nothing but glucose, the sugar in the blood, and could not survive without it. Yet in a person on the keto diet, who eats almost no carbohydrates, that organ readily learns to burn a fat-made fuel called ketones instead. Which organ makes that switch?
context: The liver's ketones can cross the blood-brain barrier — which blocks most fats — and partly replace glucose as the brain's fuel. So an organ that normally runs almost entirely on sugar ends up running on fat-derived fuel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketogenic_diet.

question: Russell Wilder built the keto diet at the Mayo Clinic in 1921 and even coined its name, but weight loss was not his goal. He designed it to control a serious condition that struck children, and doctors still treat that condition with keto today. What was the condition?
context: Dr. Russell Wilder coined 'ketogenic diet' at the Mayo Clinic in 1921 to control severe childhood epilepsy. It works: in a landmark Johns Hopkins study of nearly 1,000 children (reported 1977), over half became completely seizure-free and another quarter improved markedly. Keto is still prescribed today for drug-resistant childhood epilepsy. Source: news-medical.net History of the Ketogenic Diet; Johns Hopkins Epilepsy Center; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketogenic_diet.

question: Hugh Conklin treated sick children around 1912 with something so harsh it was miserable and could only be kept up for short stretches. Later, Russell Wilder built the keto diet to trigger the same body chemistry in a way patients could safely keep up for months. What was Conklin's treatment?
answer: Making patients go hungry for weeks
choices: Making patients go hungry for weeks
context: Around 1912, Dr. Hugh Conklin fasted epileptic patients for weeks because going without food often stopped seizures. Fasting shifts the body into ketosis; Wilder's insight was that a very high-fat diet could reproduce that same fasting chemistry — the seizure control — without the patient actually starving. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketogenic_diet; news-medical.net History of the Ketogenic Diet.

question: Loren Cordain built his paleo diet to allow meat, fish, eggs, vegetables and fruit while banning bread, beans, dairy and refined sugar. Every banned food shares one trait, and that trait is exactly why paleo rejects them. What is it?
answer: They all arrived only with farming and industry
choices: They all arrived only with farming and industry
They all carry far too many calories to burn off
They all come from animals, not from plants
They all spoil too fast to store safely
context: Loren Cordain popularized paleo in his 2002 book 'The Paleo Diet' (building on Walter Voegtlin's 1975 'The Stone Age Diet'). Its guiding idea, the 'discordance hypothesis' (Eaton and Konner, 1985), is that human genes are still tuned to a pre-farming diet, so grains, beans, dairy, refined sugar, and processed oils — all brought by farming and industry — clash with a body that never adapted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic_diet.

question: Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila have eaten the strictest form of the carnivore diet, nicknamed the 'lion diet'. Ordinary carnivore eaters drop every plant and eat only animal foods, but the lion diet strips the whole menu down to a single meat plus salt and water. Which meat?
context: Former orthopedic surgeon Shawn Baker popularized the carnivore diet on social media in 2018 and wrote 'The Carnivore Diet.' Its strictest form, the 'lion diet' followed by Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila, cuts the menu to just beef, salt, and water. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivore_diet.

question: Vilhjalmur Stefansson, an Arctic explorer, lived on meat alone for a full year under doctors' watch and never got scurvy. He also warned of 'rabbit starvation', and when the doctors had him eat only very lean meat, he sickened within days. Adding one thing back to his plate cured him fast. What had his body been missing?
context: Vilhjalmur Stefansson and Karsten Anderson ate only meat for a year under observation at New York's Bellevue Hospital (begun 1928, reported 1929-1930) and never developed scurvy. Early on, at the investigators' request, Stefansson ate lean meat only; he soon had intestinal trouble, which cleared once fat was added back. He called the sickness of living on very lean meat, such as rabbit, 'rabbit starvation'. Dietary fat is essential, not optional. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilhjalmur_Stefansson; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_poisoning; McClellan and Du Bois, Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1930.

question: Anthropologists have spent more than a century writing down every root, fish, insect and animal that went into the cooking pots of hunter-gatherers, from Inuit hunters on Arctic sea ice to Hadza foragers on the East African savanna. Across dozens of groups, what did the evidence show about their diets?
answer: They ranged from mostly meat to mostly plants
choices: They ranged from mostly meat to mostly plants
They were nearly all heavy meat-and-fish eaters
They varied by season but ate the same few staples
They leaned mostly on wild honey and fruit
context: Real hunter-gatherer diets varied enormously — animal food ranged from roughly a quarter to nearly all of their calories across different groups — and some ground and ate wild grains, while humans kept evolving after farming began. Paleo is a modern premise, a useful rule of thumb, not a photograph of one 'true' Stone-Age diet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic_diet.

question: Fans of the carnivore diet, animal foods only and no plants at all, post before-and-after stories online claiming it cured their autoimmune trouble, joint pain and depression. Critics warn that a diet with no fruit, vegetables or grains cannot be healthy for long. When mainstream medical reviewers read the actual studies, what did they conclude?
answer: The evidence so far is too thin to prove any benefit
choices: The evidence so far is too thin to prove any benefit
The evidence so far already confirms the benefits fans claim
The evidence so far shows it reliably lowers cholesterol
The evidence so far proves it's safe for the long haul
context: Mainstream reviewers caution that carnivore has no fiber, leans heavily on red meat, and can raise LDL cholesterol — and that there is currently no clinical evidence it delivers the benefits fans report; the long-term data isn't in. One puzzle is partly answered: fresh and organ meats (raw liver, for instance) do supply some vitamin C, which is how all-meat eaters like Stefansson avoided scurvy. The fiber question stays an honest open debate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivore_diet; doctorkiltz.com vitamin C on carnivore.

question: A doubtful cook drops one oil-packed anchovy fillet, a smelly, salty little fish from a jar, into a pan of hot tomato sauce simmering for pasta. Within about a minute the fillet dissolves and disappears completely. She tastes the sauce. How does it taste now?
answer: Rich and savory, with no fishy taste
choices: Rich and savory, with no fishy taste
No different than before it went in
context: The anchovy's flesh dissolves in the heat, leaving behind only a deep savory richness that has a name: umami. That's why cooks slip a 'secret anchovy' into a stew or tomato sauce — no one spots the fish, but everyone agrees the dish tastes better. Source: cookthismuch.com, 'Anchovies in Cooking: The Invisible Umami Secret'; thegourmethost.com.

question: Caesar Cardini tossed the first Caesar salad in Tijuana, Mexico, in 1924, and he put no anchovy fillets in it, because he found whole anchovies too strong. Yet the dressing still had a deep savory tang of the sea. Which bottled pantry sauce gave it that?
context: The secret was Worcestershire sauce — which is itself built on anchovies fermented in salt for about two years. So the anchovy was hiding in the dressing all along. Cardini's brother Alex later added real anchovy fillets, and that version is the Caesar we know today. Source: NPR, 'Caesar salad turns 100' (2024); Wikipedia, 'Caesar salad.'

question: Thai and Vietnamese cooks make nam pla and nuoc mam from anchovies and salt left to ferment for months, and the amber liquid is almost identical to Roman garum, made half a world away. Historians have looked for a link between the two traditions. What did they find?
answer: Each was most likely invented on its own
choices: Each was most likely invented on its own
Roman traders carried it east to Asia
Asian sailors carried it west to Rome
Both borrowed it from ancient Egypt
context: Scholars find no chemical or historical proof that the two traditions are linked, and think each was most likely invented on its own — a striking case of the same idea appearing on opposite sides of the world. Nam pla and nuoc mam are roughly three parts anchovy to one part salt, fermented 9–12 months. Source: The Conversation; Wikipedia, 'Fish sauce'; Sally Grainger, 'The Story of Garum' (Routledge, 2021).

question: France's marching armies needed food that would not rot, and Nicolas Appert, a Paris cook, won the prize offered for it. He packed cooked food into containers, corked and waxed them shut and boiled them for hours, and it kept for months. What did he seal the food in?
context: Nicolas Appert is still called 'the father of canning.' He corked and waxed the glass jars, then boiled them for hours, and the food kept for months instead of rotting. Napoleon-era France's 12,000-franc prize (offered 1795) went to him around 1809-10 after roughly 14-15 years of trials — the government/industry society offered it; Napoleon did not personally hand him a check. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Appert

question: Before he ever preserved a meal, Nicolas Appert had already made his name in Paris in one everyday food trade, with no formal science training at all. Then, in the early 1800s, he invented canning, sealing cooked food so it would not spoil for months. What was his trade?
context: Appert was a popular Paris confectioner and pastry-maker with no formal science education — canning came from a working cook, not a laboratory. The bitter irony: despite inventing canning, he died in poverty in 1841 and was buried in a pauper's grave. Source: nesta.org.uk (The French Food Preservation Prize); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Appert

question: Nicolas Appert's boiled, sealed food kept fresh for months, but he had the wrong idea about why. Microbes had not been discovered yet, so he never guessed that tiny living spoilers were the real problem; he believed his seal simply locked out one ordinary thing. What did he think he was keeping out?
context: Appert got the right method for the wrong reason: he thought sealing merely kept AIR out. Bacteriology didn't exist yet — Louis Pasteur wouldn't explain why heating-and-sealing actually works (it destroys and shuts out microbes) until about 40+ years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Appert

question: Rough army wagons easily broke Appert's sealed containers. Peter Durand, an Englishman, patented a much tougher one in 1810, and by 1813 it was feeding the British Army and Navy from a London factory. What was the new container?
context: Peter Durand patented preserving food in tin cans in 1810. By 1813 a Bermondsey (London) factory was supplying canned meat to the British Army and Navy. The sturdy tin can soon replaced Appert's breakable glass jars for armies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Durand

question: A soldier of the early 1800s, handed a sealed can of stew or meat to keep him fed on a long march, faced a problem: nobody would invent a can opener for about fifty more years. How did soldiers get their cans open?
answer: They pried and stabbed them open with bayonets and knives
choices: They pried and stabbed them open with bayonets and knives
They boiled them until the seams melted apart
They buried them so the metal would rust through
They tossed them in a fire until they burst
context: The can opener wasn't invented until about fifty years after the tin can, so early soldiers hacked cans open with bayonets and knives; Civil War troops reportedly even shot them open with rifle fire. Source: inventionandtech.com, 'Form Follows Failure'

question: Shoppers in the 1800s who bought canned food before anyone had invented a can opener found opening directions printed right on the paper label. The directions matter-of-factly named two heavy household tools to use on the lid. Which tools did the label name?
context: Because no opener existed yet, early cans literally carried the printed instruction: 'Cut round the top near the outer edge with a chisel and hammer.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_opener

question: John Landis Mason, a tinsmith, patented a glass jar in 1858 with a threaded rim and a screw-on metal lid. Families no longer needed a professional canner: they could seal a jar airtight at their own kitchen stove and reuse it every harvest. What did his lid squeeze down onto the rim to make that seal?
context: In 1858 New Jersey tinsmith John Landis Mason patented the glass jar with a threaded screw-top and a rubber-ringed lid, giving an airtight seal an ordinary family could get at home — and home canning went mainstream. Source: smithsonianmag.com, 'A Brief History of the Mason Jar'

question: A four-pound tin of roast veal went north with William Parry's Arctic expedition in 1824 and came home unopened. It sat in a museum for more than a century, until it was finally cut open in 1938. What was found inside?
choices: Brown and dried out, but edible
Gray rot and a foul stench
context: A 4-pound tin of roast veal, made in 1823 and packed for William Parry's 1824 Arctic expedition, sailed to the Arctic and back, then sat unopened in a museum until it was opened in 1938 (a few reports say 1939). The veal inside was reported pink and in good condition: proof that a properly sealed can keeps food a very long time. Source: inventionandtech.com, 'Form Follows Failure'; Science Museum Group, 'World's oldest tin', roast veal tin, 1823.

question: A grocery shelf holds bottles of corn and cottonseed oil beside olive oil and butter, which cooks have made by hand for thousands of years. Corn and cottonseed oil reached kitchens only in the last century or two. Why did they arrive so late?
answer: Getting their oil out took factory machinery
choices: Getting their oil out took factory machinery
Corn and cotton were unknown to farmers until then
Farmers only lately bred the seeds to hold oil
Both plants grew only in the far tropics until then
context: An olive can be crushed and cream churned by hand, but corn and cottonseed oil came with industry: corn oil is pressed from the germ that factory mills separate from the kernel, and crude cottonseed oil needs heavy refining before it is fit to eat. Other seed oils are far older: sesame oil is ancient, and Chinese mills were pressing soybeans for oil with wooden wedge presses centuries before any factory. Sources: Centra Foods extraction explainer; soyinfocenter.com, 'History of Soybean Crushing'; Wikipedia, 'Corn oil' and 'Cottonseed oil'.

question: Fresh from the crushed seeds, soybean oil is still crude, unfit for any cook. Refiners clean it up in three stages, the last two pushing it through clay filters and then blasting it with high heat and steam. What do those stages leave on the store shelf?
answer: A pale oil with almost no smell or taste
choices: A pale oil with almost no smell or taste
A dark oil with a strong, nutty flavor
A thick fat that sets solid like butter
A green oil with a sharp, peppery bite
context: These are the industry's RBD steps: refined, then bleached (clay filters strip out the color), then deodorized (high heat and steam drive off the strong smell and taste), leaving the pale, neutral oil sold in stores. Critics point to this bleaching and deodorizing as heavy industrial processing; defenders say it simply makes the oil stable and usable. Gentler cold-pressing (olive oil) skips it entirely, staying below 122°F with no solvent, but recovers the least oil. Source: Centra Foods extraction comparison.

question: Researchers checked the blood of more than 68,000 people in 13 countries for linoleic acid, the main fat in seed oils, then followed their health for years. What did the highest levels line up with?
answer: A lower risk of heart disease and stroke
choices: A lower risk of heart disease and stroke
A higher risk of heart disease and stroke
A higher rate of joint inflammation
A faster rate of weight gain
context: The people with the most linoleic acid in their blood had significantly LOWER heart-disease and stroke risk — the mainstream's strongest evidence for seed oils. Controlled trials also show linoleic acid lowers LDL ('bad') cholesterol, which is why the American Heart Association still advises getting about 5-10% of daily calories from omega-6 fats. Source: MGH 'Seed Oils: Facts & Myths'; AHA Science Advisory, Circulation, 2009.

question: Critics of seed oils describe a chain reaction: in theory, the body can turn linoleic acid, the omega-6 fat in soybean and corn oil, into arachidonic acid, which can then drive inflammation. Researchers tested the first link, feeding people linoleic acid and measuring how much of it became arachidonic acid. What did they find?
answer: Only a tiny fraction of it converts
choices: Only a tiny fraction of it converts
Roughly a quarter of it converts
context: The catch: in humans, only about 0.2% of the omega-6 people eat is actually converted into arachidonic acid — so even if arachidonic acid does drive inflammation, seed oils barely feed that pathway. Backing this up, a 2017 review of controlled trials found that raising linoleic-acid intake did not measurably change the inflammatory markers in people's blood. Source: MGH 'Seed Oils: Facts & Myths.'

question: Christopher Ramsden, a researcher, recovered the lost results of the Minnesota Coronary Experiment from 40-year-old magnetic tapes and ran the numbers again. Begun in 1968, the trial had more than 9,000 hospital patients swap butter and other saturated fat for the linoleic acid of seed oils, and their cholesterol dropped, as the researchers had hoped. What happened to the death toll?
answer: Deaths held steady, even as cholesterol dropped
choices: Deaths held steady, even as cholesterol dropped
Deaths fell sharply, in step with cholesterol
Deaths rose sharply, even as cholesterol dropped
Deaths fell slowly, only in the final years
context: When Christopher Ramsden recovered the buried data from the Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-73, 9,423 people) and the Sydney Diet-Heart Study — off 40-year-old 9-track magnetic tapes — the seed-oil diets clearly lowered cholesterol yet did NOT lower deaths; the treated groups died at equal or even higher rates. Lower cholesterol simply didn't buy longer life. It's the critics' single strongest piece of evidence. Source: Ramsden et al., BMJ 2016.

question: A cook in Caracas, Venezuela, flips an arepa, a thick, round corn cake, on a hot griddle until its outside is crisp and its inside soft and steamy. She serves it the Venezuelan way, as a handheld meal with shredded chicken, black beans or white cheese. How does the filling get into the cake?
answer: The cake is split open like a bun and filled
choices: The cake is split open like a bun and filled
The cake is rolled around the filling like a burrito
The cake is folded over the filling like a taco
The cake is stuffed with filling before it's cooked
context: The Venezuelan arepa is cooked firm, then split open like a bun and stuffed — an edible pocket, not a floppy wrap like the thin Mexican tortilla. Corn cakes like this are ancient here: griddled in the region for roughly 2,800-3,000 years, long before Europeans arrived. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arepa'.

question: A Mexican cook making tortilla dough first soaks the corn in a bath of limewater. A Venezuelan cook's arepa flour, called masarepa, skips the lime step entirely. How is the corn for masarepa handled instead?
answer: It's cooked in water and dried into flour
choices: It's cooked in water and dried into flour
It's ground raw and dried straight off the cob
It's fermented in salt water until it turns sour
It's roasted over an open fire until it chars
context: Masarepa is PRECOOKED corn flour — the corn is boiled in plain water and dried, with no alkali step, so it is NOT nixtamalized. That's the fundamental difference from Mexican masa, whose corn IS soaked in an alkaline lime solution. Two corn technologies, two different cakes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arepa' / 'Masarepa'.

question: At a market stall in Colombia, the cooks pat out arepas thinner than most and seldom open them up once they come off the griddle. Yet their arepas can still come loaded with cheese. How do they manage that?
answer: They knead the cheese right into the dough
choices: They knead the cheese right into the dough
They stack slices of cheese between two thin cakes
They stir the cheese into a broth the cakes are boiled in
They wrap each cake around a stick of firm cheese
context: In Colombia, cheese is often kneaded right into the arepa dough (the arepa de queso), and Colombian arepas tend to be thinner and topped rather than split and stuffed like Venezuela's reina pepiada. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arepa'.

question: A Venezuelan family that wanted arepas for breakfast, before bagged precooked corn flour existed, faced a hard daily chore called 'la piladera'. When the flour reached the shops, its slogan cheered the chore's end: 'Se acabó la piladera', 'the piladera is over'. What backbreaking task did the slogan celebrate the end of?
answer: Pounding maize by hand in a tall wooden mortar
choices: Pounding maize by hand in a tall wooden mortar
Grinding maize on a flat stone with a roller
Cranking maize through an iron hand-mill
Scraping maize kernels off the cob with a knife
context: 'La piladera' meant pounding soaked, dried maize by hand in a tall wooden mortar (the pilon) every day. Precooked arepa flour ended it — patented in 1954 by Venezuelan engineer Luis Caballero Mejias and later branded Harina P.A.N. (launched 1960); its slogan 'Se acabo la piladera' means 'no more pounding.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Harina P.A.N.'.

question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, a street cook fries a corn cake until it's only half-done, then slits a small pocket in its side and tucks one uncooked thing inside. The whole cake drops back into hot oil until it puffs — and that thing cooks, sealed right in the cake's middle. What does the cook tuck inside?
context: It's the 'arepa de huevo' from Colombia's Caribbean coast: a partly-fried corn cake is slit open, a whole raw egg is poured in, and the whole thing is deep-fried until the egg sets — a corn cake with an egg cooked in its middle. Source: ediblela.com, 'Ultimate Arepa Guide'.

question: At an Argentine asado, the weekend cookout that comes down from the gaucho cowboys, beef and sausages cook slowly on a low wood-fired grill called the parrilla. The meat does not cook over the roaring flames. What is it sitting above as it slowly browns?
choices: a tray of hot lava rocks
context: The grill is the parrilla, and the golden rule is 'you cook over embers, not flames.' The cook adjusts the heat by raising or lowering the grate over the coals, not by feeding the fire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asado; argentineasado.com.

question: A visitor at an Argentine parrilla expects the famous steaks to be soaking in a secret marinade of wine and spices, but the beef gets no marinade at all. Thick cuts of good grass-fed beef go on the grill with a single seasoning, rubbed on before or during grilling. What is that seasoning?
context: As Wikipedia puts it, 'the meat for an asado is not marinated, the only preparation being the application of salt before or during the cooking period.' The beef, the wood, and the fire do all the work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asado.

question: An Argentine cook chops fresh parsley very fine, minces garlic and stirs in dried oregano, olive oil, red wine vinegar and red chili flakes, then lets the bowl rest a few hours so the flavors blend. The bright green chimichurri goes over the grilled beef at the asado. How is this sauce prepared?
choices: simmered on the stove until thick
roasted over the coals, then blended
reduced in a pan of beef drippings
context: Chimichurri is an uncooked table condiment — chopped and stirred, nothing heated — spooned over grilled meat rather than cooked into it. It comes in green (verde, the parsley classic) and red (rojo, with tomato or red pepper). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimichurri.

question: A whole lamb is the showpiece of a big Argentine asado, and it never touches the flat grill. Instead the cook fastens the entire lamb to a single tall iron frame, planted at an angle beside the fire so it roasts slowly from the side. That iron frame is classically forged in the shape of a ___?
context: This is asado a la cruz ('asado on the cross'). A whole Patagonian lamb cooks bone-side to the fire for about three hours, then skin-side for a final hour, brushed with salt brine (salmuera) — roasting from radiant side heat instead of embers below. Source: argentineasado.com.

question: A newcomer at an Argentine asado reaches straight for a big, juicy steak, and the grill-master waves him off with a laugh: the prime steaks wait until near the end. The feast opens with something lighter, cooked quickly and served while everyone is still gathering. What comes off the grill first?
context: The opening course is the sausages and organ bits — chorizo, morcilla (blood sausage), and mollejas (sweetbreads); the prime steaks and ribs come later. Chimichurri traditionally dresses these early sausages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asado.

question: A grill-master building the fire for an asado reaches for charcoal of quebracho, a South American wood whose name comes from quiebra hacha, 'axe-breaker', because it is so hard it can snap an axe. What makes its coals the grill-master's favorite?
answer: They hold a fierce, even heat for hours
choices: They hold a fierce, even heat for hours
They flare up fast for a quick, hot sear
They catch light in seconds, no kindling
They burn down to a deep bed of soft ash
context: The name comes from quiebra hacha, 'break axe', because the wood is so hard it can snap an axe. As charcoal it is slow to come up to heat, then gives a very hot, long-lasting, even heat with very little smoke or ash, ideal for the slow ember method of the asado. Sources: Tasting Table, 'Why It Pays To Grill With Quebracho Charcoal'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinopsis.

question: A tourist in Bologna orders 'spaghetti bolognese', and the waiter kindly corrects him: the city's cooks never serve their meat ragù on spaghetti. It goes on a flat, porous ribbon of fresh egg pasta that catches the meat top and bottom. Which pasta is it?
context: In Bologna the ragù is served over tagliatelle — long, flat egg ribbons about 6–7mm wide — or layered into lasagne, but never spaghetti. Because the ribbons are made fresh with egg, their surface is slightly rough and porous, so the heavy meat sauce clings to every bite. On smooth, round spaghetti the same sauce just slides off and pools at the bottom of the bowl. Source: Wikipedia 'Bolognese sauce'; La Cucina Italiana; Wikipedia 'Tagliatelle'.

question: Before any meat goes into a Bologna ragù, the cook softens three finely chopped vegetables together in butter and oil. That trio is the flavor base of the whole sauce, and Bologna families never change it. Which three vegetables are they?
context: The base is called a soffritto — finely diced onion, carrot, and celery, gently sweated in fat before the meat is browned. It is the flavor foundation of the whole ragù; the official recipe even insists the vegetables be minced by hand rather than thrown in a food processor. Source: Bologna Welcome; StefanGourmet 'new official recipe'.

question: Food historians hunting for the oldest printed recipe for 'spaghetti bolognese', a dish Italians say is not really theirs, found it in a charity cookbook of 1917. The book was sold in an English-speaking country to raise money for Italian soldiers' families during the First World War. Where was it printed?
context: 'Spaghetti bolognese' is not part of Italian cuisine — Italians consider it inauthentic. Its first recorded appearance is in an American cookbook: Julia Lovejoy Cuniberti's 1917 'Practical Italian Recipes for American Kitchens,' sold to raise money for the families of Italian soldiers fighting in World War I. Spaghetti won out abroad because America had no fresh-egg-pasta tradition, and delicate fresh egg pasta didn't export well. Source: Wikipedia 'Bolognese sauce'; Cesarine 'spaghetti bolognese'.

question: Hours into the simmer of a Bologna ragù, the cook stirs in about half a glass of one everyday ingredient most people would never expect in a savory sauce of beef and tomato. It softens the meat and takes the sharp edge off the tomato. What is it?
context: The surprise ingredient is milk — about half a glass of whole milk, stirred in little by little during the long cook. Bologna's official recipe says it is added to soften the tomato's acidity, and it also tenderizes the meat and mellows the whole sauce. It is the ingredient outsiders almost never guess; in the 2023 update it was demoted from mandatory to merely 'advisable.' Source: Bologna Welcome; Accademia Italiana della Cucina.

question: A Bologna cook browns the ground beef for her ragù in a heavy pot, then pours in about half a glass of wine and scrapes up the tasty browned bits stuck to the bottom. Every household in the city knows the recipe by heart. In the classic version, which wine goes in?
context: It surprises people: a rich, meaty ragù is splashed not with red wine but with dry WHITE wine — only about half a glass, added after the beef browns. And despite its reputation abroad, Bolognese is a meat sauce, not a tomato sauce: the classic recipe is built on roughly 300g of ground beef with only a modest spoonful of tomato, so the meat, not the tomato, dominates the pot. Source: Bologna Welcome; Wikipedia 'Bolognese sauce'.

question: The savory backbone of a traditional Bologna ragù goes into the pan before the beef. Small cubes of an Italian cured pork belly, salt-cured, sometimes rolled and never smoked, melt slowly until they release their fat and turn golden, and only then does the ground beef brown in that fat. Which cured pork is it?
context: Before the beef ever browns, about 150g of pancetta — cured pork belly — is gently melted in the fat. Rendering the fatty pork first lays down a deep, savory base, and the beef then browns in that rendered fat, so the whole sauce tastes richer for it. Source: StefanGourmet 'official recipe'; Bologna Welcome.

question: Alberto Alvisi, private cook to a man named Barnaba Chiaramonti, made the earliest ragù on record served over pasta, near Bologna in the 1790s. A few years later his employer took a far greater title, known all across Europe. Which office did Chiaramonti hold?
context: The earliest documented ragù served over pasta comes from late-18th-century Imola, near Bologna — created by Alberto Alvisi, private cook to Barnaba Chiaramonti. In 1800 Chiaramonti was elected Pope Pius VII, so the 'pope's cook' has a fair claim to the very first ragù-with-pasta, decades before Bologna's own version was written down. Source: Wikipedia 'Bolognese sauce'.

question: A boy's body needs only a speck of vitamin B12 a day, yet without it he would fall very sick, because the vitamin does two jobs his body cannot skip. One is helping build red blood cells. What is the other?
choices: Keeping his bones strong and dense
Keeping his eyesight sharp at night
context: B12 does two jobs the body can't do without: it keeps nerve cells healthy and it helps build red blood cells. It comes from meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and essentially not from plant foods. Adults need only about 2.4 micrograms a day, a speck, but that speck is non-negotiable. Source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin B12 Health Professional fact sheet (ods.od.nih.gov).

question: A fishmonger's counter holds salmon and tuna, but some of the richest sources of vitamin B12 on Earth sit in the shellfish case beside them. A single three-ounce serving of one shellfish delivers several times a full day's B12 by itself, leaving the popular fish far behind. Which shellfish?
context: After liver, shellfish are the B12 champions: a 3-ounce serving of cooked clams delivers about 17 micrograms — many times a full day's need — and eastern oysters about 14.9. Fish like salmon trail far behind at roughly 2.6 micrograms per serving. Source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin B12 Health Professional fact sheet (ods.od.nih.gov).

question: George Minot and William Murphy, two American doctors, cured pernicious anemia in 1926, a disease that had been a death sentence: a patient's blood slowly wasted away. They fed each patient about half a pound of one raw food every day until the blood came back. What was that food?
context: Before B12 was even discovered, pernicious anemia was fatal — until 1926, when George Minot and William Murphy cured patients by feeding them about half a pound of raw liver every day; within six to eight weeks their blood recovered. It worked because liver is the richest B12 food on Earth: a single 3-ounce serving of beef liver packs about 70.7 micrograms, roughly 30 times an adult's daily need. Minot and Murphy shared the 1934 Nobel Prize in Medicine (with George Whipple) for the liver cure. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1934 Medicine; Britannica, George Minot; NIH ODS (beef liver 70.7 mcg / 3 oz).

question: A cow grazing in a field, a fish in the sea and a hen in the yard all carry vitamin B12 in their meat and eggs, yet none of them makes it; they only store it. The real B12 factory is a much tinier living thing. What builds nearly all of the world's B12?
context: The twist that surprises everyone: no animal and no plant actually makes B12 — it is synthesized only by certain bacteria and archaea (microbes). A cow or a clam merely banks the B12 that microbes made, which is why the vitamin ends up locked in animal tissue and not in plants. Source: Wikipedia, Vitamin B12 ('synthesized exclusively by certain archaea and bacteria'); corroborated by veganhealth.org.

question: A woman who cuts out every animal food and takes no supplement can feel fine for about three years before any vitamin B12 deficiency shows up. Most of the other B vitamins wash out of the body within days. Why does B12 take so long to run short?
answer: The body has stored a multi-year reserve of it.
choices: The body has stored a multi-year reserve of it.
The kidneys recycle it back into the blood.
Leafy plants slowly replace what the body loses.
The body makes its own B12 when it runs low.
context: Deficiency creeps in slowly because the liver hoards a huge reserve — roughly three to five years' worth. So someone who switches to a plants-only diet with no supplement may feel fine for about three years before B12 deficiency finally shows up; the other B-vitamins, by contrast, wash out and aren't stored. This slow onset is also why serious vegan authorities say vegans must get B12 from fortified foods or a supplement. Source: NCBI StatPearls NBK441923; liver reserve NBK114329.

question: A man can eat a plateful of vitamin B12 and still go short of it. The vitamin crosses the gut only with a protein escort, and if his own body destroys that escort by mistake, absorption stops however much he eats. Which organ makes the escort?
context: To be absorbed, B12 needs intrinsic factor, a protein made by the stomach, which ferries it across the far end of the gut (the ileum). If the body attacks its own intrinsic factor, absorption stops and pernicious anemia follows, a problem an ordinary diet cannot fix, which is why it is treated with B12 injections. Source: NCBI StatPearls NBK441923; corroborated by Wikipedia, Vitamin B12.

question: A girl decides to go fully vegan, with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy at all, and asks her older cousin whether that can truly be healthy or whether she will run short of some nutrient. Vitamin B12 comes naturally almost only from animal foods. What does the nutrition science say about a vegan diet and B12?
answer: A vegan diet is fine, but B12 has to come from a supplement or fortified food.
choices: A vegan diet is fine, but B12 has to come from a supplement or fortified food.
A vegan diet is unhealthy, because the body cannot live without animal food.
A vegan diet is complete on its own, since whole plants already supply the B12.
A vegan diet is risky, but plenty of leafy greens will cover the B12.
context: The honest verdict, steel-manning both ways: a well-planned vegan diet can be perfectly healthy as long as B12 is supplemented — and supplemented vegans often have better B12 levels than meat-eaters. But B12 is the one clear case where a plants-only, whole-foods diet genuinely cannot supply a nutrient. It's not a knock on veganism; it's simply the single unavoidable animal-food gap. Source: The Vegan Society, 'What every vegan should know about vitamin B12'; corroborated by NIH ODS.
