context: The leftover marinade, lime, raw fish juices, red onion, garlic, cilantro and Peruvian chili, is drunk on its own as leche de tigre, 'tiger's milk,' and is said to cure hangovers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_ceviche

question: Cooks in Lima will not make classic ceviche from just any fish: they reach for one prized local catch, cut it into chunks and dress it with red onion and fiery aji chili, then serve it beside sweet potato and corn. Which fish anchors the traditional Peruvian dish?
context: Classic Peruvian ceviche uses corvina — a firm white sea bass — cut in chunks and marinated in lime or bitter-orange juice with sliced red onion, aji chili, salt and cilantro, then traditionally served with sweet potato (camote) and corn-on-the-cob (choclo). Ceviche is Peru's national dish. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_ceviche

question: The Moche of coastal Peru, the story goes, soured raw fish about 2,000 years ago, long before any lime reached their shores. Limes came only on Spanish ships after Columbus, and the Spanish swapped them in. What did the Moche use to sour their fish?
answer: The juice of tumbo, a native passion fruit
choices: The juice of tumbo, a native passion fruit
The pulp of sour wild tomatoes
The juice of unripe green pineapple
The tart pulp of prickly-pear fruit
context: Limes came only with the Spanish after Columbus. Roughly 2,000 years ago the coastal Moche already marinated fish in the fermented juice of tumbo, a native passion fruit, and later Andean peoples used chicha; the Spanish simply swapped in lime and bitter orange. This deep origin is retold as culinary legend. Source: https://www.thedailymeal.com/1668429/origins-ceviche-peru/

question: Early farmers watched fresh cow's and goat's milk turn sour within a day. Then they learned to drain and salt it into firm cheese, which gave it one big advantage fresh milk never had. What was it?
answer: It could be stored for weeks or months without spoiling.
choices: It could be stored for weeks or months without spoiling.
It tasted far sweeter than the fresh milk did.
It held far more water than the fresh milk did.
It could be turned back into fresh milk anytime.
context: Cheese was humanity's way to make milk LAST: fresh milk sours in a day, but draining and salting it into a solid curd turns it into a storable, carry-able food that keeps for weeks or months. Source: University of Bristol news release, 'First cheesemaking' (2012), https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2012/9008.html

question: In Kuyavia, Poland, diggers found clay pots more than 7,000 years old. Each one was pierced with dozens of tiny holes, like a kitchen colander, and they are among the oldest cheese-making gear ever found. As early cheesemakers poured milk into these pots, what did the little holes let drip out?
answer: the watery whey, leaving the solid curds behind
choices: the watery whey, leaving the solid curds behind
the rich cream, leaving thin skim milk behind
the last of the fat, leaving a lean curd behind
the salty brine, leaving a washed rind behind
context: The perforated pots worked like a modern cheese colander: the holes let the watery whey drip out while the fatty, protein-rich curds stayed behind. Among the oldest evidence of cheese-making anywhere, these Linear Pottery culture pots (dated to roughly 5500-4900 BC by different studies) had milk residue detected on 34 of them. Sources: University of Bristol news release (2012), https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2012/9008.html; Salque et al., Nature 2012, https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11698; Wikipedia, 'Cheese'.

question: A desert traveler, the old legend goes, set out across the hot sands with fresh milk in a canteen that swung from his saddle all day. When he opened it to drink, the milk had set into soft white lumps floating in a thin, watery liquid. What was his canteen made from?
answer: a pouch made from a young animal's dried stomach
choices: a pouch made from a young animal's dried stomach
a flask carved from a large dried gourd
a skin bag tanned from a whole ox hide
a jar fired from smooth riverbank clay
context: This is the classic origin LEGEND of rennet. Rennet is an enzyme (chymosin) from the stomach lining of a young milk-fed animal — usually the fourth stomach (abomasum) of a calf or goat kid. It coagulates the milk protein casein, splitting milk into solid curds and liquid whey, and is the same substance cheesemakers still use to set milk. The story goes that stomach enzymes left in a stomach-skin canteen curdled the milk on the journey. Sources: Caglificio Clerici, 'Rennet: What Is and How is it Made', https://www.caglificioclerici.com/en/rennet-what-is-how-is-it-made-caglificio-clerici-guide/; Secret Lands Farm, 'Rennet for Cheese Making: History and Types'.

question: A lump of cheese about 3,200 years old, whitish and crumbling, is one of the oldest pieces of real cheese ever found, and chemists could still analyze it in a lab. It had survived in a place few would expect a food to last. Where had it lain for over three thousand years?
answer: sealed in the tomb of a high Egyptian official
choices: sealed in the tomb of a high Egyptian official
frozen in a glacier high in the snowy Alps
sunk in a shipwreck on the deep sea floor
buried beneath a stone-paved Roman kitchen
context: One of the oldest lumps of real cheese ever found, about 3,200 years old, came from the Saqqara tomb of Ptahmes, Mayor of Memphis and a top official under pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II (~1290-1213 BC); cheese on mummies of the Xiaohe cemetery in China is older still, about 3,600 years. Ptahmes's cheese was buried with him as a prized grave-good, surviving as a solid whitish mass inside a broken jar, still wrapped in canvas cloth; analysis showed it was made from cow's milk mixed with sheep's or goat's milk. Sources: Sci.News, 'World's Oldest Solid Cheese Found in 3,200-Year-Old Jar in Egypt', https://www.sci.news/archaeology/worlds-oldest-solid-cheese-egypt-06312.html; Greco et al., Analytical Chemistry 2018 (PubMed 30044608); Wikipedia, 'Cheese'.

question: Chemists who set out to prove that 7,000-year-old Polish pots had once held dairy faced a problem: milk itself rots away in weeks. So they tested the clay, and found one part of the ancient milk still locked inside. Which part had survived to give the pots away?
context: Scientists used lipid-biomarker and stable-isotope analysis to pull out fatty acids that had soaked into the porous clay — the milk fat itself, not just the pot's shape, survived roughly 7,000 years to be identified as real dairy. It was the first hard chemical proof (Salque et al., Nature 2012) that the pierced 'cheese-strainer' pots really were used to make cheese. Sources: Salque et al., Nature 2012, https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11698; ScienceDaily, 'Chemical analysis reveals first cheese-making in Northern Europe 7,000 years ago', https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/12/121212134044.htm

question: Scientists studying a 3,200-year-old lump of cheese found that it once carried the germ that causes brucellosis, a serious disease people can still catch from raw milk and cheese. The microbes were long gone, but their proteins remained. What ordinary step at the dairy now makes store-bought milk safe to drink?
choices: skimming — taking cream off the top
context: The 3,200-year-old Ptahmes-tomb cheese carried Brucella melitensis, the bacterium behind brucellosis — possibly the earliest direct biomolecular evidence of the disease in the ancient world. The organisms themselves did not survive 3,200 years; researchers detected them through the microbe's surviving proteins (a proteomic analysis). Brucellosis spreads through unpasteurized dairy; pasteurizing (gently heating milk) kills the bacteria, which is why store milk rarely carries it today. Sources: Greco et al., 'Proteomic Analyses on an Ancient Egyptian Cheese and Biomolecular Evidence of Brucellosis', Analytical Chemistry 2018 (PubMed 30044608); Chemistry World, 'World's oldest cheese contained infectious bacteria', https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/worlds-oldest-cheese-contained-infectious-bacteria/3009398.article

question: A rock-hard wheel of Parmesan can sit in a cellar for years, while a soft round of Brie spoils within weeks. Both are cheese made from the same milk — so what lets the hard wheel keep so much longer?
answer: it holds far less water inside
choices: it holds far less water inside
it was made from fresher milk
it carries a much thicker rind
it was salted far more heavily
context: Cheese is really a way to preserve milk. Fresh milk sours in days, but draining and pressing out its water concentrates it into a food that keeps — and the drier the cheese, the longer it lasts. Low-moisture hard cheeses like Parmesan can keep for years, while soft, high-moisture cheeses like Brie last only weeks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheese.

question: A cheesemaker warms a pot of milk and stirs in a little rennet, the enzyme used to set milk into cheese. Within minutes the smooth liquid separates into two completely different things, and that split is where every cheese begins. What does the milk split into?
context: When rennet meets milk, its enzyme (chymosin) snips the casein proteins so they can no longer stay dissolved. The casein clumps with the milk fat into solid curds, while the watery whey drains away. That split is the heart of every cheese. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennet; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheese.

question: Bronze Age mummies in the dry Tarim Basin of western China were buried with cheese as food for the afterlife. In 2024, about 3,600 years on, scientists read the genes of that cheese, the oldest ever identified, to learn whose milk made it. Which two animals gave the milk?
context: Reported in 2024 in the journal Cell, this is the oldest cheese ever identified. Its DNA showed it was a kefir cheese made from cow and goat milk, tucked around the necks of people buried in the bone-dry Tarim Basin — likely food for the afterlife. The desert air preserved both the mummies and their cheese for 3,600 years. Source: smithsonianmag.com; sciencedaily.com (2024 study).

question: Blue-green mold runs through a cut wheel of blue cheese in neat, evenly spaced lines, clearly no accident. The mold was put there on purpose, and so were the lines. How did the cheesemaker get the mold to grow in tidy lines deep inside the wheel?
answer: pierced the wheel all over with needles
choices: pierced the wheel all over with needles
layered mold between stacked sheets of curd
pressed the wheel around mold-coated rods
context: The blue veins are an edible mold, Penicillium roqueforti, and it needs oxygen to grow. But the inside of a dense wheel has none — so cheesemakers pierce the young loaf all over with needles, opening air channels the mold creeps along. That's why the veins run in lines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_cheese.

question: A beef steer raised on the western plains in the 1870s had to become dinner for a family clear across the country in Boston, and fridges had not been invented yet. How did such a steer usually reach an eastern butcher shop?
answer: Alive on the hoof, packed into a cattle car
choices: Alive on the hoof, packed into a cattle car
Salted into barrels and shipped as brine beef
Smoked into dry slabs and shipped in sacks
Boiled, canned in tin, and shipped in crates
context: Live cattle rode east for days in crowded cars — the animals lost weight, got bruised, and some died on the way. Worse, a live steer is mostly freight nobody can eat: bone, hide, and innards. Only the meat was ever worth the trip east. Source: Wikipedia, 'Swift Refrigerator Line' and 'Gustavus Franklin Swift.'

question: Chicago was the nation's great cattle hub in the 1870s when Gustavus Swift set up there as a meatpacker. He meant to slaughter the cattle in Chicago and ship only the beef east, but fresh beef spoils within a few days on the rails. What kind of railcar did Swift build to keep it good?
answer: A railcar chilled by blocks of ice
choices: A railcar chilled by blocks of ice
A boxcar packed with dry salt
A car flooded with vinegar brine
context: Swift's answer was the refrigerated railcar. Packers killed and dressed the steer in Chicago, then loaded only the chilled beef into an ice-cooled car — no wasted freight and cheap to run. One cold car could replace a whole cattle car of live animals. Source: Wikipedia, 'Swift Refrigerator Line.'

question: Andrew Chase, an engineer, took on a puzzle when Gustavus Swift hired him in 1878: where to pack the melting ice in a cold railcar so that its chill reached a whole load of beef evenly. Where did Chase put the ice so the cold would spread over all the meat at once?
answer: In bins across the top of the car
choices: In bins across the top of the car
Inside the two long side walls
In a single tank at one end
context: Chase hung the ice up top so the cold air sinks down through the beef, which was stacked low to keep the car's center of gravity down and stop the load from shifting. The first of these cars rolled in 1880. Source: Wikipedia, 'Swift Refrigerator Line.'

question: Philip Armour built Chicago's first modern large-scale packing plant in 1867, and his men could take a steer apart faster than any village butcher alive. His edge was not a better knife but the way he divided the cutting among the men on his floor. How was the work split up?
answer: One man made a single cut, over and over
choices: One man made a single cut, over and over
One man handled a single quarter of the carcass
One man took every cut on a single side
One man rotated through every cut in turn
context: Each man on Armour's floor stood at one station, specialized to a single repeated cut as the carcass came to him. Packers called it a 'disassembly line' — an assembly line running in reverse, taking the whole animal apart instead of building a product up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Union Stock Yards.'

question: Carl Sandburg opened his 1916 poem 'Chicago' by pinning a swaggering nickname on the city, whose vast stockyards and packing plants had become the very symbol of industrial America. The name stuck for a century. What did Sandburg call Chicago?
context: Sandburg's poem opens, 'Hog Butcher for the World, / Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat...' — crowning Chicago the meatpacking capital of America. The stockyards had become the defining image of the industrial age. Source: Wikipedia, 'Union Stock Yards.'

question: Gustavus Swift built his own fleet of cold railcars, and America's biggest railroads flatly refused to pull them, because cheap chilled beef threatened the fortunes they had sunk in cattle cars and stockyard pens. Swift got his beef to the East Coast anyway. How did he beat the boycott?
answer: He ran his beef north through Canada and back
choices: He ran his beef north through Canada and back
He ran his beef east by Great Lakes steamer
He ran his beef south to the Gulf, then by sea
He ran his beef east on track he laid himself
context: Swift struck a deal with the Grand Trunk Railway, which ran east through Canada and had almost no livestock trade of its own to protect. The big U.S. railroads had boycotted his cold cars to guard their cattle-hauling profits, so he financed his own cars and routed his beef up through Canada and back down to the East Coast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Swift Refrigerator Line.'

question: Henry Ford built his Model T on a moving assembly line in a fraction of the old time. In his 1922 autobiography he wrote that the idea came, in a general way, from Chicago's packing houses, which his man William 'Pa' Klann had toured. Which piece of the packers' beef-dressing setup did Ford name as its seed?
answer: An overhead trolley rolling carcasses past the men
choices: An overhead trolley rolling carcasses past the men
A floor conveyor sliding cut beef between the men
A rolling table the men pushed each carcass along
A chain of hooks the men carried the meat between
context: Ford wrote that the idea came 'in a general way from the overhead trolley that the Chicago packers use in dressing beef': the packers' disassembly line, running in reverse. Klann had toured Swift's plant and carried the concept back. Sources: Henry Ford, My Life and Work (1922); Wikipedia, 'Assembly line.'

question: A butcher's cold room quits on a hot Tuesday for four hours before a repairman gets it running, and the steaks inside go back on ice. That room is one link in what engineers call a cold chain, an unbroken line of cold from the killing floor to a kitchen icebox. Why do they still count the chain as broken?
answer: The beef grew bacteria in those warm hours, and cold won't undo it
choices: The beef grew bacteria in those warm hours, and cold won't undo it
The beef's texture is ruined once it has been chilled a second time
The beef's juices ran out while it was warm and can't soak back in
The beef browned while it was warm, and cold can't bring the red back
context: A cold chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Warm hours let bacteria multiply on the meat, and going back on ice doesn't reverse that growth — re-chilling stops the clock, it doesn't reset it. That's why one failed link breaks the whole chain. Swift's refrigerated railcar was one of the first links in the first great cold chain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cold chain.'

question: A diner bites a raw chili pepper and his mouth feels on fire, yet he is not really tasting anything. One chemical in the pepper is firing up his nerves. What is that chemical called?
context: Capsaicin (cap-SAY-uh-sin) is the compound behind every chili's heat. It doesn't burn or damage anything — it just fools the nerves into reporting a burn. (Menthol pulls the same trick in reverse, tripping the cold sensors.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Capsaicin'.

question: Chili growers rank peppers on the Scoville heat scale, from the Carolina Reaper at over a million units down to one mild pepper that scores zero. Which everyday grocery-store pepper sits at that zero?
context: A bell pepper makes no capsaicin whatsoever, so it scores 0 Scoville Heat Units — a chili that forgot to be hot. A jalapeño runs a few thousand; a habanero, over 100,000. Source: Wikipedia, 'Scoville scale'.

question: A cook adding chili to a family dinner wants to keep the heat mild for the younger diners at the table. Most of a hot pepper's burn is packed into one particular part of the pod. Which part should she cut away to strip out most of the heat?
context: Surprise — it's not the seeds most people blame. Capsaicin is made in and soaks into the pale, spongy pith (the placenta) that the seeds cling to. Cutting out that white rib cuts out most of the burn. Source: Food Republic, 'Pepper spice isn't in the seeds'.

question: Police officers and hikers clip a can of pepper spray to their belts for self-defense. What is inside rates from 500,000 to 5,000,000 units on the Scoville heat chart, as fierce as the hottest peppers that grow. What gives the spray its fire?
answer: Oil drawn from hot chili peppers
choices: Oil drawn from hot chili peppers
Oil of mustard seed and horseradish
context: Pepper spray really is weaponized chili: its active ingredient is capsaicin, usually as oleoresin capsicum, a resin extracted from ground chili peppers, which is why it lands on the same Scoville scale used for food. Despite the name, black pepper plays no part. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pepper spray'; Wikipedia, 'Scoville scale'.

question: Hungarian cooks treat their deep-red paprika as a national treasure, stirring it into goulash and dusting it over roast chicken. A jar of the fine crimson dust looks nothing like the whole ingredient it comes from. What is paprika made of?
context: Paprika is nothing exotic — just sweet or mild chilies, dried and ground to powder, which Hungary turned into a national spice (famous from Szeged and Kalocsa). Smoke those same peppers over smouldering oak instead of sun-drying them to get Spanish smoked paprika, pimentón. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paprika'.

question: Ed Currie, the man behind the Carolina Reaper, produced a new chili that took the Guinness title of world's hottest in 2023, scoring about 2.7 million Scoville units, around 1,000 times fiercer than a jalapeño. It was no lucky find. How did Currie create it?
answer: By crossbreeding peppers for ten years
choices: By crossbreeding peppers for ten years
By soaking them in pure capsaicin
By growing them in volcanic ash
By blasting the seeds with radiation
context: Ed Currie — who also bred the earlier record-holder, the Carolina Reaper — crossbred 100 kinds of pepper every year for a full decade to make Pepper X, averaging 2.693 million SHU. Source: Guinness World Records, 2023.

question: Wilbur Scoville, a pharmacist, set out in 1912 to measure how hot a chili really is. He had no machine that could detect a pepper's fiery chemical, only alcohol, sugar water and a panel of human tasters. How did his test work?
answer: He diluted the pepper's extract until tasters felt no burn
choices: He diluted the pepper's extract until tasters felt no burn
He timed how long the burn lasted on each taster's tongue
He ranked the peppers by how far the burn spread down the throat
He counted the sips of milk a taster needed to quench each pod
context: Scoville dissolved a pepper's extract in sugar-water and kept diluting it until his testers could no longer feel any heat — the more dilution required, the hotter the pepper. His original method fed the watered-down extract to a panel of five trained tasters; the score was how many dilutions it took until at least three of the five could no longer feel any heat. Machines (HPLC) took over the job in the 1980s. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Scoville scale'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper

question: A girl's mouth is ablaze from a too-hot Indian curry. Gulps of ice water barely help and may even spread the burn, because the chili's fiery chemical is oily, yet a glass of cold milk calms the fire within seconds, though milk is mostly water too. What makes milk work when water fails?
answer: A soap-like protein in milk lifts the capsaicin off
choices: A soap-like protein in milk lifts the capsaicin off
The cream in milk simply numbs the burning nerves
Milk neutralizes the chili the way an antacid does
Milk forms a cool film that seals off the nerves
context: Capsaicin is oil-like (hydrophobic) and barely dissolves in water at all, so a gulp of water just smears it around the mouth. Milk works because a protein in it, casein, acts like a soap that lifts the capsaicin off the nerves and rinses it away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Capsaicin'.

question: A wild chili plant guards its pods like a picky bouncer at the door: most animals that bite them feel a fierce burn and leave them alone. But one whole group of creatures can gulp down the hottest peppers and feel nothing at all, because their nerves lack the receptor the chili's chemical sets off. Which creatures feel no burn?
context: Birds' version of the TRPV1 sensor doesn't respond to capsaicin, so they feel no heat. The chili 'bribes' them: birds swallow the fruit and drop the seeds intact and plantable, far away — while the same burn repels seed-crushing mammals whose grinding molars would destroy the seeds. Source: EurekAlert, 'Why chili peppers are hot'.

question: A girl bites into a fiery chili and her mouth feels scalded, though the pepper sits at room temperature and her tongue is not harmed. One chemical from the plant is fooling her heat-sensing nerves into shouting fire. Which chemical is pulling that trick?
context: Capsaicin doesn't raise the temperature of anything — it binds to pain receptors in the mouth and throat and fools the brain into feeling burned, even though the tissue is completely unharmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin

question: The first Chinese writer to mention the chili pepper, in 1591, was not describing a food at all, and Chinese cooks would not use chili for about another century. What did that first record present the exotic new plant as?
context: China's earliest record of the chili (1591) treats it as an ornamental pot plant, admired for its beauty and kept indoors — not eaten. It took another century-plus for chili to enter Chinese cooking. Source: Brian Dott, 'The Chile Pepper in China: A Cultural Biography'

question: A jar of Korean kimchi today holds napa cabbage stained red-orange with fiery chili paste. Yet chili reached Korea only around 1600, so for most of its long history kimchi had none. What did kimchi look like before the chili came?
context: Early kimchi was white or pale green — vegetables in a light salt brine, with no chili at all. Chili is first recorded in Korea in the 1614 encyclopedia 'Jibong yuseol,' and red-chili kimchi only became widespread in the 1800s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimchi

question: Paul Rozin, a psychologist, went to Mexico in the 1980s to study villagers who loved chili, a food whose burn is real pain warning the eater off. He wanted to know why they chased that burn meal after meal. What did he find behind their love of it?
answer: They had trained themselves to like it, bit by bit
choices: They had trained themselves to like it, bit by bit
They had inherited the taste from chili-eating parents
They had toughened their tongues over years of hot food
They had kept eating it to impress their friends
context: Psychologist Paul Rozin argued that chili tolerance is learned, not inborn — people creep up on more heat a little at a time — and he named the liking of harmless pain 'benign masochism,' the same pull behind sad movies and roller coasters. Source: penntoday.upenn.edu/news/spicy-foods-eat-or-not-eat

question: A child today who hears the word 'chocolate' pictures a solid bar to unwrap and bite into. For most of its history, though, in the old kingdoms of Mexico and Central America, chocolate came in a very different form. What was it?
context: For roughly its first three thousand years, chocolate was strictly a beverage: ground cacao mixed with water. The idea of a solid bar a person could actually eat came only in the 1800s. Source: worldhistory.org/Chocolate_in_Mesoamerica; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate

question: Aztec shoppers spent cacao beans as real money, cash that grew on trees. A market price list that survives from 1545 shows what each purchase cost in beans. What could a shopper buy with just a single bean?
context: The 1545 Tlaxcala list: one bean bought a fully ripe avocado (a newly picked one cost three) or a large tomato; 30 beans a small rabbit; 100 a turkey hen; 300 a turkey cock. A cotton cloak ran 65 to 300 beans. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/maya/chocolate/beanz-meanz-money; worldhistory.org/Chocolate_in_Mesoamerica

question: Many of the Spaniards who first tasted Aztec chocolate disliked it, bitter and foamy as it was, and went on disliking it for decades. Europeans reworked it with several new additions to suit their own tastes, and one mattered more than all the rest. Which one?
context: Europeans sweetened the bitter ritual drink with sugar, and also stirred in vanilla and cinnamon. Many Spanish colonists actually disliked chocolate — especially the foam — until about the 1590s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate

question: Bernardino de Sahagún, a friar, compiled the Florentine Codex, his chronicle of Aztec life, and in it he described cheats who faked the cacao beans that served as money, to swindle honest traders. What trick did the counterfeiters use?
answer: Hollowed out the shells and stuffed in filler
choices: Hollowed out the shells and stuffed in filler
Painted ordinary pebbles a rich cacao brown
Hammered fake beans out of thin copper
Split real beans and glued them back doubled
context: The Florentine Codex, compiled by friar Bernardino de Sahagun, describes cheats emptying real cacao shells and repacking them with ash, dough, wax, or avocado pits — or slipping worthless wild beans into a batch. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/maya/chocolate/beanz-meanz-money

question: Columbus's crew seized a Maya trading canoe in 1502, loaded with strange beans no European had ever seen. When some spilled out on the deck, the Maya lunged to grab up every last one. A Spanish account says they snatched each fallen bean as carefully as if they had dropped what?
context: Columbus's crew, on his fourth voyage, were the first Europeans to encounter cacao — without realizing the beans were precious money. A later Spanish account said the Maya grabbed the spilled beans 'as if an eye had fallen.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate; history.com/articles/the-sweet-history-of-chocolate  (Legend.)

question: Rodolphe Lindt, a Swiss chocolatier, faced a problem in 1879: the chocolate bars of his day were coarse and gritty on the tongue. He found a way to give them their famous smooth melt without adding a single new ingredient. What did he do to the chocolate?
answer: Stirred it for hours on end
choices: Stirred it for hours on end
Chilled it slowly in cold cellars
Baked it slowly in a low oven
Aged it in barrels for months
context: In 1879 the Swiss chocolatier Rodolphe Lindt invented what he called conching: stirring the chocolate for hours on end. He added nothing new — the long, patient agitation alone turned coarse, gritty chocolate into the melt-in-your-mouth smoothness that fine bars are prized for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate

question: Coenraad van Houten built a press in 1828 that split cacao into two parts, and it opened the way to the first chocolate bar to eat. The problem it solved was old: raw ground cacao simply will not set firm and smooth on its own. What did his press squeeze out of the cacao?
context: Coenraad van Houten's 1828 cocoa press (the 'Dutch process') squeezed the fatty cocoa butter out, leaving solids that could be ground into cocoa powder. Fry's later melted cocoa butter back into powder and sugar to make a smooth, mouldable paste — the idea behind every bar since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._S._Fry_%26_Sons

question: In the hot, wet forests of Central and South America, the cacao tree hangs football-shaped pods whose beans become chocolate. Most fruit trees set their fruit at the tips of thin branches, but the cacao's pods sprout from an unexpected place. Where do they grow?
answer: Straight out of the trunk and thickest limbs
choices: Straight out of the trunk and thickest limbs
Directly out of the broad, flat leaves
High on slender stalks above the canopy
context: This trunk-flowering habit — fruit growing straight from the woody trunk and big branches instead of the twig tips — is called cauliflory. It's handy for farmers: the pods grow low enough to cut off by hand. Each pod holds roughly 20-60 beans packed in white pulp. Source: Wikipedia, 'Theobroma cacao'.

question: A farmer cracks open a fresh cacao pod, and the beans inside lie packed in a slippery white pulp. In the tropics people suck that pulp straight off the beans as a snack. What does it taste like?
answer: Bright and citrusy, like lychee or lemonade
choices: Bright and citrusy, like lychee or lemonade
Deep and bitter, like unsweetened cocoa
Salty and briny, like a green olive
Sharp and vinegary, like a pickle
context: The pulp is genuinely delicious — often compared to lychee, tropical melon, or lemonade. Rather than throw it away, farmers heap the pulp-covered beans in piles, where they begin their transformation into chocolate. Source: Wikipedia, 'Theobroma cacao'.

question: Bars of dark, milk and white chocolate lie side by side, two of them brown and one pale ivory, and some people insist the white one is not real chocolate at all. What is the real reason it is the odd one out?
answer: It contains none of the brown cocoa solids
choices: It contains none of the brown cocoa solids
It uses a rare white variety of cacao bean
It's whipped full of air to lighten its color
context: White chocolate really is made from the cacao bean — but only from cocoa butter, the pale fat pressed out of the bean, plus sugar and milk. With none of the brown cocoa solids, it simply can't turn brown. US rules (since 2004) require white chocolate to be at least 20% cocoa butter. Source: Wikipedia, 'White chocolate'.

question: Chocolate factories grind roasted cacao beans into a thick, greasy, dark paste, and from that one paste they make two very different products: dry cocoa powder for baking and pale, solid cocoa butter, the pure fat. How do they separate the fat from the powder?
answer: They crush the paste in a powerful press
choices: They crush the paste in a powerful press
They freeze it until the fat crystallizes off
They dissolve it in water and skim the top
They bake it until the extra fat evaporates
context: In 1828 the Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten patented a hydraulic press that squeezed the fatty cocoa butter out of ground cacao (called chocolate liquor, though it is completely non-alcoholic), leaving a dry cake that is ground into cocoa powder. So cocoa powder and cocoa butter are literally the two halves of the same bean. Recombining them — cocoa solids, cocoa butter, and sugar, plus milk for a milk bar — in different ratios is what makes dark chocolate versus milk chocolate. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chocolate'.

question: Doctors used to warn families to eat fewer eggs because eggs have cholesterol. But almost all of that cholesterol is packed into just one part of the egg. Which part carries nearly all of it?
context: The yolk holds essentially all of an egg's cholesterol, fat, and fat-soluble vitamins; the white is mostly protein and water with virtually none. So the yolk was the exact part that decades of diet advice told people to cut. Source: thehealthy.com; USDA FoodData Central — cholesterol is in the yolk, not the white.

question: Eggs and shrimp are rich in cholesterol, and from the 1970s American doctors warned families to eat far fewer eggs, since cholesterol was thought to clog the arteries. The whole scare rested on one intuitive idea about such food. What did people assume its cholesterol would do once eaten?
answer: Pass almost one-for-one into the blood
choices: Pass almost one-for-one into the blood
Get burned off first as energy
Block the gut from absorbing iron
context: This intuitive one-for-one logic drove the egg warnings for nearly 50 years — but when researchers actually measured it, the 2015 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee reported 'no appreciable relationship between consumption of dietary cholesterol and serum [blood] cholesterol.' The idea was reasonable; it just turned out to be wrong. Source: McNamara 2015 / DGAC, PMC4632449.

question: Scientists eventually measured where the cholesterol in human blood comes from, and the numbers undercut the whole egg scare. Food supplies only around one part in five of it. Where does the rest come from?
answer: The body makes it, mostly in the liver
choices: The body makes it, mostly in the liver
Gut bacteria produce it during digestion
It builds up from years of past meals
The skin makes it from sunlight
context: Harvard: 'your liver and intestines make about 80% of the cholesterol you need... Only about 20% comes from the foods you eat.' The liver alone makes on the order of 800 mg a day, far more than the ~186 mg in a large egg. Because the body itself is the main supplier, the food on the plate is a minor contributor. Source: health.harvard.edu, 'How it's made: Cholesterol production in your body.'

question: A man sits down to a big breakfast of bacon and eggs, packed with cholesterol. His liver does not work blindly, like a factory with no manager: it senses how much cholesterol has just come in with the meal. What does the liver do next?
answer: Throttles back its own production to compensate
choices: Throttles back its own production to compensate
Speeds up its own production to match
Dumps the extra into the blood unchanged
Stores the extra away in the muscles
context: This is a negative feedback loop: eat more cholesterol and the liver throttles down its own manufacturing (the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase gets dialed back), partly cancelling out the meal. It is the core reason dietary cholesterol shifts blood cholesterol far less than the old one-for-one logic predicted. Source: Soliman 2018, 'Dietary Cholesterol and the Lack of Evidence in CVD,' PMC6024687.

question: Health officials in the United States spent nearly half a century warning Americans to cut back on the cholesterol in eggs, shrimp and butter. Then research showed that dietary cholesterol barely moves blood cholesterol in most people, and the 2015 U.S. Dietary Guidelines made a famous about-face. What did those guidelines do?
answer: Removed the specific daily limit on dietary cholesterol
choices: Removed the specific daily limit on dietary cholesterol
Declared dietary cholesterol completely harmless to everyone
Raised the daily cholesterol limit to a much higher number
Told Americans to cut their egg intake even further
context: The 2015-2020 Dietary Guidelines dropped the longstanding 300 mg/day cap, stating cholesterol 'is not considered a nutrient of concern for overconsumption' — and the egg was, in effect, rehabilitated after about 47 years. Note the precise wording, though: they scrapped the numeric LIMIT; they did NOT declare cholesterol irrelevant to health, and blood LDL still matters for heart disease. Source: 2015-2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans / DGAC report.

question: Researchers who took a second look at the egg found that the cholesterol in food was not the main thing raising LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol in the blood. Something else in the diet does more to push it up. Which nutrient turned out to be the bigger driver?
context: Saturated fat impairs the liver's ability to clear LDL from the blood and raises apolipoprotein B — so a food's saturated-fat content turned out to matter more for blood cholesterol than its cholesterol number did. That shift in understanding is a big part of why the old cholesterol limit was dropped. Worth knowing: that is about LDL specifically. Whether raising LDL this way actually drives heart disease is itself a live debate -- later meta-analyses (Siri-Tarino 2010, Chowdhury 2014) failed to confirm the link -- so the saturated-fat story is contested, not closed. Source: National Geographic, 'Egg yolks, cholesterol and heart disease.'

question: A sunbather's skin turns cholesterol into vitamin D as the sunlight hits it, and every cell in her body wraps itself in a membrane built from cholesterol. Far from a poison, it is raw material the body cannot do without, and the body builds one more essential class of chemicals straight from it. What else does it make?
answer: Steroid hormones such as cortisol and testosterone
choices: Steroid hormones such as cortisol and testosterone
Red blood cells and the oxygen they carry
Insulin, the hormone that lowers blood sugar
Keratin, the protein in hair and nails
context: Cholesterol is essential raw material: the body uses it to build every cell membrane and to make vitamin D, bile acids for digesting fat, and all the steroid hormones — including cortisol and the sex hormones like testosterone and estrogen. No one can live without it, which is exactly why the liver makes its own steady supply. Source: StatPearls, 'Biochemistry, Cholesterol,' NIH (NBK513326).

question: Bare, unfilled cream puffs come out of the oven crisp and light. To finish them, a pastry chef pipes custard into each one through a single small hole in the side. What lets the custard flow in and fill the puff?
context: A cream puff or eclair bakes into a thin, crisp shell wrapped around a big empty pocket - and that hollow is the whole point: a built-in cup waiting to be piped full of cream or custard. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry

question: A baker pipes a blob of raw choux dough onto a tray, and in the oven it swells into a rounded little puff. French bakers thought it looked so like one round vegetable that they named the whole pastry after it. Which vegetable?
context: 'Choux' is simply the French word for cabbage. A piped blob of the dough puffs up into a bumpy, rounded little ball that reminded French bakers of a small round cabbage - and the name stuck to the whole pastry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry

question: A pastry chef makes choux dough with no yeast to raise it like bread and no baking powder to fizz it like a cake. Yet in a hot oven each piped blob balloons into a big, hollow puff. What force blows it up?
choices: egg whites beaten to stiff peaks
context: Choux has no yeast and no baking powder - its only leavening is steam. The dough is loaded with water; in the oven's heat that water flashes to steam and inflates the soft dough like a balloon, hollowing out the middle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry

question: Choux, the dough of a French bakery's cream puffs and eclairs, breaks a rule nearly every other dough keeps: bread, pie and cookie dough all go into the oven raw. Before a choux puff is baked, what has its dough already been?
answer: cooked into a paste on the stove
choices: cooked into a paste on the stove
toasted dry in a hot oven first
steamed soft over a boiling pot
context: Choux is the dough you cook twice. First you boil butter and water, beat in the flour, and cook it into a smooth paste on the stovetop; only then is it piped and baked. Almost no other dough is cooked before it goes into the oven. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry

question: Heat swells and bursts the starch granules in a choux paste of flour and water, and the recipe demands it for a real chemical reason. That gelled starch can now do something raw flour never could. What does it let the dough do?
answer: soak up far more egg and water
choices: soak up far more egg and water
rise all on its own, without eggs
brown into a deep caramel crust
stretch and snap back like gum
context: Raw flour starch can hold only so much liquid. Cooking the paste gelatinizes - swells and bursts - the starch granules, so the dough can soak up far more egg and water. That extra trapped water is the very fuel that flashes to steam in the oven and puffs the shell hollow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry; foodcrumbles.com/the-science-of-choux-pastry-in-profiteroles/

question: Cooks in the Burgundy region of France take choux, the dough behind sweet, cream-filled eclairs and profiteroles, and beat one savory ingredient into it. They bake it into little puffs and serve them cold with wine down in the cellars. What do they beat in?
context: That savory cousin is the gougere, from Burgundy: choux dough with grated Gruyere or Comte cheese beaten in, baked into cheese puffs and classically served cold with wine in the cellars. The same batter also makes eclairs, cream puffs, the wheel-shaped Paris-Brest, and the towering croquembouche - one dough, a whole family of pastries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gougere; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choux_pastry

question: French and Breton fishermen gave chowder its name, from their word 'chaudière.' Most soups are named for what floats in the bowl, like pea or onion soup. What did they name this one after?
answer: the cauldron they boiled it in
choices: the cauldron they boiled it in
context: 'Chaudière' was the big iron cauldron fishermen boiled their catch in on the docks. It traces through Late Latin 'caldaria' (cooking pot) back to Latin 'calidus,' meaning warm/hot — so a chowder is literally 'what comes out of the hot cauldron.' Source: etymonline.com/word/chowder; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chowder.

question: Colonial New England sailors ate chowder by the potful, though their earliest chowders had no clams, no milk and no potatoes, the three things that define a modern bowl. The pot still turned thick and hearty. What did the old cooks thicken it with?
context: The very first chowders were thickened not with flour but with crushed hardtack — the rock-hard ship's biscuit sailors carried — crumbled straight into the pot. Milk, potatoes, and clams are all later New England additions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chowder; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clam_chowder.

question: New England clam chowder builds its rich, savory backbone before anything else goes into the pot. First the cook dices up a fatty, cured pork, and then he melts out its fat and softens onions in that pork fat. Which cured pork traditionally starts the pot?
context: Rendering diced salt pork (sometimes with butter) and softening onion in that fat is the classic flavor base for New England's creamy white chowder, before the potatoes and milk go in. It's usually served with oyster or saltine crackers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clam_chowder.

question: Eleanor Early, a Boston writer, loathed the red, tomato-tinted chowder coming out of New York and called it a terrible pink mixture. Tomatoes and clams, she scoffed, went together no better than two other foods that clash horribly on one spoon. Which pair did she name?
context: Early called the red version 'a terrible pink mixture... only a vegetable soup,' and wrote that 'tomatoes and clams have no more affinity than ice cream and horseradish.' From Eleanor Early, 'A New England Sampler' (1940). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clam_chowder.

question: Rhode Island cooks make a clam chowder of their own and call it 'South County style.' Each stretch of the American coast has its own version of the soup. What does a Rhode Island clam chowder look like in the bowl?
answer: clear, almost like a light stock
choices: clear, almost like a light stock
creamy and white, rich with milk
red and tangy, built on tomato
thick and tan, heavy with crackers
context: Rhode Island (or 'South County style') clam chowder skips both cream and tomato, leaving a clear broth of clams, potatoes, onion, and salt-pork stock. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clam_chowder.

question: A cook following the oldest known printed chowder recipe, a jaunty rhyming poem from a Boston newspaper of 1751, layers onions, sliced pork and fish in the pot. The poem also calls for one boozy ingredient no modern clam chowder would touch. What does the poem pour in?
context: Printed in the Boston Evening Post on Sept. 23, 1751, the verse opens: 'First lay some Onions to keep the Pork from burning; Because in Chouder there can be no turning...' The layered dish held fish, salt pork, onions, hardtack, spices, and red wine. Source: theoldfoodie.com/2010/09/original-chowder.html; whatscookingamerica.net/history/chowderhistory.htm.

question: Cleveland Sleeper, a Maine lawmaker revolted by tomatoes in clam chowder, carried the chowder feud into the statehouse in 1939 with a bill to outlaw them entirely. He dreamed up a wonderfully petty punishment for anyone who dared defy it. What was an offender's sentence?
answer: dig a barrel of clams at high tide
choices: dig a barrel of clams at high tide
eat a gallon of the red soup
pay a barrel of clams in fines
shuck clams for the town feast
context: Digging a barrel of clams at high tide is impossible — the clam flats are underwater then. Rep. Cleveland Sleeper of Rockland never got his bill passed; the 'war' was settled instead by a public cook-off, which the New England white chowder won with the Maine governor among the judges. Source: newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/maines-great-clam-chowder-war-of-1939/.

question: A boy takes one bite of fresh cilantro and shoves his plate away: to him the herb tastes like a mouthful of dish soap, and he is not just being picky. Scientists hunting the cause found it in the genes for one sense. Which sense?
context: In a 23andMe study, roughly 1 in 8 people (about 13-14%) reported that cilantro tastes soapy -- and they genuinely perceive it that way. The reaction traces to smell-receptor (olfactory) genes on chromosome 11, not to the taste buds on the tongue, so it's really the herb's AROMA they're reacting to. Source: Eriksson et al., Flavour (2012), 'A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference.'

question: Suppose you taste soap in cilantro and your friend does not. Scientists really did find a 'cilantro gene' that reads the herb as soap, yet in the huge 23andMe study it explained only about half a percent of why people differ. What shapes whether you taste soap far more than that gene does?
answer: How much you grew up eating it
choices: How much you grew up eating it
How much you like other herbs
How spicy your other food is
How old you were when you tried it
context: In the 23andMe study, the OR6A2 smell-gene variant explained only about half a percent of the difference between people -- the gene is real but far from the whole story. Culture, cooking, and how much cilantro you grew up eating shape the reaction just as much, which is why people raised on cilantro-rich food rarely taste soap. Source: 23andMe blog, 'Cilantro Taste Gene'; Cleveland Clinic, 'Do You Love or Hate Cilantro?'

question: Most of the world's true cinnamon still grows on one tropical island in the Indian Ocean. Old maps and tea tins called it Ceylon, a name the spice still carries. What is the island called today?
context: Sri Lanka — called Ceylon until 1972 — is the native home of Cinnamomum verum, the 'true cinnamon' tree, and still grows 80–90% of it. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Cinnamomum verum.')

question: Arab middlemen in the cinnamon trade told a wild tale long before Europe knew where the spice grew. Giant 'cinnamon birds', they said, built their nests of it on cliffs no one could climb. Why did the traders really spread the story?
choices: to honor birds they held sacred
to scare rivals away from the cliffs
context: Pure marketing. Middlemen invented the 'cinnamon bird' to hide the real source and charge staggering prices; the Roman writer Pliny the Elder scoffed that such tales were a traders' fiction, made up to raise the price. Herodotus recorded the meat-bait version around 440 BCE (Histories 3.111). (Sources: Wikipedia, 'Cinnamon bird'; Herodotus 3.111.)  (Legend.)

question: Nero's wife Poppaea died in AD 65, in a Rome where a workman might need years of wages to buy one pound of cinnamon. Nero seized her funeral as a chance to flaunt both his grief and his riches. What did he reportedly do?
answer: burned a whole year's supply of Rome's cinnamon
choices: burned a whole year's supply of Rome's cinnamon
built her coffin from solid cinnamon wood
served cinnamon wine to every citizen of Rome
scattered cinnamon across the whole Forum
context: Cinnamon was a Roman status symbol — Pliny claimed a pound could cost a laborer years of wages. At Poppaea Sabina's funeral in AD 65, Nero reportedly burned a whole year's supply of Rome's cinnamon to display his grief and wealth. (Sources: Wikipedia, 'Cinnamon'; imperiumromanum.pl.)

question: A Dutch sea captain made a boast about Ceylon after his countrymen seized the cinnamon island in the 1600s. A passing ship, he claimed, could tell the island was near from eight leagues out, about 24 miles. By his account, what gave the island away?
answer: its scent drifting on the wind
choices: its scent drifting on the wind
its surf booming on the reefs
its smoke rising over the hills
context: A Dutch captain wrote that 'when one is downwind of the island, one can still smell cinnamon eight leagues out to sea' — roughly 24 miles. Ceylon's air was famously thick with the spice. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Cinnamon.')

question: Ceylon's cinnamon harvest belonged to the Dutch East India Company by 1658, and the company meant to keep the bark precious. To make sure the market was never flooded and the price never crashed, it took a drastic step with the island's cinnamon trees themselves. What did it do?
answer: destroyed its own surplus cinnamon trees
choices: destroyed its own surplus cinnamon trees
taxed rival growers until they gave up theirs
moved every tree to one guarded secret plantation
let only its own men plant new cinnamon trees
context: The Portuguese first seized Ceylon, then the Dutch East India Company took control of the cinnamon harvest by 1658. To keep prices high they capped how much bark could be peeled and destroyed surplus cinnamon trees to stop overproduction and smuggling. (Sources: ceylonhistory.com; Grokipedia, 'Dutch Ceylon.')

question: A cook drops a cinnamon stick, a small brown tube, into hot cider. Only a paper-thin layer of the cinnamon tree, about half a millimetre thick, ends up as that spice. Which part of the tree is it?
context: A cinnamon stick is literally a strip of the tree's inner bark, peeled off and rolled into a tube called a 'quill.' It is not a leaf, a seed, or a root. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinnamon

question: A worker cuts a cinnamon branch, peels a long thin strip from it, and lays the strip in the sun, still flat and wet. Over the next few hours, what does the drying do to that strip?
answer: It curls itself up into a tight coil
choices: It curls itself up into a tight coil
It shrinks down into hard little pellets
It bleaches into a pale, silvery gold
It splits apart into loose, dry flakes
context: Workers strip off the rough outer bark, loosen the thin inner layer, and peel it away in a strip only about half a millimeter thick. Left out to dry for a few hours, the wet strip curls up all on its own into the familiar rolled quill -- no mold or machine needed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinnamon

question: A shopper takes down a jar labelled 'cinnamon' at the supermarket. Most often the hard, dark sticks inside are not the prized true Ceylon kind but a cheaper, bolder cousin from China, Indonesia and Vietnam, sold as the same spice. What is that cousin called?
context: Most 'cinnamon' sold is actually cassia, a cheaper cousin -- most often Cinnamomum cassia from China (so it's also called Chinese cinnamon), plus Indonesian and Vietnamese kinds. Cassia tastes bolder and spicier than delicate true cinnamon. Source: https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/ceylon-vs-cassia-cinnamon

question: A sharp-eyed baker can tell true Ceylon cinnamon from the cheap supermarket kind just by looking at a stick. The cheap one is dark reddish-brown, thick and hard, rolled into one tough curl like a newspaper. What does a true Ceylon stick look like?
answer: Pale and thin, made of many soft papery layers packed like a cigar
choices: Pale and thin, made of many soft papery layers packed like a cigar
Pale and thin, made of one thin hollow shell like a drinking straw
Pale and thin, made of one smooth solid rod like a wooden dowel
Pale and thin, made of short flat chips snapped like dry bark
context: Cassia sticks are dark reddish-brown, thick (2 to 3 mm), and hard, curling into one tough scroll like a rolled-up newspaper. True Ceylon sticks are pale, thin, and made of many soft, papery layers packed together like a cigar, so they crumble easily in your hand. Source: https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/ceylon-vs-cassia-cinnamon

question: The cheap supermarket kind of cinnamon carries far more of a natural compound called coumarin than true Ceylon cinnamon does. A light sprinkle on toast or oatmeal is fine. Eaten in large amounts every single day, though, coumarin can be hard on one organ in particular. Which organ?
context: Cassia carries far more coumarin than Ceylon -- roughly 1 percent versus about 0.004 percent. Coumarin can be hard on the liver in large daily doses. European food-safety agencies set a safe daily limit of about 6 mg for an adult, and around half a teaspoon of cassia every day would pass it. An occasional sprinkle is completely fine; Ceylon is the safer pick for someone eating a lot. Sources: https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/ceylon-vs-cassia-cinnamon ; https://www.bfr.bund.de/en/service/frequently-asked-questions/topic/faq-on-coumarin-in-cinnamon-and-other-foods/

question: Herodotus, the Greek historian, told of huge birds that built their nests out of cinnamon high on cliffs no person could scale. In his tale the spice traders still found a clever way to bring the cinnamon down. What did they do?
answer: They set out heavy chunks of meat, and the loaded nests broke off the cliff
choices: They set out heavy chunks of meat, and the loaded nests broke off the cliff
They trained nimble monkeys to scramble up and pull the nests off the cliff
They lit thick, smoky fires to drive the nesting birds right off the cliff
They shot burning arrows to knock the flaming nests loose off the cliff
context: As Herodotus told it, the Arabians chopped oxen into heavy chunks and left the meat near the cliffs; the giant birds carried it up to their nests, the extra weight broke the nests loose, and the traders simply gathered the cinnamon that tumbled down. Told as ancient legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinnamon_bird

question: Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer, scoffed at the old story of giant birds that nested in cinnamon high on unclimbable cliffs. Traders made up such monsters on purpose, he said, to hide the real source of their spice. Where did Pliny say the cinnamon actually came from?
answer: It arrived by trading ship from lands in the East
choices: It arrived by trading ship from lands in the East
It came from deep mines beneath the African desert
It came from divers working the deep ocean floor
It grew wild across the sunny hillsides of Greece
context: Pliny the Elder saw through the bird tale, writing that traders invented such stories to raise their prices. The unmagical truth: cinnamon simply came by sea from the East, and the wild legend was a cover story to disguise that real source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinnamon_bird

question: A cook wipes down a kitchen counter until it looks spotless — no crumbs, no smears, nothing greasy anywhere she can see. But a health inspector walks by and warns her the counter still might not be safe to prep food on. How can a surface that looks perfectly clean still be dangerous?
answer: Germs too small to see can survive on it after wiping
choices: Germs too small to see can survive on it after wiping
The cleaning spray leaves a harmful film behind
Rinsing with tap water only adds new dirt
It has to fully dry before it counts as clean
context: This is the whole reason 'clean' and 'sanitize' are two different jobs. Cleaning REMOVES the dirt, grease, and food bits you can see; sanitizing REDUCES the pathogens you can't see down to a safe level. A counter can look spotless and still be crawling with germs. Source: ServSafe/NRAEF 'Cleaning VS. Sanitizing' fact sheet; FoodSafePal 'Cleaning vs. Sanitizing'.

question: Spray bottle in hand, a cook mists sanitizer straight onto a greasy, food-smeared counter, breaking the kitchen's golden rule: clean first, then sanitize. Why can't the sanitizer do both jobs at the same time?
answer: The leftover grease and food scraps shield the germs from it
choices: The leftover grease and food scraps shield the germs from it
The grease makes the trapped germs multiply too fast to kill
Soaking into the food scraps turns the sanitizer poisonous
The greasy film is too slippery for the sanitizer to stick
context: Cooks call it the golden rule of surface safety: 'You cannot sanitize a dirty surface — cleaning always comes first.' Leftover grease, oils, and food proteins physically shield the germs, so a sanitizer sprayed on a dirty surface can't even reach the bugs it's meant to kill. Some sanitizers, like quats, are even chemically weakened by contact with food residue. Clean the food off first, and the sanitizer can finally make contact. Source: 360training 'Difference Between Cleaning and Sanitizing'; Cornell Produce Safety Alliance; University of Minnesota Extension; FoodSafePal.

question: A line cook scrubs a prep counter, rinses it, and sprays it down with bleach sanitizer. The health inspector's swab still comes back crawling with germs. Bleach and iodine sanitizers both carry one demand this cook broke — what is it?
answer: It has to be left sitting wet for its full contact time
choices: It has to be left sitting wet for its full contact time
It has to be mixed fresh with cool water each morning
It has to be sprayed on before the rinse water dries
It has to be scrubbed in until the surface foams up
context: A chemical sanitizer has to stay WET on the surface for its 'contact time' to work — roughly 10 seconds for a chlorine/bleach solution, about 30 seconds for iodine or quats. Wipe it dry too soon and it never had time to do its job. (The other way to sanitize is heat: a dish machine's final rinse hits at least 180°F.) Source: FoodSafePal 'Cleaning vs. Sanitizing'; StateFoodSafety 'Cleaning and Sanitizing'; datcp.wi.gov sanitizing fact sheet.

question: A cook's sanitizer has sat on a counter long enough to do its job, and the wet surface now needs drying. A food-safety guide says to leave the towel alone and let the counter dry in the air. How would toweling it dry leave it germier than before?
answer: A used towel smears germs from itself right back onto the surface
choices: A used towel smears germs from itself right back onto the surface
The towel's fibers scratch tiny grooves where germs can hide
Rubbing warms the surface just enough to revive the germs
The towel leaves behind lint that lingering germs feed on
context: This is the final step of the clean-then-sanitize routine: (1) scrape, (2) wash, (3) rinse, (4) sanitize, (5) air-dry. FoodSafePal puts it bluntly: 'never use a cloth or towel for drying, since this can recontaminate the surface.' A used towel just smears the germs right back on — so let the surface dry by itself in the air. Food-contact surfaces in constant use need this whole routine at least every four hours. Source: FoodSafePal 'Cleaning vs. Sanitizing' (quoted verbatim); ServSafe 5-step process, Step 5 'Allow the surface to air dry'.

question: Every clove on Earth once came from one small corner of the planet, the only place the tree grew, and Europeans did not find it until their ships came in the 1500s. Where did the world's cloves grow?
answer: The volcanic islands of the Maluku
choices: The volcanic islands of the Maluku
The Malabar coast of southern India
context: Cloves grew on just five tiny volcanic islands in the Maluku (the Moluccas, or Spice Islands) of what is now Indonesia -- Ternate, Tidore, Moti, Makian, and Bacan -- and nowhere else on Earth. That scarcity made them worth their weight in gold and pulled traders from China, Arabia, and eventually Europe halfway around the world. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clove'.

question: In the court of Han-dynasty China, over two thousand years ago, an official had a strict rule to follow. He could not address the emperor until he had first tucked a whole clove into his mouth. Why did the official need the clove first?
context: Cloves were prized as a breath freshener in ancient China, where the spice earned the nickname 'chicken-tongue spice' for the little bud's shape. An official approaching the emperor was expected to hold one so that his breath would be sweet. Source: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Clove'; corroborated by leminhkhaiblog.com and woksoflove.com.

question: Families on the remote islands where cloves grew wove the fragrant tree into their biggest moments, above all a child's birth. On the day a baby was born, what did island tradition call for?
answer: Planting a clove tree for the newborn
choices: Planting a clove tree for the newborn
Burying the birth-cord beneath the oldest tree
Bathing the newborn in clove-scented water
Carving the child's name into a tree
context: By island tradition a family planted a clove tree at a child's birth and treated it as the child's own, believing the tree's health mirrored the child's fate. That belief is why what the Dutch would later do to the trees felt to the islanders like an attack on their children. Source: The Treeographer, 'The Clove Tree that Ended a Monopoly'; corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Clove'.  (Legend.)

question: Arab and Asian traders who carried cloves west guarded the secret of where the trees grew, so Europeans filled the silence with legend. One belief, repeated for generations, held that the cloves could only be grown and picked by whom?
context: With the true source hidden for so long, wild stories filled the gap -- including the tale that cloves could only be raised by genies (jinn) using magical arts. Keeping outsiders in the dark about the five islands was exactly how the middlemen kept clove prices sky-high. Source: Fairchild Garden, 'Cloves.'  (Legend.)

question: Soldiers of the Dutch East India Company fanned out across the clove islands from 1652 with a strict order about every clove tree growing outside the company's own plantations. The company wanted cloves rare and prices sky-high. What were the soldiers told to do to those trees?
answer: Chop them down and burn them
choices: Chop them down and burn them
Guard them under lock and key
context: Starting in 1652 the Dutch enforced an 'extirpation' policy: soldiers uprooted and burned every clove tree the company did not own across North Maluku, so that no one else could grow the spice. Many of the destroyed trees were the islanders' birth-trees, and the islanders fought back fiercely to save them. Source: The Treeographer, 'The Clove Tree that Ended a Monopoly'; Fairchild Garden, 'Cloves'.

question: The Dutch had guarded their clove monopoly for more than a century when, around 1770, a Frenchman slipped clove and nutmeg seedlings past them and broke it for good. His name was Pierre Poivre, and his surname is the French word for a spice. Which spice?
context: Pierre Poivre -- whose surname is literally French for 'pepper' -- smuggled clove and nutmeg seedlings out of the Dutch-held islands around 1770 and carried them to French colonies in the Indian Ocean, ending the monopoly. The man who cracked the spice trade was, fittingly, named Pepper. Source: The Treeographer, 'The Clove Tree that Ended a Monopoly'.

question: Clove seedlings smuggled past the Dutch around 1770 thrived far from the islands where the tree first grew. One island off East Africa took to them so well that it grew into the world's clove capital during the 1800s. Which island?
context: Zanzibar, off the coast of modern Tanzania, embraced the smuggled cloves and grew into the world's clove capital in the 1800s. The spice's home had crossed the entire Indian Ocean -- from the Maluku on one side to Zanzibar on the other. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clove'; The Treeographer, 'The Clove Tree that Ended a Monopoly'.

question: A dentist dabs clove oil on a patient's aching tooth, and the sore spot slowly goes numb, just as the tongue does when someone bites down on a whole clove. The oil's main compound, eugenol, causes that numbness. How does eugenol stop the pain?
answer: It blocks the nerve's pain-signal channels
choices: It blocks the nerve's pain-signal channels
It chills the nerve endings like ice
It burns the pain nerve away for good
It seals the tooth under a hard cap
context: Eugenol, which makes up most of clove oil, blocks the tiny sodium channels a nerve uses to fire -- the very same channels that prescription local anesthetics target -- so the pain signal never reaches the brain. Dentists still mix eugenol with zinc-oxide powder to make a soothing temporary filling for a sore tooth. Source: Medical News Today; Wikipedia, 'Clove'.

question: A clove grower dries his harvest hard in the sun, and each whole clove comes out a tiny dark-brown spike with a round little ball at the very top. What is that little ball, really?
answer: A flower bud, closed up tight before it could open
choices: A flower bud, closed up tight before it could open
A hard seed, like the pip inside an apple
A berry that shriveled small as it dried on the mat
A leaf bud that curled up tight on the stem
context: A clove is a flower that never got to bloom. Growers pick the buds just before they would open -- the little head is the four unopened petals balled up over the center -- then sun-dry them from bright red to dark brown. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clove'; McCormick Science Institute, 'Cloves' (the dried, unopened flower buds).

question: Traders prized a handful of tiny volcanic islands so highly that they called them the Spice Islands, for every clove on Earth came from there and grew nowhere else for hundreds of years. Which country are those islands part of today?
context: The clove's home is the northern Maluku (Molucca) islands of Indonesia -- five tiny volcanic specks off Halmahera: Ternate, Tidore, Moti, Makian, and Bacan. For centuries they were the world's only source of cloves. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Clove'; Sea Trek, 'Spices in the Spice Islands'.

question: A man bites down on a whole clove, and once the warm, sharp taste fades, the spot on his gum goes oddly tingly, then numb. Old-time dentists used the very same trick on aching teeth to dull the pain. Where does a clove's numbing power come from?
answer: The aromatic oil packed inside it
choices: The aromatic oil packed inside it
A mild acid in its dry skin
The sugar stored in the dried clove
The grit of its powdery coating
context: That numbing comes from the clove's own fragrant oil, which is mostly a compound called eugenol -- the source of the warm, penetrating smell, and the same stuff old-time dentists dabbed on a sore tooth to deaden it. Source: McCormick Science Institute, 'Cloves'; Wikipedia, 'Clove'.

question: A cook preparing Christmas dinner pushes dozens of whole cloves into a ham in a neat diamond grid and drops a few more into a pot of simmering stock, then fishes those out before serving instead of stirring in ground clove. Why cook with whole cloves and then pull them back out?
answer: A single clove is so strong that a whole one, later removed, seasons without overpowering
choices: A single clove is so strong that a whole one, later removed, seasons without overpowering
Ground clove is not safe to swallow and has to be strained out of the dish first
Whole cloves are far cheaper to buy by weight than the same amount of ground clove
A clove loses almost all of its smell within seconds of being ground into powder
context: A single clove packs a huge punch, so cooks use them whole and remove them: a clove-studded ham, or an onion spiked with a couple of cloves to season a stock and then thrown away -- flavoring the dish without turning it bitter or medicinal. Source: McCormick Science Institute, 'Cloves'.

question: A cook lifts a steaming green bundle of cochinita pibil out of the oven, and the meat inside is so tender it falls apart. That fragrant green wrapper traps the steam and flavors the meat as it cooks. What is the wrapper made from?
context: Cochinita pibil is a Yucatan slow-roasted dish. The meat is wrapped in banana leaves, which trap steam and perfume it so it falls apart tender. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cochinita pibil.'

question: A diner ordering cochinita pibil hears its meat in the name: 'cochinita' is Spanish for a baby version of one farm animal, and the old recipe roasted a young one whole. Which animal is it?
context: 'Cochino' is Spanish for pig, and the diminutive '-ita' makes 'cochinita' a little pig or baby pig. The most traditional version roasts a whole young suckling pig. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cochinita pibil.'

question: Cochinita pibil comes out of the oven glowing a deep sunset burnt-orange. One special ingredient, rubbed onto the raw meat before it is wrapped and cooked, gives the dish that color. Which ingredient is it?
context: The burnt-orange color of cochinita pibil comes from achiote, also called annatto: a paste ground from a tropical seed, with a mild, sweet, peppery flavor. Despite the color, it is not chili and not tomato. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cochinita pibil.'

question: Cooks thin the bright orange-red marinade of cochinita pibil with the juice of a local Yucatan citrus fruit, one prized for its sharp, puckery tang rather than for sweetness. The meat cooks for hours in it. Which fruit gives the marinade its bite?
context: Traditional cochinita pibil uses the juice of the sour orange, also called the Seville or bitter orange, not vinegar or lemon. Outside the Yucatan, sweet orange juice mixed with lime, lemon, or vinegar is the common substitute. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cochinita pibil.'

question: Cochinita pibil owes the last part of its name to the piib, the oven Maya cooks used long before the Spanish reached the Yucatán. The pork goes in wrapped in leaves and comes out hours later, tender enough to fall apart. What kind of oven is a piib?
answer: A pit of hot stones, covered over with earth
choices: A pit of hot stones, covered over with earth
A clay dome heated by a fire inside it
A flat stone griddle set over the coals
A smokehouse of poles roofed with leaves
context: The Maya earth oven, the piib, is a hole lined with hardwood and stones and fired until the stones glow; the leaf-wrapped meat goes onto the stones and the pit is covered over with earth, so the food cooks low and slow underground. 'Piib' means 'buried' in Maya, and it is the root of the '-pibil' in the dish's name. Source: Wikipedia, 'Piib'; Wikipedia, 'Cochinita pibil.'

question: Spanish explorers in the Caribbean wrote down a Taino word, barbacoa, in 1526, and English later turned it into the everyday word 'barbecue.' To the Taino who coined it, what was a barbacoa at first?
answer: a rack of green sticks over a fire
choices: a rack of green sticks over a fire
a clay pot buried in hot coals
a flat stone laid on the flames
an iron spit turned by hand
context: The Spanish word 'barbacoa', from the Taino 'barbacoa/barabicu', named a framework of green sticks raised over a fire to cook or cure meat, and it is the origin of the English 'barbecue.' It first appeared in print in Spanish in 1526, in Gonzalo Fernandez de Oviedo's account of the West Indies. In Mexico the Spanish later applied 'barbacoa' to the indigenous pit / earth-oven method, and that pit-cooking sense carried into English. Sources: Wiktionary, 'barbacoa'; Vocabulary.com, 'The Origins of Barbecue.'

question: Maya cooks made the buried-pit dish behind cochinita pibil long before Spanish ships brought its modern meat to the Yucatan in the 1500s. Back then they cooked it with a big wild bird they hunted. Which bird did they use?
context: The pit (pibil) technique is ancient Maya, but pork is post-Columbian: the Spanish introduced pigs in the 1500s. The pre-Hispanic dish used native game. The turkey version is 'pibil kuts,' the deer (venison) version is 'pibil keh,' and wild boar/peccary was also used. Sources: Undiscovered Mexico, 'History of Cochinita Pibil'; The Yucatan Times, '5 Things You Need to Know.'

question: A seed that Yucatan cooks use for cochinita pibil is sold around the world as annatto, ground fine and hidden in the ingredient list of something on an ordinary supermarket shelf. Which supermarket item owes its orange color to annatto?
context: Achiote/annatto is the same natural seed dye that turns cheeses and butter orange around the world, including red Cheddar, Red Leicester, Gloucester, Mimolette, Colby, and Muenster, plus butter and margarine. Its orange-red comes from carotenoid pigments (mainly bixin and norbixin) in the seed's waxy coating. Source: Wikipedia, 'Annatto.'

question: Ships carried the potato, the tomato and cacao away from the Americas to feed the rest of the world, but coffee made the voyage the other way, an Old World crop from the start. In which African country did the wild coffee shrub first grow?
context: Coffee is the mirror image of the great American crops. The wild coffee shrub grows in the highlands of Ethiopia, and the drink was first brewed across the Red Sea in Yemen -- so coffee was an Old World plant all along, unlike the potato and tomato that sailed OUT of the Americas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_coffee

question: Gabriel de Clieu, a French naval officer, spent months at sea in 1720 carrying a single coffee seedling to the Caribbean island of Martinique. He watched over the tiny plant the whole voyage. What sacrifice is de Clieu remembered for making to keep the seedling alive?
answer: He shared his own drinking-water ration with it
choices: He shared his own drinking-water ration with it
He sheltered it under his coat from the salt wind
He sat up guarding it through every storm
He hid it near the ship's warm galley fire
context: de Clieu's seedling thrived on Martinique and helped stock the Caribbean's coffee estates. His voyage captures coffee's backwards path: while the potato and tomato sailed OUT of the Americas, coffee -- an Old World plant -- was carried IN by Europeans during the 1700s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_coffee

question: Coffee farmers in one New World country now grow roughly a third of the coffee on Earth, far more than any other nation, though the plant never grew wild anywhere in the Americas. That makes it the surprise homeland of a bean not native to it. Which country is it?
context: Brazil grows about a third of the world's coffee -- the planet's biggest producer by far -- even though the coffee plant is native to Africa and Arabia, not the Americas. A Portuguese officer, Francisco de Melo Palheta, planted Brazil's first coffee bush in 1727. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_production_in_Brazil

question: Pickers on a coffee farm gather small, glossy globes by hand once they have ripened from green to red, from bushes that bear no beans at all, though most people picture coffee as brown beans. What is each globe, botanically?
answer: a fruit, which growers call a cherry
choices: a fruit, which growers call a cherry
a nut, which growers call a burr
a seed-pod, which growers call a hull
a flower bud, which growers call a pip
context: The 'bean' a coffee drinker grinds is really the seed hidden inside that little red fruit, the coffee cherry. Some varieties ripen yellow or orange instead of red (like Yellow Bourbon). Source: jayarr.coffee, 'Coffee Cherry Anatomy Explained.'

question: Growers making 'washed' coffee press the red skins off what they have picked, yet every seed is still wrapped in a sticky, sugary coat. They tip the coated seeds into tanks of water and leave them for a day or two, and when the seeds come out, the coat is gone. What made it disappear?
answer: the wild microbes fermented it away
choices: the wild microbes fermented it away
the tank water dissolved it away
the seeds sprouted and shed it
the warm water softened it off
context: That sugary slime is called mucilage, and its sugar level rivals wine grapes, which is what the microbes feed on. Over roughly 8 to 36 hours they and the enzyme pectinase eat the sticky fruit-layer off the seed; growers know it's done by FEEL, when the coating turns from slimy to rough and 'pebbly.' Not ALL coffee is washed: in the 'natural' (dry) process the whole cherry dries in the sun for up to four weeks with the fruit still on, giving a sweeter, fruitier cup while washed coffee tastes cleaner and brighter. Same bean, different process, different cup. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coffee production'; jayarr.coffee, 'Coffee Cherry Anatomy Explained.'

question: A roaster tips a sack of roasted coffee onto a tray. Nearly every bean is rounded on one side and flat on the other, though now and then one comes out small and round all over. What pressed the flat face onto most of the beans?
answer: A twin seed growing pressed against it
choices: A twin seed growing pressed against it
The hot drum of the roasting machine
The rollers that peeled off its skin
The patio floor where it dried in sun
