context: Most coffee cherries hold two seeds pressed flat against each other, and that pressure gives an ordinary bean its one flat face. Now and then only a single seed develops, and with no twin to flatten it, the seed grows into a small round bead called a peaberry. Peaberries show up in only a small share of any harvest, so growers often sort them out and sell them on their own; some roasters insist the rounder bean roasts more evenly, though that claim is more coffee-lore than settled science. Source: jayarr.coffee, 'Coffee Cherry Anatomy Explained.'

question: Leftover beef stew goes into a fridge set to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit, far warmer than a freezer. Left there long enough, the stew still turns sour and spoils. What is the fridge's chill doing to the germs living in the stew?
answer: Slowing them down but not killing them
choices: Slowing them down but not killing them
Killing them all within a day or two
Killing off only the harmful ones
Killing them the instant it turns cold
context: The USDA says that at fridge temperatures (40 degrees F or below), illness-causing bacteria 'either don't grow or grow very slowly' -- the cold is a brake pedal, not an off switch. The germs are still alive and still slowly at work, which is why nothing in the fridge lasts forever and even cold leftovers eventually spoil. Source: USDA FSIS, 'How Temperatures Affect Food' -- https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/how-temperatures-affect-food

question: A cook freezes leftovers at 0 degrees Fahrenheit, and the bacteria in them stop growing completely. It would be easy to believe the cold had finally killed them off. What really becomes of those germs in the deep freeze?
answer: They fall dormant and revive when the food thaws
choices: They fall dormant and revive when the food thaws
They are killed by ice crystals piercing them
They are killed, but their toxins survive the cold
They mutate into a hardier cold-loving strain
context: USDA's exact words: freezing to 0 degrees F 'inactivates any microbes -- bacteria, yeasts, and molds' by slowing molecular movement so much that the bacteria 'enter a dormant stage.' Inactivated, not dead. 'Once thawed, however, these microbes can again become active,' multiplying to levels that can cause illness -- so a thawed food is only as safe as it was the day it went into the freezer. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Freezing and Food Safety' -- https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/freezing-and-food-safety

question: A forgotten steak comes out of the freezer covered in grayish-brown, dry, leathery patches -- classic freezer burn. Is that food dangerous, and what has actually gone wrong with it?
answer: It's still safe to eat -- those spots just lost moisture
choices: It's still safe to eat -- those spots just lost moisture
It's spoiling -- bacteria have begun breaking it down
It's gone rancid -- germs multiplied in the freezer
It's turned toxic -- the deep cold made harmful compounds
context: Freezer burn happens when air reaches the food's surface and moisture escapes, leaving those dry, leathery, grayish-brown patches. USDA says the food is 'safe to eat, merely dry in spots' -- food kept constantly at 0 degrees F is always safe; only quality suffers. The fix is a knife, not the trash: cut the burned parts away, before or after cooking, and eat the rest. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Freezing and Food Safety'; Iowa State University Extension AnswerLine, 'Freezer Burn and Food Safety' (2024) -- https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2024/03/19/freezer-burn-and-food-safety/

question: Bottles stashed in the fridge door make an easy grab, but the door swings open more than any other spot, so it is the warmest, most changeable place in the whole fridge. Which everyday items should live on a cold inside shelf instead?
context: The door is opened more than anywhere else, so its temperature jumps every time you reach in, and the door gasket lets warm air creep past -- making it the fridge's warmest, swingiest spot. That's why USDA recommends storing eggs in their original carton on an interior shelf, not the door, and milk keeps best inside too. Sturdier, high-acid or high-sugar items like ketchup, pickles, and jam handle the door's swings just fine. The coldest, most stable real estate is the back of the lower shelves, where cold air sinks farthest from the door. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Refrigeration & Food Safety'; Tasting Table, 'The Warmest Place In Your Fridge' -- https://www.tastingtable.com/1929505/warmest-spot-in-fridge-door/

question: Suppose you eat a steak. Collagen, the protein that makes up roughly a third of all the protein in your own body, is in there too, because animals are built from it as well. Which part of a steak is the collagen?
answer: The chewy gristle running through it
choices: The chewy gristle running through it
The red juice that pools on the plate
The lean red muscle you slice into
The dark crust the hot pan leaves
context: That gristle -- and the pale, ropey stuff wrapped around a joint -- is collagen: the body's built-in scaffolding, the stringy glue holding skin, tendons, bones and cartilage together. It is about 30% of your body's dry weight, and a tendon is roughly 40-50% collagen. Type I collagen alone accounts for about 90% of all the collagen in you, the fibre that gives skin, bone, tendon and ligament their tensile strength. Sources: Cleveland Clinic, 'Collagen' (my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/23089-collagen); Wikipedia, 'Collagen'; The Meat Stick, 'The Science of Collagen'.

question: A pot of beef bones and knuckles simmers for six hours at a lazy bubble; then the cook strains the broth and chills it overnight. By morning she can spoon it out in trembling blocks. What did those six slow hours do to the bones?
answer: Unravelled their collagen and dissolved it into gelatin
choices: Unravelled their collagen and dissolved it into gelatin
Melted their marrow into a fat that stiffens as it chills
Cooked their blood proteins until they set like an egg white
Boiled the broth down until its salt and solids thickened it
context: Low, slow, moist heat unravels collagen and dissolves it into gelatin -- a process called hydrolysis. It begins around 160F (71C) and finishes between roughly 180-200F (82-93C), which is exactly why braising liquid stays at a gentle simmer and never a hard boil. Gelatin's melting point sits just below body temperature, so the jelly slumps back to broth the moment you reheat it -- and 'melts in your mouth'. That same melt is why the cheap, collagen-rich cuts (shank, oxtail, brisket, chuck, pork shoulder, short ribs) braise into meltingly tender meat with a silky, sticky sauce, while a lean, tender cut cooked the same way just dries out. Sources: The Meat Stick, 'The Science of Collagen'; scienceofcooking.com, 'Slow Cooking'; Freja Bone Broth, 'Jelly'; Wikipedia, 'Gelatin'.

question: Hans Riegel, a confectioner in Bonn, cooked up a chewy, fruit-flavored bear in 1922 and called it the Tanzbaer, the 'Dancing Bear,' the first gummy bear. A century on, Haribo's bears still get their chew from the setting agent that gives a marshmallow its squish. What is that setting agent cooked out of?
answer: The skin and bones of pigs and cattle
choices: The skin and bones of pigs and cattle
The hooves and horns of dairy cattle
The peel and cores of apples and lemons
The sap and bark of acacia trees
context: Gelatin is simply collagen that heat has unravelled: denatured, partly hydrolysed collagen taken from the skin, bones and connective tissue of animals such as cattle, pigs and fish, then purified until it is colourless, flavourless and translucent. Which means a gummy bear, a marshmallow and a bowl of wobbling jelly are all built from animal collagen. Hans Riegel of Haribo sold his Tanzbaer in Bonn in 1922; a century on, the bear is still set the same way. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Gelatin'; Wikipedia, 'Gummy bear'.

question: A cook warms cream with sugar, stirs in one small spoonful of gelatin and chills it overnight: that is nearly the whole recipe for panna cotta, 'cooked cream' in Italian. Next day the bowlful stands up in a dome out of its mold. How does one spoonful of gelatin hold all that cream?
answer: It weaves the cream's water into a wobbling web
choices: It weaves the cream's water into a wobbling web
It soaks the cream's water into a thick paste
It hardens the cream's fat into a cold block
It links the cream's proteins into a smooth custard
context: Purified gelatin can trap five to ten times its own weight in water, locking it into a wobbling network called a hydrogel -- that trapped-water web IS the 'set' of a jelly. And gelatin is simply collagen that heat has unravelled: denatured, partly hydrolysed collagen taken from the skin, bones and connective tissue of animals such as cattle, pigs and fish. So a delicate cream dessert is held up by animal collagen -- old Italian recipes even call the setting agent colla di pesce, 'fish glue'. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Gelatin'; Wikipedia, 'Panna cotta'.

question: Christopher Columbus sailed three small ships west from Spain in August 1492, gambling on a shortcut to the rich 'Indies' of Asia. He was not after empty land but the luxury Europeans wanted most from the East. What was he hunting?
context: Columbus set out from Spain on August 3, 1492 with three ships — the Nina, Pinta and Santa Maria — gambling that sailing WEST would be a shortcut to Asia's spice markets, where black pepper, cinnamon and cloves were treasures on European dinner tables. He made landfall October 12 — not in Asia, but on a Bahamian island. Source: Wikipedia, Voyages of Christopher Columbus; history.com.

question: A chili pod and a black peppercorn come from two unrelated plants, yet English still calls the fiery pod a 'chili pepper,' and German calls it 'Pfeffer.' Why does the chili carry a pepper's name?
answer: Columbus, hunting black pepper, tasted the fiery pods and called them 'pepper' too
choices: Columbus, hunting black pepper, tasted the fiery pods and called them 'pepper' too
Venetian traders, low on peppercorns, sold the ground pods as a cheap 'pepper'
Lisbon cooks, tasting the burn, swore the pods came off the black-pepper vine
Magellan's crew, trading in Asia, brought the pods home as an Eastern 'pepper'
context: Columbus was hunting Asia's black pepper (Piper nigrum, an Asian vine, whose bite comes from piperine). The fiery pods he carried home were an unrelated New World plant — chili, a Capsicum, whose burn comes from capsaicin — that he misnamed 'pepper' because it was hot like the peppercorns he knew. That single guess is why chilies are still called 'peppers,' 'pimiento' and 'Pfeffer' around the world. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'Why called pepper'; Wikipedia, Chili pepper.

question: Columbus started the biggest food swap in history. Chocolate, chili, tomato and potato all sailed east from the Americas. Foods went the other way too. Which food came west, from the Old World into American kitchens?
context: Columbus's failure to find Asian spices accidentally launched the Columbian Exchange — a term historian Alfred Crosby coined in 1972 — the great two-way food swap between the hemispheres. Chocolate (cacao), chili, tomato and potato sailed EAST to the Old World; wheat, sugar, citrus and coffee came WEST to the Americas. Source: Wikipedia, Columbian exchange.

question: A farm cook in Gascony rubs duck legs with salt and lays them in a pot. For hours they cook low and slow, sunk below the surface, and they never sizzle or brown. What liquid covers them?
context: This is confit (from the French confire, 'to preserve'). Salted duck or goose legs poach fully submerged in rendered fat kept low - around 85C / 185F, never hot enough to fry or brown. A deep-fryer, by contrast, runs 160-230C: confit is a warm bath, not a sizzle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confit

question: A farm family with no fridge packs cooked duck legs into a crock and pours fat over them until it sets into a hard cap. In a cool cellar the legs keep for months. How does that cap stop the meat below from rotting?
answer: It seals the meat off from all air.
choices: It seals the meat off from all air.
It is salty enough to kill any germ that lands on it.
The cellar's chill keeps the meat frozen hard.
Acids in the fat slowly pickle the meat like vinegar.
context: No oxygen can reach the meat under an airtight (anaerobic) seal of grease, so it can't spoil - kept cool and dark, confit lasts up to about three months. This is the dinner-test payoff: you drown the duck in fat not for taste but for a fat lid that locks out the air. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confit

question: A Gascon cook is strict about what counts as real confit: only one part of a duck or goose will do. Give another cut, or another bird, the same slow bath in fat, and he will call the result only 'en confit,' a copy. Which part makes true confit?
context: Confit de canard (duck) and confit d'oie (goose) are always made from the legs. Gascony is 'confit country,' where cooks prize rich duck and goose fat the way an Italian prizes olive oil, spooning it over everything. Poach a chicken the same way and it's only 'poulet en confit,' not the real thing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confit

question: A whole day before the duck legs go anywhere near the fat, the cook buries them in salt and herbs. Confit keeps for months because two tricks work together, and this is the first. What does the salt do to help the meat keep?
answer: pulls the water out of the meat
choices: pulls the water out of the meat
melts down into the fat below
keeps the fat from going rancid
makes the meat swell with juice
context: The fat cap is only half the trick. Before the legs ever meet the fat, they are salted (and herbed) for about a day: the salt pulls moisture out of the meat and starts a cure that holds back bacteria. Then the slow cook in fat dries the meat further and the hardened fat seals it. Salt + fat together = meat that survives a winter without a fridge. Source: https://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/article/1073828/truc-confit-fat-fabulous-way-preserve-meat

question: Duck confit, sausage and chunks of pork all go into cassoulet, the slow-baked feast of the Languedoc. Yet the humble ingredient at its heart is far cheaper than the meat, and over hours of baking it soaks up the fat and gives the dish its body. What is cassoulet built around?
context: Cassoulet is the great bean-and-meat bake of the Languedoc: white haricot beans slow-cooked for hours with duck or goose confit, sausage and pork. The food writer Elizabeth David called it 'that sumptuous amalgamation of haricot beans, sausage, pork, mutton and preserved goose, aromatically spiced with garlic and herbs.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet

question: A cook in the Languedoc, a sunny farm region of southern France, layers beans with pork, sausage and duck confit, then bakes the dish low and slow for hours until a golden crust forms. French food lore traces the name cassoulet back centuries. What is the dish named after?
answer: the clay pot it bakes in
choices: the clay pot it bakes in
the cook who first made it
context: Cassoulet is literally named after its own dish: the cassole, a conical red-clay bowl (wide mouth, narrow base) prized for holding heat, first made in the village of Issel and still hand-made from Issel clay near Castelnaudary. Its wide top gives the bean stew the biggest surface for the prized golden crust. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassole

question: Rui Hai Liu, a food scientist at Cornell, heated tomatoes near boiling for half an hour and compared their lycopene, the red pigment the body uses to fight disease, with raw ones. What happened to it?
answer: It jumped far higher than in raw tomatoes
choices: It jumped far higher than in raw tomatoes
It barely changed from raw either way
Heat destroyed almost all of it
Raw tomatoes had far more of it
context: Food scientist Rui Hai Liu heated tomatoes to 88 C (about 190 F): the usable trans-lycopene rose 164% after 30 minutes, and the tomatoes' overall antioxidant activity climbed 62%. The result flipped the old 'raw is always healthiest' rule — cooked sauce and canned tomatoes can beat a raw slice for lycopene, because heat breaks down the tough cell structure so more of the pigment is freed. Source: Cornell Chronicle, 2002 (news.cornell.edu/stories/2002/04/cooking-tomatoes-boosts-disease-fighting-power).

question: A cook tips broccoli into a big pot at a hard boil, and it comes out with far fewer vitamins than broccoli steamed above the water. What happens to most of the missing vitamins?
answer: They dissolve into the cooking water and get drained away
choices: They dissolve into the cooking water and get drained away
They burn up completely and turn to ash
They float off into the air as steam
They soak deeper into the broccoli's core
context: Some vitamins, like vitamin C and the B vitamins, are water-soluble: they dissolve right into the cooking water, which you then pour down the drain. Hard boiling can wash out nearly all of a vegetable's vitamin C, while steaming (no direct water contact) keeps roughly 80% compared with raw. Steam it, don't drown it. Source: PMC6049644, 'Effect of different cooking methods on the content of vitamins and true retention.'

question: Crunched raw, a carrot lets the body absorb only about a tenth of its beta-carotene, the orange pigment that becomes vitamin A. Cooked, the same carrot yields roughly three-quarters. What does the heat do to free so much more of the pigment?
answer: It bursts the tough cell walls that trap the pigment inside
choices: It bursts the tough cell walls that trap the pigment inside
It creates brand-new beta-carotene out of the heat
It changes the pigment straight into vitamin A
It dries out the carrot to concentrate the pigment
context: Only about 11% of a raw carrot's beta-carotene is absorbable, versus roughly 75% from a stir-fried one. Heat ruptures the rigid plant cell walls and frees the pigment, and a little oil at the same meal boosts it further. Cooked carrots beat raw for these vitamin-A building blocks. Source: HealWithFood, 'Beta-Carotene in Carrots and How its Bioavailability is Affected by Cooking.'

question: Raw egg white plays a trick on anyone who swallows it. A protein in it, avidin, grabs a B vitamin called biotin with the strongest bond of its kind found anywhere in nature, and the vitamin slips out of the body unused. What simple step breaks avidin's grip and rescues the vitamin?
answer: Cooking the egg until it sets
choices: Cooking the egg until it sets
Eating the egg white very fresh
Separating the white from the yolk
Whisking the white into a stiff foam
context: Avidin clamps onto the B-vitamin biotin with the strongest non-covalent (non-permanent) bond known in nature. Heat above about 70 C unfolds the avidin, and by about 85 C it releases the vitamin, so cooking disarms the egg's own trap. Like the kidney bean's lectin, it is a defense that heat takes apart. Source: Avidin, Wikipedia (biotin-binding; thermal denaturation about 70-85 C).

question: A cook tips a bag of rock-hard dried beans into a bowl, covers them with plenty of cold water and leaves them for hours. What do the beans slowly do?
answer: Swell up to about double their size
choices: Swell up to about double their size
context: Dried beans are stored bone-dry and hard. Given hours in water, they drink it back up and swell to roughly twice their size, so when they finally hit the heat it can reach all the way to the center and cook them evenly instead of leaving a chalky, gritty core. Most cooks soak them at least five hours, often overnight, before the pot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bean; Food Safety News, 'How to Avoid Poisoning From Red Beans' (2021).

question: After beans soak, the water turns cloudy and a little foamy. A careful cook pours that water down the drain and boils the beans in fresh water instead. Besides being tidier, what does dumping the old soaking water wash away?
answer: Sugars that would give you gas
choices: Sugars that would give you gas
context: Beans carry a group of sugars (oligosaccharides) that humans have no enzyme to digest. Whole, they slide down to your gut, where bacteria feed on them and make gas. But those sugars dissolve in water, so as beans soak they leach out into the water; pouring off the cloudy soak water carries much of the gas away with it, and soaked-and-rinsed beans sit easier on the stomach. Source: Food Safety News, 'How to Avoid Poisoning From Red Beans' (2021); NutrientsReview on raffinose and stachyose.

question: A pot of chili gets its body from red kidney beans, yet the same beans eaten raw can make a grown adult violently sick within hours, and as few as four or five will do it. What is the raw bean carrying that does it?
answer: A natural toxin in the bean
choices: A natural toxin in the bean
context: Raw red kidney beans hold a natural toxin called phytohaemagglutinin, a type of lectin. It is the specific reason kidney beans can't be eaten raw or barely warmed: as few as four or five raw beans can bring on nausea and vomiting, then diarrhea, within one to three hours (recovery is usually quick, within a few hours more). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytohaemagglutinin; StateFoodSafety, 'Toxic Beans.'

question: Soaked overnight, dried red kidney beans go into a fresh pot of water and up to a hard, rolling boil. A poison strong enough to sicken a grown adult sounds as if it should take hours to destroy. At a full boil, how long does the toxin take to break down completely?
context: A real boil fixes it fast: 10 minutes at 100 C (212 F) completely destroys the toxin, and 30 minutes is the belt-and-suspenders recommendation. In lab units, raw red kidney beans measure up to about 70,000 toxin units; a proper boil drops that to only a few hundred. Source: Food Safety News, 'How to Avoid Poisoning From Red Beans' (2021); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytohaemagglutinin.

question: A slow cooker set to Low warms raw red kidney beans to around 80 C: hot enough for a stew, but never a true boil. That gentle heat sounds safer than no heat at all. What does it actually do to the beans' toxin?
answer: Makes them several times more toxic
choices: Makes them several times more toxic
Removes about half of the toxin
Cooks the toxin away for good
context: This is the counterintuitive part: gentle heat activates the toxin more than it destroys it. Warming raw kidney beans to about 80 C — the temperature a slow cooker on Low reaches — can make them roughly five times as toxic as raw. Half-cooking is worse than no cooking; only a genuine, hard boil makes them safe. Source: FDA Bad Bug Book (phytohaemagglutinin); StateFoodSafety, 'Toxic Beans'; University of Illinois Extension (2024).

question: Straight from a tin, red kidney beans go onto a cold salad with no cooking at all. Yet the same kind of bean, bought dried and cooked carelessly at home, can make someone sick. Why are the canned beans already safe to eat?
answer: A cannery boils them under pressure before sealing
choices: A cannery boils them under pressure before sealing
The beans slow-cook themselves in the sealed can
Vinegar in the canning liquid dissolves the toxin
Canneries use a naturally milder kind of bean
context: Canned kidney beans are safe to eat straight from the can — cold, on a salad, no cooking needed — because the cannery already boiled them under pressure before sealing the can, long before it reached your shelf. The risk is only with dried beans you cook, or undercook, yourself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_bean; StateFoodSafety, 'Toxic Beans.'

question: A wild chimp chews raw fruit, tough leaves and raw meat for about half its day; a human chews for under an hour. Richard Wrangham argues that cooking, by cutting that time so sharply, paid for one huge change in the ancestors of humans. Which?
answer: Bigger brains — the extra calories fed them
choices: Bigger brains — the extra calories fed them
Stronger jaws — grinding hard food needs muscle
Longer guts — fermenting raw fiber needs room
Sharper teeth — slicing raw meat needs blades
context: Humans spend about 4.7% of their day feeding, against the roughly 48% predicted for a primate of human size, an order of magnitude less. Humans are the outlier of the whole primate order, because their food arrives pre-broken-down. Richard Wrangham's version of the same gap: wild chimps burn 5-7 hours a day feeding, and cooking hands those hours back for something other than chewing. Organ, Nunn, Machanda & Wrangham, 'Phylogenetic rate shifts in feeding time during the evolution of Homo', PNAS (2011); Harvard Gazette, 'Big gains in better chewing' (March 2016), reporting Zink & Lieberman — https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2016/03/big-gains-in-better-chewing/

question: Rocky Balboa, the film boxer, gulps raw eggs for protein, yet volunteers in a 1998 tracer study absorbed about 91 percent of cooked egg's protein and only about half of raw egg's. As an egg white sets in a hot pan, what is the heat doing to each protein molecule?
answer: It unfolds, and the amino-acid chain stays completely intact
choices: It unfolds, and the amino-acid chain stays completely intact
It splits, and the amino-acid chain breaks into fragments
It curls tighter, and the amino-acid chain winds into a knot
It shrinks, and the amino-acid chain sheds its outer links
context: This is called denaturing, and it is not damaging: the molecule unfolds while the amino-acid chain stays completely intact. Digestive enzymes can only cut the bonds they can physically reach, so an unfolded protein is an opened parcel, not a broken one. Grokipedia, 'Cooking' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Cooking; mechanism corroborated by Evenepoel et al. 1998, Journal of Nutrition — https://jn.nutrition.org/article/S0022-3166(23)01855-2/fulltext

question: Victoria Wobber and Richard Wrangham offered captive chimpanzees carrot, sweet potato and beef, each raw or cooked. These apes have never used fire, and nobody knew which way an animal with no cooking in its past would choose. What did the chimps pick?
context: The chimps preferred cooked carrot, cooked sweet potato and cooked beef. They showed no preference at all on white potato and apple. Wrangham reads the result as a taste for cooked food that predates the control of fire — the appetite came first, the campfire second. Wobber, Hare & Wrangham, 'Great apes prefer cooked food', Journal of Human Evolution 55(2):340-348 (2008) — https://evolutionaryanthropology.duke.edu/sites/evolutionaryanthropology.duke.edu/files/site-images/Wobber%20et%20al_%202008_%20Great%20apes%20prefer%20cooked%20food(1).pdf; summarized at https://grokipedia.com/page/Richard_Wrangham

question: Volunteers ate oats, wheat, plantain, green banana and potato, first raw and then cooked, while researchers measured what their small intestines took up. Cooking raised the starch their bodies absorbed by anywhere from 28 to 109 percent. What is the heat doing to the starch itself?
answer: Bursting the starch's tight crystal packing into loose mush
choices: Bursting the starch's tight crystal packing into loose mush
Splitting the starch straight into sugar inside the pan
Burning off the fibre skin that seals each granule
Driving the water out until each granule dries and cracks
context: Gelatinization. Raw starch sits locked in tough semicrystalline granules — packed tight enough that digestive enzymes cannot get at it — and heat turns that packing into amorphous stuff the enzymes hydrolyse easily. Water goes in and the granules swell as this happens; they do not dry out. Across the five plants the median gain in net energy was 30.2%. Richard Wrangham, 'Control of Fire in the Paleolithic: Evaluating the Cooking Hypothesis', Current Anthropology 58(S16):S303-S313 (2017) — https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/692113

question: Rachel Carmody fed lab mice lean beef, raw to some and cooked to others. Over four days the mice on cooked beef ate less than those on raw, about 54 grams against 65. Then she put both groups on the scales. What did the weights show?
answer: The cooked-meat mice lost less weight
choices: The cooked-meat mice lost less weight
The raw-meat mice lost less weight
Both groups lost the same weight
Both groups gained a little weight
context: On beef, every group of mice lost weight, but cooking cut the loss; on sweet potato, the raw-fed mice lost weight while the cooked-fed mice held theirs. The cooked-meat mice ate 53.7 g against the raw group's 64.5 g and still did better: the smaller cooked meal delivered more energy than the bigger raw one. Carmody, Weintraub & Wrangham, 'Energetic consequences of thermal and nonthermal food processing', PNAS 108(48):19199-19203 (2011) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3228431/

question: Katherine Zink and Daniel Lieberman taped sensors to volunteers' jaws and fed them tough raw goat, which chewed like gum. Then they prepared the meal the Stone Age way, slicing the meat with a stone flake and pounding the plants, with no fire at all. What happened to the chewing?
answer: Both the force of each chew and the daily count fell by nearly a fifth
choices: Both the force of each chew and the daily count fell by nearly a fifth
The force of each chew fell by nearly a fifth; the daily count held
The daily count fell by nearly a fifth; the force of each chew held
Both the force of each chew and the daily count held firm
context: Nearly 20% off both the muscular effort per chew and the number of chews a day — about 2.5 million fewer chews a year, bought with a sharp flake and no fire at all. Raw unsliced meat, by contrast, is 'like chewing gum': it can be chewed for ages without breaking down. In Lieberman's reading, that is why early humans reached for a stone flake long before they reached for a hearth. Zink & Lieberman, 'Impact of meat and Lower Palaeolithic food processing techniques on chewing in humans', Nature 531:500-503 (2016) — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16990; figures via https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2016/03/big-gains-in-better-chewing/ and https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/03/160309135656.htm

question: Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler weighed guts across the primates and found that the bigger the animal, the bigger its gut, since leaves and tough raw fruit need a large fermenting tank. By that rule a 65 kg primate should carry about 1.88 kg of gut. What does a human of that weight carry?
answer: About 1.1 kg — around 60% of the prediction
choices: About 1.1 kg — around 60% of the prediction
About 1.5 kg — a little under the prediction
About 1.9 kg — right on the prediction
About 2.6 kg — well over the prediction
context: About 1.1 kg against a predicted 1.88 kg — roughly 60%, a ~40% reduction. The human gut is stunted for an ape, and it only works because human food arrives easy to digest. Aiello and Wheeler also found a hard rule running the other way: across 18 primate species relative brain size correlates negatively with relative gut size (r = -0.69, p < 0.001) — the bigger a primate's gut, the smaller its brain. The gorilla sits at the far end, eating low-quality leaves, running an enormous fermenting gut to break them down, and carrying a brain small for its body; frugivores and omnivores like the chimpanzee, living on richer food, run smaller guts and bigger brains. The human sits at the opposite extreme. Aiello & Wheeler, 'The Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis: The Brain and the Digestive System in Human and Primate Evolution', Current Anthropology 36(2):199-221 (1995) — https://web.math.princeton.edu/~sswang/literature_general_unsorted/aiello_wheeler95_curr_anthropol.pdf; summarized at https://grokipedia.com/page/expensive_tissue_hypothesis

question: German scientists checked 513 people who ate mostly raw food, by choice, for almost four years. Supermarkets sat on every corner. The men lost about 10 kg and the women about 12. A quarter of the women dropped under a normal BMI (Body Mass Index). One more effect made the team say the diet 'cannot be recommended on a long-term basis.' What was it?
answer: About 30% of the women had stopped menstruating
choices: About 30% of the women had stopped menstruating
About 30% of the women had lost bone density
About 30% of the women had developed anaemia
About 30% of the women had lost tooth enamel
context: Partial to complete amenorrhea in about 30% of the women under 45, worse in those eating over 90% raw. A body in a deep enough energy deficit shuts down reproduction — the clearest sign that raw food, even with a modern supermarket behind it, struggles to keep a human fuelled. (Scientific American's write-up says 'up to 50 percent'; that figure belongs to the strictest 100%-raw subgroup, not the study-wide rate.) Koebnick et al., 'Consequences of a Long-Term Raw Food Diet on Body Weight and Menstruation', Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism 43(2):69-79 (1999) — https://www.karger.com/Article/Pdf/12770

question: A 65 kg human carries a brain about 0.85 kg heavier than a primate that size should have, and running it costs some 9.5 extra watts. Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler added up the body's costly organs, brain, gut, heart, liver and kidneys, and set the total against what a 65 kg primate carries. What did it come to?
answer: About 4.3 kg — exactly what a primate that size carries
choices: About 4.3 kg — exactly what a primate that size carries
About 5.2 kg — a fifth over what that size predicts
About 6.1 kg — half again what that size predicts
About 3.4 kg — a fifth under what that size predicts
context: The books balance. The gut, running at 60% of its predicted size, saves almost exactly the 9.5 watts the oversized brain costs, so total expensive-organ mass in a 65 kg human stays ~4.3 kg — the same as any primate of that weight. A shrinking gut paid for a growing brain, and the bill came out even. The brain is the priciest tissue per gram: 2% of body mass, 16-20% of resting energy, burning about nine times faster than the body average (11.1 W/kg vs ~1.2 W/kg). Aiello & Wheeler, Current Anthropology 36(2):199-221 (1995) — https://web.math.princeton.edu/~sswang/literature_general_unsorted/aiello_wheeler95_curr_anthropol.pdf; figures as summarized at https://grokipedia.com/page/expensive_tissue_hypothesis

question: Richard Wrangham argues that people were cooking by about 1.8 million years ago, the time the small teeth and the big brain arrive. At Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, diggers have found the oldest firm, in-place fire yet: wood ash, burnt bone and earth cooked past 300°C. How old is it?
answer: About 1.0 million years old — 800,000 years after Wrangham's date
choices: About 1.0 million years old — 800,000 years after Wrangham's date
About 1.8 million years old — landing right on Wrangham's date
About 2.6 million years old — 800,000 years before his date
About 400,000 years old — 1.4 million years after his date
context: Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, ~1.0 million years: microscopic wood ash, burnt bone, ashed plant remains, sediments heated past 300°C. Habitual hearths only become common ~400,000-300,000 years ago, and brain expansion began ~2 million years ago — before the fire evidence. That gap is the whole argument: Wrangham inferred his early date from anatomy, not from ash, so his 1.8-million-year date is his hypothesis, not a settled fact. (The oldest direct evidence of a cooked meal is younger still — carp teeth at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel, 780,000 years ago, whose enamel crystals grew at 200-500°C.) Grokipedia, 'Control of fire by early humans' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans; Berna et al., 'Microstratigraphic evidence of in situ fire in the Acheulean strata of Wonderwerk Cave', PNAS (2012); Zohar et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2022) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-022-01910-z

question: In a mouse trial, Rachel Carmody pitted a rock against a fire. Hammering a strip of meat or mashing a root breaks food down too, with no hearth and no flame, so she fed mice pounded food, cooked food, and food both pounded and cooked. Which way did it come out?
answer: Cooking improved a pounded diet; pounding did not improve a cooked one
choices: Cooking improved a pounded diet; pounding did not improve a cooked one
Pounding improved a cooked diet; cooking did not improve a pounded one
Each improved the other; the two effects simply added together
Pounding matched cooking on the plant foods, but not on the meat
context: Fire beat muscle. Cooking improved a pounded diet (P < 0.001); pounding did not improve a cooked diet (P = 0.707). Overall, cooking mattered (P < 0.001) and pounding didn't (P = 0.138). In mice, at least — whether stone tools got to the problem first is a separate argument, and still very much live. Carmody, Weintraub & Wrangham, 'Energetic consequences of thermal and nonthermal food processing', PNAS 108(48):19199-19203 (2011) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3228431/

question: Daniel Lieberman reads the story differently from Richard Wrangham. At Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, stone tools and the bones they cut go back 2.6 million years, long before any ash yet found, and Lieberman ran the chewing tests himself. In his account, what did fire do?
answer: Fire came second, and made an already-chewable meal easier still
choices: Fire came second, and made an already-chewable meal easier still
Fire came second, and added nothing the stone flake had not done
Fire came second, and served only for warmth, never for the food
Fire came second, and only then did the teeth begin to shrink
context: Lieberman does not deny cooking helped — in his account it made chewing easier still. It just arrived second. Stone tools go back 2.6 million years, with cut-marked bones at Olduvai Gorge, comfortably before any fire evidence, and Katherine Zink and Daniel Lieberman argue that slicing meat and pounding tubers alone could explain the smaller teeth and jaws. Lieberman: 'Once you start processing it mechanically, even just slicing it, the effects on chewing performance are dramatic.' Zink & Lieberman, 'Impact of meat and Lower Palaeolithic food processing techniques on chewing in humans', Nature 531:500-503 (2016) — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16990; quote via https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/03/160309135656.htm; critique summarized at https://grokipedia.com/page/Richard_Wrangham

question: A cook in an American kitchen adds fresh cilantro leaves to a dish, then a spoon of round coriander seeds. A gardener would grin at the pair. What do the two come from, out in the garden?
choices: two different plants in the same family
a plant and its wild ancestor
context: Both come from Coriandrum sativum -- a single herb. In American kitchens 'cilantro' means the fresh leaf and 'coriander' means the dried seed, but it's all one plant (British cooks even call the leaf 'coriander' too). Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriander'.

question: A fresh cilantro leaf tastes bright and citrusy, almost like lime. A cook toasts and crushes a handful of dried round coriander seeds from the spice jar. What do those seeds taste like?
context: One plant, two completely different flavors. The fresh leaf's bright lemon-lime punch comes from aldehyde compounds; the dried seed's warm, nutty, orange-ish note comes from a compound called linalool. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriander'.

question: A girl who hates fresh cilantro is not just being fussy: a quirk in her genes, one that runs in families, changes how the leaf tastes to her. What does it taste like to her?
context: It's a real quirk of smell genes, not fussiness. A smell-receptor gene (OR6A2) is finely tuned to the aldehyde chemicals that give the leaf its aroma -- the same class found in soaps and even stinkbugs -- so some people smell the 'soapy' side strongly. It runs in families (identical twins agree about cilantro roughly 80% of the time, fraternal twins about 50%) and varies by ancestry (about 21% of East Asians and 17% of Europeans dislike it, down to just 3-7% of South Asian, Hispanic and Middle Eastern people). It's a small, real effect -- a tendency, not destiny. Sources: Wikipedia, 'OR6A2' and 'Coriander'; Eriksson et al., Flavour, 2012.

question: Small, ridged, yellow-brown seeds about the size of a rice grain lie heaped on a table at an Indian market. A cook toasts them dry in a hot pan, then grinds them into a warm, earthy powder, the top flavor of American chili powder and a backbone of garam masala and most curry blends. Which spice is it?
context: It's cumin (Cuminum cyminum). The ancient Egyptians prized it as both a spice and a preservative used in mummification. In North Indian and Pakistani cooking it's paired with coriander seed in a blend literally called 'dhana jeera' -- dhana (coriander) plus jeera (cumin). Source: Wikipedia, 'Cumin'.

question: Cooks in ancient Greece who bruised the fresh green leaves of coriander caught a smell they found downright fetid, like a bug squashed underfoot. The herb's Greek name, koriandron, may come from koris, their word for a tiny household pest. Which pest?
context: The word 'coriander' traces back to the Ancient Greek 'koriandron', which may be rooted in 'koris' -- meaning 'bedbug'. Bruised coriander leaves were thought to give off a buggy, fetid smell, so the bug link was baked into the herb's name thousands of years ago. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriander'.  (Legend.)

question: Two seeds in a spice pantry look almost like twins, small, ridged and boat-shaped, so cooks grab the wrong jar constantly. One is earthy, warm cumin, a workhorse of Indian curry blends. Its lookalike has a sharper bite and tastes distinctly of rye bread. Which seed is the cumin impostor?
context: It's caraway (Carum carvi) -- the seed you taste in seeded rye bread, its sharp flavor coming mostly from an oil called carvone. Cumin and caraway look so alike that even their names got tangled: caraway's name traces back through Latin cuminum and Greek karon, words that originally meant cumin. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Caraway' and 'Cumin'.

question: A botanist lays the seeds of coriander, dill and fennel beside their seed-spice cousins, and few would guess they are kin: all belong to a single big plant family, the Apiaceae. Three everyday vegetables from the produce aisle belong to that family too. Which trio?
context: They're all umbellifers -- the family Apiaceae (also called Umbelliferae) -- and carrots, celery and parsley are cousins of every one of those seed-spices. The family is named for its flowers: tiny blossoms sit on spokes that fan out from a single point like a little umbrella, a cluster called an 'umbel' (from Latin umbella, 'parasol' or 'sunshade'). Source: Wikipedia, 'Apiaceae'.

question: A heap of couscous on a Moroccan plate looks like tiny round seeds picked straight from a field. They are not. Each bead was rolled by hand from the flour of one crop and then dried hard. Which crop?
context: It's wheat. Couscous is basically the world's tiniest pasta — not a seed that grew in a field, but wheat flour rolled into little balls and dried, made from the very same wheat as dried Italian pasta. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couscous; bobsredmill.com/articles/what-is-couscous-made-of

question: At a flour mill in Tunisia, one grain comes out gritty and gold, not soft and white like bread flour. That coarse flour is semolina, and every bead of couscous from Morocco to Tunisia is rolled from it. Which grain is semolina milled from?
context: Durum wheat — 'durum' is Latin for 'hard,' the root of 'durable' — is the hardest wheat grown. Its coarse golden flour is called semolina, and that same durum semolina is rolled into couscous and pressed into dried Italian pasta. Sources: bobsredmill.com/articles/what-is-couscous-made-of; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couscous

question: An Algerian grandmother sits with a wide wooden bowl of semolina and sprinkles a little water over it. Then she repeats one steady motion with the damp flour, over and over, until it has become thousands of tiny, even beads of couscous. What is she doing with her hands?
context: She rubs handfuls of moist semolina between her palms until they roll into little pellets, then sifts them so the too-small bits fall through to be rolled again — until every grain is an even bead. The skill passes down by watching and imitating. Sources: cookswithoutborders.com/new-story/couscous-celebration; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couscous

question: Cookbook writers working in Arabic in the 13th century set down some of the oldest couscous recipes known, and they already wrote of it as an everyday dish. They lived in a shining medieval land of scholars, poets and gardens. Where were those cookbooks written?
context: Some of the earliest known couscous recipes appear in 13th-century Arabic cookbooks of al-Andalus — Muslim-ruled Spain — over 700 years ago, showing the dish was already settled and recorded by then. Cooking tools found in older North African tombs hint it may be far older still. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couscous; webfoodculture.com/couscous-history-information-interesting-facts

question: A pastry cook whisks heavy cream into stiff, glossy peaks, then whisks skim milk the same way; it froths for a second, then flops back flat. What does the cream have plenty of that skim milk lacks?
context: Whipped cream is a foam: beating drives thousands of tiny air bubbles into the cream, and the fat globules crowd around each bubble and cling together into a soft scaffold that holds the shape — which is why cream stands in peaks but milk just splashes. It only works with high-fat cream: 'whipping cream' is 30-36% milk fat and 'heavy cream' is 36% or more, while skim milk and half-and-half simply don't have enough fat to build the foam. Sources: scienceinsights.org/how-does-whipped-cream-work; healthline.com heavy-cream guide.

question: Halfway through whipping cream for a dessert, a cook reaches stiff peaks and keeps going, hoping for something fluffier. Instead the smooth white foam turns gritty and breaks into pale yellow lumps in a thin, watery liquid. What has she started making by accident?
context: Whip too far and the fat globules stop half-joining and clump together completely, so the foam collapses. The pale lumps are butterfat and the watery liquid is buttermilk — you've begun the very same process that turns cream into butter. Source: kingarthurbaking.com, 'How to fix (or avoid) over-whipped cream.'

question: Sweetened cream left alone in the freezer sets into a hard, icy block that has to be chipped with a spoon. In an ice cream maker, the very same mix turns smooth and scoopable. What is the machine doing to it the whole time it freezes?
context: The churning never lets the ice sit still: a blade called the dasher scrapes freezing crystals off the cold barrel wall and smashes them, so the water sets into countless tiny crystals instead of a few big ones. Crystals around 10-20 micrometres across feel silky on the tongue; let them grow larger and you taste them as gritty or icy. Frozen without churning, you'd get one solid, crunchy brick. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ice cream'; icecreamscience.com, ice-crystals-in-ice-cream.

question: A tray of water in the freezer turns into rock-hard ice, yet a tub of ice cream in the same freezer never sets fully solid, and a scoop still slides through it. Ice cream is mostly water too, and the dissolved sugar is the reason. What does the sugar do to that water?
answer: lowers the temperature at which it freezes
choices: lowers the temperature at which it freezes
gives off heat as it dissolves
coats the ice in a syrup shell
soaks up the water like a sponge
context: This is called freezing-point depression: sugar dissolved in the water lowers its freezing point, so at freezer temperature not all of the water turns to ice — some stays as a thick, unfrozen syrup. That leftover liquid is exactly what lets you push a scoop through ice cream instead of chipping at a rock. Source: foodcrumbles.com, 'The secret of ice cream: freezing point depression.'

question: An industrial ice cream factory takes one gallon of creamy mix and churns out two full gallons of finished ice cream — doubling it in the machine without stirring in a single extra drop of cream, milk, or sugar. Ice cream makers call this trick 'overrun.' What did the factory pump into the mix to make it fill twice as many tubs?
context: The whipped-in air is called 'overrun.' Cheap economy brands (think Breyers or store brands) run near 90-100% overrun — meaning roughly half of what's in the tub is air — while premium pints like Ben & Jerry's and Haagen-Dazs pack in far less air (about 20-30% overrun) plus more butterfat, so a premium pint feels noticeably heavier and denser in your hand. Sources: dreamscoops.com, air-in-ice-cream; thekitchn.com on ice-cream overrun.

question: A crème brûlée sits in front of a first-time diner, and she asks how to start. In the classic ritual, the part that makes this dessert fun, what does she do first?
answer: Crack through the hard, glassy top
choices: Crack through the hard, glassy top
Stir it into a smooth pudding
Peel the thin skin off the top
context: Creme brulee's whole signature is that thin, glassy sugar crust -- the delicate, sharp 'snap' as your spoon breaks through the hardened top is the point of the dessert. Source: Wikipedia, 'Creme brulee'; Saveur, 'Blow Hard.'

question: Moments before serving a crème brûlée, or 'burnt cream,' a bistro cook scatters one ingredient over the custard and torches it brown and glassy. Only that part is truly burnt. Which ingredient?
context: 'Creme brulee' is French for 'burnt cream' -- but the 'burnt' is the caramelized sugar crust torched on top, not the custard, which stays pale and smooth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Creme brulee.'

question: A pastry cook gently heats cream and vanilla with one more ingredient, and it sets into the custard under a crème brûlée's crackly top, so silky it trembles when the dish is tapped. Which ingredient sets it?
context: Creme brulee's custard is cream set with egg yolks, sugar, and vanilla -- and modern versions skip flour entirely, which is what makes it silky and wobbly instead of firm like a pie. The yolks also carry natural emulsifiers that keep the cream and egg smooth instead of separating. Source: Wikipedia, 'Creme brulee' and 'Custard.'

question: Long before kitchen blowtorches, cooks browned the top of a burnt-cream custard with a red-hot iron disk on a long handle, glowing straight from the fire. They named this fiery tool after a creature that old legends claimed could live inside fire and cross through flames unharmed. Which creature?
context: The classic tool for burning the top is a 'salamander' -- a red-hot iron disk on a long handle, swung from the fire onto the sugar. It's named after the mythical lizard people once believed could live in fire (a legend). Source: Saveur, 'Blow Hard.'

question: Crème brûlée custards go into an oven that can ruin them: a few degrees too hot, and the eggs seize into grainy, scrambled curds instead of a smooth, glossy gel. Pastry cooks have one classic trick to shield the custards from the oven's fierce heat. What is the trick?
answer: set the ramekins in a pan of hot water
choices: set the ramekins in a pan of hot water
cover each ramekin with a tight foil lid
beat a spoon of flour into the custard
turn the oven to its lowest setting
context: Custards bake in a water bath -- a bain-marie, where the ramekins sit in a pan of hot water -- so the gentle, even heat sets the eggs into a smooth gel instead of scrambling them. Custard is fussy: it starts setting around 70C and turns grainy if it climbs past about 80C, so the surrounding water slows the heat down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Custard.'

question: A cook makes crème brûlée and its cousin crème caramel, or flan, from the very same silky egg custard. The brûlée is capped with a hard, scorched crust, while the flan reaches the table under a soft caramel sauce running down its sides. How does the flan get its caramel?
answer: Caramel is poured under the custard, then the flan is turned upside down.
choices: Caramel is poured under the custard, then the flan is turned upside down.
Caramel is drizzled onto the custard after the baked flan has cooled.
Caramel is whisked into the custard, then floats up while it bakes.
Caramel is torched onto the custard, then melts into a soft sauce.
context: Creme brulee's cousin creme caramel (flan) is baked in a plain mold with liquid caramel poured into the bottom first and the custard on top; then the whole thing is turned out upside down ('renversee') so the caramel runs down over it as a soft sauce -- the exact opposite of creme brulee's hard caramel torched crisp on top and cracked with a spoon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Creme caramel.'

question: A fresh croissant shatters into thin, crackly flakes at the first bite, and no special flour made them. What does the baker do to the dough, over and over, to build those flakes?
context: A croissant is a laminated dough: the baker folds sheets of cold butter into the dough over and over, building alternating paper-thin layers of dough and butter. Those layers ARE the pastry -- no special flour needed. Source: King Arthur Baking, 'When less is more: Why fewer folds make a better croissant.'

question: A French pastry cook stacks crisp sheets of puff pastry with vanilla cream between them and glazes the top. The dessert's name, mille-feuille, describes all those layers. What does it mean in English?
context: 'Mille-feuille' means 'a thousand leaves' (feuille = leaf or sheet) -- the name is the lamination trick in three words. North Americans call it a Napoleon; the British call it a vanilla or custard slice; it's the same crisp puff-pastry stack. Source: Wikipedia 'Mille-feuille.'

question: A baker building a croissant's layers rolls out the dough and makes the same fold again and again, one that bakers compare to folding a common everyday object. What is that fold like?
answer: folded in thirds, like a business letter
choices: folded in thirds, like a business letter
folded in half, like a book
folded back and forth, like an accordion fan
context: Each 'turn' is a letter fold -- folding the dough in thirds, like a letter tucked into a business envelope. King Arthur notes that a single letter fold makes almost three times as many layers as the dough started with, so just a few folds explode into dozens of paper-thin sheets. Source: King Arthur Baking, 'When less is more.'

question: A French baker starts a batch of croissants with the step she calls the lock-in, the first move toward dozens of paper-thin sheets of butter in every pastry. How does the butter go into the dough at that first step?
answer: as one big cold slab, wrapped up in the dough
choices: as one big cold slab, wrapped up in the dough
as a thin layer smeared over the rolled-out dough
as small cold cubes worked into the dough
as warm melted butter brushed across the dough
context: Lamination begins by locking one flat slab of cold butter inside a sheet of dough -- bakers call it the 'lock-in' -- then rolling it flat and folding, spreading that single block into ever-thinner alternating sheets with each turn. One slab becomes dozens of layers. Source: The Culinary Pro, 'Laminated Dough.'

question: A tray of croissants goes into a hot oven, each one layered with thin sheets of butter. Butter is not pure fat: about a sixth of every stick is water, and that hidden water gives the pastry its whole flaky character. What does the water do when the heat hits it?
answer: flashes to steam and forces the layers apart
choices: flashes to steam and forces the layers apart
quietly soaks into the dough and vanishes
bubbles up and browns the crust golden
boils off and leaves the pastry tough
context: Butter is only about 14-18% water. In the oven that trapped water flashes to steam and pries the alternating butter-and-dough layers apart into airy pockets -- that tiny bit of water doing the lifting is the whole flake. Source: voilachef.com 'Croissant lamination' and dessert-recipes.com lamination science.

question: Between folds, a croissant baker keeps sliding her dough back into the fridge so the butter stays cool and clay-like, never soft. A rushed beginner lets his butter warm up and go soft as he works. What happens when his croissants bake?
answer: the butter melts in, the layers merge, and it bakes dense and greasy
choices: the butter melts in, the layers merge, and it bakes dense and greasy
the dough stops rising and bakes out flat as a cracker
the pastry turns sour and tastes sharply of fermentation
the crust browns too fast while the center stays raw and doughy
context: The butter block must stay cold and clay-like -- bendable but not melting. If it warms and soaks into the dough, the separate layers merge and the croissant bakes dense and greasy instead of flaky. (Too cold, and the butter shatters into lumps; bakers aim for the in-between.) Source: Brod & Taylor 'How To Level Up Your Lamination.'

question: Croissants and puff pastry come out of the same French bakery, both built from thin layers. A croissant bakes soft and springy inside; puff pastry bakes into crisp flakes all through. What does croissant dough rise with that puff pastry never uses?
answer: Yeast, the way bread dough does
choices: Yeast, the way bread dough does
Baking soda, the way soda bread does
Baking powder, the way a scone does
Egg whites, the way a soufflé does
context: Viennoiserie means 'things in the style of Vienna': the yeast-raised, butter-rich family of croissants and pain au chocolat that sits between bread and pastry. Puff pastry is laminated the same way but has no yeast at all; it rises only on the steam from the butter's water. A croissant gets a double lift, from yeast and from its laminated butter. The phrase 'patisseries viennoises' first appeared in print in an 1877 Alphonse Daudet novel. Source: Wikipedia, 'Viennoiserie'; Wikipedia, 'Puff pastry.'

question: A Paris bakery of the late 1830s sold a crescent-shaped roll called the kipferl, and French bakers copied it; the croissant grew out of that roll. The kipferl had come to Paris from another European country. Which country was it?
context: The croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl. An Austrian officer, August Zang, opened the Boulangerie Viennoise at 92 rue de Richelieu in Paris in 1838-39, selling kipferl and Vienna loaves; French bakers copied him. The buttery LAMINATED croissant of today is an early-1900s French refinement. Source: Wikipedia 'Croissant.'

question: Alfred Gottschalk, a twentieth-century writer, spread a favorite tale: that Viennese bakers invented the croissant in 1683, shaped like the Ottoman crescent, to celebrate the city's victory over the invading Ottoman army. Historians call it a legend. What hard evidence sinks it?
answer: crescent rolls were already eaten in Vienna centuries before 1683
choices: crescent rolls were already eaten in Vienna centuries before 1683
the famous 1683 battle was really fought far from Vienna
no bakery existed anywhere in Vienna until after 1700
wheat flour didn't reach Austria until long after that
context: These beloved origin tales -- that the croissant was shaped like the Ottoman crescent flag to celebrate Vienna's 1683 victory over the Turks, or that Marie Antoinette carried it from Austria -- are legends with no contemporary sources, popularized by 20th-century writer Alfred Gottschalk. A crescent roll called 'chipfen' was recorded in Vienna as far back as 1227, centuries before 1683 -- so the pastry is far older than the battle it supposedly celebrates. Source: Wikipedia 'Croissant' and 'Kipferl.'

question: A cook slices raw chicken on a wooden board and, without washing it, chops lettuce for a salad there. Both now carry the bacteria, but the chicken is bound for a hot pan. Why is the salad the dangerous one?
answer: The salad is never cooked, so no heat step kills its germs.
choices: The salad is never cooked, so no heat step kills its germs.
Lettuce is porous and soaks up far more bacteria than meat.
The germs die on warm meat but thrive on cold vegetables.
Dressing feeds the germs, so the salad's bacteria multiply.
context: Cooked chicken is safe because heat kills the germs — but a raw salad gets no such 'kill step,' so any bacteria the knife carried over ride straight to your plate. That's why the FDA's 'Separate' rule says raw meat and ready-to-eat foods must never share a board or knife. Source: FDA / FoodSafety.gov, 'Four Steps to Food Safety' — Separate (foodsafety.gov/keep-food-safe/4-steps-to-food-safety).

question: A shopper at the checkout reaches for her reusable bags, with raw chicken, ground beef, apples and lettuce to pack. Germs from raw meat can spread even here. How should she split the groceries?
answer: Bag the raw meats on their own, away from the fruit and lettuce.
choices: Bag the raw meats on their own, away from the fruit and lettuce.
Bag everything cold together so the meat keeps the produce chilled.
Bag the heaviest packages alone so they don't crush the lettuce.
Bag the meat with the apples but keep the lettuce on its own.
context: Raw meat, poultry, and seafood leak juices, and those juices are the carrier — so the separation has to start in the cart and continue in the fridge, not just at the cutting board. Source: USDA, 'Check Your Steps! SEPARATE Raw Meats from Other Foods' (usda.gov/about-usda/news/blog/check-your-steps-separate-raw-meats-other-foods).

question: A line cook in a busy restaurant reaches for a board to chop salad, and the kitchen's one simple system makes it nearly impossible for her to grab the board that just held raw chicken. What is that system?
answer: A set of boards color-coded so each food type gets its own.
choices: A set of boards color-coded so each food type gets its own.
A dishwasher that sterilizes every board between tasks.
A rule that only the head chef may cut any raw meat.
A habit of always chopping the vegetables before the meat.
context: Many pro kitchens use a color code so raw and ready-to-eat foods never touch the same surface: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, green for fruits and vegetables, blue for raw fish and seafood, white for dairy. Source: FoodDocs cutting-board color chart; Grokipedia, 'Cutting board'.

question: Loading the fridge, a cook holds a plate of raw pork chops and a bowl of cut melon that will be eaten just as it is. To be sure the pork can never contaminate the melon, where should the pork go?
answer: The shelf below the melon, in a sealed dish.
choices: The shelf below the melon, in a sealed dish.
The shelf above the melon, so cold air sinks onto it.
The same shelf, pushed to the far opposite side.
The door shelf, kept well away from the melon.
context: Gravity does the damage: juices drip down, so raw meat belongs on the bottom shelf in a sealed dish, with ready-to-eat foods like salad and melon up top where nothing can drip on them. Source: High Speed Training, 'Storing Food on Fridge Shelves'; NY DMNA, 'Preventing Cross-Contamination During Storage'.

question: In a restaurant's walk-in fridge, cooks stack raw meats top to bottom by the temperature each must reach to be safe. The one needing the highest goes on the very bottom shelf, so any drips fall on meats that will be cooked hotter still. Which meat goes lowest?
context: Pros stack the fridge top to bottom by cooking temperature: ready-to-eat on top, then whole fish, then whole beef and pork, then ground meat, with raw poultry at the very bottom. Poultry needs the highest cooking temperature, so any drip lands on food that will get even hotter. Source: High Speed Training, 'Storing Food on Fridge Shelves'; StateFoodSafety fridge storage guide.

question: Researchers at Furtwangen University in Germany swabbed one everyday kitchen item in 2017 and turned up 362 different species of bacteria, up to 54 billion cells packed into a single cubic centimeter, as dense as human waste. Which kitchen item was it?
context: A 2017 German study (Cardinale et al., Scientific Reports) found 362 bacterial species in used kitchen sponges at densities up to 54 billion cells per cubic centimeter — comparable to human feces. The sponge is a bacterial hotel because it's damp, warm, and packed with food bits, and 5 of the 10 most common species had 'pathogenic potential.' Source: Cardinale et al. 2017, Scientific Reports (nature.com/articles/s41598-017-06055-9); Forbes coverage.

question: Out in the backyard, a cook carries raw burger patties to the grill on a big platter, cooks them through, then reaches to pile the finished burgers back onto that same platter. Another, more careful cook stops his hand: it is a classic cross-contamination mistake. What is the fix?
answer: Grab a fresh, clean platter for the cooked burgers.
choices: Grab a fresh, clean platter for the cooked burgers.
Wipe the platter with a paper napkin before reloading.
Let the burgers rest a minute before setting them down.
Tip the leftover juices off the platter, then reload.
context: The raw patties leave bacteria-laden juices on the platter, and putting cooked food back on it re-contaminates the meat — so the USDA's rule is simple: never return cooked food to a plate that held raw meat or poultry. Grab a clean one. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Grilling and Food Safety' (fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/grilling-and-food-safety).

question: Every day a cook rinses and microwaves her kitchen sponge, sure she is keeping it free of germs. In 2017, researchers at Furtwangen University in Germany compared sponges their owners cleaned regularly with sponges nobody had ever cleaned. What did they find in the cleaned ones?
answer: Just as many bacteria, and the survivors were even tougher.
choices: Just as many bacteria, and the survivors were even tougher.
Far fewer bacteria, proving regular cleaning really works.
Fewer germs at first, but they returned within a few hours.
The same germs, but too weak to make anyone sick.
context: The 2017 study found sponges people said they cleaned regularly had no fewer bacteria than dirty ones — and cleaning can actually select for tougher, more pathogenic germs. The real fixes: microwave a wet sponge, or just replace it about weekly. Wiping counters with an old sponge only smears germs around. Source: Cardinale et al. 2017, Scientific Reports; metagenomic microwave study, PMC7284620.

question: Raw chicken has soaked for hours in a garlicky marinade, and the cook would love to brush the same sauce over the meat as it finishes on the grill. Straight from the bowl, it could make everyone sick. How can the used marinade be made safe to baste with?
answer: Bring it to a rolling boil for a few minutes first.
choices: Bring it to a rolling boil for a few minutes first.
Brush it on early so the grill's heat burns it clean.
Stir in extra vinegar to kill off the bacteria.
Chill it in the fridge for an hour before basting.
context: Once a marinade has soaked raw meat, it's full of raw-meat bacteria and can't go on as a sauce. Two safe fixes: set aside a clean portion before it ever touches the meat, or bring the used marinade to a boil for a few minutes to kill the bacteria before basting or serving. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Grilling and Food Safety'.

question: A diner pulls meat from a lobster's tail. Her own skeleton sits deep inside her, under muscle and skin. On a lobster, crab or shrimp, what is the hard frame that holds the whole body up?
answer: Its shell, worn outside like armor.
choices: Its shell, worn outside like armor.
A stiff spine buried along its tail.
A ring of little bones around its gut.
A cage of ribs just under the surface.
context: Shrimp, prawns, crabs, lobsters and crayfish are 'decapods' — crustaceans that wear their skeleton on the OUTSIDE as a hard shell (an exoskeleton). Instead of bones inside like a human's, the shell is both armor and frame, which is why eating them means cracking and peeling to reach the muscle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapoda

question: A cook following a shrimp recipe is told to 'devein' each one, pulling out the dark line that runs down its back. Despite the name, the line is no vein or blood vessel at all. What is that dark line really?
answer: The shrimp's gut — the intestine that carries waste.
choices: The shrimp's gut — the intestine that carries waste.
A nerve cord running down to its tail.
A thin muscle it used to curl its body.
A strand of dark pigment from the shell.
context: The dark 'vein' cooks remove is the shrimp's digestive tract — its intestine. It is taken out because it can be gritty and slightly bitter, NOT because it is dangerous: cooking kills any bacteria and eating it does no harm. Source: biologyinsights.com, 'The Shrimp Gut: The Science Behind the Black Vein'

question: Every shrimp, prawn, lobster, crayfish and crab walks on ten legs, so biologists call them decapods, Greek for 'ten feet.' Of their nearly 15,000 species, one of those five kinds makes up almost half. Which one?
context: 'Decapod' is Greek for 'ten feet' — the ten walking legs shrimp, crabs and lobsters share. There are nearly 15,000 decapod species, and crabs alone make up almost half of them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapoda

question: A lobster crawling over the cold Atlantic floor off New England spots a hungry seal. Its long, muscular tail, the sweet meat diners pay top dollar for, is also its way to escape. What does the lobster do with it?
answer: Snaps it under and shoots backward through the water.
choices: Snaps it under and shoots backward through the water.
Slaps it flat on the seabed to bury itself in sand.
Waves it gently to steer as it strolls away.
Puffs it up with water to look too big to eat.
context: A lobster flees with a 'tail-flip': it contracts the muscles on the underside of its abdomen to curl the fan-shaped tail and shoot backward, away from danger. That hard-working muscle is exactly the firm, sweet meat diners prize. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caridoid_escape_reaction

question: After storms in colonial New England, lobsters piled up knee-deep on the beaches, by early accounts, and nobody wanted them. Lobster was cheap 'poor man's food,' fed to servants and apprentices and used as bait. What did farmers do with all that extra lobster?
answer: Spread it on their fields as crop fertilizer.
choices: Spread it on their fields as crop fertilizer.
Boiled it down into lamp oil for lanterns.
Dried it into bricks to build sea walls.
Fed it to prize horses before races.
context: Early New England accounts say lobster washed ashore in piles up to two feet high and was disdained as food for servants, apprentices and children, used as bait, and even spread on fields as fertilizer. It is widely-told history — colorful and broadly true about lobster's low status. Source: history.com, 'A Taste of Lobster History'  (Legend.)

question: Sandy Oliver, a food historian, went looking for the colonial prisoners said to have revolted over too many lobster dinners. She found no such prisoners in the records, only a tale from the 1900s, and the earliest 1800s version of the complaint was about a different cheap food. Which food?
context: The 'prisoners revolted over too much lobster' story is largely folklore: food historian Sandy Oliver found NO colonial records of prisoners eating lobster, the tale only surfaces in the 1900s, and the earliest 1800s version was about SALMON, not lobster. Lobster genuinely WAS cheap and low-status — but the prison detail is a later exaggeration. Source: boston.com/news/wickedpedia (food historian Sandy Oliver)  (Legend.)

question: In a good fish market, the fillets sit on ice, but the lobsters swim in tanks and the shrimp keep their heads on, packed in ice. The moment a crustacean dies, its meat spoils far faster than a fish fillet. What is it about a shrimp's or lobster's body that ruins the meat so quickly?
answer: Its own gut enzymes leak out and digest its muscle.
choices: Its own gut enzymes leak out and digest its muscle.
Its blood turns to a bitter green jelly.
The shell seals in heat and cooks it from within.
Salt from the seawater draws all the moisture out.
context: Once a crustacean dies, powerful digestive enzymes stored in a gland (the hepatopancreas) leak out and begin digesting the animal's OWN muscle — a process called autolysis — turning firm, sweet meat mushy within minutes. Fast-multiplying gut and surface bacteria (lobsters carry Vibrio from the seafloor) speed the spoilage. That is why markets keep lobster alive in tanks and sell shrimp head-on and iced: the animal is kept alive right up until it is cooked. Source: globalseafood.org, 'Enzymes in Seafood'

question: A farm family slaughters a pig in late autumn, long before refrigerators, and the meat must last through winter and spring. For most of history, what was the main way people kept meat from rotting?
choices: Keeping it in a cold cellar
context: Salt-curing was the main way to preserve meat for most of history, and it stayed the primary method right up to the late 1800s, when mechanical refrigeration finally replaced it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curing_(food_preservation)

question: Sailors aboard Moshulu, a Finnish tall ship, were still eating the old seafarers' ration in 1938, on grain runs of over 100 days from Australia to Europe. Besides rock-hard biscuit, what preserved meat filled their wooden barrels?
context: Salt beef and salt pork in barrels, eaten with hard ship's biscuit, were the classic sea ration that kept crews — famously Britain's Royal Navy — fed on voyages lasting months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt-cured_meat

question: A cook slices salty pink corned beef for a Saint Patrick's Day dinner, yet there is no corn in it. In older English a 'corn' was any small grain or hard pellet, like a 'corn' of gunpowder. What were the corns packed onto the beef?
context: In older English, 'corn' meant any small grain or pellet. Corned beef is named for the coarse grains of salt rubbed into the meat to keep it from spoiling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt-cured_meat

question: Sailors and farmers once packed hams, bacon and whole fish in heavy salt to last through long voyages and winters. Salt is no poison, yet no rotting bacteria grow inside a heavily salted ham. How does plain salt stop the microbes from ruining the meat?
answer: It draws the water out of them until they dry up
choices: It draws the water out of them until they dry up
It heats them until their insides cook
It seals them in a hard shell they cannot break
It turns the meat too acidic for them to live
context: This is osmosis: the concentrated salt pulls water out of both the meat and any microbe cells, so bacteria dry out and cannot grow — salt starves them of water rather than poisoning them. A salt concentration near 20% reliably stops unwanted bacteria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt-cured_meat

question: A curer's salt stops almost every spoilage microbe, but one tiny killer, Clostridium botulinum, shrugs it off; it grows deep inside sealed sausages and hams, and its toxin causes botulism. What second salt does the curer add to block it?
context: The second salt is nitrite. Historically it came from saltpeter (potassium nitrate), which bacteria in the cure break down into nitrite. Nitrite blocks Clostridium botulinum, the microbe behind botulism. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrite

question: A butcher curing bacon adds only a pinch of the second salt that blocks botulism, because too much of it would poison the eater. He buys it ready-mixed with plain salt as 'pink curing salt,' which its makers color a bright pink on purpose. Why do they dye it?
answer: So cooks never confuse it with ordinary salt
choices: So cooks never confuse it with ordinary salt
So the cured meat turns a deeper pink
So cooks can see when it has dissolved
So buyers can tell fresh batches from old
context: Pink curing salt (Prague Powder #1) is only about 6.25% sodium nitrite blended into 93.75% ordinary salt. A little nitrite cures meat safely, but too much is toxic — so it is dyed pink as a warning not to grab it like table salt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curing_salt

question: A beef roast turns gray-brown all the way through in the oven, yet a slice of ham, a grilled hot dog or a crisp rasher of bacon stays bright pink even when fully cooked. The trick comes from the same small addition the curer made to block botulism. What keeps cured meat pink?
answer: The nitrite locks the meat's own pigment as pink
choices: The nitrite locks the meat's own pigment as pink
The pink curing salt dyes the meat as it cooks
The heavy salt bleaches out the meat's gray tones
The long curing seals red blood inside the meat
context: Nitrite releases nitric oxide, which binds the meat's own pigment (myoglobin) into bright-red nitrosomyoglobin; cooking sets it into stable pink nitrosohemochrome. The pink is the meat's own locked-in pigment — not added dye or blood. Color-fixing is the second job nitrite does, alongside blocking botulism. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrite

question: In the hills around Parma in northern Italy, a whole raw pork leg becomes prosciutto: silky, ruby-pink slices that a diner eats without ever cooking them. Each leg hangs for more than a year before anyone slices it. What two simple things make the raw ham safe to eat?
answer: Salt and months of cool air
choices: Salt and months of cool air
context: Prosciutto crudo ('crudo' means raw) is never cooked. Parma ham hangs in cool air for at least 14 months — up to 3 years — using only sea salt; the protected recipe forbids even nitrites. Salt plus long, slow drying pull the water so low that nothing can grow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosciutto

question: An inspector in the town of Langhirano, near Parma, walks the rows of hanging hams before any may wear the five-pointed Ducal Crown. He pierces each ham in several places with a slender needle, then sniffs the needle to check that the ham has cured cleanly. What is that needle made of?
context: The inspector's needle is carved from horse bone. Each ham is pierced in several places and smelled; those that pass are branded with the five-point Ducal Crown of Parma, while the rest are sold as ordinary ham. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosciutto

question: An Indian home cook asked for 'curry' would look puzzled: India has no single dish of that name. English speakers in the 1600s borrowed the word from Tamil, a language of southern India, where kari had a simpler, plainer meaning. What did kari mean?
answer: A spiced sauce eaten over rice
choices: A spiced sauce eaten over rice
A rice dish steamed in banana leaf
A blend of dried yellow spices
A clay pot for cooking stews
context: 'Kari' (kaṟi) is a Tamil word for a spiced sauce or relish of meat, fish, or vegetables eaten over boiled rice — one kind of dish, not a whole food category. British colonizers stretched it into the catch-all English word 'curry.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Curry.'

question: A small tin of bright yellow curry powder, one blend for everything from chicken to rice, sits in many Western pantries but in no traditional Indian kitchen. The British invented it and sold it in London by the late 1700s. What job was it made to do?
answer: Let cooks fake Indian flavor without fresh spices
