context: Black pepper is the dried fruit — botanically a drupe — of Piper nigrum, a tropical woody vine that climbs trees and poles up to about 4 m (13 ft). Each peppercorn is one shrivelled little berry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_pepper

question: In the rainforests of southern Mexico, where the vanilla vine first grew wild, a tiny native insect pollinates each vanilla flower. Move the vine anywhere else and the insect stays home. How does every vanilla pod grown outside Mexico get pollinated?
answer: By hand, one flower at a time
choices: By hand, one flower at a time
By bees shipped in from Mexico
By the wind carrying its pollen
By spraying the fields with pollen
context: Vanilla is native to Mexico, where a native insect pollinates its flowers. Grown anywhere else, the orchid must be pollinated entirely by hand, because its natural pollinator doesn't live outside its home range — which makes vanilla one of the most labour-intensive spices in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla

question: Vanilla vines on Réunion, an island of French sugar plantations, would not fruit because their pollinator from Mexico was missing. In 1841 Edmond Albius solved what trained botanists could not, with a sliver of bamboo and a flick of his thumb, and growers worldwide still use his method. What did he do to each flower?
answer: Lifted the flap between its male and female parts
choices: Lifted the flap between its male and female parts
Brushed pollen onto it from a small glass jar
Sliced it open to scrape out the ripe seeds
Tied its petals shut around a trapped insect
context: Edmond Albius lifted the rostellum — the flap separating the flower's male and female parts — with a thin sliver of bamboo and pressed them together with his thumb. A vanilla flower opens for only one morning and must be pollinated that day, so the work is demanding; his exact 1841 method is still used worldwide, including on Madagascar, which now grows most of the world's vanilla. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Albius; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla

question: Edmond Albius saw his bamboo-sliver trick for pollinating vanilla build a worldwide trade, yet France never paid him a penny for it. Freed when France ended slavery in 1848, he fell into poverty and later went to jail for theft. Then he was let out early, for a surprising reason. What was it?
answer: Officials cut his sentence to honour his discovery
choices: Officials cut his sentence to honour his discovery
A planter he'd taught to pollinate bribed the judge
New evidence surfaced and cleared his name
He slipped out during a fire at the prison
context: Despite unlocking a worldwide vanilla industry, Edmond Albius was never rewarded. Freed when France abolished slavery in 1848, he was later jailed for theft, then released early in recognition of his contribution to vanilla — and he died in poverty in 1880. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Albius

question: At a street stall in Cairo, a cook fries balls of falafel crisp and brown in hot oil and tucks them into warm pita with pickles and sauce, as carts and stalls do all across the Middle East. What is a falafel ball mostly made of?
context: Falafel is entirely plant-based — no meat, no egg — which is exactly why it became a beloved vegetarian street food across the Middle East. It's served tucked into flatbreads like pita, laffa or samoon with salad and a sesame tahini sauce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falafel

question: A cook starts a batch of falafel the night before, tipping dried chickpeas into a bowl of water to soak until they swell to double their size. The next step is the secret that makes the whole dish work. What does she do to the soaked beans before shaping them for the hot oil?
context: Dried chickpeas soak for roughly 24 hours, at least doubling in size — but traditional falafel never boils them. The swollen beans are ground raw and then deep-fried at about 375°F. Source: themediterraneandish.com/how-to-make-falafel

question: Short on time, a cook skips the overnight soak of dried chickpeas that traditional falafel calls for and tips a can of pre-cooked chickpeas into the blender instead. She shapes the paste into balls and lowers them into the hot oil. What happens to them?
context: Raw soaked beans hold a sticky natural starch that acts like internal velcro when ground, gluing the fritter together with no egg or flour. Boiling or canning bursts those starch granules, so the glue is gone and the falafel disintegrates in the oil — as one cook put it, you'd 'essentially be trying to fry hummus.' Source: culinarylore.com/dishes:canned-chick-peas-for-falafel; themediterraneandish.com/how-to-make-falafel

question: A diner in Beirut bites a fresh falafel in half, and inside the crisp brown shell the paste glows a bright, mossy green. Chickpeas are pale gold, so the color is not coming from the beans themselves. What turns the inside of a falafel green?
answer: a big handful of fresh herbs
choices: a big handful of fresh herbs
a pinch of green food coloring
a swirl of bright olive oil
context: The green comes from a big handful of fresh parsley and cilantro (coriander), sometimes mint, blitzed raw into the paste — the chlorophyll in the leaves dyes the whole batter green. Those same herbs give falafel its fresh, savory flavor. Source: burpy.com/what-makes-falafel-green; themediterraneandish.com/how-to-make-falafel

question: In Egypt, a cook making ta'ameya, the country's own falafel, reaches for a different bean from the soaked chickpeas behind most falafel in Lebanon, Syria and Israel. Many food historians think Egypt's version is the original, and by some accounts Coptic Christians made it first, to eat on meatless fast days. Its balls come out a little greener and softer inside. Which bean gives ta'ameya its flavor?
context: Egypt's ta'ameya (ta'amiya) is the fava-bean original, and many food historians believe falafel began in Egypt. Fava beans give it an earthier taste and a brighter-green inside, while the Levantine chickpea version comes out nuttier, sweeter and more golden. So falafel is not always a chickpea food. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falafel; tastingtable.com/901336/the-real-difference-between-taameya-and-falafel

question: Historians say the pharaohs never ate falafel: nothing like it appears in their texts, and the dish turns up in Egyptian records only in the 1800s. One reason is the sky-high ancient price of a kitchen staple it needs in large amounts. Which staple?
context: Falafel most likely emerged in the Egyptian port city of Alexandria, appearing in records only after the British occupation of 1882 — there's nothing like it in ancient Egyptian texts. Deep-frying swallows a lot of oil, which was a costly luxury in the ancient world, so a fried-bean fritter simply wasn't practical then. Source: historytoday.com/archive/historians-cookbook/falafel

question: A cook follows an 1890s recipe calling for 'a lump of butter' and 'a teacup of flour', and the cake comes out different every time, depending on whose lump and whose cup. Fannie Farmer's fix began with filling the measuring cup. What did she tell cooks to do next?
answer: Scrape the top flat and level with a knife's edge
choices: Scrape the top flat and level with a knife's edge
Round the flour up into a small heaping dome
Pack the flour down firmly with the back of a spoon
Shake the cup gently to help the flour settle even
context: Farmer's 1896 cookbook spelled it out: 'To measure a cupful, put in the ingredient by spoonfuls or from a scoop, round slightly, and level with a case knife, care being taken not to shake the cup.' Fill it, then scrape the top flat so every cook gets the exact same amount — which is why 'shake the cup to settle it' was exactly the wrong move. Source: The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, 1896 (gutenberg.org/files/65061); Greenfield Recorder, 'In the kitchen with Fannie Farmer.'

question: When Fannie Farmer's cookbook first went to press, she paid for the printing herself, as the story goes, because her publisher, Little, Brown, was so sure it would flop that it ran only 3,000 copies. It went on to sell more than four million in her lifetime. What nickname did the hit earn her?
choices: the queen of the Boston kitchen
the first lady of American baking
the high priestess of home cooking
context: The publisher doubted the book, capped the first printing at 3,000 copies, and reportedly had Farmer foot the bill herself — yet 'The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book' sold over four million copies in her lifetime and never went out of print, and she became known as 'the mother of level measurements.' (The commercial-drama details are a well-worn retelling; the nickname is solidly documented.) Source: amazingwomeninhistory.com, 'Fannie Farmer, the mother of level measurements'; Boston Magazine (bostonmagazine.com/news/2016/01/07/fannie-farmer-cookbook).

question: Fannie Farmer measured every ingredient in her 1896 Boston cookbook exactly, in standard cups and spoons, where older recipes had said vague things like 'flour enough to make a stiff dough'. With exact amounts, a recipe could finally promise something no cookbook ever had before. What could it promise?
answer: that a beginner and an expert would end up with the same dish
choices: that a beginner and an expert would end up with the same dish
that the finished dish would taste better than any restaurant's
that any dish could be cooked in half the usual time
that a cook could use cheaper ingredients without anyone noticing
context: Before Farmer, two cooks with the 'same' recipe could get wildly different food, because they guessed the amounts. With exact leveled measures the recipe became reproducible — hers was the first cookbook where a beginner and an expert following the same recipe got the same result, turning cooking from guesswork into something repeatable. Source: Boston Magazine; massmoments.org, 'Fannie Farmer Cookbook Published.'

question: An American baker scoops flour into a measuring cup, though bakers across most of the world weigh theirs in grams on a kitchen scale. Fannie Farmer locked that habit in with her 1896 cookbook and its exact measurements for every ingredient. Why was the cup the more practical choice in the late 1800s?
answer: Scales then were costly and unreliable, but a cheap leveled cup was consistent
choices: Scales then were costly and unreliable, but a cheap leveled cup was consistent
Flour was sold loose by the cupful, so a scale was never needed at all
American recipes used too many ingredients to weigh each one by hand
Scales could not measure the tiny amounts a teaspoon was meant to hold
context: Dry ingredients are still measured by weight (250 g flour) in most of the world but by volume (1/2 cup flour) in North America — and Wikipedia credits Farmer's 1896 book with locking in the volume system. In the late-1800s American kitchen, scales were expensive and unreliable, while a cheap standard cup scraped level was cheap and consistent, so cups won out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooking_weights_and_measures; flavoralchemy.com; justhungry.com.

question: A salmon fillet glistens on ice at a supermarket fish counter, pink and fresh under the bright lights. Where did that salmon most likely grow up?
answer: A netted pen in a coastal bay
choices: A netted pen in a coastal bay
A fast river bound for the sea
context: Roughly 70% of the salmon produced worldwide is farm-raised — grown in large net pens anchored in sheltered coastal water, not caught in the wild. The 'wild-looking' fillet at the fish counter was almost certainly grown on a farm. Source: TIME, 'Your Wild Salmon Is Probably Farmed'; NOAA Fisheries, Atlantic Salmon Aquaculture.

question: A home cook reads that ocean-caught shrimp tastes sweeter than pond-raised and hunts his grocery store for a bag marked 'wild-caught'. Bag after bag in the freezer says 'farm-raised', and the fresh case holds no wild shrimp at all. What is the main reason?
answer: Most shrimp sold is raised on farms
choices: Most shrimp sold is raised on farms
Wild shrimp costs far too much to stock
Wild shrimp is banned from most shops
Wild shrimp spoils within a single hour
context: Most shrimp sold today is farmed, about seven-tenths of the world's shrimp by weight, and most reaches shops frozen, shipped from farms in Asia and Ecuador, so wild-caught shrimp is the smaller slice of the market, and a single farmed species dominates the farmed supply. Source: Faunalytics / Rethink Priorities, 'How Many Shrimps Are Killed For Food?'; Wikipedia, 'Whiteleg shrimp'.

question: The earliest fishermen worked with nets and spears, and for all of human history since, people have taken their seafood wild from rivers, lakes and seas. Then, around 2022, the global numbers flipped for the first time. What changed?
answer: Farms now grow more seafood than is caught wild
choices: Farms now grow more seafood than is caught wild
Wild fish catches finally began climbing again
People suddenly started eating far less seafood
Nearly all wild fish species had run out
context: In 2022, aquaculture — farming fish and shellfish — produced about 51% of all aquatic animals and roughly 57% of the seafood destined for people's plates, passing wild capture for the first time in history. Aquaculture has been the fastest-growing food-production sector on Earth for about 50 years, expanding around 5–6% a year. Source: FAO, State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture (SOFIA) 2024.

question: On a salmon farm, an Atlantic salmon's life runs on a strict two-year schedule, from a fertilized egg to a fillet at harvest. Its wild cousins hatch in freshwater rivers and only later swim out to the salty ocean. Where does a farmed Atlantic salmon spend its very first year of life?
choices: In saltwater pens out at sea
Drifting free in the open ocean
In tidal pools along the shore
context: Farmed Atlantic salmon start in on-land freshwater hatcheries, where eggs are fertilized and the young fish grow for about a year. Only then are they moved to marine net pens in coastal water, and harvested at roughly two years old — the fillet was, in effect, grown to schedule. Like wild salmon, they naturally begin life in freshwater before heading to the sea. Source: NOAA Fisheries, Atlantic Salmon Aquaculture.

question: Along the coasts of Vietnam, Thailand, India and Ecuador, shallow ponds teem with one small sea creature, farmed there by an estimated hundreds of billions every year. Asked for the most-farmed animal on Earth by sheer numbers, most people would guess the chicken, but this creature is probably the true champion. Which creature is it?
context: The whiteleg shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) is likely the most-farmed animal on the planet by sheer headcount. Shrimp farms raise an estimated 300 to 620 billion shrimp a year, several times the number of farmed chickens, and the whiteleg makes up most of that farmed shrimp. Source: Faunalytics / Rethink Priorities, 'How Many Shrimps Are Killed For Food?'; https://grokipedia.com/page/Whiteleg_shrimp

question: Workers on a big Atlantic salmon farm toss feed pellets to the fish, but they cannot fatten them on grain the way a chicken farm feeds its birds. Salmon are hunters that eat other fish, and need the protein and oily fats only ocean animals give. What was long ground up and pressed into those pellets?
answer: Small wild fish like anchovies and sardines
choices: Small wild fish like anchovies and sardines
Shells from crabs, shrimp, and lobster
context: To grow carnivorous fish like salmon, farms have long netted small 'forage' fish — anchovies, herring, sardines, menhaden, capelin, mackerel — and ground them into feed pellets. These small ocean fish supply about 70% of the world's fishmeal and fish oil. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Feeds for Aquaculture'.

question: Wild Atlantic salmon roam thousands of miles of open ocean, spread thin. Farmed salmon live packed together by the tens of thousands, and that crowding lets a tiny parasite spread from fish to fish. What small creature is the biggest health headache in salmon farming?
context: Because farmed salmon are crowded together, they are plagued by sea lice (Lepeophtheirus salmonis) — a tiny parasite that clamps onto the fish and eats its mucus, skin, and blood. It is the single biggest health threat in salmon farming and costs the industry well over $1 billion a year. To fight it, farmers even stock 'cleaner' fish — wrasse and lumpfish — that eat the lice right off the salmon, alongside warm-water baths and resting a pen site between crops. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salmon louse'; Marine Resource Economics, 'The Cost of Lice'.

question: Wild salmon flesh glows a bright pink-orange on the fishmonger's ice. A farmed salmon raised on plain feed pellets would turn out a dull grey instead, a color no supermarket shopper will buy. How do farmers give the farmed fillet its familiar pink?
answer: They add a pigment to the fish's feed
choices: They add a pigment to the fish's feed
They inject a food-safe dye before sale
They breed the fish for pinker flesh
They raise the mineral level in the pen
context: Farmed salmon flesh would be grey or beige on its own; its pink comes from the pigment astaxanthin added to the feed. It is not an artificial dye — wild salmon get the exact same pigment naturally by eating krill and shrimp. Source: The Conversation, 'The colour of farmed salmon comes from adding an antioxidant to their feed'; Global Salmon Initiative.

question: Critics of fish farming long complained that it drains the ocean: by their count, several pounds of small wild fish must be caught and ground into pellets to grow each pound of farmed salmon or shrimp. It sounds like a bad trade. When researchers add up all of fish farming today, fish, shellfish and seaweed together, what does the honest math show?
answer: Farming now grows more seafood than the wild fish it uses
choices: Farming now grows more seafood than the wild fish it uses
Farming still burns far more wild fish than it produces
Farming uses wild fish and grows seafood in equal weight
Farming no longer uses any wild fish at all
context: Globally, aquaculture now uses about half a ton of wild whole fish to produce a full ton of farmed seafood — so it is a net producer of fish, and it takes pressure off wild stocks. Farmed salmon still eats some wild forage fish, but the old figure is out of date: in Norwegian salmon farming the wild-fish cost per kg of salmon fell from about 7.2 kg around 1990 to roughly 1.5 kg by 2013. 'Farmed = bad' is too simple. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Feeds for Aquaculture'; SeaChoice, 'Wild Fish in Feed'.

question: A salmon farmer picks in advance roughly what shade of pink-orange his fish will turn out, from pale to deep. Feed companies even sell farmers a small hand-held tool for picking the exact shade a supermarket buyer has ordered. What is this tool like?
answer: A fan of paint-chip color swatches
choices: A fan of paint-chip color swatches
A dial on the feed tank that sets it
A dye chart keyed to the sale price
A water filter that deepens the tint
context: Feed companies sell farmers a 'SalmoFan' — a fan of paint-chip-style color swatches — so they can pick the exact pink-orange shade before the salmon even grows; the most popular shades sit around numbers 24 to 28. The color itself comes from the pigment astaxanthin in the feed. Source: The Conversation, 'The colour of farmed salmon...'.

question: Laid side by side on a fish counter, a farmed Atlantic salmon fillet carries roughly twice as much fat as a wild Alaskan one. Nobody injects it; the fat builds up because a farmed fish never has to swim hard against ocean currents the way a wild salmon does all its life. Where does that extra fat show in the raw fillet?
answer: In wide white stripes marbling the flesh
choices: In wide white stripes marbling the flesh
In a thick layer of skin on the back
In the deep red color of the meat
In how large the raw flakes look
context: A farmed salmon serving carries roughly 27 g of fat versus about 13 g in wild — nearly double. Those wide, creamy-white stripes marbling a raw fillet ARE that fat, so heavy marbling is the visible signature of a farmed fish; wild salmon is leaner, firmer, and more deeply colored because it swims hard and eats krill. Source: Healthline, 'Wild vs Farmed Salmon'; Cleveland Clinic, 'Fish Faceoff'.

question: A nutrition teacher writes all thirteen vitamins on the board, then circles the four that will not dissolve in water at all, only in fat. Those four can be soaked up only from a meal with some butter, oil or egg yolk in it. Which four has she circled?
answer: Vitamins A, D, E and K
choices: Vitamins A, D, E and K
Vitamins A, C, E and K
Vitamins B, C, D and E
Vitamins A, B, D and K
context: A, D, E and K are the four fat-soluble vitamins; the other nine - the B-vitamins and vitamin C - dissolve in water instead. A handy memory hook: the odd-ones-out spell A-D-E-K. Because they ride in fat, your body can only absorb them from a meal that has some fat in it. Source: Wikipedia 'Fat-soluble vitamin' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat-soluble_vitamin) - 'In humans there are 13 vitamins: 4 fat-soluble (A, D, E, and K) and 9 water-soluble.'

question: A boy who nibbles a carrot raw absorbs only about a tenth of the vitamins locked inside it. Prepared one simple way, the same carrot gives up nearly three-quarters, over six times as much. What kitchen step unlocks the difference?
answer: Sauteing it in a little oil or butter
choices: Sauteing it in a little oil or butter
Grating it raw over a green salad
Boiling it in plenty of plain water
context: From a raw carrot you absorb only about 11% of its orange pigment (beta-carotene); stir-fried in a little oil, that jumps to about 74% - the study found cooking in oil raised the usable vitamin yield 6.5-fold. The fat dissolves the pigment and ferries it across your gut wall, so a pat of butter is really a delivery truck. Source: British Journal of Nutrition, 'The effect of food preparation on the bioavailability of carotenoids from carrots' (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effect-of-food-preparation-on-the-bioavailability-of-carotenoids-from-carrots-using-intrinsic-labelling/C4E2B9F580B2F6D142A7E48DC52953D9) - raw ~11% vs stir-fried ~74%, retinol yield 'enhanced by a factor of 6.5 by stir-frying.'

question: Suppose you skip vitamin A for a few weeks: you stay perfectly fine. Skip vitamin C, the nutrient in oranges, peppers and broccoli, for just a few days, though, and your body starts running low, so you need some every single day. Why can your body not stockpile vitamin C?
answer: It dissolves in water, so your body flushes the extra out
choices: It dissolves in water, so your body flushes the extra out
Stomach acid destroys it within a few hours of eating
Your body burns through it faster than any other vitamin
It breaks down quickly once a fruit is cut or picked
context: Vitamin C is water-soluble: it dissolves in water, so your body can't build a reserve and simply flushes the surplus out in urine - you need a fresh supply daily (citrus, peppers, berries). The fat-soluble four (A, D, E, K) are the opposite: they ride in fat and your body can hold onto them far longer. Source: Wikipedia 'Fat-soluble vitamin' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat-soluble_vitamin) - water-soluble vitamins 'dissolve easily in water and... are readily excreted from the body,' so 'more consistent intake is important.'

question: A carrot, a baked sweet potato and a wedge of ripe cantaloupe sit sliced open on a board, the same vivid orange in all three. One natural pigment does the work, and the body takes it apart to build vitamin A, which keeps eyes sharp in dim light. What is the pigment called?
context: A carrot's orange comes from beta-carotene, a carotenoid pigment. It's a 'provitamin' - a precursor, not the finished vitamin: your gut uses an enzyme (BCO1) to split one beta-carotene molecule and build vitamin A from it, so the plant supplies the raw material and your body does the final assembly. Chlorophyll is the green of leaves, lycopene the red of tomatoes, and melanin the brown of skin and hair - but only beta-carotene is the orange one your body turns into vitamin A. Source: Grokipedia 'Vitamin A' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_A) - beta-carotene is 'centrally cleaved by the enzyme beta-carotene 15,15'-monooxygenase 1 (BCO1)' to yield vitamin A.

question: A cook simmers tomatoes low and slow in a little olive oil for a pasta sauce, and one of their prized nutrients ends up several times more absorbable than in a raw slice. The tomato breaks the rule that raw vegetables always beat cooked ones. Why does the oily, cooked sauce win?
answer: The heat ruptures the cells, freeing the pigment for fat to carry
choices: The heat ruptures the cells, freeing the pigment for fat to carry
The heat builds brand-new vitamins that a raw tomato lacks
Cooking turns the tomato's water into extra vitamins
The oil donates its own vitamins for the tomato to soak up
context: A tomato's red color is lycopene, a fat-soluble pigment. Gentle cooking in oil ruptures the tomato's tough cell walls, releasing the lycopene, and the oil carries it into you - lycopene in oil-simmered tomato paste is up to four times more absorbable than in a raw tomato. It's the rare case where cooking makes a nutrient MORE available, not less. Source: Wikipedia 'Lycopene' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycopene) - 'Lycopene in tomato paste is up to four times more bioavailable than in fresh tomatoes.'

question: Suppose you ran short of vitamin A in your food: your body would draw on a reserve it banks, instead of washing the vitamin out the way it does water-soluble ones. More than 90 percent of that reserve, often nearly a year's worth, sits inside one organ. Which organ is the body's vitamin A vault?
context: Because they dissolve in fat, A, D, E and K can be banked in your body - over 90% of your vitamin A reserve is stored in the liver, often close to a year's worth. (It's also why liver and cod-liver oil are so rich in vitamin A: they're an animal's own vitamin vault.) The catch: stored vitamins A and D CAN build up to toxic levels if you badly overdo them - a problem called hypervitaminosis. Source: StatPearls 'Biochemistry, Fat Soluble Vitamins' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534869/) and Wikipedia 'Fat-soluble vitamin' - fat-soluble vitamins are 'stored... mainly in the liver.'

question: A cook sets out four spoonfuls of exactly the same size, each holding a different food. Every food carries chemical energy the body can burn, measured in calories. Gram for gram, which spoon packs by far the most?
context: Fat is the body's densest fuel: a gram of fat carries more than double the energy of a gram of sugar (a carbohydrate) or of protein — the old 'four-four-nine' rule of nutrition. That is why a single spoonful of oil is so calorie-rich. Source: Merck Manual, 'Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats'; corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Fat.'

question: A nurse pinches the soft layer just under a patient's skin: that is subcutaneous fat. Most people think of it only as spare fuel saved for a hungry day, but doctors point to two other jobs it does every day. Which pair?
choices: Filtering the blood and making urine
context: The fat just under the skin, subcutaneous fat, insulates the body and helps regulate its temperature, and it also pads and cushions the organs against knocks and shocks. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fat' (insulate organs against shock, regulate body temperature).

question: A cook swirls a knob of cold butter into a pan of tomato sauce just before serving, and the sauce suddenly tastes fuller and rounder than it did a minute before. What is the fat doing to the flavor?
answer: Dissolving and carrying the sauce's flavor and aroma
choices: Dissolving and carrying the sauce's flavor and aroma
Breaking the tough fibers down into sugar
Killing off the bacteria that dull the flavor
Soaking up and hiding the sauce's extra salt
context: Many of the compounds that give food its taste and aroma are fat-soluble: they dissolve into fat but barely into water, so fat carries flavor and smell across the tongue. Strip the fat out of a food and much of its taste goes with it, which is why finishing a sauce with butter deepens it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fat' (dietary fats carry flavor and aroma compounds).

question: A runner deep into a hard workout draws on two fuel tanks. The fast one, a quick-burning store, runs nearly empty after only 90 to 120 minutes of hard exercise, while the other holds enough to keep a person going for days or even weeks. What is that big, long-lasting tank made of?
context: About 80-85% of a healthy adult's stored energy is held as body fat — enough to last days or even weeks. The fast-access glycogen (sugar) store holds only about 1,800-2,000 calories, roughly 90-120 minutes of hard exercise before it runs low. Fat is the body's long-term battery. Source: Human Kinetics, 'The Body's Fuel Sources'; nutri.it.com.

question: Under a microscope, a single cell sits wrapped in a thin, flexible skin, the cell membrane, which holds it together and decides what passes in and out. The human body is built from some thirty trillion such cells, every one wrapped the same way. What is that living wall mostly built from?
context: Every cell is enclosed by a cell membrane — a double layer of fat molecules called a phospholipid bilayer — that separates and protects the cell's interior and controls what enters and leaves. Fat is structure, not just fuel. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cell membrane.'

question: A man on a gym treadmill sweats to burn off fat as if it were the enemy. Yet one organ of the human body is built from fat more than anything else, about 60 percent by dry weight, and there the fat is no fuel at all, but the stuff its cells are shaped from. Which organ is it?
context: The brain is the fattiest organ in the body — roughly 60% fat by dry weight. There the fat isn't fuel; it's the structural material the brain is built from, since phospholipids form the shell of every brain cell. Source: ScienceDirect and Nature (lipids make up ~50-60% of dry brain mass).

question: A nerve signal travels out to a muscle along a long, thin fiber wrapped in a fatty sheath called myelin, much like the plastic coating on an electrical wire. That insulation does more than protect the nerve: it changes the way the signal moves. What does the fatty wrapping let the signal do?
answer: Leap along in jumps instead of crawling
choices: Leap along in jumps instead of crawling
Split apart into two weaker copies
Slow right down to keep its place in line
Turn back when it meets a blockage
context: The insulation around nerves, called myelin, is 60-75% fat by dry weight. Like the plastic coating on an electrical wire, this fatty sheath lets the nerve signal jump from gap to gap — 'saltatory conduction' — instead of crawling steadily along, so signals travel far faster. Source: Wikipedia, 'Myelin.'

question: A fat-free rice cake leaves its eater hungry within an hour, while the same snack with a smear of peanut butter keeps hunger off far longer, even at the same calories. Nutritionists say the fat does two jobs down in the gut that together stretch out the feeling of fullness. Which pair of jobs?
answer: Slows stomach emptying and quiets appetite with gut hormones
choices: Slows stomach emptying and quiets appetite with gut hormones
Forms a thick gel and swells to fill the stomach
Releases quick sugar and satisfies the brain fast
Soaks up stomach acid and settles the hunger
context: When fat reaches the small intestine it slows the stomach from emptying and triggers appetite-quieting gut hormones — which is why a fatty meal keeps hunger away for hours, while a fat-free snack leaves its eater hungry again soon. Source: Cambridge, Proceedings of the Nutrition Society (fat in the small intestine slows gastric emptying and suppresses appetite).

question: Ancel Keys, a physiologist, championed the idea in the 1950s that dietary fat causes heart disease, and in 1977 the American government's first official diet advice urged everyone to eat less of it. Critics later said Keys had been so fixed on fat that he overlooked another common ingredient that may, in their view, drive heart disease itself. Which ingredient did they point to?
context: Fat became the diet villain through real science, not from nowhere: in the 1950s physiologist Ancel Keys pushed the 'diet-heart' idea that fat caused heart disease, and in 1977 Senator George McGovern's 'Dietary Goals for the United States' told Americans to eat less fat — the first such advice from the U.S. government. Later critics argued that his focus on fat overlooked sugar's role, and that his country comparison left out high-fat, low-heart-disease France. There were real reasons for the low-fat advice, but many now argue fat was over-vilified. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ancel Keys'; MDPI Nutrients (Lipid-Heart Hypothesis and the 1977 Dietary Goals).

question: Two doughs come out of the same oven: a lean bread dough, chewy and stretchy, and a rich one worked with plenty of butter, soft and crumbly. In the rich one the fat coats every grain of flour in a greasy film. What does that film keep away from the flour?
context: Fat is greasy and repels water, so a film of it around each flour grain keeps water out — and without water, the flour's proteins can't link up and toughen the dough. That's why a rich, buttery dough bakes soft while a lean bread dough turns chewy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Shortening'; Chemistry LibreTexts, Chemistry of Cooking, ch.3 Fat.

question: A baker creams solid shortening into flour, and the fat stops one thing in the dough from growing into the long, linked strands that make bread chewy. Old cooks named the fat for that job long before food science could explain it, the same 'short' as in shortbread. What is the fat cutting short?
context: Gluten is the stretchy protein network that gives bread its chew; fat coats the flour and stops it forming long strands, effectively cutting the gluten 'short' — which is exactly why solid baking fat is called shortening (the same 'short' in shortbread and shortcake). Source: etymonline, 'shortening'; Wikipedia, 'Shortening'.

question: Two bowls of the same butter and flour sit on a baker's counter, one for pie crust and one for shortbread, and only her handling of the fat tells them apart. For shortbread she rubs the butter in until the mix looks like damp sand; for pie crust she stops while the cold butter sits in pea-sized lumps. In the oven, what does each lump do to leave a flake?
answer: It melts away and leaves a flat gap that lifts into a thin layer.
choices: It melts away and leaves a flat gap that lifts into a thin layer.
It swells with trapped air and lifts the crust like a bubble.
It hardens into a crisp little nugget studding the crust.
It soaks into the dough and fries it into a crisp shell.
context: Leaving the fat in pea-sized lumps (pie crust) makes it flaky; rubbing it in completely until the mix looks like damp sand (shortbread) makes it evenly crumbly instead. Lump size is the whole difference between flaky and short. Source: Boston Girl Bakes, 'The Rubbing-In Method'; The Kitchn, 'How to Make Perfectly Flaky Pie Crust'.

question: A pie crust comes out of the oven greasy, hard and flat, without a single flake, because the kitchen was warm and the butter softened and soaked into the flour before the pan went in. Butter kept cold and solid would have propped the layers open. What else does cold, solid butter do in the oven's heat?
answer: Its trapped water flashes to steam and forces the layers apart.
choices: Its trapped water flashes to steam and forces the layers apart.
Its trapped air expands and inflates the crust like a balloon.
It caramelizes into a crisp brown sheet between the layers.
It melts into hot oil that fries each layer until crisp.
context: Butter is only about 80% fat — the rest is mostly water. Kept cold and solid, that water flashes to steam in the oven and puffs the pastry layers apart; but if the butter warms and soaks into the flour first, there's no water pocket left to steam and no gap to lift, so the crust bakes greasy and hard. It's the croissant's cold-butter trick on a small scale. Source: Food52, 'Baking Fats: Butter Versus the World'; The Kitchn flaky pie crust guide.

question: A baker makes the same cookie dough twice, once with butter and once with white vegetable shortening. The shortening batch bakes up tall and puffy while the butter batch spreads into thin, flat disks. Shortening is nearly pure fat and melts at a higher temperature than butter. Why does that give a taller cookie?
answer: The fat stays solid longer, so the cookie sets before it can spread.
choices: The fat stays solid longer, so the cookie sets before it can spread.
The extra heat needed to brown the top locks the shape in early.
The firmer fat grips the flour and holds the dough from relaxing.
The stiffer dough simply has less room to spread outward.
context: Vegetable shortening and lard are nearly 100% fat with no water and a higher melting point than butter (~44-47C vs butter's ~38C), so they stay solid longer in the oven and the bake sets before the fat can spread — giving taller, more tender cookies and crust, though with less flavor and no steam-flake of their own. Source: Chemistry LibreTexts, Chemistry of Cooking, ch.3 Fat; bakeitwithlove.com, 'Butter vs Shortening'.

question: Volunteers at Iowa State University ate hearty salads of spinach, romaine, carrots and tomatoes, but poured on fat-free dressing. Careful blood tests afterward gave a startling result about the carotenoids, the orange and red plant pigments, some of which become vitamin A inside the body. What had happened to them?
answer: almost none of them reached their blood
choices: almost none of them reached their blood
about half of them reached their blood
about a quarter of them reached their blood
about as many as usual reached their blood
context: With fat-free dressing, essentially no carotenoids -- alpha-carotene, beta-carotene, lycopene -- showed up in the volunteers' blood; the vegetables' provitamin A passed straight through, and absorption was called 'negligible.' A diner can eat the pigment and still absorb almost none of it. Source: Brown et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 80(2):396-403, 2004 (PubMed 15277161).

question: A patient eats food full of the four fat-soluble vitamins, yet tests show him short of every one, because a blocked bile duct keeps his bile from the gut. Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, is squirted into the small intestine whenever fatty food arrives. What is bile doing for those vitamins?
answer: bundling them into droplets the gut can absorb
choices: bundling them into droplets the gut can absorb
breaking them down into smaller vitamins
neutralizing the stomach acid around them
carrying them straight into the bloodstream
context: Dietary fat triggers the gallbladder to release bile, which bundles the fat-soluble vitamins into tiny droplets called micelles that the gut wall absorbs; they're then wrapped in chylomicrons and shipped through the lymph. No fat means no micelle, so no carrier -- which is why people who can't digest fat (cystic fibrosis, celiac, a blocked bile duct) go deficient even with plenty of A, D, E and K in their food. Source: NCBI Bookshelf NBK534869 (Fat-Soluble Vitamins -- bile/micelle/chylomicron pathway).

question: Mario Ferruzzi, a food scientist at Purdue, fed volunteers the same salad with dressings made from different fats, and the kind of fat made a difference. With one, the vegetables' carotenoids came through on just a few grams of fat, while the others took more fat to match it. Which dressing worked with the least fat?
context: In Ferruzzi's Purdue feeding trial, published by Goltz and colleagues in 2012, 29 volunteers ate salads dressed with butter, canola oil or a polyunsaturated oil at 3, 8 or 20 grams of fat. The monounsaturated canola dressing gave about the same carotenoid absorption at 3 grams as at 20, while the butter and the polyunsaturated oil needed more fat to catch up; overall the authors found the amount of fat mattered more than its source, and more fat generally meant more absorption. Source: Goltz et al. (Purdue), Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, 2012; Purdue news release, June 2012 (purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2012/120619FerruzziSalad.html).

question: Douglas Mawson and Xavier Mertz, stranded and starving on the Antarctic ice in 1913, ate the only food they had left: the livers of their own sled dogs. Within days their skin was peeling off in sheets, and Mertz was dead. What is the classic explanation for what poisoned them?
context: Because fat-soluble vitamins are STORED in the liver and body fat rather than flushed out daily like water-soluble ones, they can build up to toxic levels -- hypervitaminosis A, with peeling skin and headaches. Some animal livers are extraordinarily vitamin-A-rich: about 500 g of polar bear liver is an acutely toxic dose, which is why the Inuit refuse to eat it. The vitamin-A poisoning of the Mawson-Mertz party is the widely cited explanation for their sled-dog-liver deaths. Source: Wikipedia, Hypervitaminosis A (Mawson/Mertz Far Eastern Party 1913; 500 g toxic dose; Inuit avoidance); NCBI Bookshelf NBK534869.  (Legend.)

question: A diner calls butter, cream and a marbled steak 'rich', and takes that richness to be pure texture, how silky they feel on the tongue. Food scientists at Purdue, led by Richard Mattes, made a bolder claim about fat in 2015. What did they argue fat really is?
answer: a real sixth basic taste of its own
choices: a real sixth basic taste of its own
just the fifth taste, umami, in disguise
only an aroma, not a taste at all
a mild cousin of chili's spicy heat
context: The five tastes everyone agrees on are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory). In 2015, Richard Mattes and his team at Purdue argued that fat belongs on that list as a taste in its own right — something the tongue detects, separate from the slippery feel of grease. Source: Purdue University newsroom, 2015 (purdue.edu).

question: Scientists had volunteers sample pure fat with its smell and its silky feel both taken away, and everyone expected something as good as butter, bacon or cream. Instead it was startlingly bad. What did the pure taste of fat taste like?
context: Richard Mattes described pure fat-taste as tasting like rancid oil — 'very unpleasant... a warning signal telling you this is not the best thing to eat.' The idea: the tongue senses free fatty acids so it can catch fat that has spoiled. Source: National Geographic and Purdue University newsroom, 2015.

question: A taster handed a strong dose of pure fat wants to spit it out, yet a faint trace of the same taste makes food more appealing. Scientists found fat behaves like one of the five classic tastes, one people are built to reject in strength but learn to love in a whisper. Which taste?
context: Bitterness is the classic 'love it in small doses' taste: a strong hit makes a taster recoil, but a little is exactly what makes coffee, dark chocolate, and red wine so good. Scientists found fat-taste behaves the same way — repellent when strong, appealing when faint. Source: Purdue University newsroom, 2015 (purdue.edu).

question: A cook simmers a broth for hours with garlic and onions and finishes it with aged Parmesan, and the dish takes on a deep, round, lingering fullness. Japanese food science calls this quality kokumi, 'mouthfulness', and it works differently from sweet, sour or salty. How does kokumi create that fullness?
answer: it boosts the salty and savory tastes already in the food
choices: it boosts the salty and savory tastes already in the food
it delivers a strong new flavor of its own
it coats the tongue with a thick, oily film
it cancels out bitterness so nothing tastes harsh
context: Kokumi compounds — like glutathione, found in garlic, onions, and aged cheese — are nearly tasteless on their own. They switch on a sensor on the taste cells (the calcium-sensing receptor) that amplifies salty, sweet, and umami, which is why a long-simmered broth or aged cheese tastes so full and satisfying. Source: 'Kokumi Substances, Enhancers of Basic Tastes' (PMC3325276).

question: Suppose you ate plenty of carbohydrate and protein but no fat: your body could build nearly every fat it needs from scratch, all but two, which must come from food. Each of these essential fatty acids heads a whole family of fats, named for where a chemical bond sits in the molecule. Which two families?
context: The only two fats the human body can't build for itself are alpha-linolenic acid (parent of the omega-3 family) and linoleic acid (parent of the omega-6 family) — the 'essential' fatty acids. Everything else, including omega-9, the body makes from carbs, protein, or other fats. Source: Linus Pauling Institute, 'Essential Fatty Acids'; Wikipedia, 'Essential fatty acid.'

question: Most of the fat in olive oil is monounsaturated, each molecule bent by a single kink, and the oil pours in a smooth, glossy stream at room temperature. A cook leaves a bottle in the fridge overnight. How does the oil look the next morning?
choices: Clear and runny, just as before
Frozen into a hard white block
Split into oily and watery layers
context: Monounsaturated fat — the main fat in olive oil (oleic acid) — has a single double bond that puts ONE kink in the chain. That kink keeps it liquid at room temperature but lets it turn cloudy and semi-solid when chilled, so the fridge is a handy test for it. Source: Mayo Clinic, 'Dietary fats'; Graza, 'Does olive oil solidify?'

question: Fish oil stays pourable even straight from a cold fridge, because it belongs to the polyunsaturated fats, whose molecules are kinked in several places. One common kitchen oil, rich in omega-6 fat, belongs to the same family and pours just as freely when chilled. Which oil is it?
context: Polyunsaturated fats have several double bonds, several kinks, so the molecules can't pack together, and they stay liquid even in the fridge. Corn oil, like the other seed oils, is mostly polyunsaturated omega-6 fat; fish oil's omega-3s belong to the same family. Olive and avocado oil are mostly monounsaturated, and palm oil is about half saturated. Source: Mayo Clinic, 'Dietary fats'; Wikipedia, 'Corn oil'.

question: A veteran Italian chef keeps two olive oils on his bench. He fries in the cheap, refined one, nearly flavorless and stable up to a high smoke point, and pours the peppery green extra-virgin bottle only raw, over a finished plate of pasta or grilled fish, never into a hot pan. Why won't he fry with the extra-virgin oil?
answer: the very compounds that give it flavor scorch at a low temperature
choices: the very compounds that give it flavor scorch at a low temperature
extra-virgin oil holds far more calories than refined oil
heating instantly destroys all of the oil's healthy fats
refined oil is the only cooking oil that is safe to eat hot
context: Extra-virgin olive oil has a low smoke point (about 325-410°F) precisely because the chlorophyll and volatile aroma compounds that make it taste so good also burn easily. Refining strips those out and raises the smoke point, which is why chefs deep-fry in refined, high-smoke-point fats (beef tallow smokes around 400°F, refined avocado oil 480-520°F) and save fragile EVOO as a finishing drizzle. Push any fat past its smoke point and heat wrecks it. Source: MasterClass, 'Cooking Oils and Smoke Points'; ThermoWorks, 'Oil Smoke Point Temps.'

question: Researchers find that people in the modern West eat roughly fifteen times more omega-6 fat than omega-3, though they propose that people long ago ate the two in about equal measure. Their advice for rebalancing is not to fear fat itself, but to eat more of one food. Which food is it?
context: Omega-6 and omega-3 compete in the body, so the lopsided modern ratio — roughly 15:1 to 17:1, versus a proposed ancestral 1:1 — matters, not just the total amount of fat. The fix nutritionists point to is more oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel) to bring omega-3 back up, NOT going fat-phobic; just 2-3 servings a week clears the recommended 250-500 mg/day of EPA+DHA. Source: Simopoulos 2002, 'The importance of the ratio of omega-6/omega-3 essential fatty acids' (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12442909); Healthline, '12 omega-3-rich foods.'

question: Cooks who swear by butter, tallow, and olive oil point out that modern seed oils aren't simply pressed the way olive oil is. To wring oil from tough little seeds like soybeans and corn, factories flake them and wash them with an industrial solvent, then bleach and deodorize the result into a clear, flavorless oil. Which solvent does that extraction use?
context: Most commodity seed oils are solvent-extracted with hexane (a light fraction refined from petroleum), then RBD — refined, bleached, and deodorized — into a clear, neutral oil. Traditional-foods critics argue this heavy processing, plus the fragile omega-6 fat these oils carry, is reason to prefer butter, tallow, and olive oil. Note: the health-harm claim is contested, not settled. Source: SeedOilFreeCertified, 'What is hexane extraction'; ACS ChemMatters, 'Seed Oils.'

question: 'Seed oils are toxic,' one online slogan shouts, and 'seed oils are perfectly safe,' answers another, yet nutrition scientists say both miss the real disagreement. Some trials found that swapping butter for these oils cut heart disease, while others found no benefit at all. Stripped of the shouting, they say, the honest fight is not about whether fat is bad. What is it really about?
answer: the processing and the repeated heating, not fat itself
choices: the processing and the repeated heating, not fat itself
the price and the packaging, not fat itself
the color and the flavor, not fat itself
the calories and the salt, not fat itself
context: The honest crux of the seed-oil fight is three things: heavy industrial processing, whether repeatedly heating fragile omega-6 fats oxidizes them into reactive compounds, and the lopsided omega-6-to-omega-3 balance of the modern diet. The human evidence genuinely disagrees — the Minnesota Coronary Experiment and Sydney Diet Heart Study found no benefit (even worse outcomes) from swapping saturated fat for high-omega-6 oil, while the American Heart Association points to trials showing about 30% less heart disease and Stanford's Christopher Gardner argues the oils need not be feared. The fight is over the crux, not over whether fat itself is bad. Source: 2025 narrative synthesis (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12923254); AHA, 'There's no reason to avoid seed oils' (2024).

question: A Brazilian family gathers on a Saturday around a big black pot bubbling low on the stove. Inside, feijoada, Brazil's national dish, has been simmering for hours and fills the house with a rich, smoky smell. Which two ingredients form its heart?
context: This is feijoada, Brazil's national dish. A full 'feijoada completa' slow-cooks black beans all day with many cuts of pork — salted ears, tail and feet, smoked ribs, bacon, sausage, and dried jerked beef — until the broth turns a dark purplish-brown. Source: Wikipedia, 'Feijoada (Brazilian dish).'

question: A plate of feijoada always arrives with the same companions: fluffy white rice, sauteed collard greens, and a dusting of toasted cassava flour called farofa. One more thing sits on the side — a fresh fruit whose sharp acid cuts the fatty pork and is said to aid digestion. Which fruit?
context: Feijoada's fixed spread is white rice, sauteed collard greens (called 'couve'), farofa (toasted manioc/cassava flour sprinkled on top), and slices of fresh orange, whose acid balances the rich pork and is traditionally said to aid digestion. Source: Wikipedia, 'Feijoada (Brazilian dish).'

question: Carlos Augusto Ditadi, a Brazilian historian, calls it modern folklore that enslaved Africans invented feijoada from the pork scraps their masters threw away. Cuts like pig's feet and ears were prized food in Europe, never garbage, and the stew comes from an older European bean-and-pork dish. From which country's northern kitchens?
context: Feijoada descends from the Portuguese 'cozido,' a northern-Portugal pork-and-bean stew. Historian Carlos Augusto Ditadi calls the 'slave leftovers' story 'born of modern folklore, in a romanticized vision' of slavery, and food scholar Raul Lody says the idealized image of turban-wearing enslaved women stirring clay pots hides slavery's real brutality. Two facts sink the myth: Iberians prized pig's feet and ears as food, and the African cultures enslaved people came from did not traditionally cook beans with pork — Latin Europe did. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Feijoada (Brazilian dish)'; Southern Cultures, 'Feijoada and Hoppin' John.'  (Legend.)

question: Three pots simmer in three countries: feijoada in Brazil, cassoulet in France and fabada in Spain, each holding beans slow-cooked with salted, smoked pork. Food historians count all three as one family. Whose old meat-and-bean stews are the shared ancestor?
context: Feijoada, France's cassoulet (white haricot beans with sausage and duck or pork confit), and Spain's fabada asturiana (fat white 'fabes' beans with chorizo and morcilla blood sausage) all belong to one Old-World family of beans slow-cooked with preserved pork — descended from ancient Roman meat-and-bean stews. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Feijoada' and 'Fabada asturiana.'

question: Feijoada's ingredients crossed oceans to meet in the pot. Its black beans are a New World crop, but its pork was a newcomer, since pigs were unknown in the Americas until European ships carried the first ones over. Which voyage brought them?
context: Feijoada is a three-continent fusion on one plate: the black beans are a New World crop (domesticated in Mesoamerica over 7,000 years ago), the pig is an Old World animal (Europeans brought the first pigs to the Americas on Columbus's 1493 second voyage), and the slow-simmered bean-and-meat method is European. Sources: Wikipedia, 'New World crops'; Texas A&M feral-hog history (feralhogs.tamu.edu).

question: A cook making sauerkraut, the traditional German pickle, packs a crock with one plain vegetable and one simple pantry ingredient, then leaves it in a cool cellar for weeks. Out comes a sharp, tangy, sour pile that keeps all winter. What went into the crock?
context: Cabbage and salt — that's the whole recipe, and no vinegar is ever added. Shredded cabbage salted and packed airtight is soured by its own good bacteria into a tangy food that survives for months rather than spoiling. The German name says it plainly: 'sauer' means sour and 'kraut' means cabbage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauerkraut

question: Korean families gathered every autumn for gimjang, the great communal effort of making a whole winter's worth of kimchi in one go, long before anyone owned a refrigerator. How did they keep all that kimchi cool and slowly fermenting for months?
answer: They sealed the pots and buried them in the ground
choices: They sealed the pots and buried them in the ground
They packed the pots in mountain snow and ice
They lowered the pots into cold stone wells
They stored the pots high in shaded rafters
context: Families packed kimchi into brown earthenware jars called onggi and buried them in the ground, where the steady cool earth kept it fizzing slowly and safely through winter. The big communal autumn kimchi-making, traditionally led by the community's women, is called gimjang. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimchi.

question: Garum, a salty sauce of fermented fish, went onto nearly every dish in a Roman kitchen. The very finest grade was sealed into clay jars and shipped across the whole empire under a luxury brand name. Roughly what might a wealthy Roman have paid for just a couple of gallons of it?
answer: About a legionary's whole year of pay
choices: About a legionary's whole year of pay
About a month of a workman's wages
About the price of a fine warhorse
About the cost of a good wool cloak
context: Pliny the Elder said scarcely any liquid except perfume cost so much by volume, and premium 'garum sociorum' from Cartagena could fetch on the order of a legionary's whole year's pay for only a couple of gallons — a fortune, for salted fermented fish. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garum; National Geographic History, 'What is garum?'

question: A Roman winemaker watched a vat of crushed grapes go to work all by itself for days, no hand touching it, as though something inside were alive, long before anyone knew microbes existed. The Romans named the process for what the sight reminded them of, and the word 'fermentation' still carries their Latin verb. What does that verb mean?
context: 'Fermentation' comes from the Latin fervere, 'to boil.' When the Romans watched fermenting vats bubble and fizz with carbon-dioxide gas, the frothing liquid looked exactly as though it were boiling — even though nothing was hot. The name stuck for centuries before anyone understood that living microbes were making the gas. Source: etymonline.com.

question: Ferran Adrià set down before a diner at elBulli what looked exactly like a shiny green olive resting in a spoonful of oil. The diner lifted it expecting a familiar snack, but the moment the 'olive' touched the tongue and the mouth closed on it, it did something no real olive could. What happened?
answer: Its thin skin burst, flooding the tongue with olive juice.
choices: Its thin skin burst, flooding the tongue with olive juice.
It crackled apart into shards of crisp olive candy.
It slowly melted into a warm olive-flavored cream.
It fizzed away into a puff of olive-scented air.
context: The 'liquid olive' (2005) was created by Ferran Adria and his brother Albert at elBulli. It is not an olive at all: it is real olive juice held inside a skin so thin it bursts the moment a diner bites. The trick is called spherification. Source: molecularrecipes.com (el-bulli-spherification-history); thebazaar.com 'Bazaar Classics: Liquid Olives'.

question: A diner at elBulli in 2003 scooped up a spoonful of tiny, glistening orange beads, Ferran Adrià's first spherified dish, which looked exactly like fish eggs. Expecting the briny, salty taste of caviar, the diner bit down and got a total surprise. What did the beads taste of?
context: This was 'melon caviar' (2003), Ferran Adria's first spherified dish at elBulli on Spain's Catalan coast: dozens of tiny orange beads of sweet cantaloupe-melon juice made to look exactly like fish caviar. Spherification turns a plain liquid into a soft little sphere with a skin that holds until it pops in the mouth; Adria didn't invent it, he made it world-famous. Source: theworlds50best.com '12 iconic dishes of elBulli'; molecularrecipes.com el-bulli-spherification-history.

question: A small glass arrived at an elBulli table holding nothing but a trembling cloud, with no solid food in it at all. It was one of Ferran Adrià's foams: he took the pure flavor of a single food and whipped it into a weightless, airy cloud. What flavor filled the diner's mouth?
context: Ferran Adria invented culinary foam (Spanish 'espuma') in 1994 using a whipped-cream siphon. This one was 'Espuma de humo' (Smoke Foam, 1997): a cloud made from smoked water that tasted of pure smoke, with nothing solid in it at all. Source: theworlds50best.com '12 iconic dishes of elBulli'.

question: A diner orders the Spanish potato omelette at elBulli, and it arrives as three warm layers in a tall glass, onion, then liquid egg, then potato foam, to be eaten with a spoon. Ferran Adrià kept every flavor of the familiar dish and rebuilt only its form, an idea known as deconstruction. What did he say happens to the omelette?
answer: It finishes being made in the diner's mouth.
choices: It finishes being made in the diner's mouth.
It grows hotter with every spoonful.
It turns slowly sweeter as it is eaten.
It tastes like a grandmother's tortilla.
context: Adria called this his deconstructed Spanish omelette (tortilla de patatas): confited onion, a liquid-egg layer, and warm potato foam, spooned up from the bottom so the flavors combine only as the diner eats: 'the tortilla finishes being made in your mouth.' His very first deconstructed dish was a chicken curry (1995), served with every ingredient separate on the plate. Source: eldiario.es (Adria's tortilla); theworlds50best.com '12 iconic dishes of elBulli'.

question: A single dinner at elBulli could run past 40 tiny courses, served one small bite at a time for hours on end. Yet Ferran Adrià opened the restaurant to diners for only about half of each year, leaving the dining room dark the rest of the time. What were he and his team doing in those closed months?
answer: Experimenting on brand-new dishes in a workshop in Barcelona.
choices: Experimenting on brand-new dishes in a workshop in Barcelona.
Resting the worn-out staff and repainting the dining room.
Touring the world's great kitchens to learn other chefs' recipes.
Tending the gardens that grew the restaurant's own produce.
context: To keep inventing, Ferran Adria closed elBulli for about six months every year so his team could experiment full-time at a Barcelona workshop, elBulliTaller, where they created hundreds of brand-new dishes before each season. That flood of invention is how a single dinner could reach more than 40 courses. Source: finedininglovers.com '12 ways elBulli changed the food world'; en.wikipedia.org 'El Bulli'.

question: At the very peak of elBulli's fame in 2011, with around two million booking requests a year chasing its roughly 8,000 seats a season, Ferran Adrià shut its doors for good. He was not quitting cooking, and the restaurant had not failed. What did he turn it into?
context: Adria closed elBulli on July 30, 2011, to turn it into a food-research lab (later the elBulliFoundation). It had actually run at a loss since 2000 -- the real money came from books and lectures, not dinners. He said what he thrived on was creativity, not repeating the same dishes night after night. The restaurant could seat only about 8,000 diners a season against more than two million booking requests a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'El Bulli'; newsweek.com (Ferran Adria interview).  (Legend.)

question: Beans, oats and an apple with its crunchy skin sit on a lunch tray, all packed with fiber, the tough, stringy part of a plant. Suppose you eat them: your gut pulls their sugar and protein into your blood, but the fiber does something different. What happens to it?
answer: It passes through you largely undigested.
choices: It passes through you largely undigested.
It digests into sugar faster than anything else.
It's absorbed straight into your bloodstream.
It gets stored in your liver as fuel.
context: Fiber is the part of plant food your digestive enzymes can't break down, so it passes through largely intact instead of being absorbed for energy — and that indigestibility is exactly the point. It lives in beans, oats, whole grains, vegetables, and fruit skins. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dietary fiber.'

question: Suppose you swap a bowl of sugary cereal for oatmeal at breakfast: instead of going hungry by mid-morning, you stay full until lunch, even for the same calories. The secret is the soluble fiber in the oats. What does it do down in your stomach?
answer: It swells into a thick gel that slows your stomach from emptying.
choices: It swells into a thick gel that slows your stomach from emptying.
It coats your tongue so the food tastes richer.
It hardens into dry flakes that pack your stomach.
It races through your gut, dragging food along.
context: Soluble fiber dissolves in water and forms a viscous gel during digestion, slowing the emptying of the stomach — that gel is why oatmeal keeps you full longer. It's found in oats, barley, beans, and psyllium. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dietary fiber.'

question: A spoonful of wheat bran soaks up water like a sponge without ever dissolving: it is insoluble fiber, the kind carried in the gritty skins of whole grains. Rather than being broken down for fuel, it travels almost all the way through the gut unchanged. What is its main job on the way?
answer: It adds bulk that keeps everything moving along.
choices: It adds bulk that keeps everything moving along.
It slowly releases sugar for steady energy.
It's burned for a quick shot of energy.
It's absorbed and tucked away as body fat.
context: Insoluble fiber does not dissolve; it absorbs and holds water, adding bulk that promotes bowel-movement regularity and keeps things moving. It's found in wheat bran, cellulose, and whole grains — two kinds of fiber, two jobs: gel versus bulk. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dietary fiber.'

question: A mill grinding grain into flour sifts off the thin, papery jacket around each kernel, its bran. Gram for gram, one grain's bran is the fiber king of the whole pantry, nearly 80 percent fiber and ahead of any bean or leafy green. Which grain's bran wins the crown?
context: Corn bran is about 79 grams of fiber per 100 grams — one of the most fiber-dense foods there is. Wheat bran, itself very high, is about 43 grams per 100 grams. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dietary fiber.'

question: Suppose you could follow the fiber from a bowl of oatmeal all the way down: your body makes no enzymes to break it apart, so it reaches your large intestine still whole. It is not wasted there, because something is waiting to feast on it. What feeds on the fiber you eat?
context: Humans lack the enzymes to break down most dietary fiber, so it passes intact into the large intestine, where gut bacteria ferment it. Feeding the bacteria and microbiota of your gut is exactly what the word 'prebiotic' means. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Dietary fiber'; PMC3735932.

question: Trillions of bacteria live in the colon, fermenting the fiber that human enzymes cannot break down and pumping out a short-chain fat as their waste. Suppose you eat a bowl of beans: which part of your body then runs mainly on that fuel?
answer: The cells lining your colon wall
choices: The cells lining your colon wall
The neurons firing in your brain
The muscle in your beating heart
The red cells in your blood
context: When gut bacteria ferment fiber they release short-chain fatty acids — acetate, propionate, and butyrate. Butyrate is the main energy source of colonocytes, the cells lining the colon, supplying roughly 70% of their energy; the cells prefer it even when glucose is available. So fiber feeds your own gut wall through a bacterial middleman. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Short-chain fatty acid'; Nutrients 2017 (MDPI 9/12/1348); PMC5748798.

question: A firm, green banana sits on the counter, packed with resistant starch, a starch that slips past digestion and feeds gut bacteria the way fiber does. Suppose you let it ripen soft and sweet, or bake it into bread: that gut-feeding starch changes. What does it turn into?
answer: Ordinary starch your body digests into sugar.
choices: Ordinary starch your body digests into sugar.
An even tougher starch your gut can't break down.
Pure fiber that passes straight through you.
A protein your muscles can burn for fuel.
context: Green bananas and raw potatoes are naturally packed with resistant starch (type RS2), which resists digestion in the small intestine and reaches the colon, where gut bacteria ferment it just like fiber. But ripening or cooking turns that RS2 back into ordinary digestible starch — a firm green banana feeds your gut, while a soft ripe one feeds it much less. Source: Wikipedia, 'Resistant starch.'

question: Suppose you start every morning with a bowl of oatmeal: it genuinely lowers the cholesterol in your blood, by a sneaky route. The oats' soluble fiber grabs bile acids, the digestive juice your liver builds out of cholesterol, and drags them out of your body. Why does losing those bile acids pull your blood cholesterol down?
answer: Your liver pulls cholesterol from your blood to make replacement bile.
choices: Your liver pulls cholesterol from your blood to make replacement bile.
The bile acids carry loose blood cholesterol out along with them.
The fiber digests the lost cholesterol into harmless sugar.
Your gut simply stops absorbing any cholesterol from food.
context: Oat beta-glucan, a soluble fiber, forms a gel that traps bile acids so they leave the body in stool; the liver then pulls LDL cholesterol out of the blood to make the replacement bile — that's how oats lower cholesterol. The FDA allows the cholesterol-lowering claim for about 3 grams a day of oat or barley beta-glucan. Sources: Frontiers in Nutrition 2019, 'The Cholesterol-Lowering Effect of Oats and Oat Beta Glucan'; HEART UK, 'Oats and barley.'

question: Two potatoes come out of the same oven. One is eaten piping hot, and the body digests its starch into sugar; after one extra step, the other's starch turns into a form human enzymes cannot break down, so it feeds gut bacteria instead. What was that extra step?
answer: Letting it cool in the fridge
choices: Letting it cool in the fridge
context: Cook a potato or rice, then cool it, and some starch re-crystallizes — a process called retrogradation — into 'resistant starch' (type RS3) that your body can't digest but your gut bacteria love. Cooling boiled potatoes overnight at 4°C increased their resistant starch by a factor of 2.8 — nearly triple, just from chilling — so cold potato salad feeds your gut more than hot fries from the same potato. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Resistant starch'; Healthline, 'Cooling Some Foods After Cooking Increases Their Resistant Starch.'

question: At an English chip shop, a cook dips raw white fish in batter and lowers it into hot oil. Minutes later the outside is a crunchy golden jacket, while the fish inside comes out moist and flaky, barely touched by the oil. What cooked the fish inside?
answer: Steam from its own trapped moisture
choices: Steam from its own trapped moisture
Hot oil soaking through the batter
Boiling water released from the batter
Heat conducted from the metal basket
context: The batter forms a crisp shell that the hot oil browns and crisps, but the fish inside barely meets the oil at all - it gently steams in its own moisture, so it stays soft and flaky while the coating crunches. The fish is almost always cod or haddock. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish and chips'; Scientific American, 'Beer Batter Is Better.'

question: Sephardic Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal brought battered fried fish to England, cooking white fish in a crisp coating so it could be eaten cold the next day. Fish and chips feels British to the bone, but this half of it began with them. Why did they want fish that still tasted good cold?
answer: So they could eat it on the Sabbath, when cooking is forbidden
choices: So they could eat it on the Sabbath, when cooking is forbidden
So it could survive the long sea voyage from Spain
So it could be sold cheaply from a street cart
So it would keep right through the winter months
context: The dish was 'pescado frito' - fish fried on Friday to be eaten cold on Saturday, the Sabbath, when Jewish law forbids lighting a fire to cook. In England fried fish was long known as fish cooked 'in the Jewish manner.' Source: Wikipedia 'Pescado frito'; lostjews.org.uk.

question: A chip-shop cook mixes the batter with cold beer instead of water, then dunks in the fish. The instant that batter hits the screaming-hot oil, the coating blooms into a light, crisp crust instead of a dense, doughy one. What is it about the beer that lightens the crust?
answer: Dissolved carbon dioxide rushing out into tiny bubbles
choices: Dissolved carbon dioxide rushing out into tiny bubbles
Sugar in the drink caramelising into a glaze
Yeast in the beer rising and expanding
Alcohol thickening the flour into a gel
context: Fizzy drinks are packed with dissolved carbon dioxide. When the cold batter hits the hot oil, that gas rushes out of solution and froths into thousands of tiny bubbles locked into the crust - giving a lacy, crisp coating instead of a heavy one. Source: Scientific American, 'Beer Batter Is Better'; Food Republic.

question: Spain and Portugal expelled their Jewish families in the 1490s, and many of these Sephardic Jews settled in England with a Friday tradition of fried fish. Back home they had fried nearly everything in one everyday fat, far more often than in butter, lard or beef drippings. Which fat was it?
context: Hard animal fats like tallow and goose fat turn waxy and unpleasant as they cool, but olive oil - the everyday oil of Spain and Portugal - stays light and crisp even stone cold, perfect for a fish fried the day before. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish and chips'; 'Pescado frito.'

question: Fried fish, long a treat for the well-off, turned cheap enough in 1800s Britain to feed whole factory neighbourhoods, and fish and chips was born. Two new things made fish cheap and plentiful in the cities, and one was the railway, racing each haul inland. What was the other?
context: Steam trawlers dragged huge nets and landed vast catches, and the new railways raced the fish inland to the cities. Cheap fish plus cheap potatoes made fish and chips the hot, filling, affordable meal of the industrial working class. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish and chips.'

question: A British family in the Second World War got only a fixed weekly share of meat, butter, sugar and eggs, as rationing reached nearly everything on the table. Fish and chips mattered so much to the nation's morale that the government made a special decision about it. What did rationing do with fish and chips?
answer: It was never put on the ration books at all
choices: It was never put on the ration books at all
Chip shops got priority coupons for fish and oil
Everyone was allowed a small guaranteed weekly portion
The fish was rationed but not the chips
context: Fish and chips was one of the very few foods never rationed in wartime Britain; the government deliberately protected fish and potato supplies. Winston Churchill called the pair 'the good companions,' and, as the story goes, on D-Day in 1944 some British soldiers used 'fish' and 'chips' as a night password to tell friend from foe. Source: Forces News; Wikipedia 'Fish and chips.'

question: In Thai and Vietnamese kitchens, a thin amber liquid is splashed into almost every dish for salt and savor. It is called nam pla in Thailand and nuoc mam in Vietnam. It looks a lot like soy sauce, but it is not made from soybeans. What is it actually made from?
context: Fish sauce — Thai nam pla, Vietnamese nuoc mam — is the everyday salt-and-savor of Southeast Asian cooking. It can look like soy sauce, but there's no soybean in it at all: just small fish and salt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_sauce

question: A fish-sauce maker in Southeast Asia packs a wooden barrel tight with tiny whole fish, bones and all, layers on coarse salt and leaves the mash to ferment for months. The little silvery fish crammed into the barrel are almost always one kind, small and oily. Which fish is it?
context: They're almost always anchovies, packed whole into coarse salt — bones and all — at roughly two to three parts fish to one part salt, then left to ferment for many months, often a year or more (up to two years), with no cooking at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_sauce

question: Wooden barrels packed with nothing but small fish and a lot of salt sit for many months in Southeast Asia, with no broth, no spices and no cooking. Slowly, all on their own, the fish dissolve into a rich, savory brown liquid. What actually breaks them down?
choices: wild yeast from the open air
the heat of the tropical sun
context: This is autolysis: the fish's own natural enzymes slowly break its proteins down into free glutamate, the amino acid behind umami — the deep, savory 'fifth taste' that makes food taste rich and 'complete.' The bottle is basically bottled umami; that taste was isolated and named by chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_sauce; umamiinfo.com/ikedakikunae/

question: A cook uncaps a bottle of fish sauce, and the smell is sharp enough to wrinkle her nose. She stirs it by the spoonful into a simmering curry all the same, as cooks do across Southeast Asia. What happens to that shocking smell once it cooks into the dish?
answer: It mellows into a round, savory depth.
choices: It mellows into a round, savory depth.
It grows even sharper and fishier.
It fades away, adding nothing at all.
context: Fish sauce smells shockingly pungent straight from the bottle, but cooked into a dish it turns to gentle, round savoriness — a few drops add a depth plain salt never could, without tasting 'fishy' at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_sauce

question: A gardener who forgets to pick a head of broccoli sees its tight green beads loosen within weeks. They were flower buds all along, and now they open into tiny flowers. What colour are those flowers?
context: A head of broccoli is a mass of unopened flower buds, so a diner is eating the plant before it can bloom; unpicked, it opens into small four-petaled yellow flowers. The name comes from the Italian broccolo, 'the flowering crest of a cabbage.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broccoli

question: A cauliflower grows its head, a dense dome of unopened flower buds, out in the open garden. Left alone, that head can turn a blotchy red-purple instead of staying snow-white. To keep it white as it grows, what have farmers long done?
answer: fold the big leaves over the head
choices: fold the big leaves over the head
water the plant only after dark
dust the head with white flour
context: The white head, called the 'curd,' is a mass of underdeveloped flower buds. Sunlight triggers the plant's purple pigment, so shading the head under its own leaves keeps it pale; grown in full sun it flushes red-purple. Left unharvested, it finally bolts and flowers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauliflower

question: A diner peels an artichoke's tough scales one at a time and finally reaches the soft heart. She has been eating a giant flower bud, picked young before it could open. Left on the plant, it would open into the flower of what spiny plant?
context: The artichoke is the immature flower bud of a cultivated thistle. A diner eats the fleshy base of the bracts (the 'scales') and the receptacle at the base — the 'heart.' The bud on sale is only a few inches across, but the thistle that grows it can tower to about 2 metres (6+ feet). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artichoke

question: Capers go into the brine as tight buds, pinched off a Mediterranean bush before they can open. A bud left on the branch blooms and sets fruit, and the bush then gives a second, bigger pickle: plump, about the size of an olive and packed with soft seeds. What is it sold as?
context: It's one plant caught at two moments: pick the tight bud and it's a caper; let it bloom and fruit and it's a caper berry (caperberry). Both are brined. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caper

question: A cousin of cauliflower stands out in the produce aisle as a bright lime-green cone built from smaller spiral cones. Every little turret on it is a tiny copy of the whole head, a mathematical fractal pattern rarely seen in food. What is this vegetable called?
