Other American shell beans, such as kidney and cranberry beans, turn up in old recipes too, but fava beans, mung beans and soy beans are Old World crops, far from the first succotash pots. Source: grokipedia, 'Succotash' (etymology corroborated); infoarizona.com, 'Three Sisters.'

question: Twenty or so amino acids link up to build every protein in food, from a bowl of beans to a steak. Nine of them, lysine, methionine and tryptophan among them, are singled out as 'essential', though the label says nothing about which matter most. What sets those nine apart?
answer: The body cannot make them itself
choices: The body cannot make them itself
Only they can build new muscle
context: The nine essential amino acids - lysine, methionine, tryptophan, threonine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, phenylalanine, and histidine - are the ones the human body can't build for itself, so they must come from food. A single food that supplies enough of all nine is called a 'complete' protein. Source: Wikipedia, 'Complete protein.'

question: A Mexican cook wraps beans in a corn tortilla, never having traded a recipe with the cooks of India who spoon lentils over rice, or with those of the Middle East who scoop hummus with pita. Yet all of them landed on the same grain-plus-legume plate. What drove them to it?
answer: each is short of protein building blocks the other supplies
choices: each is short of protein building blocks the other supplies
grains and beans grow best in the very same soil
the two foods stay fresh far longer when stored together
beans cook much faster when boiled beside a grain
context: This grain-plus-legume trick is called protein complementation. No single staple plant - not rice, wheat, corn, or beans on its own - supplies enough of every one of the nine essential amino acids: grains run low in lysine, beans in methionine. Eaten together, the two fill each other's gaps, and they need not even share a meal, only the same day's eating. That's why cultures with no contact all invented the same pairing. Source: Wikipedia, 'Protein combining'; vivolife.com, 'protein complementation'.

question: A botanist lays a wheat stalk, a rice plant, a cornstalk and an oat stem on her bench. They look nothing alike, yet she files all four in one family of plants. What kind of plant are they?
context: All four are members of the grass family (Poaceae). The 'grain' we harvest is simply the grass's seed, packed with starch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryopsis

question: A miller tips a sack of wheat into his hopper, every grain in it crammed with starch. That store never grew to feed people: the parent plant packed it as a first meal for something else. For what?
answer: the baby plant that sprouts from it
choices: the baby plant that sprouts from it
the birds that come to peck it
the mice that raid the field
the mold that grows on damp grain
context: A seed's starchy store is a packed lunch for its own embryo — it fuels the sprout until the new plant grows leaves and can feed itself by sunlight. We just happen to eat the lunch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryopsis

question: A combine rolls through a field at harvest, filling its hopper with the grain people grow more of, by weight, than any other. Each year the world harvests well over a billion tonnes of it, more than wheat and more than rice, to feed people and livestock by the billions. Which grain tops them all?
context: Maize (corn) leads all grains at roughly 1.1 billion tonnes a year, ahead of both wheat and rice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize

question: George Beadle set out to prove that scraggly teosinte, not some lost plant, was the true ancestor of maize. Doubters scoffed that its rock-hard little kernels could never have fed anyone. As the story goes, Beadle answered them with a simple kitchen trick. What did he do to the kernels?
context: This popular anecdote makes Beadle's point: teosinte really was edible, and he ate the popped kernels to prove it. His breeding experiments showed only a few genes separate the wild grass from modern corn — few enough for ancient farmers to bridge. Source: sciencemadefun.net/blog/a-humble-ear-of-corn/  (Legend.)

question: Christiaan Eijkman, a Dutch doctor, fed his lab chickens nothing but polished white rice in 1897. The birds grew too weak to stand, like sailors struck with beriberi, and they recovered once he fed them the bran that milling had thrown away. Doctors of his day hunted a germ behind every illness. What did his test suggest was the real cause?
answer: the sickness sprang from something missing in their food
choices: the sickness sprang from something missing in their food
the sickness sprang from a germ hidden in the rice
the sickness sprang from a poison in the polished rice
the sickness sprang from a diet too meager to live on
context: Feeding the thrown-away bran cured the birds. Eijkman had shown a disease could come not from a germ but from something MISSING in food — the first clue to vitamins. He shared the 1929 Nobel Prize. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beriberi

question: Tiny yeasts get to work on a jar of sweet grape juice left sitting out, eating the grape sugar. They turn it into bubbles of gas and one other substance, the one that makes the juice into wine. What else do the yeasts make?
context: That's the whole trick of fermentation: yeast cells eat the grape's sugar and, with no oxygen around, split each sugar molecule into ethanol (the alcohol) and carbon-dioxide gas (the bubbles). No other ingredient is needed to turn grape juice into wine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winemaking

question: A winemaker crushes a vat of grapes and simply waits. She never stirs in a pinch of yeast, yet the juice soon begins to ferment. Where is the wild yeast hiding, ready to work the moment the sugary juice runs out?
answer: In the dusty bloom on the grape's skin
choices: In the dusty bloom on the grape's skin
Deep in the grape's sugary core
Floating unseen in the cellar air
Down in the roots of the grapevine
context: Grapes wear a dusty, powdery coating called the 'bloom,' and wild yeast lives right in it — a single berry can carry anywhere from a few hundred to tens of thousands of yeast cells. So the instant the grapes are crushed, fermentation can begin on its own, no packet of yeast required. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeast_in_winemaking

question: In a vat of crushed grapes, many wild yeasts start the ferment and die out. The yeast that usually completes the job, turning the juice all the way into wine, also works in kitchens. What other everyday job does it do?
context: The wild yeasts pounce first but often stall out. The one that usually finishes the wine is Saccharomyces cerevisiae — the exact same species bakers use to make bread rise. Because a purely wild ferment can stall or turn to vinegar, winemakers often add a measured dose of this same cultured yeast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeast_in_winemaking

question: Inky-dark purple grapes go into the press, and the juice that runs out is a pale grayish color, not red at all. Yet the same grapes end up as a deep-red wine. Where does the wine get its color?
answer: From soaking the dark grape skins
choices: From soaking the dark grape skins
From the grape seeds soaking in it
From red dye the winemaker stirs in
From the copper of the fermenting vats
context: Crushed grapes give clear-grayish juice; red wine gets its color only by fermenting WITH the dark skins soaking in it — a step called maceration — as red pigments (anthocyanins) and tannins leach out of the skins. Pull the skins out early and even dark red grapes make a pale wine: that's exactly how rosé (brief skin contact) is made. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maceration_(wine)

question: Dom Pérignon, a French monk, worked in a chilly abbey cellar where trapped fizz built up such pressure that finished bottles kept bursting on the racks. Legend makes him the inventor of Champagne's bubbles, though the real story is the reverse. What job did the abbey actually give him?
answer: Chase the bubbles out of the wine
choices: Chase the bubbles out of the wine
Pour the wine into much thicker bottles
Turn the pale wine a deep red
Sweeten the wine with spoonfuls of honey
context: The legend runs backwards. Dom Pérignon was actually told to get RID of the bubbles, because the pressure kept exploding bottles in his cellar. The method for deliberately fizzing wine in a sealed bottle had already been written down earlier, by the English scientist Christopher Merret in 1662. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne

question: A jar of grape juice bubbles away for weeks, then one day goes still and quiet. The winemaker tastes it and finds it's actually still a little sweet — so the yeast clearly didn't run out of sugar to eat. What made the tiny yeast quit and die off?
answer: The alcohol they made built up and poisoned them
choices: The alcohol they made built up and poisoned them
The chilly cellar slowly cooled them to sleep
A layer of vinegar soured them from the top
They simply grew too old and wore themselves out
context: Fermentation ends one of two ways: the yeast either eats all the sugar (a 'dry' wine) or makes so much alcohol that it poisons itself — the alcohol attacks the yeast cells' own membranes, and common wine yeast dies off around 15% alcohol. That ceiling is why plain wine can't reach the strength of a spirit; to go higher, a maker has to distill it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeast_in_winemaking

question: A soda factory pumps carbon-dioxide gas into each can to give it fizz. Champagne makers in northern France never pump any gas into their famous sparkling wine, and they seal the bottles quiet and still. How does the gas end up trapped inside a sealed bottle of Champagne?
answer: The wine is sealed up so it ferments a second time
choices: The wine is sealed up so it ferments a second time
The wine is shaken hard until it froths up
The wine is boiled so steam bubbles rise through it
The wine is frozen, then thawed until it fizzes
context: Champagne's fizz is a SECOND fermentation done inside the sealed bottle. The winemaker adds a little sugar and fresh yeast, then caps it; the new burst of carbon-dioxide gas has nowhere to escape, so instead of bubbling away it dissolves into the wine under pressure — and only reappears as bubbles when the bottle is opened. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne

question: Inside a sealed bottle of Champagne, the trapped gas pushes on the glass at about 90 pounds per square inch, more than twice the pressure in a car tire. Something has to stop that force from firing the fat cork across the room. What pins the cork down?
answer: A little twisted-wire cage over the cork
choices: A little twisted-wire cage over the cork
A ring of hardened candle wax
A strip of sticky cloth tape
A tight band of woven straw
context: That trapped gas builds real force — about 5 to 6 atmospheres, roughly 90 psi, more than twice a car tire — so the cork is a fat mushroom shape pinned down by a little twisted-wire cage called the muselet, invented in 1844. One bottle holds enough dissolved CO2 for tens of millions of bubbles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparkling_wine

question: In a heavy stone bowl, an Aztec cook mashes one soft fruit into a rich, creamy paste, then works in salt and chili to make guacamole. Which fruit is the base of the whole dish?
context: Guacamole is essentially mashed ripe avocado with salt and chili, and it goes back to the Aztecs of Mesoamerica. The lime juice, onion, and cilantro that brighten guacamole today came later - those are Old World foods the Spanish brought to the Americas after 1519. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guacamole

question: A fruit seller's crate of apples, grapes and bananas is mostly sugar and water, like nearly every fruit. The avocado beside them is the rebel: about three-quarters of its calories come from one thing hardly any other fruit carries. What is it?
context: An avocado's flesh is about 15% fat - mostly monounsaturated oleic acid - and only around 0.66 g of sugar per 100 g, so roughly 75% of its calories come from fat, the opposite of nearly every other fruit, which is mostly sugar and water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avocado

question: Cooks in Mexico mashed avocados into guacamole by hand, centuries before anyone owned a food processor, and their tool still sits in Mexican kitchens today. What is that tool called?
context: Guacamole is traditionally mashed in a molcajete - a mortar and pestle carved from a single block of vesicular (volcanic) basalt. The little hand grinder is called a tejolote, and the tool is pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican, used by both the Aztec and the Maya. A metate is a flat grinding slab, a comal is a griddle, and a molinillo is a wooden whisk for frothing chocolate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molcajete

question: A Cajun cook starts her gumbo the way nearly every Louisiana cook does, by chopping the same three vegetables into the pot. Cooks there call this base the 'holy trinity'. Which three are they?
context: The holy trinity is Louisiana's answer to the French mirepoix, which uses carrot where the trinity uses green bell pepper. The Acadians — French colonists exiled from Nova Scotia around 1755 — reached for the pepper because it grew better and cheaper in the Louisiana heat, and German and Italian immigrants added the celery in the late 1700s. Chef Paul Prudhomme popularized the name 'holy trinity' (first documented 1981) — and Louisiana cooks joke that adding garlic is adding 'the Pope.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Holy trinity (cuisine).'

question: A bowl of gumbo, the thick Creole and Cajun stew of Louisiana, goes together in two layers. First a scoop of something starchy drops into the empty bowl, then the spicy stew is ladled on top to soak into it, never stirred through. What goes in first?
context: Gumbo is always ladled over a scoop of white rice, never with the rice stirred through — the grains soak up the broth spoonful by spoonful. Source: Cajun Food Tours, 'The Ultimate Guide to Cajun Gumbo Styles.'

question: Enslaved West Africans, shipped in chains to Louisiana's plantations in the 1700s, carried seeds and words with them. One green, ridged pod they had grown for centuries went straight into their stew pots, and its name, ki ngombo, softened in Louisiana cooks' mouths into 'gumbo'. Which vegetable was it?
context: 'Ki ngombo' (Kimbundu 'quingombo,' Bambara 'gombo') crossed the ocean with the okra itself. In the pot okra does double duty: as the sliced pods simmer, they release a natural slippery sap — a mucilage — that thickens the whole stew with no flour at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gumbo.'

question: A cook stirs two simple ingredients together over the heat for the base of a gumbo, the roux that came from the French side of the dish's family. It darkens from pale gold to peanut-butter brown to dark chocolate, then thickens the pot and gives it a deep, nutty flavor. Which two ingredients make it?
context: A roux — flour cooked in fat — is the French contribution to gumbo, used to both thicken and flavor the stew, and it's the base behind the classic French sauces too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Roux.'

question: A jar of filé sits beside the stove in a Cajun kitchen: a green powder for giving gumbo body, first made by a Native people of the Gulf Coast long before the French arrived. It is nothing fancy, just the dried leaves of one North American tree, ground fine. Which tree?
context: Filé is the dried, ground leaves of Sassafras albidum, a tree of the North American South — a third way (besides okra and a roux) to thicken and flavor a gumbo. Source: Wikipedia, 'Filé powder.'

question: LaPlace, a little town just west of New Orleans, bills itself as the world capital of one coarse pork sausage, packed with black pepper and slow-cured over pecan or sugarcane wood. Cajun cooks lean on it for the smoky backbone of their gumbo. What is the sausage called?
context: Coarse, smoky andouille — a heavily seasoned, double-smoked pork sausage — carries the flavor of a Cajun gumbo. LaPlace, Louisiana, on the Mississippi, calls itself the 'Andouille Capital of the World.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Andouille.'

question: A New Orleans cook making city-style Creole gumbo adds one red ingredient that a country Cajun cook on the bayou would never touch. The Creole pot turns red with it and leans toward seafood; the Cajun pot goes without and runs darker. What is the ingredient?
context: Creole ('city,' New Orleans) gumbo often includes tomatoes and leans toward seafood; Cajun ('country') gumbo uses no tomato and a darker roux — two distinct styles from the same state. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gumbo.'

question: A roux stirred low and slow in oil darkens to a deep chocolate brown and a rich, nutty flavor. Next to a pale, barely cooked roux, what has all that cooking done to its power to thicken the gumbo?
answer: Weakened it — a dark roux thickens far less
choices: Weakened it — a dark roux thickens far less
Strengthened it — a dark roux thickens far more
Left it unchanged — the color doesn't affect thickening
Set it — a dark roux thickens only when cooled
context: Counter-intuitively, the darker a roux gets, the MORE it flavors but the LESS it thickens: a chocolate-brown roux has only about a quarter of the thickening power of a pale one, because the long heat breaks the starch down. That's also why cooks reach for high-smoke-point vegetable oil, not butter, for a dark roux — the oil survives the long, hot cooking without burning. Source: Wikipedia, 'Roux.'

question: The gumbo has simmered all afternoon when the cook lifts it off the burner, waits for the boil to die down, and only then whisks in a spoonful of filé, the green leaf powder Cajuns use to season and thicken the stew. Every cook down the bayou knows filé must never boil. What goes wrong if the pot keeps cooking after it goes in?
answer: The gumbo turns stringy and ropey
choices: The gumbo turns stringy and ropey
The gumbo goes bitter and burnt
The gumbo loses all its color
context: Boiled filé turns a gumbo stringy and ropey — which is exactly why it goes in last, off the heat. Fittingly, the name comes from the French 'filer,' 'to make threads' or 'to become ropy.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Filé powder.'

question: West Africans gave gumbo its name and the French gave it the roux. Its third thickener, filé, came from a people native to the Gulf South, who had ground a local tree's leaves into seasoning before any Frenchman came. Which people gave it?
context: Filé is a gift from the Choctaw of the Gulf South, the first to grind sassafras leaves into a seasoning — their word for it was 'kombo.' So a single bowl of gumbo blends three eighteenth-century Louisiana cultures: West African okra, French roux, and Choctaw filé — three different ways to thicken one pot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Gumbo'; Wikipedia, 'Filé powder.'

question: An Icelander sets out a plate of hakarl, small pale cubes of meat whose cure began with weeks buried in a gravel pit. The meat comes from one huge, slow fish of the freezing Arctic deep, and its fresh flesh is truly poisonous. Which fish becomes hakarl?
context: Hakarl is Iceland's fermented shark, made from the Greenland shark - a fish whose fresh meat really is poisonous to eat. Instead of wasting the catch, Icelanders learned to turn that poison into a meal by letting it rot on purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakarl

question: A sled dog that gulps raw meat from the hakarl shark gets too sick to stand. People are hit hard as well, because a compound packed in the fresh flesh turns into a poison inside the gut. What does that poison do to a person?
answer: Leaves him staggering as if drunk
choices: Leaves him staggering as if drunk
Gives him a raging high fever
Turns his skin a sickly yellow
Covers him in itchy red welts
context: The compound is TMAO, which the gut turns into trimethylamine, leaving a person dizzy and staggering as if drunk; in northern Norway an old expression, 'hai full', calls the state 'shark drunk'. The same untreated meat makes sled dogs so ill they cannot even stand up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark ; National Geographic on Morten Stroksnes's book Shark Drunk.

question: In a shallow gravel pit, a curer lays a gutted, headless shark and piles heavy stones on top of it, and there it stays for weeks. What is all that weight doing to the meat?
answer: Squeezing the poisonous fluids out of it
choices: Squeezing the poisonous fluids out of it
Crushing the tough flesh until it is tender
Keeping hungry Arctic foxes away from it
Sealing out the air so it cannot spoil
context: Pressed under piled stones in a gravel pit, the shark slowly drains its toxic fluids - the first step toward making it safe. Buried like this, it ferments for about six to twelve weeks depending on the season. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakarl

question: The Greenland shark behind hakarl spends its whole life in the freezing Arctic deep. It keeps a heavy load of one chemical stored right in its flesh, which helps it cope with the cold, salty sea and is one reason the fresh meat is unsafe to eat. Which chemical is it?
answer: Urea, the waste chemical in urine
choices: Urea, the waste chemical in urine
Cyanide, the poison in bitter almonds
Lactic acid, made by tired muscle
context: Like other sharks, the Greenland shark keeps its waste urea (the same chemical in urine) in its flesh rather than flushing it out, along with a related compound, TMAO. Those chemicals are not a flaw: they help the shark float and keep its body fluids in balance with cold, salty, deep Arctic water. Both make the fresh meat unsafe, and the TMAO turns into a toxin in the gut. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakarl

question: A newcomer in Iceland raises a small cube of properly cured hakarl. It tastes milder than he fears, but the smell arrives first and hits hard, so he pinches his nose before the cube reaches his mouth. What does the eye-watering reek smell like?
choices: Burnt rubber, like a tire fire
context: That ammonia reek is the finishing sign of the whole cure: the urea and related chemicals that once made the meat poisonous have broken down, and ammonia is what remains. The smell really is worse than the taste, which is why hakarl is served in tiny cubes on toothpicks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakarl

question: Icelanders have eaten hakarl for centuries, and the gravel pit is only the start of its cure. When the shark comes out from its weeks under the stones, it is still not ready to eat. What is the second half of the cure?
answer: It is cut into strips and hung to dry for months
choices: It is cut into strips and hung to dry for months
It is packed into barrels of brine for months
It is smoked over smouldering birch for months
It is boiled soft and sealed under fat for months
context: The gravel pit is only stage one. The drained shark is cut into strips and hung out to dry for several months. Over that long hang a brown crust forms on the outside, and the crust is trimmed away before the shark is cut into the little cubes served on toothpicks. Rot first, then wind - that is the whole recipe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakarl

question: A thick steak hits a screaming-hot cast-iron pan on a bare burner and sizzles at once. A dark crust forms first on the side pressed to the metal as the steak cooks from the outside in. How is the heat getting into the steak?
choices: By a moving hot liquid or gas
By invisible waves across a gap
context: This is conduction: heat marches straight out of the hot metal into whatever it touches, cooking contact-point by contact-point from the outside in. It's why the side pressed against the pan browns first. Source: 123foodscience.com, 'Heat Transfer Methods'.

question: Three pots work side by side in a busy kitchen: pasta boiling, dumplings steaming in a basket, oil deep-frying. They look like three different ways to cook, yet all of them carry heat into the food the same way. What do they share?
context: All three are convection — a moving hot fluid (water, steam, or oil) sweeps the heat onto the food. A boiling pot and a deep fryer look nothing alike, but the fluid doing the work is the same idea. Source: 123foodscience.com, 'Heat Transfer Methods'.

question: A camper holds a marshmallow a few inches above glowing embers, up in the air and touching no flame, and it still browns and blisters. A red-hot overhead grill browns the top of a casserole below it the same way, with no one flipping the dish. Which of the three ways heat travels are both using?
choices: Direct touch with a hot surface
context: This is radiation — infrared waves stream across open space and heat the surface with no contact and no fluid in between (radiation needs no matter to travel through). It's why a broiler browns a casserole's top without you ever flipping it. Source: 123foodscience.com, 'Heat Transfer Methods'.

question: A cook turns the burner all the way up under a pot of boiling water. But the water can't get any hotter. It just boils harder. Past 100°C / 212°F it turns to steam and leaves the pot. Given that hard ceiling, what is one thing boiling water can never do to food?
answer: Give it a browned, crisp crust
choices: Give it a browned, crisp crust
Cook it all the way through
Kill the germs on its surface
context: Boiling and steaming top out at 100°C, but the Maillard browning that builds a crust only runs at roughly 140°C and up — so a wet method can never brown, no matter the time. That is exactly why a crust needs a hot dry pan, hot oil, or a hot oven. Source: Wikipedia, 'Maillard reaction'.

question: A cookware maker shapes frying pans from aluminum or copper, never from wood, glass or plastic. Those metals beat water hundreds of times over, and air thousands of times over, at one particular job, and that job is why pans are metal. What is that job?
choices: Holding onto heat for a long time
Standing up to very high heat
Being cheap and easy to make
context: Metal's superpower is thermal conductivity — how fast it passes heat along. Copper carries heat at about 385 and aluminum about 205 watts per meter-kelvin, versus water at only ~0.6 and air at ~0.026 — metal shuttles heat hundreds of times faster than water and thousands of times faster than air. Source: thermtest.com, 'Thermal Conductivity and Cooking Technique'.

question: A baker reaches a bare hand into a 100°C oven for a second and barely feels a sting, while a splash of boiling water at the very same 100°C would scald her badly. Why does the water burn so much worse than the air?
answer: Water carries far more heat than air
choices: Water carries far more heat than air
Water soaks deeper into the skin
Water covers more skin at once
Air blows away before it can burn
context: Same temperature, wildly different heat delivered: a gram of water holds about four times the heat energy of a gram of air (specific heat ~4.18 vs ~1.0 J/g·°C). The water dumps far more energy into your skin — the same reason a wet, water-carrying method cooks so much faster than dry oven air at the same temperature. Source: USGS, 'Specific Heat Capacity and Water'.

question: A cook pinches a sprig from each pot on her windowsill, basil, mint, oregano and sage, for her sauce. Kitchens call all four herbs, never spices, for one reason. Which part of each plant does she use?
context: An herb is the leafy green part of a plant; a spice is any OTHER part -- a seed, bark, root, flower, or fruit. That one rule sorts the whole spice rack. Basil, mint, oregano, sage, thyme, and bay laurel are all herbs for the same simple reason: the part used is the leaf. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Herb' -- 'Herbs generally refers to the leafy green or flowering parts of a plant, while spices are usually dried and produced from other parts of the plant, including seeds, bark, roots and fruits.')

question: A gardener buries a knobbly piece of supermarket ginger with one of its pale bumps facing up and keeps it warm and damp. Within weeks a green shoot pushes up from the bump, new roots reach down, and a whole new plant grows. What part of the ginger plant is that knob?
context: The knob is a rhizome, an underground stem, whatever the shop label says. Its little bumps are nodes, the joints of a stem: a rhizome like ginger (and its cousin turmeric) can push a new shoot up and new roots down from any of them, while a true root has no nodes and ends in a root cap. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Rhizome' -- 'Roots do not have nodes and internodes and have a root cap terminating their ends,' whereas rhizomes 'retain the ability to allow new shoots to grow upwards.')

question: Bees fly some 55,000 miles and visit about two million flowers, by common estimates, to make one pound of honey. What does a forager gather at each flower to carry home and turn into honey?
context: Raw flower nectar is roughly 70-80% water, thin as sugar-water; bees dry it down to honey's final ~17%. Foragers gather pollen too, but as protein food for the young, not to make honey. The figures of about 55,000 colony-miles and some 2 million flowers per pound are widely cited approximations. Source: blog.aghires.com/honey-bees; Wikipedia, 'Honey' and 'Honey bee'.

question: Inside the warm hive, an army of worker bees sets about turning a thin, sweet flower juice, about three-quarters water, into thick, gooey honey. What do the bees do to the juice to thicken it?
answer: fan it hard with their wings
choices: fan it hard with their wings
knead it with their front legs
coat it in a layer of wax
pack it tight into the cells
context: The hive runs about 35°C (95°F), and the bees' wing-fanning evaporates the water — dropping nectar from ~70-80% water down to honey's ~17%. Source: Wikipedia, 'Honey'.

question: Worker bees ripening honey in the hive add an enzyme that turns some of its sugar into acid, plus tiny traces of a common antiseptic, the same germ-killer found in a bottle in the medicine cabinet. Which antiseptic does honey make a little of?
context: A bee enzyme, glucose oxidase, converts some glucose into gluconic acid plus small amounts of hydrogen peroxide — the antiseptic that fizzes on a scraped knee. That, plus honey's acidity (around pH 3.9), backs up its main water-pulling defense. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Science Behind Honey's Eternal Shelf Life'.

question: A baker sweetens one cake with honey and another with sugar, and the honey cake stays soft and moist for days after the sugar cake has gone dry and stale. The same power lets an open jar of honey slowly turn watery and even ferment. What unusual thing does honey do?
answer: It soaks up moisture straight from the surrounding air.
choices: It soaks up moisture straight from the surrounding air.
It slowly leaks out its own stored water over time.
It kills off the yeasts and molds that dry cake out.
It holds onto heat and stays slightly warm for hours.
context: Honey is hygroscopic — it draws water out of the air. That keeps honey-sweetened cakes moist, but it also means an unsealed jar can absorb enough water (above ~20-25%) for yeast to grow and ferment it. So 'honey never spoils' holds only while it stays sealed and low in water — the preservation is about low water, not magic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Honey'; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: In a cave in eastern Spain, there is an 8,000-year-old painting of a person high on a cliff, clinging to rope ladders, holding a basket in one hand, and pushing the other arm deep into a hole in the rock. What is the climber after?
answer: Honey from a wild bees' nest
choices: Honey from a wild bees' nest
Eggs from a cliff bird's nest
Bats from a roost in the crack
Snails from the damp rock face
context: The cave is the Cuevas de la Arana - the Spider Caves - at Bicorp, Valencia, and the figure, nicknamed the Man of Bicorp, is reaching into a wild bees' nest on the cliff while bees swarm around him. It is the earliest known depiction of bees and of honey-gathering by humankind. He wasn't climbing for a treat: cane sugar only spread to the West in the medieval era, so honey was the single sweetest, most energy-dense food a person could get - worth a rope ladder and a cloud of stings. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuevas_de_la_Ara%C3%B1a ; https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/man-of-bicorp-cave-painting

question: Egyptian workers sealed pots of honey inside the pharaohs' tombs more than three thousand years ago, as gifts for the afterlife. Archaeologists who opened such pots reported the honey unspoiled, with no mold and no rot. What does honey do to a mold spore or germ that lands in it?
answer: Pulls the water out of it until it dries up and dies
choices: Pulls the water out of it until it dries up and dies
Coats it in a wax film that seals it off from the air
Poisons it with a toxin the bees gather from flowers
Traps it in sugar crystals that crush it as they grow
context: Honey is only about 17-18% water, and sugar packed that tightly pulls hard on any water near it. A microbe that lands in honey has the moisture yanked out through its own wall, so it dries out and dies before it can grow. The bees stack a second defense on top: an enzyme they add (glucose oxidase) makes gluconic acid and a trace of hydrogen peroxide, leaving honey acidic enough to kill bacteria. As UC Davis honey expert Amina Harris puts it, as long as the lid stays on and no water gets in, 'honey will not go bad.' Honey was among the goods placed in Egyptian tombs, including Tutankhamun's - though the famous tale of tomb honey still being edible rests on reports of unspoiled pots rather than settled proof. The chemistry underneath it is not in doubt. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-science-behind-honeys-eternal-shelf-life-1218690/  (Legend.)

question: Ancient Egyptian beekeepers kept their bees in long tubes of clay and mud, stacked into walls of hives. The flowers bloomed at different seasons along different stretches of the country. By traditional accounts, how did the keepers keep their colonies in fresh blossom all year?
answer: Floated the hives along the river on rafts
choices: Floated the hives along the river on rafts
Hauled the hives into the hills on donkeys
Ringed each stack of hives with flower gardens
Rebuilt the colonies in new hives at each grove
context: By traditional accounts of Egyptian beekeeping, the keepers loaded their clay hives onto rafts and floated them along the Nile, drifting the bees to wherever the flowers were blooming that season and returning laden with honey - a migrating apiary on the water. The stacked tubes of clay and Nile mud ran roughly 1.2 m long and 30-40 cm wide, a design still used in the region thousands of years later. The earliest known picture of beekeeping itself, rather than wild honey-raiding, is a relief in the sun temple of the pharaoh Nyuserre Ini from about the mid-2400s BCE: a beekeeper blows smoke into the hives while other men pour honey into jars and seal them. In Egypt honey was sweetener, wound medicine, cosmetic, and temple offering all at once, and the bee was the symbol of Lower Egypt. Sources: https://livebeekeeping.com/history-of-beekeeping/beekeeping-egypt/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beehive  (Legend.)

question: André and Édouard Michelin launched the Michelin Guide in 1900, and today one of its stars can make a chef famous overnight. Yet the brothers were neither chefs nor food critics, and their little red book was meant to help drivers find good stops on long trips. What did their company make?
context: In 1900 there were fewer than 3,000 cars in all of France, and Andre and Edouard Michelin ran the Michelin tire company in Clermont-Ferrand. The award that now crowns the world's finest restaurants began life as a giveaway from a rubber company. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michelin Guide'.

question: A motorist in 1900 could pick up a slim red book for nothing, one of 35,000 copies the Michelin brothers printed and gave away. Flipping through that very first Michelin Guide, what would he have found filling most of its pages?
context: That first free guide was really a survival manual for early motorists: maps, where to find petrol, how to change or repair a tire, plus lists of mechanics and hotels. Restaurant listings were just one small corner of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michelin Guide'.

question: The Michelin brothers began handing out thousands of guidebooks for nothing in 1900, when the cars on all of France's roads numbered under 3,000. The brothers had a plan for those few drivers. How did giving the guide away help them sell more tires?
answer: it got people driving more, wearing their tires out
choices: it got people driving more, wearing their tires out
it charged restaurants a fee to be listed inside
it came bundled with a coupon for cut-price tires
it named the cheap tire brands drivers should avoid
context: More driving meant more worn-out tires and more replacement sales. The free guide was clever marketing: get France's few motorists to travel farther, and they would wear through their Michelin tires and come back to buy more. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michelin Guide'.

question: A Michelin inspector settles quietly into a Paris restaurant for dinner, and nobody in the kitchen knows who she is. In a small leather notebook she weighs whether the place has earned a star. The guide insists its stars are awarded for one thing only. What is it?
context: Michelin insists the decor, the tablecloths, and even the service do not affect a restaurant's star count -- only what's on the plate. That's why a tiny bistro with plastic chairs can outrank a glittering palace. Source: guide.michelin.com, 'What is a Michelin star?'.

question: A diner planning a trip around Michelin's stars reads the guide's famous ladder of phrases. One star means a restaurant is 'worth a stop' if she is passing by; two mean it is 'worth a detour', out of her way. What do three stars promise her?
answer: worth a special journey -- cross the whole country to eat there
choices: worth a special journey -- cross the whole country to eat there
worth a passport stamp -- fly abroad for a single dinner
worth a weekend away -- turn one meal into a holiday
worth a mountain drive -- wind for hours up to the door
context: Michelin's official ladder: one star is 'high-quality cooking, worth a stop'; two stars, 'excellent cooking, worth a detour'; three stars, 'exceptional cuisine, worth a special journey' -- worth crossing the whole country just to eat there. Source: guide.michelin.com, 'What is a Michelin star?'.

question: Plush chairs and sparkling chandeliers fill a grand dining room. Michelin rates that comfort and luxury with a separate mark of its own, running from one for 'quite comfortable' up to five. What symbols make up that mark?
context: Michelin ranks comfort with fork-and-spoon symbols -- one for 'quite comfortable' up to five for real luxury. Because it has nothing to do with the cooking, a grand five-fork dining room can still hold zero stars. Source: Tasting Table, on Michelin's fork-and-spoon rating.

question: A chef who spotted a Michelin inspector in the dining room would cook the meal of his life for that one table, and every other diner would leave thinking the restaurant better than it really is. Michelin's famous fix has been in place since the 1920s. What do its inspectors do?
answer: book under fake names and pay the bill like ordinary diners
choices: book under fake names and pay the bill like ordinary diners
send a disguised assistant to eat while they wait outside
order every dish as delivery so they are never seen
come only on the busiest nights, hidden in the crowd
context: Michelin inspectors reserve under fake names, eat, and pay the full bill exactly like any other guest, so no kitchen can spot them and put on a special show. The secrecy runs deep -- inspectors are advised not to reveal their job even to close friends, and one may eat around 250 restaurant meals a year. Source: Elite Traveler and Forbes, on anonymous Michelin inspectors.

question: In an Indian kitchen a cook wants fresh paneer for dinner, but there is no cheese-making kit in the house: just a pot of milk heating on the stove. Twenty minutes later a block of homemade paneer sits draining in a cloth. One ordinary kitchen ingredient made that hot milk curdle. What was it?
context: Paneer is acid-set: the lemon's acid alone curdles the hot milk, with no other setting agent. It is never aged and does not melt, so it stays firm, which is why a cook can fry it or simmer it in a curry. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paneer'.

question: A small bottle of rennet sits on a cheesemaker's shelf, and she stirs just a few drops into a whole vat of milk. Plain acid would curdle the same milk almost for free, yet she would never swap it in. What does rennet do to milk that acid cannot?
answer: sets it into a firm, springy gel
choices: sets it into a firm, springy gel
adds the sharp tang cheese needs
kills the bacteria that spoil it
gives it a rich, buttery flavor
context: Acid alone makes soft, fragile curds; rennet instead sets a firm, elastic gel that can be pressed and aged into hard cheeses. Nearly every hard cheese on Earth depends on it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cheese'.

question: An Italian cheesemaker refuses to throw out the runny whey left from a batch of firmer cheese. She gently reheats the whey until soft, fluffy new curds float to the top. Then she skims those off as a second, softer cheese made from the leftovers. What is this cheese?
context: Ricotta means 'recooked' in Italian, because the whey is cooked a second time. Nothing is wasted: the leftovers of one cheese become a whole new one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ricotta'.

question: A cheesemaker in the Swiss Alps slices open a fresh wheel of Emmental cheese and reveals its famous secret — big round holes, called 'eyes,' scattered through the pale yellow paste. No one drills them and no one presses them in; the wheel forms them all on its own during the months it ages down in the cellar. What actually creates each of those perfectly round holes?
answer: a bubble of gas given off by bacteria
choices: a bubble of gas given off by bacteria
a pocket of air trapped between the curds
a drop of whey that dried and shrank
a lump of salt that dissolved away
context: A bacterium (Propionibacterium freudenreichii) feeds on the lactic acid inside the cheese and releases carbon dioxide gas. Trapped in the firm paste, the gas collects into round bubbles, the 'eyes' of Swiss and Emmental. Source: Wikipedia, 'Emmental cheese'.

question: A freshly made block of cheese tastes mild and a bit bland. A year or more in a cool cellar turns the same cheese sharp, nutty and deeply complex, though nothing new is added the whole time: no salt, no herbs, no fresh milk, no spices. Where does all that new flavor come from?
answer: microbes and enzymes break its proteins and fat apart
choices: microbes and enzymes break its proteins and fat apart
trapped water dries out and concentrates the taste
salt from the rind creeps in and seasons it through
milk sugars slowly toast and turn the paste nutty
context: Over weeks to years, enzymes and microbes break cheese's bland proteins and milkfat down into a rich mix of savory, tangy, nutty compounds. This slow breakdown is exactly what 'aging' is for. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cheese'.

question: A supermarket cheese counter is stacked with wheels and blocks, most of them set with rennet that never came near a calf. For thousands of years cheesemakers took that enzyme from the stomachs of young calves, lambs and kids, but since the 1990s the animal source has grown rare. Where does modern rennet come from?
answer: grown by microbes in big tanks
choices: grown by microbes in big tanks
context: It is called 'fermentation-produced chymosin': gene-edited microbes carry a copy of the calf's own gene and brew the identical enzyme in tanks. It was the first genetically engineered enzyme the FDA ever approved, and it now sets the large majority of American and British cheese; traditional animal rennet is down to a small fraction. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rennet'.

question: A pot of fresh milk gets a dose of rennet, the enzyme first taken from calf stomachs. In the milk drift tiny bundles of casein protein that never clump on their own, because each wears a fuzzy, negatively charged coat that pushes its neighbors away like magnets turned the same way. Within minutes the milk has turned to curd. What does the enzyme do to the bundles?
answer: snips off their fuzzy coating so they stop repelling and clump
choices: snips off their fuzzy coating so they stop repelling and clump
adds a positive charge that pulls the negative proteins together
heats them until they melt and fuse into a solid sheet
wraps each one in fat so they stick together like glue
context: The coating is a hairy piece of the protein called kappa-casein. Chymosin makes a single precise cut to remove it; stripped bare, the caseins lose their mutual repulsion and bond into a solid curd. The clipped-off piece, glycomacropeptide, floats away in the whey. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chymosin'.

question: Swiss cheesemakers watched the famous round holes in their Emmental shrink and even vanish, and for years nobody could say why. Researchers found the answer in 2015: each hole needs a tiny seed to start forming around, and spotless modern milking had stripped that seed out of the milk. What does each hole grow around?
context: A 2015 Agroscope study found the carbon-dioxide bubbles need microscopic specks of hay dust as seeds to form around. Old open-bucket milking let bits of hay fall into the milk; spotless modern milking machines removed them, so the holes grew smaller and fewer. Source: dairyreporter.com, 2015 (Agroscope study).

question: A spoonful of tahini spreads on toast like peanut butter and even tastes a bit like it, a smooth, oily, tan paste, yet not a single peanut goes into the jar. It is nothing but one kind of seed, toasted and ground. Which seed?
context: Tahini is made by hulling sesame seeds, toasting them, and grinding them into an oily paste — nothing else. It's the same sesame base used in halva and baba ghanoush, and it's one of the two things (with chickpeas) that make up hummus. Source: Wikipedia 'Tahini' & 'Hummus'.

question: A cook in a Middle Eastern kitchen blends cooked chickpeas with a spoonful of tahini, the pale seed paste, and tastes a bland, pasty mush. It only becomes hummus once she stirs in two classic Mediterranean flavors for a bright, tangy kick. Which pair does she add?
context: That lemon-and-garlic finish is what turns plain blended chickpeas into hummus. It's traditionally served with a puddle of olive oil, a few whole chickpeas, a sprinkle of parsley, and a dusting of red paprika on top. Source: Wikipedia 'Hummus'.

question: A shopper in a Beirut market writes 'hummus' on her list. In Arabic the word is no fancy name for a dip, just the everyday grocery word for one ingredient. Which ingredient does it name?
context: 'Hummus' (حُمُّص) is literally the Arabic word for 'chickpea,' so ordering hummus means ordering 'chickpeas.' The dish's full name, 'hummus bi tahina,' translates word-for-word as 'chickpeas with tahini.' Source: Wikipedia 'Hummus'.

question: A beginner unscrews a fresh jar of tahini, the Middle Eastern seed paste, and it looks split and spoiled: clear oil floats over a stiff, pale paste. He is ready to toss it in the trash, but the tahini is perfectly fine. What should he do with the jar?
context: Because real tahini is just ground sesame and its own natural oil, the oil separates and rises to the top in the jar — exactly like natural (no-stir-added) peanut butter. Stir it smooth again before using. Source: Wikipedia 'Tahini'.

question: A diner at a Lebanese restaurant gets hummus as silky as pudding, spreading in soft ribbons across the plate. At home he blends the same cooked chickpeas with the same tahini in the same blender, and his batch comes out gritty and grainy. The restaurant's cooks take one extra, tedious step that he skips. What is it?
answer: They peel the skin off every bean
choices: They peel the skin off every bean
They blend in a handful of ice cubes
They soak the beans in lemon juice
They chill the beans overnight first
context: The papery skins are exactly what make cheap hummus feel gritty. Boil the chickpeas soft enough and the skins slip right off, leaving the ultra-smooth purée that good restaurants serve. Source: America's Test Kitchen 'For Creamier Hummus, Skin Your Chickpeas'; smittenkitchen 'ethereally smooth hummus'.

question: A pot of chickpeas simmers on the stove for hummus, and the cook tosses in one pinch of a common white kitchen powder. The beans turn tender in half the time and blend up perfectly smooth. Which powder does the cook add?
context: A pinch of baking soda makes the cooking water alkaline, which breaks down the tough chickpea skins so they loosen and float away — and softens the beans faster too. (Cream of tartar would do the opposite: it's acidic.) Source: Jerusalem Post 'baking soda trick'; Ottolenghi & Tamimi method via America's Test Kitchen.

question: About 300 cooks gathered near Beirut in 2010 and filled one bowl with more than 10,000 kilograms of hummus, more than double the world record a rival nation had set earlier that year. Lebanon took the title, one more round in the feud nicknamed the Hummus Wars. Whose record did the cooks smash?
context: The colossal batch weighed roughly 10,450 kg — over 23,000 pounds — and claimed the Guinness World Record. Because Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Syria, and Egypt all claim hummus as their own, the ongoing feud has been nicknamed the 'Hummus Wars.' Source: Wikipedia 'Hummus'.

question: A gardener picks a vegetable on a hot summer day and bites into a cool, crisp slice, and it is almost like taking a drink: about 95 percent of its weight is water, held inside a thin, edible skin. It turns up in salads and gets pickled by the jarful. Which vegetable is it?
context: Harvard Health lists cucumber, celery, and romaine lettuce all around 95% water — so watery they hydrate you almost like a drink. Denser roots like carrots, potatoes, and beets hold far less. Source: Harvard Health, 'Using food to stay hydrated'; NCBI Nursing table 6.2 places cucumber, lettuce, and celery in the 90–99% water band.

question: A cook unwraps a thick raw steak on the counter, dense, deep red and cool to the touch. It feels like a solid block of protein, yet weighed gram for gram, well over half of it turns out to be something most people never guess. What makes up most of a raw steak?
context: Even a 'solid' steak is mostly water. The USDA notes fresh beef muscle is roughly 65–75% water: an eye-of-round roast is about 73% water raw and still ~65% after roasting — cooking is what drives the moisture out, which is why meat shrinks and lightens in the pan. Source: USDA Food Safety & Inspection Service, 'Water in Meat & Poultry.'

question: Heinz Valtin, who studied kidneys at Dartmouth, looked in 2002 for the science behind the well-known rule of eight glasses of water a day, and found none. The rule apparently began with a 1945 report advising about that much water in total, but readers forgot its next line. What did that line say?
answer: That most of that water is already in your food
choices: That most of that water is already in your food
That the amount depends on how much you weigh
That children need far less than adults do
That coffee and tea should not be counted
context: Kidney physiologist Heinz Valtin of Dartmouth reviewed the evidence in 2002 and wrote that he found 'no scientific proof that absolutely every person must drink at least eight glasses of water a day.' The rule traces to a 1945 Food and Nutrition Board report that advised about 2.5 quarts (~1 mL per calorie) — whose very next sentence read, 'Most of this quantity is contained in prepared foods.' People remembered the number and forgot the caveat. Source: Valtin, Am. J. Physiology 2002; 1945 Food and Nutrition Board via Dartmouth/Geisel.

question: A basketball player pushing hard through a game can lose more than a liter of sweat an hour. Sports scientists who collect and test that sweat find it full of electrolytes, but one mineral makes up the bulk of the loss, the one athletes scramble to replace with sports drinks and salty snacks. Which electrolyte does sweat carry away the most of?
context: Sodium is the main electrolyte in sweat — roughly 1 gram per liter (people range from about 0.2 to 2 g/L), which is why hard sweat tastes salty and stings the eyes. Potassium is the runner-up at only ~150–300 mg per liter. The body even adapts: after 1–2 weeks in the heat it conserves sodium, cutting sweat-sodium losses by up to half. Source: Precision Hydration/MySportScience; American Heart Association.

question: A runner sweats for hours through an endurance race and refills on nothing but plain water, glass after glass. Sports doctors have documented that such runners can end up seriously ill, the opposite of the usual warning about drinking too little. What goes wrong inside the body?
answer: Their blood's salt gets diluted dangerously low
choices: Their blood's salt gets diluted dangerously low
Their stomach can't absorb that much at once
Their kidneys shut down from the overload
Their body temperature crashes too fast
context: Drinking only plain water through hours of heavy sweating can dilute the blood's sodium — 'water intoxication,' or exercise-associated hyponatremia. A New England Journal of Medicine study found about 13% of Boston Marathon runners had it (mostly mild), and at least 8 endurance-event deaths have been recorded since 1985. The lesson isn't that water is dangerous — it's that after heavy sweat, plain water alone isn't the whole story, so athletes add electrolytes. Source: Almond et al., NEJM 2005; Am. J. Medicine 2015.

question: A guest sits down to dinner in an Ethiopian home. There is no fork, no spoon and no plate; a huge, spongy, sour flatbread called injera lies spread like a tablecloth, with spicy stews in mounds on top. How does he eat the meal?
answer: Tear off pieces of the injera and use them to scoop up the stew
choices: Tear off pieces of the injera and use them to scoop up the stew
Lift the whole flatbread and let the stew slide into his mouth
Sip the stew first, then eat the bare bread on its own
Roll each bite up inside a fresh green leaf like a wrap
context: Injera is both the serving platter and the utensil: the stews sit on top and diners tear off spongy pieces to pinch up each bite — no cutlery needed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera' ('often both the serving platter and utensil for a meal').

question: All through an Ethiopian meal, the stews soak down into the injera underneath. By the end, the top dishes are gone but the bottom sheet of bread is drenched in juices. What happens to that gravy-soaked layer of injera?
answer: It's eaten last of all, the prized final bite of the whole dinner
choices: It's eaten last of all, the prized final bite of the whole dinner
It's peeled up and tossed out, now far too soggy to enjoy
It's dried in the sun and saved to crisp up the next day
It's carried off to the kitchen for the cook to finish alone
context: Nothing is wasted — the bottom 'tablecloth' of injera soaks up all the juices and is eaten at the end of the meal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera' ('the injera served on the bottom soaks up the juices... this tablecloth of injera is also consumed').

question: Injera starts as a runny batter of water, salt and one flour, milled from a grain so tiny that about 100 of its seeds weigh as much as a single grain of wheat. What is this smallest grain in the world called?
context: Teff is the smallest grain in the world — roughly 100 teff seeds equal one wheat grain — and it's the base flour of injera. Source: Seward Community Co-op, 'Talking Teff: The Story of the World's Smallest Grain'; Ancient Grains Alliance.

question: An Ethiopian cook spreads one enormous round of injera on the tray and spoons different stews over it in colorful mounds, with no separate plates at all. How is that single bread meant to be eaten?
answer: Two or three people share it, all reaching into the same bread
choices: Two or three people share it, all reaching into the same bread
Guests tear off portions to carry back to their own seats
The host eats first, then passes what's left down the line
It's cut into equal wedges and handed out one per person
context: The meal is communal — two or three people eat from one shared platter of injera, reaching into the same bread. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera' ('Two or three people may share the same injera').

question: Doro wat, chicken slow-simmered for hours in spiced clarified butter with sweet onions and chili, is the most famous of the stews served on injera. A cook making a proper doro wat tucks one surprising extra into the pot whole. What is it?
context: Doro wat, the most famous wat, is a spicy chicken stew traditionally served with a whole hard-boiled egg simmered in the sauce. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera'; Baking Hermann; Kosher Cowboy, 'Injera Recipe'.

question: A girl with celiac disease can't eat bread made from wheat, barley or rye, because her body reacts badly to one substance in those grains. In Ethiopia she could eat injera every day, since the grain it is made from contains none of it. What is that substance?
context: Teff is naturally gluten-free, so injera is safe for people with celiac disease — a nutrition win built right into a daily staple. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teff' ('Teff is gluten free'); Ancient Grains Alliance.

question: A pot of the spicy Ethiopian stew called wat glows a deep, rusty red and carries a slow, building heat — both come from one dried spice blend, stirred in by the spoonful and built on ground red chillies and warm spices. What is this signature blend called?
context: Berbere is the rusty-red Ethiopian spice blend — dried chillies, fenugreek, nigella, ginger, cardamom and more — that gives wat its color and heat. Source: Helen Graves, 'Ethiopian Spiced Butter, Berbere and Doro Wat'; The Daring Gourmet.

question: A cook in the Ethiopian highlands grinds injera's tiny grain into flour, as cooks there have for thousands of years. The grain may be the smallest on Earth, but it is a nutritional heavyweight: a plate of injera delivers a big share of the day's need for one mineral, which the grain carries more of than almost any other. Which mineral is it famous for?
context: Teff is exceptionally iron-rich — about 7.6 mg per 100 g, among the highest of any grain — so injera is a strong dietary source of iron. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teff' (7.63 mg iron per 100 g); Ancient Grains Alliance.

question: A bowl of injera batter, just flour stirred into water, sits out at room temperature for two or three days before its cook goes near the griddle. What is happening inside the batter during that long wait?
answer: It's fermenting as wild yeasts and bacteria feed on it, giving off gas and acid
choices: It's fermenting as wild yeasts and bacteria feed on it, giving off gas and acid
It's resting quietly while the raw flour swells and softens into a smoother batter
It's drying out in the open air until it stiffens into a firm dough
It's soaking up salt sprinkled across the top to cure and preserve it
context: Injera's signature sour tang comes from fermentation — the teff batter is left to bubble and sour for about two to three days, much like sourdough, before it's cooked. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera' (primary fermentation 24–72 hours); Yang's Nourishing Kitchen.

question: Thin injera batter hits a hot griddle, and steam pushes up through it, popping open hundreds of little holes across the top and leaving a soft, lacy surface. A torn piece uses those holes to grab the stew and soak it up, and Ethiopians have a name for them. What are they called?
context: The lacy holes on injera are called its 'eyes' — they form as steam bubbles up during cooking, and those eyes are exactly what let torn pieces grab and soak up the stew. Source: Wikipedia, 'Injera' ('visible bubbles known as eyes... the eyes of injera help to pick up stews').

question: At an Ethiopian table, a woman wraps a bite of stew in a torn piece of injera and feeds it to her friend with her own fingers. Ethiopians call this gursha, Amharic for 'mouthful', and some gurshas are far bigger than others. What does an extra-big gursha tell the friend?
choices: The friend has had enough to eat
The meal is about to come to an end
The cook made far too much food
context: Gursha (Amharic for 'mouthful') is the custom of using injera to scoop a bite and feed it by hand into someone else's mouth — a gesture of love and respect, and the bigger the bite, the deeper the affection. Source: Salaam Urban Village, 'Gursha'; Comboni Lay Missionaries, 'The Ethiopian Gursha'.

question: Villagers in the alpine valleys of Switzerland a century ago had necks that bulged with huge, soft lumps called goiters. The trouble sat in the thyroid, a small gland at the front of the neck that helps run the body's energy; starved of one mineral, it cannot build its hormones and swells. Which mineral does it need?
context: Iodine is so central that it makes up about 65% of the weight of the thyroid hormone T4 and 59% of T3 -- no iodine, no thyroid hormone, so the starved gland swells trying to keep up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Iodine deficiency.'

question: A sushi chef lays a bamboo mat on his counter, sets a thin, dark-green sheet on top, spreads sticky rice across it and rolls the whole thing into a tight tube. Those wrapper sheets are one of the richest natural sources of iodine, the mineral the thyroid gland needs. What are they made from?
context: Ounce for ounce, nothing beats sea vegetables -- kelp, nori, and dulse -- for iodine, because iodine steadily washes out of the land and collects in the sea. That is why seafood-eaters rarely fell short. Source: Wikipedia, 'Iodine deficiency.'

question: David Cowie, a Michigan doctor, faced a puzzle in the early 1920s: doctors knew a trace of iodine could prevent goiter, but how could a whole country take a tiny dose every day? He pushed a cheap answer, putting the iodine into one thing nearly everyone eats a little of daily. What did he add it to?
context: Salt was the perfect carrier -- cheap, eaten by nearly everyone, and used in small, steady amounts all year round. America's first iodized salt went on sale on May 1, 1924 in Michigan grocery stores, and Morton Salt carried it nationwide that same year. Source: HistoryFacts; Healio.

question: Doctors mapped whole inland 'goiter belts', in the Great Lakes states, the Appalachians and the Swiss Alps, where 1920s health surveys found swollen necks in classroom after classroom. Places hundreds of miles apart were struck the same way. What did those scattered regions share that bred so many goiters?
answer: The poor soil that fed their crops
choices: The poor soil that fed their crops
The hard water in their deep wells
The thin air of the high country
context: Iodine slowly leaches out of the land and drains into the sea, so glacier-scraped and mountainous inland soils -- the Great Lakes country, the old Appalachians, the high Swiss Alps -- grow crops and graze animals holding almost no iodine, and the families who ate that local food fell short. It wasn't the water, the air, or the cold that did it; it was the barren ground beneath the fields. US health surveys in the 1920s found goiter in 70 to 100 percent of schoolchildren in parts of Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. Source: Healio; Wikipedia, 'Iodine deficiency.'

question: Feyrer, Politi and Weil, three economists, measured decades later what iodized salt had done beyond shrinking swollen necks. In the most iodine-starved quarter of the country, that cheap pinch in the salt shaker had lifted something in the whole next generation. What did it raise in those children?
context: Because a baby's brain needs iodine to develop in the womb, iodization quietly boosted brainpower. Economists Feyrer, Politi, and Weil found that for the quarter of Americans who had been most iodine-deficient, it raised IQ by roughly 15 points -- about one standard deviation. Source: NBER working paper (Feyrer, Politi & Weil).

question: A kid who is always tired, pale and cold-handed gets a blood test, and the doctor points to low iron. Iron sits at the heart of hemoglobin in the red blood cells, where it does one job for the whole body. What is that job?
answer: Grabs oxygen in the lungs and carries it everywhere
choices: Grabs oxygen in the lungs and carries it everywhere
Fights off invading germs and viruses
Breaks down food into usable energy
Builds and repairs muscle after exercise
context: Iron is the core of hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that grabs oxygen in the lungs and ferries it body-wide. Run low and the blood carries less oxygen — that's iron-deficiency anemia: tired, pale, weak, cold-handed, and foggy-headed. Source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Iron Health Professional Fact Sheet.

question: For a patient short of iron, a doctor's first and simplest advice is to eat more of one food, the one with the richest, best-absorbed iron. Low iron is the planet's commonest nutrient shortfall, shared by more than 1.6 billion people. Which food is it?
context: Iron deficiency is the world's most common nutritional deficiency — 1.6+ billion people, and roughly 10% of toddlers, teen girls, and women of child-bearing age in the US and Canada. Red meat and seafood carry the richest, most easily-absorbed iron. (Leafy spinach is a famous trap — more on that later.) Source: NCBI StatPearls, Dietary Iron; NIH ODS Iron Fact Sheet.

question: A doctor treating low iron cares less about the milligrams on a label than about which form of iron a patient eats. Meat, fish and poultry carry the heme form; beans, lentils and greens carry the non-heme form. What is the crucial difference between them?
answer: The heme form from meat is absorbed easily; the non-heme plant form is absorbed poorly
choices: The heme form from meat is absorbed easily; the non-heme plant form is absorbed poorly
The non-heme plant form is absorbed easily; the heme form from meat is absorbed poorly
The heme form carries oxygen, while the non-heme form only stores it
The non-heme form is destroyed by stomach acid, while heme survives it
context: Heme iron — the animal form locked in the hemoglobin and myoglobin of meat, fish, poultry, and blood — is absorbed easily (about 25%) and shrugs off dietary blockers. Non-heme iron — the plant form in beans, lentils, greens, and fortified grains — absorbs poorly (often 17% or less, as little as 5–12% on an all-plant diet) and is easily blocked. Source: NCBI StatPearls, Dietary Iron; NIH ODS Iron Fact Sheet.

question: A vegetarian builds dinner on beans, lentils and grains, whose iron is the poorly absorbed plant kind. Nutritionists have a famous trick to rescue it: eat that plant iron alongside a food rich in one particular vitamin, and a single meal's absorption can leap two- to threefold. Which vitamin unlocks plant iron?
context: Vitamin C keeps iron in its soluble, absorbable form: about 100 mg (a squeeze of citrus, some bell peppers or tomatoes) can raise a single meal's plant-iron absorption two- to threefold. The honest catch — it's dramatic per meal but modest over a whole day; one controlled study found little difference in daily iron absorption across vitamin C intakes from 51 to 247 mg. So an orange helps THAT dinner more than it moves a whole day's iron balance. Source: Hallberg & Brune, Am J Clin Nutr; Cook & Reddy, Am J Clin Nutr (PubMed 11124756).

question: A diner washes down a hamburger, a solid hit of iron, with a hot mug of tea. In one classic study, the tea cut how much of the meal's iron the body kept by about 64 percent; with coffee the loss was about 39. What in tea and coffee grabs the iron and drags it out of reach?
context: Tannins (polyphenols) in tea and coffee lock iron into insoluble iron-tannate complexes. In the classic study, a cup of tea with a hamburger slashed iron absorption about 64%, coffee about 39%. Whole grains, beans, nuts, and seeds do similar damage through their storage compound, phytates. Best move: keep tea and coffee away from iron-rich meals. Source: Morck, Lynch & Cook, Am J Clin Nutr 1983; NIH ODS Iron Fact Sheet.

question: Popeye downed cans of spinach for bursts of super-strength, and generations grew up sure that spinach is the ultimate iron food. The raw leaf does contain iron, yet the body absorbs only about 1 to 2 percent of it. What in spinach locks its iron away so tightly?
context: Raw spinach really holds iron (about 2.7 mg per 100 g), but it's loaded with oxalates that bind the iron so tightly the body absorbs only about 1–2%. Popeye is legend, not nutrition — the iron is technically there, it just mostly passes straight through. Source: NIH ODS Iron Fact Sheet (oxalate inhibition); nutrition-science reviews on spinach iron bioavailability.

question: Two nutrition researchers, Brittin and Nossaman, cooked the same tomato spaghetti sauce two ways in 1986. One batch came out with barely any iron in it; the other, from the same recipe and the same tomatoes, held nearly ten times as much. What did the pair do differently to the second batch?
answer: Simmered it in a bare cast-iron pan
choices: Simmered it in a bare cast-iron pan
Stirred in a big handful of spinach
Cooked it under a blazing-hot broiler
Added an extra pinch of table salt
context: Cooking acidic, watery food in bare cast iron leaches real, usable NON-heme iron into the food. In H. C. Brittin and C. E. Nossaman's 1986 study, spaghetti sauce jumped from 0.61 to 5.77 mg iron per 100 g (about 9.5x) and applesauce from 0.35 to 7.38 mg. A new, unseasoned skillet gives up the most; a well-seasoned old one gives up less (the baked-on fat shields the metal), and more acid, moisture, simmering, and stirring all pull out more. Source: Brittin & Nossaman, J Am Diet Assoc, July 1986, 86(7):897–901.

question: A typical Western eater gets just 10 to 15 percent of his iron in the heme form from meat, yet that slice makes up about 40 percent of what his body actually absorbs. Plant iron floats loose in the gut, where other compounds grab it, but meat's iron comes protected. What is it packaged inside?
answer: The red pigments of its blood and muscle
choices: The red pigments of its blood and muscle
The white fat marbled through its muscle
The tough collagen in its sinews
The mineral salts in its juices
context: That's the honest core of the two-iron story: heme iron is only about 10-15% of the iron a Western diet EATS, yet it delivers roughly 40% of the iron actually ABSORBED, because it travels inside the meat's own hemoglobin and myoglobin, held in a ring-shaped molecule called a porphyrin, out of reach of the gut's blockers. Plant-only iron can still work, but its eaters have to work the system: vegetarians are advised to aim for about 1.8x the iron intake, lean hard on the vitamin-C pairing, and keep tea away from meals, which is why iron deficiency is more common among people who eat no meat. Source: NCBI StatPearls, Dietary Iron; NIH ODS Iron Fact Sheet.

question: Cooks out in the fields of Valencia made the first paellas in the open air. The dish's name surprises most people: 'paella' is an old Valencian word borrowed from Latin, and it has nothing to do with rice or flavor. What does the word name?
answer: the shallow pan it's cooked in
choices: the shallow pan it's cooked in
the outdoor feast it's served at
the open fire it's cooked over
context: The Valencian word 'paella' comes from the Latin 'patella,' meaning a shallow pan — it names the wide, two-handled steel pan the rice is cooked in, and the same word came to mean the food too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paella.'

question: A tourist cafe serves a paella piled with shrimp, mussels and squid. Cooks in Valencia, where the dish was born, say real paella holds no fish or shellfish at all, only meat from the land. Which three belong in a true Valencian paella?
context: Authentic paella valenciana is a farmland dish of rabbit, chicken, snails, and beans cooked over an open fire — a 2022 study found rabbit in 89% of traditional versions, and Valencians consider fish or shellfish 'absolutely out of the question.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Paella.'

question: A paella is nearly done. The cook turns the heat up high and falls silent, listening closely to the pan, because one sound means the socarrat, the prized crust of golden rice stuck to the very bottom, is forming just right. What is the cook listening for?
context: Socarrat is the crisp, caramelized layer of rice at the bottom of the pan. Over an open fire it forms on its own; cooks coax it out by turning up the heat at the end and listening for the crackle — as long as it doesn't burn, it's the most prized bite. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paella.'

question: An Italian cook stirs a pan of risotto without stopping, and that stirring is exactly what turns it thick and creamy. A cook making paella follows the opposite rule: once the broth goes into the pan, the rice is never stirred, not once, or the whole dish is wrecked. What does stirring do to paella rice that ruins it?
answer: it releases starch that turns it gummy
choices: it releases starch that turns it gummy
it makes the broth boil over the rim
it cools the pan and stops the cooking
it turns the golden rice muddy brown
context: Stirring releases the rice's starch. That creaminess is exactly what a risotto wants, but in a paella it turns the grains gummy and ruins the dish — so the cook leaves it untouched, letting firm short-grain bomba rice drink up the broth while staying separate. Source: bascofinefoods.com, 'Risotto vs Paella.'

question: Spanish settlers in New Orleans, the popular story goes, set out to cook their beloved paella. One prized spice cost far too much to ship across the Atlantic, so they made the dish without it and let tomatoes fill the gap. Which pricey spice did that first jambalaya go without?
context: The popular story says New Orleans' Spanish settlers couldn't get costly saffron, so tomatoes stood in for it — turning paella into jambalaya. (Historians note Louisiana's West African rice heritage, from enslaved people brought from rice-growing Senegal, was just as formative.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Jambalaya'; Britannica, 'Jambalaya.'  (Legend.)

question: In New Orleans, Creole cooks stir tomatoes into their jambalaya and turn it red. Out in Cajun country, cooks leave the tomato out entirely, yet their 'brown' jambalaya still comes out a deep, rich color. Where does the Cajun version get its brown?
answer: from meat seared dark in the pot
choices: from meat seared dark in the pot
from a spoonful of dark molasses
context: Creole (New Orleans) jambalaya adds tomatoes for a 'red' dish; Cajun (Acadiana) jambalaya skips the tomato and browns the meat in a cast-iron pot, so the caramelized stuck bits — the 'sucs' — give it a deep brown color. It's the same Creole/Cajun split seen in gumbo. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jambalaya.'

question: In a small Japanese home kitchen, one light knife with a short, flat blade and a slightly rounded tip does all the daily work. It slices meat, cuts up a whole fish and chops a pile of vegetables. Which all-purpose Japanese knife is it?
context: The santoku (三徳, 'three virtues' or 'three uses') was created in the 1940s to fold the strengths of older single-purpose knives into one generalist blade — the 'three' being meat, fish, and vegetables. It ends in a blunt, rounded 'sheep's foot' tip and is built for straight down-chops, not the rocking of a Western chef's knife. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santoku

question: With his traditional Japanese knife, a sushi chef slices a tomato nearly see-through; its edge is far keener than a common European knife's. That sharpness comes from an unusual way of grinding the blade. What is odd about how these knives are ground?
answer: They're ground on one side only, with the back left flat
choices: They're ground on one side only, with the back left flat
They're ground into fine saw-teeth all along the edge
They're ground steeper on the softer lower half
They're ground round on both faces, like a spoon's lip
context: This is a single-bevel edge — sharpened on one side only, the other side left flat (though the 'flat' back actually carries a shallow concave hollow, the urasuki). That one-sided geometry lets the edge reach a far more acute point than any double-bevel, V-ground knife can manage. Source: https://www.echefknife.com/blogs/blog/the-anatomy-of-the-japanese-single-bevel-knife

question: At a sushi counter, the chef picks up his yanagiba, a long, slender knife shaped like a willow leaf, and turns a block of glistening raw tuna into sashimi. His cutting motion is the mark of a master; get it wrong and the fish comes out ragged. What is that motion?
answer: One long, smooth pull-stroke, heel to tip
choices: One long, smooth pull-stroke, heel to tip
Short rocking chops along the blade's belly
A firm straight-down press, like a paper cutter
context: The yanagiba ('willow blade,' for its long willow-leaf shape) is the single-bevel sashimi knife. The chef draws the whole blade heel-to-tip through the fish in one motion — a stroke called hiki-giri — so the cut face stays smooth, shiny, and even. The standard professional size runs about 270 mm (10.6 in) precisely so a whole slice comes off in a single draw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yanagi_ba

question: A sushi master slicing sashimi would never drag his yanagiba back and forth through a block of raw tuna. Sawing the fish does not just look clumsy; it genuinely ruins the piece. What does sawing do to a slice of raw fish?
answer: It tears and bruises the flesh into a dull, mushy slice
choices: It tears and bruises the flesh into a dull, mushy slice
It warms the surface until it turns pale and opaque
It leaves a bitter, metallic taste along the cut
It packs the fibers tighter, turning the slice rubbery
context: Pushing or sawing back and forth leaves a jagged, serrated cross-section and tears and bruises the delicate flesh, turning the fish mushy and killing its glossy sheen. The long single-bevel yanagiba lets the slice part in one clean pull. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yanagi_ba

question: A cook breaking down a whole fish reaches for the deba, a heavy, thick-spined Japanese knife that powers straight through the backbone and ribs. Because it looks like a stubby little cleaver, new owners grab it to hack a chicken or pork-chop bone, and regret it. Why is that a mistake?
answer: The hard bone would chip its keen, one-sided edge
choices: The hard bone would chip its keen, one-sided edge
The greasy pork would rust its bare carbon-steel blade
The heavy blow would crack the knife's wooden handle
The dense bone would snap the brittle hardened steel
context: The deba (出刃, 'fish-preparer') is thick-spined (about 5–7 mm) and built for fish bone, not butcher bone: hacking a big pork or beef bone would chip its keen single-bevel edge. It first appeared in the Edo period in Sakai, near Osaka. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deba_bocho
