The rule holds only if the cook adds one more step right after the meat leaves the heat, the step that lets the middle finish cooking safely. What is that step?
answer: Letting it rest for three minutes before cutting
choices: Letting it rest for three minutes before cutting
Searing the outside once more over high heat
Slicing it open right away to release the heat
Brushing the surface with oil and salt
context: During that three-minute rest off the heat, the interior keeps rising and pathogens keep dying — so the pause is part of the cooking, not just a wait. Source: USDA FSIS Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart; CIDRAP.

question: American cooks spent generations cooking pork until it was gray, firm and dry, all to destroy one dangerous parasite. Once modern hog farming had nearly wiped it out, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) in 2011 approved a rosy, juicy pork chop cooked to 145 degrees. Which parasite had cooks been overcooking pork to kill?
context: The trichinella worm causes trichinosis; it once made undercooked pork risky, so pork was cooked to 160°F and beyond. With the worm nearly gone from modern hog farming, the 2011 change made a pink pork chop officially fine. Source: CIDRAP; TheNoshery.com.

question: A tiny worm parasite can hide in pork and make people miserably sick when the meat is eaten undercooked, and a hundred years ago it was common in American pigs. Modern farm rules made it rare, and in a survey published in 2024 the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) checked 3.2 million pigs from farms across the country. What did that enormous check find?
answer: Not a single pig was infected
choices: Not a single pig was infected
About one pig in ten was infected
A few thousand pigs were infected
Roughly half the pigs were infected
context: Trichinosis in the US has collapsed — from about 400 cases a year in the 1940s to roughly 15-20 now — and a USDA survey of about 3.2 million pigs, sampled over 54 months and published in 2024, turned up zero infections. Source: USDA ARS (ars.usda.gov, 2024); CDC; Food-Safety.com; Wikipedia, 'Trichinosis.'

question: On the grill, one burger can turn fully brown in the middle before it is safe to eat, while another can stay pink inside long after it is safe, for harmless chemical reasons. Since color misleads both ways, what is the only reliable way to know a burger is safe to eat?
answer: Read the temperature at its center with a thermometer
choices: Read the temperature at its center with a thermometer
Press the center and judge it by how firm it feels
Wait until the juices running from it turn clear
Go by the cooking time shown on the clock
context: USDA research found more than a quarter of patties brown before reaching 160°F, while others stay pink after they're safe. Doneness is about looks; safety is about temperature — only a thermometer in the center tells the truth. Source: USDA FSIS, 'Color of Cooked Ground Beef.'

question: A cook who wants chicken for dinner pulls a rock-hard frozen package from the freezer that morning. Food-safety experts call one slow, hands-off way the best for defrosting it: set the package in one spot and walk away for many hours. Where should the package go?
context: The fridge is the no-planning default because it holds a safe, steady 40°F or below — cold enough that bacteria can't multiply. The catch is time: a pound of ground meat needs a full day, and a big turkey about a day for every 4 to 5 pounds. The other two safe methods — cold water in a sealed bag, or the microwave — are faster but need your attention. Source: USDA FSIS, 'The Big Thaw — Safe Defrosting Methods.'

question: A frozen chicken sits on the warm kitchen counter all afternoon, thawing for dinner. Hours later the cook pokes it, finds the center still a solid block of ice and decides it must be perfectly safe to cook. Food-safety experts say she may have ruined it already. Why?
answer: The outer layer has been sitting warm for hours, growing bacteria
choices: The outer layer has been sitting warm for hours, growing bacteria
The frozen center has formed sharp ice crystals inside the meat
The whole chicken is still frozen too hard to cook evenly
The surface has dried out and lost most of its flavor
context: This is exactly why the counter is off-limits. The surface warms into the 'danger zone' — 40°F to 140°F — where bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes, all while the core stays frozen for hours. The rule of thumb: perishable food should never sit at room temperature longer than 2 hours (just 1 hour above 90°F). Source: USDA FSIS, 'The Big Thaw' and 'Danger Zone (40°F–140°F).'

question: On the microwave's defrost setting, a frozen chicken breast thaws fast, and the cook plans to leave it on the counter and make dinner a few hours later. Food-safety experts say not to wait but to get it straight into a hot pan, because a microwave never defrosts quite evenly. What has the microwave already done to the meat?
answer: Warmed the edges until a few spots got hot enough to start cooking
choices: Warmed the edges until a few spots got hot enough to start cooking
Sealed the surface so the meat's juices can no longer escape
Chilled the center below freezing while only the edges thawed
Toughened the muscle fibers so the meat needs a long rest
context: Microwaves heat unevenly. While parts of the chicken are still icy, other spots race up past 40°F and even begin to cook — putting those bits squarely in the bacteria-friendly 'danger zone.' Let it sit and those warm spots keep growing bacteria, so microwave-thawed food has to go straight into the pan or oven. Source: USDA FSIS, 'The Big Thaw — Safe Defrosting Methods.'

question: Two raw chicken breasts thaw on the same day, one overnight in the cold fridge and the other all afternoon on the kitchen counter. Then dinner plans change. Food-safety experts say the fridge-thawed breast is safe to refreeze raw, but the counter-thawed one must be cooked or thrown out. Why is the fridge-thawed breast safe?
answer: It never got warm enough for the bacteria to multiply
choices: It never got warm enough for the bacteria to multiply
The cold actually killed off the bacteria already on it
Its sealed bag kept new bacteria from getting in
It thawed so fast the bacteria never caught up
context: Because the fridge one never left refrigerator temperature, it stayed out of the danger zone the whole time, so it's safe to refreeze raw. The one trade-off is juiciness: slow thawing grows large ice crystals that rupture the meat's cells, so it 'drips' and cooks up a little drier — safe, just less juicy. The counter one, though, spent hours warming in the danger zone; refreezing would only lock the bacteria in. (Meat thawed by the cold-water or microwave methods can be refrozen too — but only after you cook it first.) Source: USDA FSIS, 'Freezing and Food Safety' and 'The Big Thaw.'

question: Three crimson threads sit at the heart of a small purple flower that blooms each autumn. Plucked by hand and dried, they become saffron, the costliest spice on Earth. Which flower gives saffron?
context: The saffron crocus, Crocus sativus, is a lilac-purple crocus that blooms in autumn; the red threads we call saffron are dried from its blossoms - and it is the priciest spice on Earth. (Wikipedia, 'Saffron')

question: The royal house of Navarre paid eight times as much for a pound of saffron around 1300 as for a pound of black pepper, and merchants weighed the crimson threads almost ounce for ounce against gold. What do traders still call saffron?
context: Saffron regularly sells above US$5,000 a kilogram and $10,000+ for top grades, so traders call it 'red gold.' (JSTOR Daily, 'Saffron: The Story of the World's Most Expensive Spice')

question: Growers need about 150,000 flowers to make one kilogram of dried saffron, which fetches over $5,000. Yet the flower is easy to grow and cheap to plant. Where does all that cost come from?
answer: Every flower is opened and its threads are pinched out by hand.
choices: Every flower is opened and its threads are pinched out by hand.
Rare, delicate machines must tease out each thread.
The threads must be aged for years before they can be sold.
The threads must be smoked over a fire for many weeks.
context: No machine can do it - a kilogram takes roughly 370-470 hours of hand labor, about 440,000 threads pinched out one flower at a time. The cost is in the picking, not the growing. (JSTOR Daily)

question: Pickers in Iran and Spain bend over field after field each autumn, plucking the three deep-red threads from the heart of every saffron flower and tossing the showy petals away. It takes thousands of blooms to fill a single ounce. Which part of the flower are those threads?
context: The three crimson threads are the stigmas - the flower's female, pollen-catching parts. Every saffron crocus yields only three. (Wikipedia, 'Saffron')

question: Because real saffron costs a small fortune, sharp dealers have sold a look-alike for centuries. It's nicknamed 'poor man's saffron,' and it's really the dyed orange petals of a completely different plant, chopped and passed off as the real crimson threads. It looks close in the spice jar, but tastes of almost nothing. Which plant do the fakers usually use?
context: Real saffron is whole, deep-crimson, trumpet-shaped threads; the common fake is safflower (Carthamus tinctorius), or powder cut with turmeric or paprika. Buying whole threads, not powder, is the best defense. (Roco Saffron)

question: A pot of Persian rice glows gold with saffron, and its perfume drifts through the kitchen. One compound in the threads gives the colour and another the scent, which chefs and spice merchants reach for strange comparisons to describe. Which two smells do they most often name?
context: That hay-and-honey aroma comes from safranal, one of three compounds at work in saffron: crocin colors it gold, picrocrocin makes it faintly bitter, and safranal gives the smell. (Wikipedia, 'Saffron')

question: Saffron pickers walk into their fields at first light every October, in a harvest that lasts only a week or two. Every flower must be gathered on the same morning it opens, never a day later. What forces them to pick at dawn?
answer: Each bloom opens at dawn and wilts in the day's heat.
choices: Each bloom opens at dawn and wilts in the day's heat.
Bees strip the threads from any flower left past sunrise.
The threads turn red only in early-morning light.
Cold night air makes the threads too brittle to pull.
context: The crocus blooms for only about one to two weeks in October, and each flower opens at dawn and wilts as the day heats up - so pickers gather them the morning each bloom opens, before the sun ruins them. (JSTOR Daily)

question: A cook suspects the 'saffron' she bought is a cheap fake, dyed petals passed off as the real threads. She drops a few threads into a glass of warm water and watches. Real saffron gives itself away by how it colours the water. What do genuine threads do?
answer: They stain the water gold slowly and stay red themselves.
choices: They stain the water gold slowly and stay red themselves.
They bleed a fast blood-red and fade to white.
They sink and turn the water cloudy grey.
They turn the water bright orange within seconds.
context: Real saffron releases its gold slowly over 10-15 minutes while the threads stay red; safflower and dyed imitations bleed a fast blood-red and the threads fade to white. (Roco Saffron)

question: A cook making paella wants saffron's gold to spread evenly through the rice instead of scorching in one spot. A common beginner's mistake is to toss the threads straight into the hot oil in the pan. What should the cook do instead?
answer: Steep the threads in warm broth, then stir that golden liquid in.
choices: Steep the threads in warm broth, then stir that golden liquid in.
Toast the threads in a dry pan until they smoke.
Grind the threads into the dry rice before adding any liquid.
Sprinkle the whole threads on top just before serving.
context: Saffron's gold pigment, crocin, is water-soluble but won't release into fat - so you steep the threads in warm water, broth, or milk for 15-20 minutes and pour that golden liquid into the dish. Fried in oil, the color just scorches in spots. (Savory Spice Shop)

question: Every plant in a saffron field is sterile and makes no seed that will grow; sow its 'seeds' and nothing ever comes up. Yet farmers have raised the flower for thousands of years. How do they make new saffron plants?
answer: They divide the underground bulbs by hand and replant them.
choices: They divide the underground bulbs by hand and replant them.
They take leaf cuttings and root them in damp sand.
They graft buds onto a hardier wild crocus stem.
They split side shoots off the flower stalk and pot each up.
context: The saffron crocus is a sterile triploid: it sets no viable seed, so every plant is a clone, propagated by hand-dividing its underground corms (bulbs). Humans have cloned this one flower for thousands of years. (Wikipedia, 'Saffron')

question: A kid helping bake a cake sneaks a lick of raw batter off the spoon. Raw batter can carry salmonella, a germ that brings fever and days of misery, and the risk rides in on just one of its raw ingredients. Which one?
context: Raw eggs are the salmonella carrier in cake batter, cookie dough, homemade Caesar dressing, mayonnaise, and eggnog — the CDC and FDA warn that these uncooked-egg foods can make people sick. (In raw cookie dough the flour is a separate germ risk, a different story.) The name 'salmonella' has nothing to do with salmon the fish — it's named for American veterinarian Daniel Elmer Salmon, whose lab first studied it in the 1880s. Sources: CDC 'Raw Flour and Dough' https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/no-raw-dough.html ; WebMD 'Eating Raw Cookie Dough' https://www.webmd.com/food-recipes/food-poisoning/eating-raw-cookie-dough-salmonella-infections ; Wikipedia 'Daniel Elmer Salmon' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Elmer_Salmon

question: A cook scrubs an egg's shell until it is spotless, sure that a clean shell means the raw egg inside is safe. Yet a perfectly clean, uncracked egg can still carry salmonella somewhere no scrubbing can reach. How did the germ get there?
answer: An infected hen sealed it in before the shell formed.
choices: An infected hen sealed it in before the shell formed.
It grew there on its own as the egg sat aging.
Nearby eggs passed it in through the carton walls.
It bred from a tiny spot of blood in the yolk.
context: A hen carrying Salmonella Enteritidis in her ovaries or oviduct can pass the bacteria straight into the yolk or white before the shell hardens — called transovarian transmission — so a clean, uncracked egg from a healthy-looking hen can still carry it. That's why scrubbing the shell does NOT make a raw egg safe. It's rare, though: only about 1 in 20,000 U.S. eggs is estimated to be internally contaminated. Sources: Discover Magazine https://www.discovermagazine.com/how-eggs-can-harbor-salmonella-even-when-they-look-perfectly-clean-48131 ; Live Science 'How Does Salmonella Get Inside Eggs?' https://www.livescience.com/10016-salmonella-eggs.html

question: A restaurant kitchen whisks up raw-egg Caesar dressing, cracking every egg from a carton stamped 'pasteurized.' The salmonella in those eggs is gone, yet each one still cracks open runny and raw. How were the eggs in that carton treated?
answer: Bathed in their shells in warm water for close to an hour.
choices: Bathed in their shells in warm water for close to an hour.
Soaked overnight in cold vinegar right through the shell.
Rinsed with a food-safe spray that kills germs on contact.
Chilled in a salt brine cold enough to kill the germs.
context: Pasteurized eggs are gently warmed in the shell in a hot-water bath at roughly 130-140°F (about 135-136°F) for close to an hour — warm enough to kill salmonella throughout the egg, but too cool to firm the white or yolk. They come out looking and pouring exactly like raw eggs, so a kitchen can safely serve raw-egg Caesar dressing, mayonnaise, hollandaise, tiramisu, meringue, or eggnog. Sources: Wikipedia 'Pasteurized eggs' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteurized_eggs ; USDA ARS 'A New Way To Pasteurize Eggs' https://agresearchmag.ars.usda.gov/2017/apr/eggs/

question: A fried egg sizzles in a home kitchen pan. Heat is the cook's kill switch for salmonella, since every germ dies in an egg cooked hot enough, but no one can see bacteria, and a home kitchen has no thermometer for a single fried egg. What sign in the pan shows the egg got hot enough all the way through?
answer: Both the white and the yolk have set firm.
choices: Both the white and the yolk have set firm.
The white has turned solid while the yolk still runs.
The edges have crisped and browned in the pan.
The egg has puffed up and stopped sizzling.
context: USDA and FDA guidance is to cook eggs and egg dishes until both the white and yolk are firm — an internal 160°F, where salmonella dies in about 2 minutes. A runny yolk is the higher-risk one: sunny-side-up, over-easy, poached, and soft-boiled eggs all leave the yolk under-heated, so any salmonella inside survives. For scale, the CDC estimates salmonella causes about 1.35 million infections, 26,500 hospitalizations, and 420 deaths in the U.S. each year — the leading cause of food-poisoning hospitalizations and deaths. Sources: FoodSafety.gov 'Salmonella and Eggs' https://www.foodsafety.gov/blog/salmonella-and-eggs ; TODAY https://www.today.com/food/egg-safety-salmonella-sunny-side-eggs-safe-eat-t127088 ; CDC 'About Salmonella Infection' https://www.cdc.gov/salmonella/about/index.html

question: At a salad bar, one common raw topping is a notorious repeat offender in salmonella outbreaks. It grows in the warm, damp conditions the germ loves, and it reaches the plate raw, with nothing on the way to kill the germ. Which topping is it?
context: Seeds like alfalfa and mung bean need warm, humid days (about 70-77°F) to sprout — the very conditions that let salmonella bloom — and sprouts are eaten raw, with no cooking kill-step. Even a few bacterial cells on a seed can multiply thousands- to hundred-thousand-fold during sprouting. The FDA advises children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with weak immune systems to avoid raw sprouts entirely. Sources: Colorado State University Food Source Information 'Sprouts' https://www.chhs.colostate.edu/fsi/food-articles/produce/sprouts/ ; CDC EID 'Infections Associated with Eating Seed Sprouts' https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/5/5/99-0503_article

question: A tub of 'edible' cookie dough waits in a supermarket fridge, made to be eaten raw from the spoon with no baking at all. Homemade dough eaten raw is risky for two separate reasons, and one of them is the flour, which can carry germs of its own. What two swaps let the store dough skip the oven safely?
context: Store-bought 'edible' cookie dough and brownie batter are made with heat-treated flour and pasteurized eggs (or no eggs at all) — the two swaps that remove both the salmonella risk from the raw eggs and the E. coli risk from the raw flour. Homemade raw dough has neither safeguard, which is why the CDC warns against eating it. Source: CDC 'Raw Flour and Dough' https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/no-raw-dough.html

question: In a German kitchen, shredded cabbage sits in a jar for weeks and turns fiercely sour on its own, though no vinegar or lemon juice ever goes in. Besides the shredded cabbage, a real jar of sauerkraut needs just one other thing. What is it?
context: The German name 'Sauerkraut' literally means 'sour cabbage.' It is nothing but shredded cabbage and salt — no vinegar — yet it turns sour by itself as it ferments. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sauerkraut'.

question: A crock of shredded cabbage turns fiercely sour within weeks, though nobody ever buys a starter culture or adds a single bacterium. The souring starts all on its own. Where do the microbes that ferment the cabbage come from?
answer: they already live on the raw cabbage leaves
choices: they already live on the raw cabbage leaves
they come up out of the cabbage's roots
they drift in from the surrounding air
they multiply out of the salty brine
context: No starter culture is needed; the fermentation is spontaneous, because the lactic-acid bacteria are already present on the raw cabbage leaves. The salt and the airless brine simply let the right, salt-tolerant ones take over while the spoilage microbes are held back, so the cook does not add the culture but selects it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kimchi'; UF/IFAS 'Fermented Foods: Sauerkraut.'

question: A cook rubs two big spoonfuls of salt through shredded cabbage and presses it into a warm jar to ferment. Raw vegetables left to ferment sound like a perfect recipe for rot, yet the cabbage never turns to slime, and the salt is the reason. What does the salt do among the microbes?
answer: it stops the rot-microbes but spares the sour-making ones
choices: it stops the rot-microbes but spares the sour-making ones
it kills the sour-makers but feeds the rot-microbes
it wipes out every microbe, the good and the bad alike
it dries the cabbage until nothing, helpful or not, survives
context: By osmosis the salt pulls water out of the cabbage to make a brine. The rot- and mold-microbes cannot tolerate it, but the helpful sour-making (lactic-acid) bacteria can, so they take over. About 2–3% salt is the sweet spot. Sources: American Homebrewers Association; Wikipedia, 'Sauerkraut'.

question: A kraut-maker weights the cabbage down so that every shred stays under the brine. A bit left poking above the surface grows fuzzy mold, while everything kept below sours cleanly for months. Why does staying under the brine keep the mold away?
answer: under the brine there's no air, and mold can't grow without it
choices: under the brine there's no air, and mold can't grow without it
under the brine the salt is simply too strong for the mold
under the brine it stays too cold for any mold to grow
under the brine the acid keeps rinsing the mold spores away
context: Submerged, the cabbage sits in an airless (anaerobic) home that starves mold and rot, while the acid-makers thrive and drive the brine sour enough (around pH 3.5) to keep bad microbes out for months. Sources: American Homebrewers Association; Wikipedia, 'Sauerkraut'.

question: A Korean family eats kimchi at nearly every meal, and these days it is usually made from big, crinkly napa cabbage. Napa reached Korea only in the late 1800s, though. For most of Korea's long history, kimchi was built around a different, humbler vegetable. Which one?
context: For most of Korean history the main kimchi vegetable was the radish; the big napa (Chinese) cabbage only arrived in the late 1800s. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kimchi'; ScienceDirect.

question: Barrels of sauerkraut went to sea with James Cook, who across three years lost not a single crewman to scurvy, a disease that killed sailors by the thousands. Nobody in his day knew that vitamins existed, yet fermented cabbage keeps much of the very nutrient whose lack causes scurvy. Which nutrient is it?
context: Fermented cabbage keeps much of its vitamin C, the nutrient that prevents scurvy — though no one understood vitamins yet. In 1776 the Royal Society gave Cook its highest honor, the Copley Medal, for his account of keeping his crew healthy at sea. Scurvy is estimated to have killed some two million sailors between 1500 and 1800; one earlier commodore, George Anson, lost more than 1,300 of about 2,000 men. Sources: Britannica, 'James Cook'; Modern Farmer.

question: A cook shakes a tiny pinch of salt over cold watermelon, rich caramel and ripe strawberries, the same salt that goes on french fries. It looks like a blunder, but cooks all over the world do it on purpose. What does the pinch do to sweet foods?
context: This is real and reproducible right at the table: the salt is kept far below the level where you'd taste 'salty,' and instead the sweetness pops — which is exactly why salted caramel and salt-on-watermelon are a thing. Salt adds no sweetness of its own; it's dialing something else down. Sources: culinarylore.com, 'why does salt make sweet foods taste sweeter'; science.org, 'Why adding salt makes fruit and candy sweeter.'

question: A pot of homemade soup tastes flat: not bad, just dull, as if something is missing. The first instinct is more herbs, more garlic, more pepper, but a seasoned cook says that nine times out of ten that is the wrong fix. What does a flat soup almost always need?
context: When a dish tastes flat, it's almost always UNDER-salted, not under-flavored — the flavors that are already there just aren't being carried forward. Piling on more herbs or spices tends to muddy it; a small pinch of salt brings the existing flavors into focus (and lifts the savory, aroma-rich notes too). Sources: scienceinsights.org, 'does salt bring out flavor or just taste salty'; parkcityculinaryinstitute.com, 'science of seasoning.'

question: A baker presses a few flakes of coarse sea salt onto each dark-chocolate cookie on her tray just before it goes into the oven. Dark chocolate is naturally a little bitter, bitter enough that a small child might spit it out, and salting a sweet cookie sounds as if it would only make things worse. Once the cookies are baked, what does the salt do to their flavor?
answer: Pushes both the chocolate and the sweetness forward
choices: Pushes both the chocolate and the sweetness forward
Turns the whole cookie faintly salty
Fades the chocolate and leaves only sweetness
Slips a sour note beneath the chocolate
context: This is the salted-caramel / flaky-salt-on-cookies trick used on purpose. The salt tamps down the bitterness of the (especially dark) chocolate, so the sweetness reads cleaner — and, because the bitter edge is out of the way, the chocolate flavor itself also comes through more strongly. Both get louder at once, from a pinch too small to taste salty. Sources: aspicyperspective.com, 'salted chocolate chip cookies'; seasaltsuperstore.com, 'how salt enhances sweet flavors in desserts.'

question: Taste researchers testing bitter foods treat table salt as two things locked together: a metal called sodium and its partner, chloride. Their careful tests show that only one half of the pair does the work against bitterness. Which half is it?
context: It's the metal ion — the sodium — that suppresses bitterness, not the crystal as a whole. Researchers proved it by swapping ions: lithium quieted bitterness just as strongly as sodium, but potassium had no bitterness-suppressing power at all — so the effect belongs to specific positive metal ions, not to 'salt' in general. That's why the concept is 'sodium,' not 'chloride.' Source: Breslin & Beauchamp, 'Suppression of bitterness by sodium: variation among bitter taste stimuli,' 1995 — pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8788095/.

question: Scientists stirred a pinch of salt into sugar water spiked with a bitter chemical in a famous 1997 experiment, and the drink suddenly tasted much sweeter. The same pinch in plain sugar water changed its sweetness not at all. What do the paired results show the salt is doing?
answer: Quieting the bitterness so the drink's own sweetness shows
choices: Quieting the bitterness so the drink's own sweetness shows
Making the bitter chemical itself taste sweet
Wearing down the tongue's bitter receptors for good
Binding the bitter chemical and dissolving it away
context: This is the cleanest proof that salt doesn't ADD sweetness — it releases the sweetness that bitterness was hiding. The control condition is the key: if salt made things sweet on its own, the plain sugar-water should have tasted sweeter too, but it didn't budge. Sweetness only jumped when there was bitterness present for the salt to suppress. Source: Breslin PAS & Beauchamp GK, 'Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness,' Nature 387:563 (1997) — nature.com/articles/42388.

question: Fishermen gutted cod, packed it between layers of salt, and dried it into a board-hard plank they could stack in a cellar or a ship's hold. Kept dry, how long would one of those planks stay good to cook?
context: Fresh fish spoils in a day or two, but drying — the world's oldest known food-preservation method — changed the math. Gutted, packed between layers of salt, and dried into board-hard planks, cod could keep for several years. That keeping power is why it fed sailors and whole armies: the original long-haul protein, a fish that could be shipped anywhere. Source: Wikipedia 'Dried and salted cod'; History Today 'A History of Salt Cod.'

question: A cook brings home a plank of bacalao, salt cod: rock-hard, crusted white with salt and dry as a board. Fried or baked like that, it would be painfully salty and almost inedible. What must the cook do before it can go into a stew or soup?
answer: Soak it in cold water for a day or more
choices: Soak it in cold water for a day or more
Simmer it in milk for an hour
Sear it in a hot, dry pan
context: Salt cod must be 'soaked back to life' in cold water for one to three days, with the water changed two or three times a day, to rehydrate it and wash out the salt before cooking. Source: Wikipedia 'Dried and salted cod.'

question: Norwegian fishermen have made salt cod for hundreds of years, and they call it klippfisk, a word that means 'cliff-fish' or 'rock-fish.' The odd name comes straight from the way they turned fresh cod into a fish that lasted without a fridge. Why 'cliff-fish'?
answer: They spread the salted cod on rocky coasts to dry
choices: They spread the salted cod on rocky coasts to dry
They fished for it from the tops of the sea cliffs
They aged it in caves cut into the cliffs
They traded it only in rocky mountain towns
context: Klippfisk means 'cliff-fish' or 'rock-fish': along Norway's coast the salted cod was laid out across the bare rocks to dry hard in the cold sea air. The same fish is bacalhau in Portuguese, bacalao in Spanish, baccalà in Italian, and 'saltfish' in the Caribbean — most from the old root 'bacal-.' Source: Wikipedia 'Dried and salted cod'; 'Stockfish.'

question: A mackerel salted and laid out to dry turns rancid, soft and stinking of spoiled oil, while a cod given the same cure dries rock-hard and keeps without a fridge. Both fish swim the same cold seas; the difference is where each stores its body oil. Where does a cod keep its oil?
context: Cod stores its oil in its liver — the source of cod-liver oil — leaving its white muscle almost fat-free. A fatty fish like mackerel or herring carries oil all through its flesh, which turns rancid and keeps salt from penetrating, so it can never dry hard and keep the way lean cod does. Source: Mark Kurlansky, 'Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World'; Wikipedia 'Cod fisheries.'

question: A medieval cook planned the household's meals around the Church's fast days, and Lent was the strictest stretch of the year. Foods a cook could still reach for on an ordinary fast day went off the table for all forty days of it. Which foods vanished once Lent began?
context: Meat was barred on every fast day — every Friday, all of Lent and Advent, and many more (medieval calendars even added Wednesdays and Saturdays), a huge share of the year. Eggs and dairy were different: legal on an ordinary fast day, they were restricted only once the stricter Lenten fast began. With meat gone year-round and eggs and cheese gone through Lent, fish was what was left, and dried salt cod was the classic 'fish-day' meal for 16th-century Catholics. Source: NPR The Salt 'The real story behind fish Fridays'; Wikipedia 'Fasting and abstinence in the Catholic Church.'

question: A Portuguese family sits down to salt cod on Christmas Eve, as tradition asks, and calls the fish its fiel amigo, its 'faithful friend.' One beloved saying captures how endlessly the Portuguese cook it. What does the saying claim?
answer: There's a recipe for every single day of the year
choices: There's a recipe for every single day of the year
No two families cook it the same way twice
A true cook never repeats a recipe in a lifetime
Every village guards one secret recipe of its own
context: In Portugal salt cod is the 'fiel amigo' ('faithful friend'). Wikipedia notes 'it is said there are more than 365 ways to cook bacalhau, one for every day of the year; others say there are 1,001 ways.' It is the traditional Christmas Eve dinner in parts of Portugal. Source: Wikipedia 'Bacalhau.'

question: Newfoundland's fishermen graded their dried cod in the 1700s and 1800s. The best went to the fine tables of Catholic Europe. The cheapest, damaged 'refuse' grade, too broken or bruised for any respectable buyer, sailed off on a route of its own. Where did it go, and whom was it meant to feed?
answer: To the Caribbean, to feed enslaved people on the sugar plantations
choices: To the Caribbean, to feed enslaved people on the sugar plantations
To Arctic Norway, to feed the fishermen through the long winter
To inland Spain, to feed the monks of the mountain monasteries
To West Africa, to feed the porters of the inland caravans
context: Salt cod became a leg of the Atlantic triangular trade. The best grades went to Europe and the Mediterranean; the poorest 'refuse' grade was shipped to the Caribbean as cheap, durable protein to feed enslaved people on the sugar plantations. Mark Kurlansky writes that the Newfoundland and Nova Scotia fisheries became geared to 'low-grade West India saltfish.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_fishing_in_Newfoundland; The Caribbean Camera, quoting historian Christopher Magra.

question: A salt farmer at Guérande, on France's Atlantic coast, floods a wide, shallow pond with seawater and simply waits. Weeks of summer sun later the pond has turned white and crusty, and he rakes up glittering heaps of sea salt. Where did all the water go?
answer: The sun slowly evaporated it into the air
choices: The sun slowly evaporated it into the air
The sand soaked it up like a sponge
The tide carried it back out to sea
The muddy floor swallowed it down below
context: Sea salt is harvested by letting seawater flood shallow ponds and evaporate in the sun; the water leaves and salt crystals are left behind to be raked up. No fuel needed - just sunshine and time. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salt' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt).

question: A cook stirs table salt into a pot of soup, then reaches for kosher salt to sprinkle over a steak. A chemist tests both and finds the same sodium chloride in each. Why, then, does one suit the soup and the other the steak?
answer: the size and shape of their crystals
choices: the size and shape of their crystals
the part of the world they come from
how much they cost to buy
how long they take to make
context: Kosher salt and flaky finishing salts differ from ordinary table salt mainly in the size and shape of their crystals, not their basic chemistry - it is all sodium chloride, though table salt is often iodized. Bigger, flakier crystals are easy to pinch and sprinkle over finished food. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salt'.

question: Seen from an airplane, the salt ponds along San Francisco Bay look like spilled paint, glowing hot pink, red and orange. The water is far too salty for fish or ordinary plants to survive. What is staining the ponds those wild colors?
choices: rust from iron in the mud
context: Salt-evaporation ponds often glow bright pink, red, and orange because salt-loving algae and microbes are the only living things that can thrive in water that salty. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salt'.

question: Miners in Kansas and Poland dig salt from beds hundreds of meters thick, buried far inland with no ocean anywhere near. It seems impossible. How did so much salt end up locked in solid rock in the middle of dry land?
answer: an ancient sea dried up and left its salt behind
choices: an ancient sea dried up and left its salt behind
volcanoes pushed the salt up from deep below
glaciers scraped the salt out of the mountains
rivers carried the salt in and left it stranded
context: Rock salt is an evaporite - the dried-up remains of ancient seas and salt lakes that evaporated long ago, leaving buried beds that can be hundreds of meters thick. Source: Wikipedia, 'Halite'.

question: A buried bed of salt is lighter than the rock above it, and on Avery Island, in Louisiana's coastal marsh, one has squeezed up into a giant dome that nearly reaches the surface. A family there began making a famous food in 1868, mixing salt mined from that dome into a mash of ground peppers. Which food?
context: Avery Island is a salt dome, a huge plug of rock salt that rose from deep underground because salt is lighter than the rock around it. By the company's own history, Edmund McIlhenny began making Tabasco sauce there in 1868, grinding tabasco peppers into a mash with salt from the island's mine and aging it in oak barrels. Salt domes draw oil prospectors too, because oil often pools against their sides. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabasco_sauce; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avery_Island,_Louisiana; grokipedia.com/page/Tabasco_sauce

question: An entire sea nearly dried up some five to six million years ago, geologists say. Its narrow gateway to the open ocean slammed shut, the water boiled away under the sun, and over a million cubic kilometers of salt piled up on the empty seabed, so much that it still holds a chunk of all the salt in today's oceans. Which sea vanished?
context: About 5-6 million years ago the Mediterranean Sea nearly dried up - the Messinian salinity crisis - dumping over a million cubic kilometers of salt on the seafloor. Roughly 5-6% of all the salt in the world's oceans is now locked in those buried layers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Messinian salinity crisis'.

question: A deer will go out of its way to find salt, and so will many other animals, people included, because a body that goes entirely without it dies. Something in salt is what lets nerves crackle and muscles twitch. Which part of salt does that job?
context: The body genuinely needs salt to live: nerves and muscles fire by letting sodium ions rush into a cell - an 'action potential' - then pumping them back out. That electrical need is a big reason humans and animals crave salt. Source: NCBI Bookshelf, physiology of the action potential.

question: Spaghetti comes out of an unsalted pot perfectly cooked but bland and flat, like wet cardboard, because the cook forgot to salt the water. No amount of salt sprinkled over the finished plate brings it to life. Why can't salt on the plate fix the noodles now?
answer: The noodles could only drink up seasoning while they swelled
choices: The noodles could only drink up seasoning while they swelled
Salt clings to sauce but slides right off bare noodles
Boiling had already driven the flavor out of the pasta
Salt melts into pasta only under very high heat
context: As the noodles hydrate and swell they absorb salted water all the way through, seasoning from the inside out — flavor you can never add back afterward, no matter how much you sprinkle on the finished plate. The old rule is to make the water 'taste like the sea,' roughly 1–2 tablespoons per pound of pasta. Source: The Culinary Center of Kansas City, 'You're Not Salting Your Pasta Water Enough' (kcculinary.com/blog/youre-not-salting-your-pasta-water-enough); Taste of Home, 'How to Season Pasta Water' (tasteofhome.com/article/how-to-season-pasta-water).

question: Two identical pots of soup simmer side by side, one salted and one plain. Samin Nosrat, the chef who wrote Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat, says the salted pot does more than taste better: it changes in a way the tongue never touches. What changes?
answer: Its aroma lifts, so it smells more strongly of itself
choices: Its aroma lifts, so it smells more strongly of itself
Its color deepens, so the broth looks richer and darker
Its body thickens, so it clings to the back of the spoon
Its steam rises hotter, so it carries more heat to the lip
context: Nosrat's canonical book puts it that salt 'unlocks many aromatic compounds' in food, so a properly salted dish literally smells more strongly of what it is. Across the board salt's job is to minimize bitterness, balance sweetness, and lift aroma — not to taste 'salty.' Source: Samin Nosrat, 'Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat' (notes: joekotlan.com/salt-fat-acid-heat; publisher PDF: cdn.bookey.app/files/pdf/book/en/salt--fat--acid--heat.pdf).

question: A chef scatters a pinch of Maldon over a finished plate at the very last second. Finishing salts such as Maldon and fleur de sel never go into the pan. What do they add that ordinary cooking salt can't?
answer: A burst of crunch and a pop of aroma on the tongue
choices: A burst of crunch and a pop of aroma on the tongue
A stronger, saltier hit than fine table salt gives
A glossy shine that makes the plate look finished
A slow, even release of salt as the food cools
context: A finishing salt is added at the very last second for CRUNCH and a burst of aroma, not deep seasoning — its big hollow crystals pop and dissolve on the tongue in salty bursts. Cook with it and the heat melts the flakes, losing the whole point. Maldon is the famous name: a British sea salt made on the Essex coast for well over a century (~140 years), prized for its hollow pyramid-shaped crystals. Source: goop, '9 Types of Salt and How to Cook with Each' (goop.com/food/tutorials/9-types-of-salt-and-how-to-cook-with-each); Koyuncu Salt Library, 'Fleur de Sel Substitutions' (koyuncusalt.com); Mongtable, 'What Is Maldon Salt?' (mongtable.click/en/what-is-maldon-salt).

question: A fresh green cabbage, shredded into a pile and salted heavily, is left on the cutting board. Half an hour later it sits in a real puddle of its own liquid, wet enough to pour off. Which way did the water travel to get there, and why?
answer: Out of the vegetable's cells, drawn toward the salty surface
choices: Out of the vegetable's cells, drawn toward the salty surface
Into the cells, which the salt made swell and split open
Straight down, as gravity pulled the loose juices free
Nowhere — the puddle is just the salt itself melting
context: On a cut surface salt runs osmosis in reverse of seasoning: water is pulled OUT of the cells toward the salty surface. Within 30–60 minutes salted eggplant or cabbage visibly weeps beads of liquid, so you rinse and pat it dry to make it brown crisp instead of steaming. The same osmosis is why little beads of juice appear on a steak minutes after you salt it. Source: Food52, 'Do You Actually Need to Salt Eggplant in Advance?' (food52.com/story/26413); ScienceInsights, 'What Makes Eggplant Bitter and How to Avoid It' (scienceinsights.org/what-makes-eggplant-bitter-and-how-to-avoid-it).

question: A cook tosses a big pinch of salt into the pasta pot, trusting the old kitchen advice that salted water boils hotter and faster. Chemists have measured the boiling points of salted and plain water side by side with great precision. What did they find salt does to the water's boiling temperature?
answer: It rises by a tiny fraction of a degree — far too little to matter
choices: It rises by a tiny fraction of a degree — far too little to matter
It rises several degrees, cooking the pasta noticeably faster
It drops, so the water boils at a cooler temperature
It holds steady, but the salt makes bubbles form sooner
context: Salt raises water's boiling point only a trace: a tablespoon lifts it under 0.5°C, and a normal ~1% pasta pot rises only about 0.17–0.3°C. You'd need roughly 60 grams per liter (about 4 tablespoons) to gain even 1°C, at which point the water is undrinkably salty. You salt pasta water purely for flavor, not speed. Source: The San Lupe Project, 'Boiling Point of Water Salt' (thesanlupeproject.org/boiling-point-water-salt-science); The Kitchn, 'Does Salting Pasta Water Have Any Scientific Merit?' (thekitchn.com/does-salting-pa-158293).

question: Slices of eggplant weep under a coat of salt on the counter, and the cook is sure the bitterness is draining away with the water. Food scientists say the bitterness never leaves at all; the salt only masks it on the tongue. What keeps the bitter taste from washing out?
answer: The bitter molecules are simply too big to slip out with the water
choices: The bitter molecules are simply too big to slip out with the water
The bitter molecules cling too tightly to the eggplant's flesh
The bitter molecules will not dissolve in the salty water
The bitter molecules sit too deep to reach the cut surface
context: A twist most people get wrong: salting eggplant does NOT actually pull the bitterness out — the bitter alkaloid molecules are too big to leave with the water via osmosis. What salting really does is draw out moisture (for better texture and browning) and mask the PERCEPTION of bitterness on the tongue. Source: ScienceInsights, 'What Makes Eggplant Bitter and How to Avoid It' (scienceinsights.org/what-makes-eggplant-bitter-and-how-to-avoid-it); Salon, 'Do you actually need to salt eggplant in advance?' (salon.com/2021/07/28).

question: A whole chicken sits uncovered in the fridge a full day before Sunday's roast, salted all over in a dry brine. At first the salt draws beads of juice out to the surface, yet by roasting time the bird is seasoned to the bone, not just on the skin. How does the salt end up deep inside the meat?
answer: The juice dissolves the salt, and the brine soaks back in
choices: The juice dissolves the salt, and the brine soaks back in
The juice evaporates, and the dry salt sinks in behind it
The juice softens the surface, and the salt seeps through it
The juice leaves gaps in the cells, and the salt fills them in
context: A 'dry brine' turns the surface weeping to advantage: salt a steak or chicken hours ahead, and the juice it first drew out dissolves the salt into a briny slurry that then gets REABSORBED — seasoning the meat deep, leaving it juicier, and drying the surface so it browns better. Rule of thumb: about 1/2 teaspoon of kosher salt per pound; thin steaks want 1–2 hours, chicken and turkey 2–4 hours up to overnight, thick roasts 12–48 hours. Source: AmazingRibs, 'Dry Brining' (amazingribs.com/tested-recipes/salting-brining-curing-and-injecting/dry-brining).

question: Table salt goes into a dish whose recipe called for a tablespoon of kosher salt, and the dish comes out more than twice as salty. Cooks prefer kosher salt for exactly this reason: it is much harder to over-salt with. Why?
answer: Its crystals are big and loosely packed, so less fits in the spoon
choices: Its crystals are big and loosely packed, so less fits in the spoon
Its grains each hold less sodium than a grain of table salt
Its crystals dissolve slowly, so less salt reaches the dish
Its grains are churned with air, so each one weighs less
context: Bigger crystals pack in loosely, so a spoonful weighs far LESS and it's much harder to over-salt. A tablespoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt weighs about 10 grams; a tablespoon of fine table salt weighs about 23 grams — more than double — so table salt is roughly twice as salty by volume, and grabbing the wrong one can nearly double the saltiness. Source: America's Test Kitchen, 'Ask Paul: What's the Difference Between Table Salt, Kosher Salt...' (americastestkitchen.com/articles/4286); Jacobsen Salt Co., 'Table Salt Versus Kosher Salt' (jacobsensalt.com/blogs/resources/table-salt-versus-kosher-salt).

question: J. Kenji López-Alt tests kitchen advice in his own lab, and on steak he is blunt: salt it right before it hits the hot pan or at least 40 minutes ahead. Salting 10 to 30 minutes ahead, he says, is the single worst choice a cook can make. What goes wrong in that middle window?
answer: The juice has been pulled out but not back in, so the surface won't sear
choices: The juice has been pulled out but not back in, so the surface won't sear
The juice has soaked back in, but the salt hasn't spread through it yet
The surface has set into a rubbery skin that won't take color
The salt has half-dissolved into a gritty paste that steams in the pan
context: The most retellable timing gem: salt a steak right before the pan OR at least ~40–45 minutes ahead, but the 10-to-30-minute window is the WORST — the salt has pulled juice to the surface but there hasn't been time for it to soak back in, leaving a wet surface that ruins the sear. Source: J. Kenji López-Alt (Serious Eats) via Tasting Table, 'Why You Should Always Salt Your Steak Before Cooking' (tastingtable.com/844510); Kenji López-Alt, TikTok @j.kenji.lopezalt video 7471317522248142110.

question: To make meat survive months at sea, sailors packed it in a cask and topped it with brine -- salt water so strong it kept the meat from rotting. Old accounts give one vivid sign that a cask's brine was salty enough. Which sign?
answer: It would float a whole egg
choices: It would float a whole egg
It held a wooden spoon upright
It stung any cut on the hand
It turned a cloudy, milky white
context: The old shipboard method: dry-rub the meat in salt, soak it in brine for days to draw out the blood, pack it in a cask with more salt, then top it with brine so heavy it could float an egg. That brimful, egg-floating cask is why sailors' meat could last a whole voyage. Source: csphistorical.com, 'Salt Pork, Ship's Biscuit and Burgoo.'  (Legend.)

question: Berber caravans of hundreds of camels crossed nearly five hundred miles of the Sahara in medieval West Africa, carrying salt cut in great slabs at the Taghaza mines to Timbuktu and the other inland cities of the Mali Empire. In some remote markets, what did traders swap the salt for, at times pound for pound?
context: Inland, salt was scarce and vital for preserving food, so where it was rare it was as good as money -- swapped for gold dust, by some accounts even pound for pound in remote markets, though historians think that famous ratio was rare at best. The giant camel caravans are a legendary image of just how far people would haul a preserving mineral. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1342 ('The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taghaza.

question: Mark Kurlansky argues that a salted, dried fish is the real reason Europeans could cross the Atlantic, because it kept long enough to feed ships on long voyages. By his account, Basque fishermen from northern Spain were already trading it far and wide by about the year 1000, well before Columbus. Which fish was it?
context: Salt cod could last years and cross oceans, so it -- not fresh fish -- became the fuel of long voyages. Chasing it, Basque, Portuguese, French, and English fleets were crossing to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland by the early 1500s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_fishing_in_Newfoundland.

question: English sea captains fishing off Newfoundland around 1600 sent home a report about the cod that made those waters sound endless. The shoals by the shore were so thick, they claimed, that a man could hardly do one simple thing among them. What was it?
choices: Haul the nets for their weight
Find clear water to swim in
context: English captains around 1600 reported cod shoals 'so thick by the shore that we hardly have been able to row a boat through them' -- an image that made the Grand Banks sound inexhaustible. A century earlier, John Cabot's crew of 1497 had claimed the sea was so full of fish they could be taken in baskets as well as nets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_fishing_in_Newfoundland.

question: On the Grand Banks in the 1500s, rival fleets from four nations cured their catch in different ways. The English prized a method that made their fish so hard and dry it could stay edible for years. How did the English cure their catch?
answer: Salted it lightly, then washed and dried it on shore
choices: Salted it lightly, then washed and dried it on shore
Salted it heavily and wet, then dried it back in Europe
Packed it in strong brine below decks, undried
Layered it in dry salt in casks for the voyage
context: The English used 'light salting, washing and drying onshore,' which made a hard, dry salt cod that 'could remain edible for years.' The French, Spanish and Portuguese fished the offshore banks, salted their catch on board and dried it only back in Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_fishing_in_Newfoundland.

question: Smugglers called faux-sauniers ran cheap salt past the king's tax collectors in old France, risking the galleys or the gallows if caught. A tax called the gabelle forced everyone to buy the king's overpriced salt, and a huge black market grew up around it. To ordinary French people, what were the salt-runners?
context: The gabelle was despised -- everyone over age 8 had to buy salt at prices the crown fixed, up to 20 times higher in Paris than in Brittany -- so the smugglers were cheered as folk heroes against an unjust tax. The gabelle became a symbol of royal injustice, and France's revolutionary National Assembly abolished it in 1790. Source: legalclarity.org, 'The Gabelle.'

question: A salt-cured ham hangs for months without rotting, because the salt pulls water out of every microbe on it until the germs are too dried-out to grow. Cooks keep food from spoiling in plenty of other ways. Which of them fights spoilage by that very same water-pulling trick?
context: Sugar preserves food the very same way salt does -- it lowers the 'free water' that microbes need to live, so water flows out of every cell toward the sugary surface and the bugs dry out. That's why a salt-cured ham and a jar of sweet fruit jam both keep for months on the shelf: one savory, one sweet, but guarded by the identical trick. The others work differently -- pickling relies on acid, smoking on antimicrobial smoke, and chilling just slows microbes down instead of drying them out. Source: scientificamerican.com, 'How do salt and sugar preserve food?'

question: A stubborn few bacteria can shrug off being dried out, and still they die inside a ham packed in heavy salt. Near the highest salt levels, the mineral turns on the microbes a second way that has nothing to do with drying. What does that much salt become to a bacterium?
answer: A poison that wrecks its inner workings
choices: A poison that wrecks its inner workings
A blanket that freezes it solid
A cage that cuts off its air
A scrub that wipes it off the meat
context: At high enough concentration the salt itself turns toxic to many bacteria, jamming the enzymes and internal chemistry they need to function. So curing attacks microbes on several fronts at once -- it dries them out, it locks up the water that's left, and it poisons them directly, which is why cured meat can sit shelf-stable so long. Source: bhooc.com, 'How Salt, Microbes, and Time Preserved Food.'

question: Romans splashed brine over almost everything they ate, and one dish on their table took its very name from what they poured across it. Two thousand years later that dish still sits on menus all over the world. Which dish is it?
context: 'Salad' descends from Latin herba salata, 'salted vegetables' — the Romans dressed their greens with salt, oil, and vinegar, and the salted part gave the dish its name. Source: etymonline.com/word/salad

question: Traders in Ethiopia bought and sold goods with hard, foot-long bars called amole right up into the early 1900s, and the empire even collected them as taxes. A trader could snap a bar into smaller pieces to make change. What were these money-bars made of?
context: Bars of rock salt called 'amole' were used as actual money in Ethiopia into the early 1900s. Each bar was roughly 10-12 inches long and could be snapped into pieces for small change. In 1903 the empire collected amole worth about 27% of its tax revenue — a sign of how precious salt was. Source: moneymuseum.com/en/coins?id=1613

question: Peter Gainsford, a classicist, combed the ancient Roman writings for the famous story that soldiers were paid in salt, the supposed root of the word 'salary.' The word does trace back to the Latin for salt, but he found not one scrap of evidence that any soldier was ever handed salt as wages. Who invented the salt-pay tale?
answer: Dictionary writers invented it in their entries
choices: Dictionary writers invented it in their entries
Latin teachers invented it in their lessons
Medieval monks invented it in their chronicles
Victorian novelists invented it in their stories
context: The 'paid in salt' story is only half true. 'Salary' does trace to Latin salarium (from sal, salt), but there is NO ancient evidence soldiers were handed salt — they were paid in coin. Gainsford: 'There isn't the tiniest scrap of evidence to suggest this.' The salt-pay idea was invented by 18th-century dictionary writers by analogy with words like vestiarium ('clothing money'); Pliny only linked the WORD salary to salt's importance along the Salarian Way. A popular tale scholars reject, not a proven fact. Source: kiwihellenist.blogspot.com/2017/01/salt-and-salary.html  (Legend.)

question: A big bowl of bread dough gets just a small spoonful of salt, and most of that salt's work has nothing to do with flavor. Yeast, a tiny living fungus, raises the loaf by eating the dough's sugars and puffing it up with gas, and the salt works directly on that living yeast. What does the salt do to it?
context: Salt is the yeast's brake. Leave it out and the yeast races — the dough over-ferments, rising fast and tall, then collapsing into a bland, over-holey loaf. And here's the reassuring part: at normal bread amounts (about 2% of the flour's weight), salt only slows the yeast, it never kills it — King Arthur's bakers say salt and yeast can even touch briefly with no harm. Source: King Arthur Baking, 'Why is salt important in yeast bread?' and 'Does salt kill yeast?'

question: A grain of salt sits in a bowl of bread dough beside a cluster of yeast cells and draws something out of them, straight through their walls. Starved of it, the yeast struggles to ferment. What does the salt pull out of the yeast?
context: This is osmosis. Salt is hygroscopic — it grabs onto water — so it pulls water out through the yeast cells' walls. Yeast needs water to ferment, so a dried-out, water-starved cell works slower. The brake, in other words, is water, drawn out by the salt. Source: King Arthur Baking, 'Salt' reference, and ChainBaker, 'This is How Salt Affects Bread Dough.'

question: A baker kneads a spoonful of salt through a batch of bread dough, and besides its work on the yeast, the salt acts on the gluten, the stretchy protein web that gives bread its chew. What does salt do to that gluten web?
answer: Tightens it so it traps the gas
choices: Tightens it so it traps the gas
Loosens it so it stretches farther
Breaks it down into a batter
context: Salt does double duty: it tightens the gluten strands so they bond more strongly and can hold the yeast's carbon-dioxide gas. In ChainBaker's side-by-side test, the salt-free dough was so weak it spread out sideways instead of rising upward, baking up spongy — and it was stickier to handle, too. Source: King Arthur Baking, 'Why is salt important in yeast bread?' and ChainBaker, 'This is How Salt Affects Bread Dough.'

question: Wooden ships of the Age of Sail spent months at sea, and one disease killed about two million of their sailors, more than storms, sea battles, shipwrecks and pirates combined. Gums bled, teeth fell out and old wounds cracked open. Which disease killed more sailors than the ocean itself?
context: Scurvy was the great killer of the Age of Sail. On months-long voyages with nothing but salt-meat and hard biscuit, it took an estimated two million sailors — more than storms, shipwrecks, and enemy cannon combined. Source: Hektoen International, 'Plague of the Sea and the Spoyle of Mariners'; Modern Farmer, 'Magical Sour Cabbage.'

question: Barrels of one humble, long-keeping food went below deck by the ton when James Cook sailed the Pacific on voyages lasting years. Fresh fruit rots in weeks, and there was no room to store it anyway, yet this food kept his crews healthy. What was in the barrels?
context: Sauerkraut is cabbage fermented in salt. Unlike fresh oranges, it keeps for months at sea and holds its vitamin C, so Cook loaded nearly four tons of it for the Endeavour's 1768 Pacific voyage. Source: Modern Farmer, 'Magical Sour Cabbage'; British Library Untold Lives, 'Sauerkraut, sugar, and salt pork.'

question: Shredded vegetables fermenting in a sealed barrel keep much of their vitamin C for months below deck on a sailing ship, though most ways of storing food for a long voyage would destroy it. What is it about fermenting that spares the vitamin?
answer: Fermenting uses no heat, and heat is what destroys vitamin C
choices: Fermenting uses no heat, and heat is what destroys vitamin C
The oak of the barrel seeps fresh vitamin C into it
The heavy salt is itself packed with vitamin C
Sealing the barrel starves the germs that would eat the vitamin
context: Heat and drying wreck vitamin C, but the lactic-acid bacteria of fermentation do not — they preserve it, and by some accounts even raise it. So a sealed barrel of sauerkraut kept vitamin C on hand for months at sea. Source: Modern Farmer, 'Magical Sour Cabbage'; Hektoen International, 'Plague of the Sea and the Spoyle of Mariners.'

question: The sour, foreign cabbage James Cook brought to keep his crew healthy met a wall of turned-up noses, and he refused to force it down them. Instead, by his own account, he used a method with sailors that he swore had 'never once failed.' What did Cook do?
answer: He served it to the officers and let the men take it or leave it
choices: He served it to the officers and let the men take it or leave it
He mixed it into the grog so the men would swallow it unnoticed
He disguised it as a sweet pudding so the cook could sneak it in
He promised an extra rum ration to any man who cleaned his bowl
context: Cook wrote that the men would not touch the kraut 'until I put in practice a method I never once knew to fail with seamen': he had it dressed every day for the officers' table and left it to the men to take as much as they pleased or none at all. 'The moment they see their superiors set a value upon it, it becomes the finest stuff in the world.' Within a week he had to put everyone on board on a ration of it. Source: Cook's Journal, Endeavour, 13 April 1769 (paulturnbull.org/project/southseas/journals/cook/17690413.html).

question: A kid bakes brownies perfectly at 350 degrees for 25 minutes, then doubles the batter in one pan and bakes it at 350 for 50 minutes, sure twice the batter needs twice the time. The edges burn; the middle stays raw. What is the real rule for a doubled batch?
answer: Keep the temperature the same, add only a little time
choices: Keep the temperature the same, add only a little time
Keep the time the same, raise the temperature instead
Double the temperature and the time together
Halve the temperature and double the time
context: Doubling the ingredients does not double the oven settings. The doubled batter just sits deeper in the pan, so 'bake twice as long' scorches the edges before the middle can cook. Keep the same temperature and expect only about 15 to 25 percent more time, and check the center with a toothpick, never the clock alone. Source: kitchenscience.scitoys.com/scaling.

question: A double batch of cornbread goes into two pans the same size as the original instead of one, split evenly and baked side by side on one rack. Compared with the original single pan, how long do the two pans take?
answer: About the same as one original pan
choices: About the same as one original pan
About twice as long as one original pan
About half as long as one original pan
A little longer than one original pan
context: Each pan still holds the original DEPTH of batter, so heat has the same short distance to travel to each center, and the bake time barely changes. It is total depth, not total amount, that sets baking time. Pile the whole double batch into one deep pan instead and the center sits twice as far from the heat, baking unevenly. Source: kitchenscience.scitoys.com/scaling.

question: A wedding cake's huge bottom tier goes into the oven far deeper than the slim top tier, and at the recipe's usual setting its center stays raw while its crust hardens. To cook the deep tier through evenly, what does the baker do to the oven temperature and the bake time?
answer: Lower the oven temperature and lengthen the bake
choices: Lower the oven temperature and lengthen the bake
Raise the oven temperature and shorten the bake
Raise the oven temperature and lengthen the bake
Lower the oven temperature and shorten the bake
context: As a cake tier gets wider it also gets thicker, so heat has farther to travel to reach the center. Cranking the heat or simply baking longer at full temperature only scorches the outside before the middle sets. So bakers do the opposite of the instinct: they drop the oven temperature, for example from 350 down to 325 degrees, and lengthen the bake, letting the heat crawl slowly all the way to the center without burning the crust. It is the same depth-and-heat rule as a doubled batch, solved by adjusting the oven instead of the pan. Source: kitchenscience.scitoys.com/scaling.

question: Two small chickens and one turkey of exactly the same total weight go into the same oven to roast side by side. The two chickens finish far sooner. Since the weight going in was identical, what really sets how long a bird takes to roast?
choices: How many birds share the oven at once
How much fat marbles the meat
How dark the roasting pan is
context: Physicist Nathan Myhrvold (Modernist Cuisine) framed it as a rule: a roast is done when its CENTER reaches temperature, and heat only travels inward from the surface, so a long, thin roast cooks faster than a short, fat one of the same weight. Each small chicken is thinner than the big turkey, so heat reaches each center much sooner; every 'hunk' in the oven cooks by its own thickness, independently. Source: amazingribs.com.

question: A baker scales a loaf up by doubling every dimension of the pan, twice as wide, twice as long, twice as tall, expecting a giant loaf. Instead it burns to a hard crust while the center stays wet dough, no matter how long it bakes. What is it about doubling every dimension that dooms the big loaf?
answer: The batter's volume grows far faster than its heat-catching surface
choices: The batter's volume grows far faster than its heat-catching surface
The thicker crust traps steam and keeps the center soggy
The bigger pan takes too long to heat up in the oven
The taller sides block the oven's heat from the top
context: Double every side and the VOLUME grows 2x2x2 = 8 times, while the SURFACE grows only 2x2 = 4 times, the square-cube idea. The surface is where heat enters, but now there is twice as much batter for every bit of crust, so the inside cannot cook before the outside dries and browns. Scitoys' example: a 5x4x8.5-inch loaf (about 3 quarts), doubled in every dimension to 10x8x17 inches, holds nearly 24 quarts, eight times the batter, with only four times the crust. Source: kitchenscience.scitoys.com/scaling.

question: A cake rockets up in the oven, then sinks into a dense, sunken middle with a faint metallic taste: its baker doubled the recipe and, to be safe, doubled the baking powder too. Why did doubling the baking powder backfire?
answer: Too much gas built up for the batter to hold, and the bubbles burst
choices: Too much gas built up for the batter to hold, and the bubbles burst
The extra powder soaked up the batter's liquid as it baked
The batter set on the outside long before the center did
The extra powder made the crumb tough and chewy
context: Double the baking powder and you make double the carbon-dioxide gas, but the batter's gluten net cannot hold the extra pressure, so the bubbles rupture and the cake collapses (and too much leavening can taste metallic). Bakers scale leavening to only about 1.5 times, or trim roughly an eighth of a teaspoon for every teaspoon. This is why baking is stricter than stovetop cooking: a stew forgives a rough double, just simmer longer and taste, but a cake's geometry, leavening, and browning all shift at once. Sources: mashed.com; pastrycal.com.

question: Grandpa slaps a raw steak onto a blazing-hot cast-iron pan at a family cookout, and as it hisses and browns he declares that the dark crust 'seals in the juices.' Food scientists have tested that by weighing steaks before and after cooking. What did they find about the crust?
answer: The browned crust is not waterproof and seals in no juice
choices: The browned crust is not waterproof and seals in no juice
The browned crust forms an airtight shell around the meat
The browned crust locks juice into thick cuts but not thin ones
The browned crust seals the juice in only if the pan stays hot
context: Food scientist Harold McGee, author of the classic 'On Food and Cooking,' puts it flatly: 'the crust that forms around the surface of the meat is not waterproof.' He calls searing-seals-the-juices the biggest myth in cooking. Nothing can lock juice inside, because meat is roughly 70% water and heating steadily squeezes that water out no matter how the outside is browned. Source: AmazingRibs, 'Myth: Searing Steaks Seals In The Juices' (quoting McGee).

question: A steak hisses and sizzles the whole time it sits on the hot pan, from the second it lands to the second it comes off. Many cooks think that sound is juice being sealed inside. What is that constant sizzle really?
answer: Moisture escaping the meat and flashing to steam on the hot metal
choices: Moisture escaping the meat and flashing to steam on the hot metal
The crust sealing tight and trapping the juices within
Fat crystallizing as it hardens into the brown outer shell
Air pockets deep in the muscle bursting under the heat
context: As McGee explains, that continuing sizzle 'is the sound of moisture continually escaping and vaporizing' — the opposite of being sealed in. The crust is no waterproof shell; water is being driven out of the meat and flashing to steam against the hot pan the entire time it cooks. Source: AmazingRibs, 'Myth: Searing Steaks Seals In The Juices' (Harold McGee).

question: Alton Brown ran a test: two matching steaks cooked to the very same doneness, one seared hard first, one never seared at all, then he weighed how much juice each one lost. If searing truly 'sealed in' the juices, the seared steak should have lost the least. What actually happened?
answer: The seared steak lost MORE juice than the un-seared one
choices: The seared steak lost MORE juice than the un-seared one
The seared steak lost far less, proving the seal had held
The seared steak lost the very same amount, down to the gram
The seared steak lost no measurable juice at all
context: In Alton Brown's test the un-seared steak lost about 13% of its weight in juice while the seared steak lost about 19% — searing cost it MORE. The reason: moisture loss rises with temperature, so the fiercer the sear, the faster water is driven off the surface. Cook's Illustrated reached the same verdict after its own tests: 'The notion of sealing in juices is thus nothing but an old wives' tale.' Source: TodayIFoundOut, 'Searing Meat Does Not Seal in the Juices'; AmazingRibs.

question: A steak hits a smoking-hot pan and comes out wearing a dark, crackly crust. Harold McGee, the food scientist, sears every steak he cooks, and Meathead, the pitmaster, says simply, 'brown is beautiful.' What does that crust give the meat?
answer: A deep, savory, roasted flavor and rich aroma
choices: A deep, savory, roasted flavor and rich aroma
A tender, juicy texture all the way to the center
A warm outer layer that keeps it hot far longer
A soft, delicate surface that is easier to chew
context: The dark crust is the Maillard reaction — amino acids reacting with sugars under high heat — plus caramelization: a huge upgrade in taste and aroma, but not a moisture seal. McGee spent decades debunking the 'juices' myth yet still sears every steak, purely because it tastes better. Source: AmazingRibs, 'Myth: Searing Steaks Seals In The Juices'; Wikipedia, 'Searing.'

question: A cook lays a steak in a blazing-hot pan to 'seal in the juices,' a rule that feels like wisdom handed down through generations of kitchens. Food historians trace it instead to one particular man, writing in 1847. Who first put the famous rule into print?
answer: A German chemist, in a book on food chemistry
choices: A German chemist, in a book on food chemistry
A Scottish doctor, in a guide to healthy eating
A French royal chef, in a grand cookbook
An English butcher, in a trade handbook
context: The chemist Justus von Liebig proposed the idea in his 1847 book 'Researches on the Chemistry of Food,' reasoning that a fierce initial blast of heat hardens the surface into a protective crust. He never tested it — and cooks believed it for nearly a century, spread even by the legendary French chef Auguste Escoffier, until simple US home-economics experiments in the 1930s weighed the meat and disproved it. A lab, not a kitchen, gave cooking its most-repeated rule. Source: TodayIFoundOut, 'Searing Meat Does Not Seal in the Juices'; Wikipedia, 'Searing.'

question: Skeptics call soybean, corn, and sunflower oils 'seed oils' because each comes from a plant's seeds. One famous kitchen oil doesn't belong in that group — it's really more like fruit juice. Which oil is the odd one out?
context: Olive oil is pressed from the flesh of the olive fruit, so it's a 'fruit oil,' not a seed oil. Avocado oil (from the green pulp) sits on the same fruit-oil side; canola, peanut, and sesame oils all come from seeds. Source: ScienceInsights, 'What Oils Are Not Seed Oils'; Wikipedia, 'Avocado oil.'

question: Cate Shanahan, a doctor and outspoken critic of modern seed oils, lumps the most common of them together, from soybean and canola to rice-bran, and blames them for modern disease. Her grim nickname for the group is borrowed from a Quentin Tarantino western. What does she call them?
context: The 'Hateful Eight' are soybean, canola, corn, sunflower, safflower, cottonseed, grapeseed, and rice-bran oil — eight industrial oils, echoing the eight outlaws in Quentin Tarantino's 2015 film. Source: Wikipedia, 'Seed oil misinformation.'

question: Plant breeders at the University of Manitoba took an old crop, grown for lamp oil and machine grease and too bitter and heart-harming to eat, and bred it into a safe kitchen oil in the 1970s. The new oil's name, canola, comes from 'Canadian oil, low acid'. What plant did they start from?
context: Canola is bred-down rapeseed. Plant breeders at the University of Manitoba cut its heart-harming erucic acid from over 40% to under 2%, and in 1978 trademarked 'canola' — short for 'CANadian Oil, Low Acid.' Source: Saturday Evening Post, 'The Creation of Canola Oil'; Wikipedia, 'Rapeseed oil.'

question: A cook in an American kitchen of 1909 almost never used one oil that, by 1999, had become the country's most-used cooking oil. Its use multiplied more than a thousand times in that century, powering the whole seed-oil boom. Which oil was it?
context: A 2011 study by Tanya Blasbalg and colleagues tracked the surge: as cheap soybean oil spread, linoleic acid climbed from 2.79% to 7.21% of Americans' daily calories over the 1900s. Source: Blasbalg et al. 2011, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.

question: A fast-food fryer reuses the same corn or sunflower oil again and again, and here both sides of the seed-oil argument agree. Under high heat the fragile double bonds of those polyunsaturated oils break apart, and with every reuse harmful compounds pile up. What class of compound forms?
context: Repeatedly heated PUFA-rich oils generate toxic aldehydes such as 4-HNE, 4-HHE, acrolein, and malondialdehyde. Chemist Martin Grootveld of De Montfort University, Leicester, calls this the strongest, best-evidenced part of the skeptic case. Source: Grootveld et al., 'Evidence-Based Challenges to... Toxic Aldehydic Lipid Oxidation Products.'

question: Martin Grootveld's team fried a batch of potatoes in fresh sunflower oil, then fried another batch in the same oil, and another, round after round, testing the oil after each one. Harmful breakdown chemicals piled up higher with every reuse. Where did those chemicals go next?
context: Grootveld's team ran repeated frying sessions at about 170°C; aldehyde levels rose with every reuse, and the compounds moved out of the oil and into the fried potatoes. This is the chemistry behind 'don't cook in old fryer oil.' Source: Moumtaz, Grootveld et al., Scientific Reports (2019), repeated domestic deep-frying of potato chips.

question: Skeptics warn that seed oils reach the dinner table laced with leftover hexane, the gasoline solvent that washed the oil out of the crushed seeds. Chemists who test the bottled oil find only the faintest trace of it. Why does so little hexane survive the trip from mill to bottle?
answer: It evaporates easily, and heat drives it off
choices: It evaporates easily, and heat drives it off
It sinks and is drained off the bottom
Sunlight breaks it down on the store shelf
The seeds' own enzymes digest it away
context: After extraction, mills drive the hexane off with heat, and the volatile solvent nearly all evaporates, so tests of refined oil find only traces; Europe has capped residual hexane at 1 mg per kilogram of oil since 1998. When the U.S. EPA studied industrial hexane in the 1980s, it found traces that small cause no nerve damage, so the 'poisoned by solvent' claim is overstated. (Hexane can harm nerves, but only at heavy industrial exposures, not dietary traces.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'Seed oil misinformation' (EPA hexane finding); OCL journal 2001, residual hexane limits (ocl-journal.org/10.1051/ocl.2001.0167).

question: Mainstream nutrition scientists answer the seed-oil critics with a measurement. When people swap butter and other saturated fat for polyunsaturated seed oil, one number at the doctor's office reliably drops, enough that the American Heart Association still recommends some omega-6 in the diet. Which number drops?
context: The AHA's 2009 Science Advisory (Harris, Mozaffarian, Rimm and colleagues, in Circulation) found no compelling evidence that omega-6 is harmful and recommended 5-10% of calories from it — even concluding that cutting omega-6 would 'more likely increase than decrease' heart risk. A 2019 pooled analysis of 30 cohorts (Marklund et al.) tied higher linoleic-acid levels to LOWER cardiovascular risk. Source: Harris et al. 2009, Circulation; Marklund et al. 2019, Circulation.

question: Servants at a lavish French dinner in the 1700s set every dish of a course on the table at once, soups, roasts and steaming stews in one enormous spread: service à la française. A seated guest could take food from only some of those dishes. Which ones?
answer: The dishes within his own arm's reach
choices: The dishes within his own arm's reach
The dishes reserved for his rank
The dishes the head carver sent down
The dishes nearest the host's seat
context: In service à la française, every dish of a course arrived together in one vast spread, and diners helped themselves only from the platters they could physically reach — so a diner's SEAT decided his dinner. Whatever sat far down the table, he never tasted. Source: Wikipedia, 'Service à la française'; instituteofetiquette.com.
