context: Farming was invented independently more than once, not spread from a single cradle: rice was domesticated in China's Yangtze valley (and maize in Mexico) around 9,000 years ago. The Fertile Crescent was simply first. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2664049/

question: The ancestors of the Inca first farmed the potato thousands of years ago, high in a great mountain range, and farmers there still grow it on steep slopes above 10,000 feet in a dozen colors: purple, red, blue and yellow. Which mountain range gave the world the potato?
context: Most people assume the potato is Irish or European, but it was first domesticated 7,000-10,000 years ago high in the Andes, around Lake Titicaca in what is now southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia. Of the world's roughly 5,000 potato varieties, about 3,000 still grow in the Andes. Source: Wikipedia 'Potato' ('first domesticated in southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia... around Lake Titicaca').

question: Andean farmers make a preserved potato called chuño that can sit in a village storehouse for years, by some accounts a whole decade, without rotting, though mold, yeast and bacteria float in the mountain air. How does chuño hold off the microbes?
answer: The freezing night bursts the potato's cells so the sun dries it out
choices: The freezing night bursts the potato's cells so the sun dries it out
The salt rubbed into the potato slowly pulls its water out
The smoke of slow fires coats the potato in bitter tars
The cold storehouse keeps the potato chilled all year round
context: Freezing at night (around -5C) ruptures the potato's cells, and the strong day sun then drives that water off, leaving a chunk so dry that mold, yeast, and bacteria can't take hold — which is why chuño keeps for 2-4 years, and by some accounts a decade or more. Salt-curing and smoking preserve other foods, but chuño's trick is the freeze-and-dry cycle of the high Andes. Source: Wikipedia 'Chuño' and 'Qullqa' (freeze-dried potatoes lasted 2-4 years, some up to 10).

question: To turn potatoes into chuño, Andean families spread them out to freeze hard on icy mountain nights, then let the day's fierce sun thaw them soft. Over the next several days they repeat one more step, again and again, until the potatoes shrink to a small chunk. Traditionally, how do whole families do that final step?
choices: They boil the potatoes in pots
They smoke the potatoes over fires
They bury the potatoes in sand
context: Over about a week the potatoes are frozen at night (around -5C), thawed and dried under the strong day sun, and trampled underfoot — traditionally by whole families — to press out the water and slip off the skins, until only a light chunk of chuño remains. Source: Wikipedia 'Chuño'.

question: In a high Andean village, two kinds of chuño dry side by side: dark black chuño, frozen each night and thawed each day, and paler white chuño, called tunta or moraya in Quechua and Aymara, which gets one extra step before drying in the sun. What is that step?
context: Black chuño is left unwashed; white chuño (tunta or moraya) is soaked in running water — often a cold stream — before sun-drying, which gives it a paler color. In Bolivia the two aren't interchangeable: the hearty soup chairo specifically calls for ground chuño. Source: Wikipedia 'Chuño'.

question: Irish farmers of the 1840s nearly all grew one potato variety, the Lumper, and every plant was a genetic clone of the next. When blight struck, not one could resist, and about one in eight Irish people died within three years. Why were the plants all identical clones in the first place?
answer: Potatoes are grown from cut-up tubers, not seeds
choices: Potatoes are grown from cut-up tubers, not seeds
Irish law banned planting more than one variety
The Lumper could not produce any flowers or seeds
Blight had already killed off all the other varieties
context: Potatoes are propagated from cut seed-potatoes (tubers), so each plant is a genetic clone with the same weaknesses. With nearly all of Ireland planted in the single Lumper variety, the blight Phytophthora infestans met no resistance, and about one in eight Irish people died in three years. Source: UC Berkeley Evolution, 'Monoculture and the Irish Potato Famine'; Potatoes in Canada, 'The Lumper'.

question: Dinner is a piece of chicken hot off the grill, a scoop of white rice, some buttered broccoli and a drizzle of olive oil. After the meal, the body takes one of the four apart into building blocks to repair muscle, skin and hair. Which food does the rebuilding?
context: Protein is the plate's build-and-repair section. It breaks down into about 20 amino acids -- the body's actual building blocks -- and proteins like collagen and keratin form your skin, hair, nails, bones and teeth. The rice (a carb) and the oil (a fat) don't do this job; the meat, eggs or beans are the part that rebuilds YOU. Source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Amino Acids: Benefits & Food Sources'; WebMD, 'Foods High in Amino Acids'.

question: Suppose you heap your dinner plate with vegetables, as Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate encourages. A cucumber is more than 90 percent water, and celery, lettuce and zucchini are nearly as watery, which is the quiet reason the model wants so many. What does all that water do for you?
answer: It means a big heap of veggies carries almost no calories
choices: It means a big heap of veggies carries almost no calories
It ferries their complete protein straight into your muscles
It lets their natural sugars release slowly for steady energy
It dissolves their healthy fats so your body can absorb them
context: Vegetables (with fruit) get to fill about half the plate -- vegetables the larger share -- because they're the lowest-calorie section, mostly water and fiber, so you can eat a big, filling volume for very few calories. Cucumber is ~96% water; iceberg lettuce ~96%, celery ~95%, tomato ~95%, zucchini ~95%, watermelon ~92%. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source, 'Healthy Eating Plate'; Cleveland Clinic, 'Foods To Help Keep You Hydrated This Summer'.

question: Scientists at Ohio State fed volunteers a plain, fat-free salad in 2005, then served the same salad again with a single fruit sliced on top. This time they measured over fifteen times as much beta-carotene absorbed from the salad's vegetables. Which fruit had they sliced on top?
context: In a 2005 Ohio State study (Unlu, Bohn, Clinton & Schwartz, Journal of Nutrition), adding avocado to a salad multiplied absorption of beta-carotene 15.3x, alpha-carotene 7.2x and lutein 5.1x versus the fat-free salad; added to salsa, it multiplied lycopene 4.4x and beta-carotene 2.6x. The fat in the avocado is what unlocks the vegetables' nutrients -- the same reason a plain salad needs a drizzle of oil. Source: Unlu NZ, Bohn T, Clinton SK, Schwartz SJ, J Nutr 135:431-436 (2005), PubMed 15735074.  (Legend.)

question: Harvard's nutrition scientists drew up their Healthy Eating Plate and made one surprising call: they flatly refused to count the humble potato as a vegetable, though the American government's own MyPlate still counts it. Harvard's reason is about what happens in the body after someone eats a plain baked or mashed potato. What is that reason?
answer: A plain potato is fast starch that spikes blood sugar like white bread
choices: A plain potato is fast starch that spikes blood sugar like white bread
A plain potato hides more fat under its skin than any real vegetable
A plain potato holds almost none of the vitamins other vegetables do
A plain potato grows underground, so it counts as a root, not a veg
context: Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate pointedly says 'Potatoes and French fries don't count' as a vegetable, reasoning that a plain potato is full of rapidly digested starch that hits blood sugar much like refined grains and sweets. Treat this as ONE model's reasoning, not settled law -- the USDA's MyPlate still counts potatoes as vegetables, and the two guides otherwise agree that about half your plate should be produce. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source, 'Healthy Eating Plate vs. USDA's MyPlate'.

question: A stew pot bubbles with carrots cut in rough, bite-sized chunks that need not match, since they will bob around in the broth for an hour. Of the four everyday knife cuts, which is this loose, anything-goes one called?
context: Chopping is the most forgiving cut of all — a generic term for cutting food into rough, bite-sized pieces that don't have to be uniform in size or shape, which is exactly why it suits a rustic stew. Source: WebstaurantStore, 'Types of Knife Cuts.'

question: A trainee in a professional kitchen is told to dice the potatoes, and a dice is fussy about one thing: every piece must come out the same size, so all of them cook at the same rate in the pan. What shape is the trainee cutting?
context: The whole game of dicing is evenness: matching cubes drop into the pan the same size and finish cooking at the same moment. Dice even comes in graded sizes — large, medium, and small. Source: Wikipedia, 'List of culinary knife cuts'; Escoffier Online, 'Why Knife Cuts Matter.'

question: A cook wants a single clove of garlic to flavor the whole pot, not just whoever bites into the big chunk. So the garlic gets cut as fine as a sharp knife can manage, until it becomes almost a smooth paste. What is this finest of the everyday knife cuts called?
context: Mince is the finest cut there is — around one-sixteenth of an inch, so small the pieces almost dissolve into the dish; it's the smallest cut you can make before food becomes puree. Cutting garlic and ginger this fine gives what chefs call 'maximum flavor dispersion.' Source: WebstaurantStore, 'Types of Knife Cuts.'

question: At the cutting board, a trained cook slices a ripe tomato into flat, even rounds and never saws the knife back and forth the way a beginner does. Each round takes a single stroke of the blade. What is that stroke?
answer: A smooth glide drawn from tip to heel
choices: A smooth glide drawn from tip to heel
A quick downward chop through the flesh
A firm straight press onto the board
A rocking pivot around the blade's tip
context: Slicing makes flat, even pieces with a drawing motion — the blade glides through the food from tip to heel in one fluid stroke, never a back-and-forth saw. That single smooth pass leaves a clean face on the food instead of a torn, ragged one. Source: Wusthof, 'Essential Knife Skills 101.'

question: A beginner cook in a hurry cuts an onion into fat chunks and paper-thin slivers and tosses the whole uneven pile into one hot, sizzling pan of oil over high heat. When the dish is done and tasted, something has clearly gone wrong. What happened in the pan?
answer: The tiny slivers scorched while the big chunks stayed raw
choices: The tiny slivers scorched while the big chunks stayed raw
The big chunks scorched while the tiny slivers stayed raw
Every piece finished cooking at exactly the same time
The whole panful steamed into mush before it could brown
context: This is the whole reason knife cuts matter: in one cooking vessel, smaller pieces overcook and scorch while larger ones stay raw or underdone in the middle. Cutting all pieces the same size means they all reach 'done' at the same moment. Source: Escoffier Online, 'Why Knife Cuts Matter.'

question: Fat chunks beside paper-thin slivers: vegetables cut fast and uneven pile up on a hurried cook's board. For most dishes that ruins the cooking, because pieces of different sizes finish at different times, but for one dish the mismatch does not matter at all. Which dish is it?
context: A loose 'rough chop' is perfectly fine for a long-simmered stock, where the vegetables cook down for hours and then get strained out anyway — but it's wrong for a quick saute or stir-fry, where each piece's size decides whether it's done. Match the cut to the cooking. Source: WebstaurantStore, 'Types of Knife Cuts'; Escoffier Online, 'Why Knife Cuts Matter.'

question: A professional cook dicing an onion never tries to carve its pieces straight off the whole onion. The first move is to slice the onion into flat slabs, and the slabs still need two more moves before they are ready for the pan. What are the next two steps, in order?
answer: Cut the slabs into sticks, then crosscut the sticks into cubes
choices: Cut the slabs into sticks, then crosscut the sticks into cubes
Crosscut the slabs straight into cubes, skipping the sticks
Roll the slabs up tight, then slice the roll into cubes
Stack all the slabs and chop straight down through them
context: Even professionals build a dice in three stages: plank, then stick, then cube. You cut a flat slab (the plank), cut the slab into sticks, then bundle the sticks and crosscut them into cubes. That middle stick stage has a French name — the batonnet, literally 'little stick.' Source: WebstaurantStore, 'Types of Knife Cuts'; Wikipedia, 'List of culinary knife cuts.'

question: A fruit bowl holds a banana, a strawberry, a raspberry and a cherry. To a botanist, a true berry is a fleshy fruit grown from a single flower that holds its seeds inside its own soft flesh, and only one of the four passes that strict test. Which fruit is it?
context: A banana ticks every botanical box for a berry: it grows from a single flower's one ovary, its whole wall ripens into soft flesh, and the seeds sit embedded inside — those tiny dark specks running down the core. The strawberry, raspberry and cherry each fail the test in a different way. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: Four fruits at a market stall carry the word 'berry' right in their names: strawberry, blackberry, raspberry and blueberry. To a botanist, a true berry grows from a single flower's ovary with its seeds spread through the flesh, and only one of the four passes. Which one?
context: Blueberry, cranberry and currant are true berries — fleshy through, grown from one ovary with the seeds embedded inside. Strawberry, blackberry and raspberry only borrow the word 'berry'; botanically each is built a different way and fails the test. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A child peels a lunchbox banana and eats right through the faint black specks down its middle, all that is left of its seeds. Its wild ancestor in the jungles of Southeast Asia is crammed with big, hard, tooth-cracking seeds, and farmers did not breed those seeds out. Why does the supermarket banana come out seedless?
answer: It swells and ripens without ever being fertilized.
choices: It swells and ripens without ever being fertilized.
Growers breed its seeds a little smaller each year.
Its seeds melt into sugar as the fruit ripens.
It is always picked green, before seeds can form.
context: The eating banana grows and swells without being pollinated — a trick called parthenocarpy — so its 'seeds' never develop past faint specks. Wild bananas still make the real thing: seeds so big and hard they can crack a tooth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A diner bites into a ripe strawberry, the most berry-sounding fruit of all, though a botanist will not call it a true berry. Its sweet red part is not the fruit's ovary; it grew from another piece of the flower, which puffed up huge and turned red. Which piece of the flower was it?
answer: The base the flower was sitting on.
choices: The base the flower was sitting on.
The petals, thickened and turned sweet.
The stalk just below the flower head.
The pollen sacs, swollen and reddened.
context: Botanists call that swollen flower base the receptacle, which makes the strawberry an 'accessory fruit' — the tasty part isn't the true fruit at all. A real berry's flesh is the ripened wall of the ovary itself, which is exactly what the strawberry lacks. Source: Wikipedia, 'Accessory fruit'.

question: On a botanist's bench lie a grape, a kiwi, a chili pepper and an eggplant, all true berries, though none looks like a supermarket berry. Two of the four are also close cousins of the tomato in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, which shares one shape of flower and one family of chemicals. Which two?
answer: The chili pepper and the eggplant.
choices: The chili pepper and the eggplant.
The kiwi and the chili pepper.
context: The nightshade family (Solanaceae) includes the tomato, the chili pepper and the eggplant — all fleshy fruits from a single ovary with seeds in the pulp, so all true berries. Grapes and kiwifruit are berries too, but from completely different plant families. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A cook runs a thumb across a strawberry and feels about 200 tiny dots freckling its red skin, and most people would confidently call each one a seed. Botanists see those little dots very differently. What is each dot, botanically?
answer: A whole tiny fruit with one seed inside it.
choices: A whole tiny fruit with one seed inside it.
A hard scale that shields the soft flesh.
A tiny pore that lets the fruit breathe.
A gland that oozes out the red juice.
context: Each dot is an achene — a complete, tiny, one-seeded fruit — so a single strawberry carries roughly 200 real fruits on its skin. The bumpy specks everyone calls 'seeds' are the only TRUE fruits the strawberry has. Source: Wikipedia, 'Accessory fruit'.

question: A girl squeezes a ripe raspberry between her fingers, and it crumbles into a dozen tiny, juicy beads, a sign it is no true berry: a true berry, such as a grape, is one solid piece of flesh. Where did all those separate beads come from?
answer: One flower with many ovaries, one bead from each.
choices: One flower with many ovaries, one bead from each.
One ovary that split into segments as it ripened.
A soft rind that puffed up around a hollow core.
Seeds that each grew their own bubble of pulp.
context: A raspberry is an 'aggregate fruit': its single flower held many ovaries, and each ovary ripened into one little bead (a drupelet), so the whole thing pulls apart. A blackberry is built the same way — which is why neither is a true berry. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A boy digs a thumbnail into the tough, oil-dotted peel of an orange and pulls apart the sweet, juice-filled segments packed tightly inside. It looks nothing like a grape, yet a botanist files the orange in the same broad class of fruit as the grape. Which class is it?
context: That citrus berry has its own name — a hesperidium — with a leathery, oil-dotted rind and juice-filled segments inside. A lemon and a grapefruit are hesperidia too. It still passes the berry test: a fleshy fruit from a single ovary with seeds inside. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A cook slices an avocado open and scoops out its soft, buttery green flesh with a spoon. The avocado is a true botanical berry, though a strange one, wrapped around one enormous pit instead of many tiny seeds. In botanical terms, what is the green flesh?
answer: The ripened fruit wall around a single seed.
choices: The ripened fruit wall around a single seed.
A thick layer of stored-up leaf tissue.
The lining of a hollow inner seed pod.
A cushion of pulp that feeds the seed.
context: By the berry test — one ovary, fleshy through, seed inside — the avocado passes: the entire green flesh is the fruit wall, the ripened ovary, wrapped around one big seed (the pit). That makes it a one-seeded berry. Source: Wikipedia, 'Berry (botany)'.

question: A watermelon heavier than a bowling ball sits on a market table, yet botanists file it in the same class of fruit as a tiny grape: the berry. It is a hard-rinded berry called a pepo, like the cucumber and the pumpkin, and its tough, striped rind lets it grow huge without splitting. Where does that rind come from as the fruit forms?
answer: Flower tissue that fused and hardened over the ovary.
choices: Flower tissue that fused and hardened over the ovary.
A thick skin of dried, flattened seed cases.
Leaves that wrapped the fruit and turned woody.
The plant's stem, swollen into a stiff shell.
context: That hard-shelled berry has its own name — a pepo, the gourd-family type. The rind forms from flower tissue fused over the ovary, and inside it's fleshy right through with no dividing walls, seeds scattered in the pulp. Cucumbers and pumpkins are pepos too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pepo (botany)'.

question: A wok cook in a Chinese kitchen tilts the knife and slices across a carrot on a slant instead of cutting straight down. A straight cut would leave a small round coin, but the slant changes that. What shape does each slice become?
context: This slanted cut is called cutting on the bias (or 'on the diagonal') — a slice made straight across a carrot, celery stalk, or scallion at about a 30-to-45-degree angle, with chefs often favoring 45. Japanese cooking even has a named version, naname-giri, a 45-degree diagonal cut for exactly these oval pieces. Source: scienceinsights.org, 'What Does Sliced on the Bias Mean in Cooking'; Wikipedia, 'List of culinary knife cuts'.

question: Carrots sliced on a diagonal for a stir-fry give every piece a much bigger, longer cut face than a round coin would. The wok is roaring hot, and the food spends only a minute or two in it. Why is that extra cut surface just what a Chinese wok cook wants?
answer: Heat reaches more of each piece at once, so it cooks faster and more evenly.
choices: Heat reaches more of each piece at once, so it cooks faster and more evenly.
The extra surface locks moisture in, so the carrot stays raw and crisp.
The wider face makes the piece heavier, so it sinks and steams gently.
The bigger cut releases more sugar, so the whole pan turns to syrup.
context: As one guide puts it, the angled cuts 'create more surface area for heat to penetrate so that food cooks faster' — perfect for the quick, screaming heat of a wok. That same extra surface does double duty: more flat area touches the pan, so the piece browns faster and soaks up more sauce, which is why the bias cut shows up constantly in Chinese, Thai, and Japanese cooking. Source: scienceinsights.org, 'What Does Sliced on the Bias Mean in Cooking'; madeincookware.com, corroborated by America's Test Kitchen.

question: A cook roll-cuts a carrot: one slanted slice, a quarter-turn of the carrot, another slanted slice, all the way down. The carrot tapers from a fat end to a skinny tip, yet she wants every tumbling chunk the same size so they all cook through together. What does she do with the knife as she reaches the skinny end?
answer: Tilt the knife to a wider slant, so even the skinny end yields a full-size chunk.
choices: Tilt the knife to a wider slant, so even the skinny end yields a full-size chunk.
Keep the same slant but cut thicker slices, so the skinny end still makes big chunks.
Keep the same slant but roll a bigger turn, so the skinny end shows more faces.
Steepen the knife toward straight down, so the skinny end drops small coins.
context: This is the roll cut (also called the oblique cut): slice on the bias, roll the carrot a quarter-turn, slice again at the same angle, and repeat all the way down. But a carrot is tapered, so a skilled cook keeps the angle sharper (more acute) at the fat end and opens it to a wider, more obtuse angle as the carrot narrows toward the tip — that way every tumbling chunk ends up about the same size and cooks at the same rate. (All those fresh-cut faces also leave a roll-cut chunk nearly all exposed surface, even more than a plain bias slice, which is why the pieces soak up sauce and cook fast in stir-fries and braises.) Source: madeincookware.com, 'How to Roll Cut'; America's Test Kitchen, 'How to Make a Roll Cut and Why'; scienceinsights.org.

question: A Paris shopkeeper named Boulanger, as French legend tells it, sold one product to tired, weak or sick customers in the 1700s and called it a 'restaurant', something restorative. The name only later passed from the food to the shop that sold it. What was the original 'restaurant'?
choices: a cup of hot spiced wine
context: The French called this reviving bouillon a 'restaurant,' from the verb restaurer — to restore (rooted in Latin restaurare, 'to renew'). People took it not to fill the belly but to rebuild their strength. Only later did the name leap from the soup to the shop that sold it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Restaurant'; Merriam-Webster, 'The History of Restaurant.'

question: A hungry traveler pulled into a French coaching inn, in the days before restaurants, and found no menu and no choice. The innkeeper decided what to cook, and everyone ate the same meal at his fixed hour, elbow to elbow at one long table. What was this take-it-or-leave-it inn meal called?
context: It was the table d'hôte — literally 'the host's table.' You ate whatever the innkeeper had cooking, whenever he chose to serve it, elbow to elbow with strangers. The restaurant's revolution was the exact opposite: your own small table, your own choice of dish, your own hour. Source: Wikipedia, 'Restaurant.'

question: A diner in one of the first Paris restaurants of the late 1700s could do something new: order a single dish from a list of separate dishes, each with its own price, and pay only for that. Paper was dear, and the dishes changed every day. Where was that list written for him to read?
context: The French word for that little board was the carte — the 'card.' Choosing your dishes off it is why, to this day, ordering individual plates is called eating à la carte, 'according to the card.' The menu was born as chalk on a board. Source: Wikipedia, 'À la carte.'

question: A palace-trained cook in a noble household lost his post in the French Revolution of 1789, when his masters were killed or fled the country. Many skilled private cooks were thrown out of work the same way. What did many of them do next?
answer: opened public restaurants of their own
choices: opened public restaurants of their own
cooked in secret for hidden nobles
went to sea as ships' cooks
sold their old recipes to bakeries
context: With their aristocratic masters dead or in exile, dozens of these palace-trained cooks opened restaurants and served anyone with coins to spend. For the first time, food once locked inside noble mansions was on offer to ordinary Parisians. The Revolution set fine French cooking loose in the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Restaurant.'

question: Parisians who told the legend of the first restaurateur, a man named Boulanger, enjoyed a joke hidden in his name. The surname is the French word for an everyday food trade, yet the man supposedly sold none of that trade's goods. What trade does 'boulanger' name?
context: The surname Boulanger literally means 'baker' in French — yet the legend says this man sold not loaves but a restorative broth. The tale was repeated in cookbooks for two hundred years, until historians began asking whether Boulanger was ever a real person at all. Source: National Geographic, 'Who Invented the First Modern Restaurant?'

question: In the Paris archives, Rebecca Spang spent years hunting for any real trace of the founder whom French cookbooks had credited, for two centuries, with opening the first restaurant in the 1760s. What did her search turn up?
answer: no record that he ever existed
choices: no record that he ever existed
proof he had died deeply in debt
a rival who had stolen his idea
context: 'In all of this, I found no Boulanger,' Rebecca Spang wrote — no birth record, no shop, not even the famous lawsuit the legend claims he fought. The 'founder' of the restaurant appears to be a man who never lived. Spang argues the real innovator was a promoter named Mathurin Roze de Chantoiseau, around 1766. Source: National Geographic, 'Who Invented the First Modern Restaurant?'; Rebecca L. Spang, 'The Invention of the Restaurant.'

question: Over the door of the first Paris restaurant in the 1760s, French legend says, hung a Latin motto: 'Come to me, all who suffer from stomach pain, and I will restore you.' Parisians recognized it as a cheeky twist on a famous line. Who first spoke that line?
choices: King Louis XIV, at his court
context: The Latin ran 'Venite ad me omnes qui stomacho laboratis, et ego vos restaurabo.' It echoed Jesus's famous welcome in Matthew's Gospel — 'Come to me, all you who are weary… and I will give you rest' — but swapped weary souls for aching stomachs and rest for a restorative broth. Like the founder himself, the sign may be pure legend. Source: Merriam-Webster, 'The History of Restaurant.'

question: Rebecca Spang traced the much-retold legend of the restaurant's founder to a single written source, set down in 1782, seventeen years after the man supposedly opened his doors. The tale had been repeated for generations. Where did the story first appear?
answer: a printed history of French food
choices: a printed history of French food
a Paris police court's case file
context: In 1782 a former Jesuit, Le Grand d'Aussy, published a history of French eating and named an otherwise-unknown 'Boulanger' as the restaurant's 1765 inventor. Every later retelling traces back to those few lines — a story set down seventeen years after the fact, by a man who could not have witnessed it. That thin thread grew into two centuries of legend. Source: National Geographic, 'Who Invented the First Modern Restaurant?'

question: The Michelin brothers gave their red guide away free for twenty years, about 35,000 copies in 1900 alone, when all of France had barely 3,000 cars. In 1920 the company began charging seven francs for it. What reason did André Michelin reportedly give?
answer: that people only value what they pay for
choices: that people only value what they pay for
that printing costs had finally caught up
that too many drivers hoarded free copies
that rival guides were undercutting them
context: André Michelin reportedly declared that 'man only truly respects what he pays for' — and charging worked: once the guide cost money, its verdicts carried real weight. Michelin added restaurant ratings, a single star in 1926 and the famous three-star scale by the 1930s, until its stars became the most coveted prize in world cooking. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michelin Guide.'

question: Shopping for a beef stew, a cook passes over the pricey steaks for the cheapest, chewiest cut: shoulder, a hard-working muscle laced with tough connective tissue. She browns it, covers it in liquid and simmers it, lidded, for hours. How does it turn out?
context: This is the whole logic of braising: cheap, hard-working cuts like chuck (shoulder) and shank are loaded with tough connective tissue, and only long, slow, moist cooking can turn that toughness into silky tenderness - the exact opposite of a fast-grilled steak, which wants a naturally tender cut. Sources: wildcountrymeats.com; recipetineats.com (beef bourguignon).

question: Boeuf bourguignon, France's most famous beef stew, braises its beef for hours almost entirely in one bold, dark liquid. That liquid stains the stew a deep purple-brown and lends it a rich, sharp, grown-up flavor. What is the braising liquid?
context: 'Boeuf bourguignon' literally means 'beef Burgundy,' and the beef braises in red Burgundy wine (usually with some beef stock alongside). The wine isn't a splash added at the end - it's the main liquid the meat slowly cooks in. Source: Wikipedia, 'Beef bourguignon.'

question: Lardons, little strips of cured, salted pork, go into the hot, empty pot first when a cook starts boeuf bourguignon or coq au vin, the two great French braises. The beef or chicken, the onions and the vegetables all wait their turn. Why do the lardons go in first?
answer: To melt out their fat and cook everything else in it
choices: To melt out their fat and cook everything else in it
To crisp them into a garnish added at the very end
To season the empty pot before the beef goes in
To render slowly, or the cured pork turns rubbery
context: Lardons are little strips or cubes of salt-cured (usually unsmoked) pork, cut from the belly or fatback - close cousins of bacon. You fry them first to render out their fat, brown everything else in that rendered fat, then scatter the crisp lardons back in near the end. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lardon.'

question: Coq au vin braises for hours in wine, until the meat falls off the bone. So slow a braise only pays off with tough meat, and the dish was born as a thrifty rescue for one tough old bird that nobody could roast into anything but shoe leather. Which bird was it created to rescue?
context: 'Coq au vin' means literally 'rooster in wine.' A coq is a mature male chicken, packed with so much tough connective tissue it's far too chewy to roast. Braising it for hours in wine was the classic way to turn that spent old rooster tender and delicious. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coq au vin.'

question: A cook pours wine over the beef for a braise, trusting the popular kitchen claim that it will tenderize the tough meat. That is mostly a myth: the slow, moist heat does the tenderizing. Left to simmer uncovered for hours, what is the wine really doing for the dish?
answer: It reduces, concentrating into a thick, glossy sauce
choices: It reduces, concentrating into a thick, glossy sauce
It boils away entirely, leaving only plain broth
It keeps the pot from ever coming to a boil
It turns the meat's fat into extra gelatin
context: The collagen-to-gelatin breakdown is what tenderizes the meat; the wine's real gift is flavor. Simmering uncovered, the wine reduces - water boils off and the wine concentrates down into the body, gloss, and deep flavor of the sauce. (This is the widely taught view; some sources still credit the wine's acidity with a small tenderizing role.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'Beef bourguignon'; ricardocuisine.com.

question: Food historians went hunting for the roots of boeuf bourguignon, a stew many diners take for a Burgundian peasant dish a thousand years old. The recipe, they found, was first written down only in 1867, and they tied the real dish to one French city. Which city made it famous?
context: Boeuf bourguignon isn't an ancient Burgundian peasant recipe at all - it was first documented in 1867 and is tied to Paris bistros, only being called a 'Burgundian specialty' in the 20th century. The 'Burgundy' in its name really points to the WINE it's cooked in, not an old regional home. (Auguste Escoffier later locked it into fine-dining canon with his 1907 Guide Culinaire.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Beef bourguignon.'  (Legend.)

question: A defiant Gallic chief, the legend goes, mocked Julius Caesar during his war on the Gauls by sending him a scrawny rooster, which the Romans cooked in wine: the first coq au vin, over two thousand years ago. Food historians say the tale is almost certainly just a story. What gives it away?
answer: No written recipe for it appears until the early 1900s
choices: No written recipe for it appears until the early 1900s
Ancient Gauls were forbidden to cook with any wine
Romans believed eating rooster brought terrible luck
The tale was first invented by a famous French novelist
context: The Caesar-and-the-Gauls tale is charming but undocumented - the coq au vin recipe simply isn't written down until the early 20th century. (A related but different dish, poulet au vin blanc, does show up in an 1864 cookbook, 'Cookery for English Households, by a French Lady.') Julia Child later brought coq au vin to American kitchens on her PBS show, The French Chef. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coq au vin.'  (Legend.)

question: At a Swedish party nobody carries dinner to the guests: the food waits in a long row down one table, and each guest walks up and fills a plate. Swedes call that table the smörgåsbord. Word for word, what does the name mean?
context: Smörgås is an open-faced buttered-bread sandwich and bord is table — so the word English reaches for whenever something is huge and varied ('a smorgasbord of options') is, in Swedish, just the sandwich table. English borrowed smorgasbord in 1893, and that figurative 'medley of anything' sense is recorded from 1948. Source: Wikipedia, 'Smorgasbord'; Etymonline, 'smorgasbord'.

question: Guests at a Swedish smörgåsbord work through it in a strict order of rounds, fetching a fresh, clean plate for each new one. The very first round gets a clean plate all its own, so no other flavor touches it. Which dish opens the meal?
context: Herring (sill) opens the smörgåsbord, and it gets that clean plate of its own for a reason: its pickled tang is strong enough that Swedes will not let it bleed into whatever you take next. From there you work through cold fish, then cold meats, then the warm dishes, then cheese — fetching a fresh plate as you go. The other hard rule: never pile hot and cold food together on the same plate. Source: ScandiKitchen, 'Little Lessons: Smorgasbord'; Wikipedia, 'Smorgasbord'.

question: Swedish merchant families as far back as the 1500s set out bread, butter and cheese beside bottles of brännvin, the spirit also called aquavit, and let their guests help themselves. They called it the brännvinsbord, the schnapps table. Where did it fit into a Swedish dinner party?
answer: An appetizer, eaten hours before the real dinner
choices: An appetizer, eaten hours before the real dinner
The dinner itself, with no courses afterward
A dessert round, brought out after dinner ended
A farewell course, offered as guests headed home
context: This little schnapps table is the ancestor of the famous Swedish spread — and it began as a warm-up, not the whole meal. Guests of the merchant and upper classes ate from the brännvinsbord standing up, sometimes two to five hours before the real dinner, and sometimes with the men and women in separate rooms. Only over the centuries did that pre-dinner table swell into the smörgåsbord we picture today — its grandest form being the julbord, the 'Christmas table,' a feast that can eat up an entire afternoon. Americans first met the spread at the 1939 New York World's Fair, at the Swedish Pavilion's Three Crowns Restaurant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Smorgasbord'; ScandiKitchen, 'Little Lessons: Smorgasbord'.

question: Catherine de' Medici was fourteen when she left Florence in 1533 to wed into France's royal family, and a famous legend grew up around her. Her Italian servants, the story claims, brought France everything from artichokes to fine table manners. Which piece of silverware does the tale falsely credit her with introducing?
context: This is the myth in miniature: the fork was one of many 'trophies' the tale piled into Catherine's luggage over the centuries -- alongside artichokes, sorbet, olive oil and truffles -- yet no early record supports any of it. Wikipedia lists 'utensils' among the fork-and-food claims that food historians have discredited. The story is a snowball that kept growing long after 1533. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Catherine de' Medici' (Culinary legend); thenewgastronome.com.

question: François Pierre de La Varenne, a French chef, swept away France's old heavy, spiced cooking in 1651, more than a century after Catherine de' Medici's wedding. He taught cooks to build flavor with roux, silky béchamel and rich stocks, none of it borrowed from Italy. How did La Varenne spread the new cooking?
answer: By writing the first true French cookbook.
choices: By writing the first true French cookbook.
By opening the king's first royal cooking school.
By cooking each night for the court at Versailles.
By founding the pastry-makers' guild of Paris.
context: La Varenne's 'Le Cuisinier Francois' (1651) is the founding text of French cuisine -- it introduced roux, bechamel, bisque, the bouquet garni, stocks, and butter in place of lard, none of it Italian. Food historian Barbara Ketcham Wheaton, in 'Savoring the Past,' showed real French haute cuisine formed about a century after Catherine's wedding, with no Italian fingerprint on it. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Francois Pierre La Varenne'; Frontiers in Nutrition (2020).

question: Susan Pinkard, a historian, tested the legend that Catherine de' Medici's 1533 wedding gave birth to French cuisine. She compared what wealthy Florentines ate in the 1530s with the food on the French court's tables, and what she found leaves no room for Italy to have taught France to cook. What did Pinkard discover about the two courts' fine dining?
answer: Their food was essentially identical, court to court.
choices: Their food was essentially identical, court to court.
France's was already far richer than Florence's.
Florence's was plain and simple beside France's.
The two had almost no dishes in common at all.
context: Pinkard, in 'A Revolution in Taste,' found the food Catherine grew up eating in Florence was 'identical in its fundamentals' to what she met at the French court: Renaissance elite kitchens across Europe all shared one complex, spicy, sweet style. There was no separate national 'French cuisine' for a single wedding to invent. The real lesson: great cuisines grow slowly, from many hands, regions and generations -- no lone hero or foreign bride creates a nation's kitchen. Sources: Susan Pinkard, 'A Revolution in Taste' (cambridgeblog.org); synthesis with Wheaton and Stephen Mennell.

question: A dad unpacking groceries sets four packages on the counter. Food scientists, he tells his kids, call a food ultra-processed when a factory builds it from extracted starches, oils and sugars plus additives no home kitchen would stock. Which package earns that label?
answer: A brick of instant ramen noodles
choices: A brick of instant ramen noodles
A block of sharp cheddar cheese
A can of plain cooked chickpeas
A bag of plain rolled oats
context: Ultra-processed foods are the everyday stuff kids already know: soft drinks, packaged snacks, instant noodles, chicken nuggets, sweetened breakfast cereals, mass-produced bread, ice cream, and artificially sweetened yogurt. Instant ramen is a factory product start to finish — refined-flour noodles plus a seasoning packet. Cheddar, canned chickpeas, and rolled oats all sit in NOVA's lower groups: whole foods and simple combinations of them. Source: news-medical.net, 'The NOVA Method of Food Classification.'

question: Suppose you stand in a supermarket with a box in your hand and want to judge how heavily processed the food inside is, no chemistry class needed. You flip the package over and read the ingredient list. What is the handy rule of thumb?
answer: The more ingredients you can't picture as real food, the more processed it is
choices: The more ingredients you can't picture as real food, the more processed it is
The brighter and shinier the box it comes in, the more processed it is
The more the food costs per pound, the more processed it is
The heavier the package feels in your hand, the more processed it is
context: NOVA's rough marker for ultra-processed food is five or more ingredients, especially ones you'd never recognize as a real food. (The 'apple = 1 ingredient, snack cake ≈ 30' contrast is an illustrative way to picture it, not a fixed count.) Source: news-medical.net, 'The NOVA Method of Food Classification.'

question: Carlos Monteiro sorted every food into four groups when he published his NOVA ranking in 2009, from Group 1, whole or barely changed, up to Group 4, the ultra-processed. Four packaged items come out of a grocery bag. Which one does NOVA still file in Group 1?
choices: A bag of plain white sugar
context: Group 1 is unprocessed or minimally processed: fresh fruit, vegetables, milk, eggs, meat. Heating, spinning, homogenizing, and cartoning milk doesn't move it out — nothing was added. Group 2 is culinary ingredients pulled from Group 1 foods — butter, oil, sugar, salt; Group 3 combines the two, like cheese or fresh-baked bread; Group 4 is the ultra-processed products, margarine and instant soup among them. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ultra-processed food.'

question: Two loaves of bread sit side by side on the same shelf. The bakery loaf is nothing but flour, water, salt, and yeast, so NOVA files it as plain 'processed food.' The soft, sliced supermarket sandwich loaf gets bumped up to 'ultra-processed' — same basic bread, higher group. What pushes the packaged loaf over the line?
answer: Emulsifiers and preservatives a home baker never uses
choices: Emulsifiers and preservatives a home baker never uses
A higher price for each sliced loaf
Being baked inside a much bigger oven
Using bleached flour instead of whole wheat
context: Same shelf, different NOVA category — decided entirely by processing. The industrial additives (emulsifiers, preservatives) are the tell-tale of Group 4, while the four-ingredient bakery loaf stays in Group 3. Source: news-medical.net, 'The NOVA Method of Food Classification.'

question: Researchers running big population surveys keep finding one pattern: people who eat lots of ultra-processed food have higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. Careful scientists who read those same surveys still refuse to convict the processing itself. What is the honest reason they stay cautious?
answer: Only a link was found; the real cause might just be extra calories
choices: Only a link was found; the real cause might just be extra calories
Only adults were studied; nobody has followed children on that diet
Only one country was surveyed; the rest of the world went unchecked
Only packaged snacks were counted; sodas were left out entirely
context: The studies show correlation, not proof of cause — as one review put it, 'the specific mechanism was not clear.' The real culprit could be sheer energy density, or ultra-processed food crowding whole foods out of the diet, rather than the processing itself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ultra-processed food.'

question: A boy who has just bitten into a fiery chili bolts for the fridge, ready to gulp down anything cold. Not every cold drink calms the burn the same way: some barely help, and one actually works. Which drink cools a chili burn best?
context: Capsaicin, the chili's fiery chemical, is oily and won't dissolve in water, so a gulp of water just smears the oil across more of your mouth. Milk can actually dissolve and carry the oil away, cooling the burn. Source: https://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/packages/spicy-foods/mouth-on-fire-myths--what-really-cools-your-palate-

question: Slow-smoked over wood and dried until its flavor changes completely, an everyday Mexican chili sold in almost any grocery store becomes a chipotle. Its deep, smoky, almost meaty taste makes people think of some rare, exotic pepper. Which familiar fresh pepper turns into a chipotle?
context: A chipotle is simply a jalapeno that has been smoked and dried — the exact same pepper, remade by smoke. A lightly smoked one is called a chile morita; a heavily smoked one, a chile meco. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chipotle

question: Mexican cooks often stuff a large, mild, dark-green poblano chili with cheese and roast it. Once a poblano has dried in the sun until it turns dark brown, wrinkled and raisin-sweet, they stop calling it a poblano and reach for a different name at the market. What name does the dried poblano take?
context: An ancho is a dried poblano — drying a chili often renames it AND deepens its flavor. The same trick shows up elsewhere: a guajillo is a dried mirasol. Source: https://pepperscale.com/ancho-vs-chipotle/

question: A cook slicing jalapenos is handling a chili most people call really spicy, yet it scores only a few thousand units on the Scoville heat scale. Another pepper plays in a completely different league, roaring into the hundreds of thousands. Which pepper is it?
context: A jalapeno sits around 2,500-8,000 Scoville Heat Units, while a habanero runs 100,000-350,000 — dozens of times hotter. The Scoville scale ranks a chili's heat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoville_scale

question: Ed Currie of the Puckerbutt Pepper Company in South Carolina held the Guinness record for the hottest chili on Earth with his Carolina Reaper, until October 2023, when he dethroned his own champion with a new pepper about three times hotter. What is the reigning hottest pepper on Earth called?
context: Pepper X averages about 2,693,000 Scoville units — roughly three times a Carolina Reaper. Both were bred by Ed Currie of the Puckerbutt Pepper Company; Pepper X took the Guinness World Record in 2023. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/news/2023/10/pepper-x-dethrones-carolina-reaper-as-worlds-hottest-chilli-pepper-759706

question: Chili burns in kitchens from India to Korea to Hungary, and those cuisines are hard to picture without its fire. Yet every chili pepper on Earth descends from wild plants of a single region. Where did chili first grow wild?
context: Every chili on Earth descends from Capsicum, a plant native to the Americas and completely unknown in Europe, Asia, and Africa until Columbus's voyages reached the New World in 1492. Before that, no one across the entire Old World had ever tasted a chili. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chili pepper' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper).

question: Royal cooks in Korea, China and Thailand around 1300 piled their banquet tables with roast meats, rice, spices and delicacies, yet not one dish carried the blazing chili heat those cuisines are famous for today. No amount of the king's silver could buy it. Why was the fire missing?
answer: Chili peppers had not yet reached Asia
choices: Chili peppers had not yet reached Asia
Chili peppers were banned as a costly luxury
Chili peppers were used only as medicine
Chili peppers were reserved for the royal court
context: Chili is a New World plant that reached Asia only after Columbus opened the Americas in 1492. So the fiery heat of Thai curry, Indian vindaloo, Korean kimchi, and Sichuan hot pot is all less than about 500 years old — before chili arrived, none of those cuisines was spicy the way we know today. Source: Splendid Table, 'How chili peppers conquered the world.'

question: Spice ships from one European nation carried chili pods east, and within about fifty years of Columbus, cooks from Africa and India to China, Korea and Japan were using them, one of the fastest spreads of any food in history. Which traders spread chili across Asia?
context: Portuguese traders carried chilies from Brazil around the Cape of Good Hope to their colony at Goa within a few years of Columbus. In roughly 50 years the chili spread across Africa, India, Southeast Asia, China, Korea, and Japan — one of the fastest food adoptions in all of human history. Source: James Hancock, 'The Columbian Exchange: dispersal of chili peppers.'

question: A chili plant loads its pods with fiery capsaicin to drive off hungry mammals, whose grinding molars crush and kill its seeds. A bird, though, feels no burn at all and swallows the pods happily. Why is that bird a welcome guest, from the plant's point of view?
answer: The bird spreads the seeds unharmed in its droppings
choices: The bird spreads the seeds unharmed in its droppings
The bird pollinates the chili's flowers as it feeds
The bird shields the plant from swarms of insects
The bird's body heat keeps the ripening pods from frost
context: The chili makes capsaicin to protect its seeds from mammals — our grinding molars destroy the seeds, so the burn drives us off. Birds lack the capsaicin-sensitive receptor, feel no heat at all, and scatter the seeds unharmed in their droppings. The chili's conquest of human kitchens was really an accident of that bird-versus-mammal defense. Source: Wikipedia, 'Capsaicin.'

question: A nutritionist unpacks her groceries, looking for foods that carry, in one serving, all nine amino acids the body cannot make for itself. Such a food is a complete protein, and most foods carry only some of the nine. Which group of everyday foods reliably has the full set?
context: The nine essential amino acids -- histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine -- are called 'essential' because your body cannot build them; they must come from food. Meat, fish, eggs, and milk reliably carry all nine at once, because the animal already assembled every one of them inside its own body. Source: Wikipedia, 'Complete protein' & 'Essential amino acid.'

question: A glass of cow's milk left to go sour curdles into soft white lumps, and those lumps are casein, milk's main protein. The protein takes its name from an old Latin word, caseus. Which everyday dairy food does caseus name?
context: Casein is the very protein that curdles into cheese curds, while the watery part left behind is called whey -- so it is fitting that 'casein' comes from Latin 'caseus,' meaning cheese (the same root behind Spanish 'queso'). Source: Wikipedia, 'Casein.'

question: H. H. Mitchell worked out a scale in 1923 for grading protein, since an ounce of one food can give the body more usable protein than an ounce of another. Scientists still score every food on it against one ordinary food whose value is fixed at a perfect 100. Which food is that gold standard?
context: Scientists set a whole egg's 'biological value' at 100 and score every other protein against it -- the method was invented by H. H. Mitchell in 1923. An egg earns the honor because it must contain everything needed to build an entire chick from scratch, so it holds all nine amino acids in nearly ideal balance. A few foods edge it out on the scale (whey ~104, milk ~91), and modern DIAAS scoring rates whole egg around 101 ('excellent'), but the egg remains the historic yardstick. Source: Wikipedia, 'Biological value.'

question: Frances Moore Lappé told a generation of vegetarians, in her bestseller of 1971, Diet for a Small Planet, to combine plant proteins carefully at every single meal or fall short on amino acids. Ten years later she revisited that rule in a new edition of the same book. What did she say about it there?
answer: She reversed it -- no need to combine at every meal
choices: She reversed it -- no need to combine at every meal
She tightened it -- combine at every snack as well
She narrowed it -- only growing children must combine
She widened it -- combine dairy and eggs at meals too
context: In the 1981 10th-anniversary edition Lappe took it back: 'In combating the myth that meat is the only way to get high-quality protein, I reinforced another myth... Actually, it is much easier than I thought.' Scientists now know the body pools amino acids over a whole day, so plant complementing still works -- you just don't have to engineer every single plate. Source: Wikipedia, 'Diet for a Small Planet'; Forks Over Knives, 'The Myth of Complementary Protein.'

question: Small clay cooking pots roughly 20,000 years old, the oldest pottery ever found, lay buried in Xianrendong Cave in southern China. Their makers shaped and fired them deep in the last Ice Age. Which kind of people made them?
context: This is the real shock of Xianrendong Cave: the potters were mobile hunter-gatherers who hunted and foraged through the coldest stretch of the Ice Age — roughly 10,000 years BEFORE farming reached that region. Pottery didn't need agriculture at all; foragers invented it first. Source: Wu et al., 'Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China,' Science 2012; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xianren_Cave.

question: The archaeologists who dug pottery about 20,000 years old out of Xianrendong Cave, in southern China, are certain those pots held more than stored grain or water: people cooked food in them. What clue on the clay itself gave the cooking away?
answer: Sooty scorch marks up the outside
choices: Sooty scorch marks up the outside
Fish bones baked into the clay
A glassy heat-glaze on the rim
context: Many Xianrendong fragments carry soot and scorch on their OUTER walls — the tell-tale sign a pot was set right in a fire. That's how we know these weren't only storage jars: people were baking, boiling, and steaming food in them 20,000 years ago. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xianren_Cave; Wu et al., Science 2012; ceramics.org, 'Oldest known pottery dates back 20,000 years.'

question: Zhijun Zhao, an archaeologist, thinks the Xianrendong pots had many uses. A clay pot set right in the fire let Ice Age cooks boil food instead of only roasting it over flames, and Zhao names one prized food from the water's edge that he thinks they boiled. Which did he name?
context: Dr. Zhijun Zhao put it plainly: the Xianrendong pots 'probably had many purposes, including boiling clams and snails.' You can't really roast a clam — but drop it in a bubbling pot and it steams open. Shellfish is exactly the kind of food a pot unlocks. Source: sci.news/archaeology/article00448.html, quoting Dr. Zhijun Zhao.

question: Hunter-gatherers were boiling water for their cooking maybe 30,000 years ago, long before anyone fired a clay pot. Their only containers were floppy skin bags and woven bark baskets, which would catch fire the moment they touched the flames. How did they bring the water to a boil without burning the bag?
answer: They dropped fire-heated stones into the water
choices: They dropped fire-heated stones into the water
They held the bag low over the flames
They stirred hot ash and embers into it
They left the bag out in the hot sun
context: This is 'stone boiling,' and it's about 30,000 years old — far older than pottery. People heated rocks in the fire, then dropped them into a skin bag, bark basket, or hide-lined pit until the water rolled and boiled. So a clay pot didn't INVENT boiling — it made boiling easy and repeatable, because you could finally set the pot straight on the fire instead of reheating rocks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_boiling; NPR The Salt, 'Stone Age Stew? Soup Making May Be Older Than We'd Thought' (2013).

question: After a kill, Ice Age hunters cracked the long bones open for their marrow, then smashed the crumbly bone ends to bits and boiled them for hours. As it all simmered, a food rose to the surface that they scooped off and kept. What was it?
answer: A thick layer of bone grease
choices: A thick layer of bone grease
context: The prize was bone grease. Crushing the spongy ends of bones and boiling the fragments liquefies the fat, which floats up to be skimmed off the top. Hunter-gatherers valued it hugely — calorie-dense, easy to store, and easy to carry on the move. A pot turned a pile of smashed bones into portable food. Source: Outram, 'Experiments in bone boiling: Nutritional returns and archaeological reflections,' ResearchGate 284261364.

question: Native Californian cooks turned raw acorns, far too bitter for anyone to eat straight, into an everyday staple: they boiled and rinsed them for hours, until the nuts finally turned sweet. What is the bitter compound locked inside a raw acorn?
context: The bitter compounds are tannins — the same astringent stuff that puckers your mouth in strong tea and young red wine. Because tannins dissolve in water, boiling leaches them out of the nut and into the cooking water, which is then poured away; some methods boiled the acorns for 6-8 hours and changed the water up to 7-10 times, until they were finally sweet enough to eat. A pot doesn't just cook food — it can wash the poison out. Source: nativehistory.info, 'Native American Acorn Processing: Leaching Techniques'; smv.org, 'The Science of Eating Acorns.'

question: Three whipped eggs go into a hot pan for a soft French omelette, cooked in about two minutes and rolled up soft and yellow. Delicate eggs like these cling to bare metal and tear apart. Which pan is built to handle them without sticking?
context: Nonstick pans are coated in Teflon (PTFE), a plastic that's built for eggs and delicate fish at low-to-medium heat. Nothing browns onto it, so it can't build a sear — but nothing sticks or tears either. It's rated safe up to about 500 F (260 C). Source: healthline.com/nutrition/nonstick-cookware-safety

question: A cook drops a cold, wet steak into a screaming-hot cast iron skillet, and it sears into a dark crust the moment it lands. The same steak in an equally hot stainless steel pan steams into a sad gray slab. What does thick, heavy cast iron have that thin stainless steel lacks?
answer: It banks a big reserve of heat, so cold food barely cools it.
choices: It banks a big reserve of heat, so cold food barely cools it.
Its dark, baked-on coating grips and browns the meat directly.
It reacts with the steak's juices to keep the sizzle going.
Its rough cast surface scrapes a crust onto the meat as it cooks.
context: Cast iron has roughly 3x the thermal mass of a comparable stainless pan. When a cold steak lands on stainless the surface can crash 150-200 F, killing the browning; on cast iron the drop is usually under 50 F, keeping it in the Maillard browning zone. The flip side: that mass is slow to charge, so preheat cast iron a full ~5 minutes for an even surface. Sources: pantryjoy.com/blogs/kitchen-tips/cast-iron-steak-vs-stainless; misen.com/blogs/news/how-to-sear-a-steak-mastering-cast-iron-skillet-techniques

question: A bright tomato-and-wine sauce bubbles through a long, gentle simmer. In a bare cast iron pan the acidic sauce can take on a dull, metallic, off taste, so the cook reaches for a different pan, and the sauce stays clean and bright. Which pan, and why?
answer: Stainless steel — it won't react with the acid in the food.
choices: Stainless steel — it won't react with the acid in the food.
Aluminum — its oxide skin seals the metal off from the acid.
Carbon steel — its baked-on seasoning keeps the acid off the iron.
Copper — it's far too tough for kitchen acids to corrode it.
context: Stainless steel is non-reactive: it won't react with acids the way bare iron, aluminum, or copper can, so tomato, wine, and citrus dishes come out clean-tasting. That's why acidic pan sauces and long tomato simmers belong in stainless. Source: greenpan.us/blogs/the-cooks-journal/the-chemistry-of-cooking-how-different-cookware-materials-react-with-food

question: A nonstick pan sits blazing empty on a high burner, and its Teflon coating, a plastic perfectly safe at low heat, starts to break down and give off fumes. The fumes give a cook flu-like chills and a headache, but to one kind of household pet they are deadly. Which pet?
context: Above about 570 F (300 C), PTFE breaks down and releases fumes that cause 'polymer fume fever' — nicknamed Teflon flu — with chills and headache, and the same fumes are quickly lethal to pet birds. An empty nonstick pan on high heat can hit 500 F+ in just 2-3 minutes, which is why you never crank a nonstick pan. Source: docquity.com/articles/teflon-flu-about-polymer-fume-fever/

question: A chef sets a good stainless steel pan on the burner. Plain stainless is one of the worst heat conductors of any common pan metal and, on its own, cooks with fierce hot spots and cold dead zones, but this pan hides a trick sealed inside its walls. What is hidden inside them?
answer: A layer of aluminum or copper sealed inside to spread the heat.
choices: A layer of aluminum or copper sealed inside to spread the heat.
A honeycomb of air pockets sealed inside to even the heat.
A ceramic core sealed inside to soak up and release heat.
A steel-and-magnet disc sealed inside to drag heat across.
context: Plain stainless steel is a poor heat conductor — among the worst of common cookware metals — so it heats unevenly on its own. That's why good stainless pans are 'clad': built with a hidden aluminum or copper core sandwiched inside to spread the heat evenly. Source: misen.com/blogs/news/how-to-cook-with-stainless-steel

question: A well-loved cast iron skillet, one that's been cooked on for years, wears a slick, black, almost-nonstick surface all over the inside. Cooks call that coating the pan's 'seasoning' and treat it with real care — never scouring it with harsh soap or a metal scrub brush. But what is that black seasoning layer actually made of?
answer: Layers of oil baked on until they harden into a film.
choices: Layers of oil baked on until they harden into a film.
A sprayed-on Teflon layer, the same as a nonstick pan.
A thin coat of stainless steel bonded over the iron.
Ground-in soot and carbon from years of smoky cooking.
context: Seasoning is a baked-on layer of hardened fat that does double duty: it IS the nonstick surface AND the rust shield. Cast iron and carbon steel REQUIRE it — bare, they rust rapidly — while stainless and nonstick never get seasoned (and you can't season Teflon). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seasoning_(cookware)

question: Seasoning a cast iron pan, a cook wipes a very thin layer of runny oil over the inside and bakes the pan in a hot oven for an hour or so. It comes out wearing a hard, dark, glassy coating that no soap or scrubbing will wash off. What happens to the oil's molecules in the oven?
answer: The heat links the oil's small molecules into one big solid network.
choices: The heat links the oil's small molecules into one big solid network.
The oil soaks deep into the iron's pores and clogs them shut tight.
The oil burns down to carbon, and the black ash bakes on hard.
The heat fuses the oil into the metal like a tiny weld.
context: Heat the oil past its smoke point and it polymerizes: the fat's triglycerides split (the glycerol burns off as the smoke you see), and the fatty acids' reactive double bonds break open and cross-link into a hard, solid film bonded to the metal — not oil sitting on top. Some oil even reacts directly with the iron oxide to form 'iron carboxylate,' a metal-organic compound that chemically glues the film to the pan, which is why real seasoning doesn't wash off. 'Drying oils' high in polyunsaturated omega-3 form the hardest film (flaxseed is ~57% ALA versus canola's ~10%); chemist Sheryl Canter recommends heating to 500 F to push past the smoke point and drive the polymerization. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seasoning_(cookware); ironpatina.com/the-chemistry-of-cast-iron-seasoning-how-polymerization-creates-a-non-stick-surface/; sherylcanter.com/wordpress/2010/01/a-science-based-technique-for-seasoning-cast-iron/

question: A miner's wife in Cornwall packs beef, potato and onion into her pasty completely raw, seals the pastry and bakes it, and the filling steams itself into a rich gravy inside. One more root vegetable goes in raw beside them. Which one?
context: Beef, potato, swede and onion — and nothing is pre-cooked before it goes in. Swede is the yellow root Americans call rutabaga. The shortcrust is sealed around a raw filling, and the filling cooks in its own steam during the bake, the meat juices and onion making a rich gravy inside the pastry. Baked in the morning, a pasty kept its filling warm for hours. Sources: Historic UK, 'History of the Cornish Pasty'; Wikipedia, 'Pasty'.

question: Deep in a Cornish tin mine, a miner sits down to the pasty his wife baked that morning. His hands are black with ore dust that sometimes carries arsenic, and there is no water down there to wash them. The traditional story says the pastry itself solved the problem. What was built into it?
answer: A fat rope of crimped pastry gave him a handle to grip, then throw away.
choices: A fat rope of crimped pastry gave him a handle to grip, then throw away.
A pointed tip let him tip the filling into his mouth, hands well clear.
A thick pastry lid peeled back, so only the lid met his black fingers.
A stiff pastry base held it upright, so he bit down with no hands at all.
context: Miners worked too deep to climb out at midday, so their wives baked an all-in-one meal that fit in a pocket — held against the body it warmed the man as well, and it was sturdy enough to survive being dropped down a mine shaft. Historians dispute the throw-away-the-handle tale, though: the earliest Cornish pasty recipe book (1929) says pasties were wrapped in paper or muslin bags and eaten from end to end, calling that 'the true Cornish way' — and food was far too precious for a hungry miner to discard. Sources: Historic UK, 'History of the Cornish Pasty'; Wikipedia, 'Pasty', citing the 1929 Cornish recipe book.

question: A baker in Cornwall gets his pasty's traditional filling exactly right, uses local ingredients and bakes it in Cornwall itself. European law has protected the name since 2011, and one small slip in shaping the pastry still bars him from selling it as a Cornish pasty. Which slip costs him the name?
answer: He seals the join across the top, not down one side.
choices: He seals the join across the top, not down one side.
He rolls the pastry out thin, not thick, before filling.
He crimps the join into a thick rope, not a thin one.
He makes one big pasty to share, not a small one each.
context: Since 20 July 2011 'Cornish pasty' has carried PGI (Protected Geographical Indication) status. To use the name it must be a 'D' shape, crimped on the side and never over the top, and prepared in Cornwall — a top-crimped pasty legally cannot be called a Cornish pasty. The filling rules are exact too: at least 12.5% beef and at least 25% vegetables (potato, swede and onion), all raw when sealed in, chunky, and seasoned only lightly with salt and pepper. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasty'; Cornish Pasty Association, 'About the pasty'; UK Government PGI file.

question: A baker beats softened butter and white sugar with a spoon or a mixer for three or four full minutes, until the mix turns light and fluffy. Only then do the eggs and flour go in. What is all that beating doing to the butter?
answer: Whipping thousands of tiny air bubbles into it
choices: Whipping thousands of tiny air bubbles into it
Blending it smoothly together with the sugar
Warming it up so the eggs will mix in later
Dissolving the sugar completely into the fat
context: 'Light and fluffy' is simply what butter looks like once it is packed with air. Creaming is not blending the butter and sugar to combine them — it whips thousands of tiny air bubbles down into the solid fat. Source: Sally's Baking Addiction, 'How to Cream Butter and Sugar'; corroborated by Completely Delicious, 'The Creaming Method'.

question: Chocolate chip cookies start with softened butter and sugar beaten together with a mixer for several minutes. As the beaters spin, the mix puffs up thicker and slowly changes color, starting from a bright buttery yellow. What color does it turn into?
context: That pale, puffed-up look is the visible proof the air is in: done right, creaming almost doubles the volume and lightens the mix from bright yellow to pale ivory. Source: Completely Delicious, 'The Creaming Method' ('almost doubled in volume,' 'very light in color'); corroborated by CraftyBaking / Sarah Phillips ('pale ivory') and Sally's Baking Addiction.

question: Softened butter beaten on its own, with no sugar, barely fluffs at all, however long a baker keeps at it. With sugar in the bowl, the same minutes of beating leave it light and fluffy, though in this step the sugar is not there to sweeten. What job is the sugar doing to the butter?
answer: Its jagged crystals dig tiny air pockets into the butter
choices: Its jagged crystals dig tiny air pockets into the butter
It melts into a syrup that traps steam as it heats
It soaks up water and dries the butter into flakes
It softens the fat so the beater can spin faster
context: Sugar's hard, jagged crystals act like tiny shovels, digging little pockets of air into the soft butter with every turn of the beater. Take the sugar away and the butter barely fluffs — in this step the sugar is the aerator, not the sweetener. Source: Abbey the Food Scientist, 'What's the Point of Creaming Butter with Sugar?' ('jagged sugar crystals act like tiny shovels'); corroborated by Completely Delicious.

question: In a bakery, one baker rushes the creaming, the slow beating of butter and sugar before any flour goes in, and gives it only a few seconds. Then he dumps in extra baking powder to rescue the rise, and the cake still bakes dense and heavy. Why can't the powder make up for the rushed creaming?
answer: It can only puff up pockets that exist already, not make new ones
choices: It can only puff up pockets that exist already, not make new ones
It stops working the moment the batter hits the hot oven
It needs the sugar fully dissolved before it can switch on
It only lifts the top of the cake, never the dense middle
context: Creaming (and beating eggs) is the only step that actually CREATES air pockets. Baking powder, baking soda, steam, and yeast make no new bubbles at all — each can only inflate the ones already whipped in. Skimp on creaming and there are too few pockets to blow up, so the cake bakes dense. Source: CraftyBaking / Sarah Phillips ('leaveners simply enlarge the air bubbles that already exist'); corroborated by Baker Bettie, 'What Is Leavening?'.

question: Butter left to grow too warm slumps into liquid oil before a baker can cream it. Chilling it solid again and beating it does not bring it back, which is why every cake recipe asks for butter 'softened, not melted.' What lasting harm has melting done to the butter?
answer: The fat breaks down and releases the trapped air for good
choices: The fat breaks down and releases the trapped air for good
The sugar dissolves so it can no longer cut air in
The butter separates into oil and a watery liquid
The fat sets into hard grains that won't smooth out
context: Warm butter past about 68°F and the fat breaks down and lets go of the air you creamed in — and that emulsion breaks for good, so you can't re-cream it. With the air gone, cookies spread thin and greasy and cakes bake dense. That's the whole reason recipes insist on 'softened, not melted.' Source: CraftyBaking / Sarah Phillips ('fat starts to break down and release the previously creamed-in air bubbles'); corroborated by Completely Delicious.

question: British bakers of the 1700s, before baking powder existed, raised a tall cake on nothing but ten minutes of beating butter and sugar. Its plain name was easy to remember in an age when many people could not read. Where does the name 'pound cake' come from?
answer: It used a pound each of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour
choices: It used a pound each of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour
It was sold by the pound at every village market
It was heavy enough to weigh a pound for each slice
It was pounded flat with a mallet before baking
context: As the story goes, it was called 'pound cake' because it used one pound each of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour — an easy recipe to remember when many people couldn't read. With no chemical leavener invented yet, its whole rise came from beating the butter and sugar for a full ten minutes. Source: What's Cooking America and Windy City Baker, histories of pound cake ('no leaveners... other than the air whipped into the batter... beat for 10 minutes').  (Legend.)

question: Two cooks in a friendly bake-off follow the same cake recipe step for step, with one difference: one reaches for regular granulated sugar, the other for superfine caster sugar with its tiny, powder-fine crystals. The caster-sugar cake comes out taller and lighter, its crumb finer and softer. Why does the caster sugar give a finer crumb?
answer: Its many small crystals cut more and smaller air pockets
choices: Its many small crystals cut more and smaller air pockets
It dissolves fully and gives off more gas while baking
It melts faster and seals moisture into the crumb
It weighs less, so the batter goes in lighter
context: Superfine (caster) sugar has far more, smaller crystals than regular granulated, so it cuts more and smaller air pockets into the butter — giving a lighter, higher, more even crumb. Coarse sugar cuts fewer, bigger pockets and bakes denser. Same recipe, finer sugar, finer texture. Source: C&H Sugar, 'Crystal Clear: How Sugar Shapes Your Cake'; corroborated by Bakers Authority and US Sweeteners on caster vs. granulated ('more, smaller air pockets... lighter, more delicate crumb').

question: Suppose you have just cut raw chicken on a wooden board, and ripe tomatoes wait to be sliced for a salad eaten raw. Chicken juice can carry salmonella, and the tomatoes will never be heated. Which food-safety habit matters most right now?
answer: Give the tomatoes a fresh board before you start slicing.
choices: Give the tomatoes a fresh board before you start slicing.
Rinse the tomatoes under cold running water before slicing them.
Salt the tomato slices to keep bacteria from growing on them.
Let the board air-dry for a minute between the two foods.
context: Raw chicken juices carry bugs like Salmonella. NC State food-safety specialist Ben Chapman's rule: keep raw meat and ready-to-eat foods (salad, bread) on separate boards, or wash the board between them. Slicing tomatoes on the same unwashed board hands the bacteria a free ride onto food you won't cook. Source: NC State News (Ben Chapman), https://news.ncsu.edu/2014/09/cutting-boards-food-safety/

question: A wooden cutting board lies soaking in a sink full of water. Wood is thirsty and drinks it up. Suppose you leave your board there, or run it through a dishwasher's long, blistering-hot cycle. What goes wrong with it?
answer: It swells up, then cracks and warps out of shape.
choices: It swells up, then cracks and warps out of shape.
It grows a fuzzy mold that no amount of scrubbing removes.
It leaches a bitter, woody taste into the next food you cut.
It turns slippery with a slime the knife can never grip.
context: Waterlogged wood swells, then cracks, warps, and splits, and those splits become permanent crevices where bacteria really can hide. A dishwasher's heat plus a long soak is the worst of both. The move: wash a wood board fast in warm soapy water and dry it right away. Source: The NW Co., 'Do Wooden Cutting Boards Harbor Bacteria?', https://nwboards.com/blogs/care-maintenance/do-wooden-cutting-boards-harbor-bacteria

question: Smearing disease bacteria onto a wooden cutting board, Dean Cliver, a food scientist at the University of California, Davis, set out to test whether its porous grain was the germ trap people feared. Minutes later he went looking for the bacteria. What had become of them?
answer: They'd been pulled down into the grain, where they slowly die off.
choices: They'd been pulled down into the grain, where they slowly die off.
They'd multiplied into a sticky film across the top.
They'd stayed put on the surface, alive and ready to spread.
They'd soaked into the wood and thrived in the damp.
context: UC Davis food scientist Dean O. Cliver found disease bacteria smeared on a wood board were unrecoverable within minutes, pulled into the grain and unable to be cultured back to the surface. In his words, once inside the wood the bacteria 'do not multiply, and they gradually die.' Porous wood, counterintuitively, is not the germ trap people feared. Source: Dean O. Cliver, UC Davis Food Safety Lab (naturalhandyman reprint), https://www.naturalhandyman.com/iip/infxtra/infcuttingboard.html

question: Slicing on a wooden board, a worried cook wonders whether her knife will drag the germs buried in its grain back up to the surface and onto the food. Dean Cliver, the food scientist, checked exactly that fear. What did his evidence show about cutting and the buried bacteria?
answer: Cutting has never been shown to bring the buried bugs back up.
choices: Cutting has never been shown to bring the buried bugs back up.
Cutting drags a fresh batch of them up to the surface each time.
Cutting reaches them only when the blade digs in deep.
Cutting brings them up only while the board is still damp.
context: Cliver was careful not to overclaim. Bacteria driven into the grain, he wrote, 'are not killed instantly, but neither do they return to the surface,' and their 'resurrection... via knife edges has not been demonstrated.'
