context: Over 5,000 emigrants who died at sea or of shipboard fever were buried at the quarantine station on Grosse Isle in Quebec. Of the more than 100,000 Irish who sailed to Canada in 1847, roughly one in five did not survive the crossing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland).

question: Even as roughly a million people starved, Ireland's farms never stopped producing — grain, cattle, and butter kept coming off the land in quantity. Yet almost none of it reached the mouths of the starving Irish. What became of that food?
answer: It was shipped out of Ireland to Britain.
choices: It was shipped out of Ireland to Britain.
It was locked in landlords' storehouses in Dublin.
It was left to rot in barns before sale.
It was burned to keep grain prices high.
context: For most of the famine Ireland stayed a net exporter of food. In 1847 alone almost 4,000 ships carried food out to ports like Bristol, Liverpool, Glasgow and London, and nearly 10,000 calves were shipped to Britain — about a third more than the year before. Whether the era's landlords and free-market policy turned a crop failure into mass death is still fiercely argued by historians; the plain fact is that food kept leaving Ireland while its people starved. Source: historyireland.com/food-exports-from-ireland-1846-47 (Cecil Woodham-Smith, The Great Hunger).

question: A baker brushes a raw challah with beaten egg before sliding it into the oven, and it bakes up with a glossy, deep-golden top instead of a dull, pale one. Why does a coat of egg boost the browning like that?
answer: It paints extra protein and sugar onto the surface for browning to work on
choices: It paints extra protein and sugar onto the surface for browning to work on
It seals in steam so the surface can climb to a higher temperature
It adds a layer of water that slows the crust until the inside catches up
It coats the dough in fat that fries the surface like shallow oil
context: An egg wash turbo-charges browning because the reaction runs on protein and sugar, and egg carries both. The egg WHITE's protein gives the shine; the YOLK's fat and pigment give the deep golden color; a whole-egg wash gives the best-balanced mahogany top on challah and pastry. Source: https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2022/02/15/understanding-the-maillard-reaction-in-baking

question: Jean-Marie Lehn, a chemist who won the Nobel Prize, once named one chemical reaction 'by far the most widely practiced in the world.' He did not mean anything done in a factory or a laboratory, but something people carry out in their own kitchens every day. Which everyday act did he mean?
answer: Browning food in the oven or a hot pan
choices: Browning food in the oven or a hot pan
context: Lehn was pointing at the Maillard reaction, the browning that runs every time a cook toasts bread, sears a steak, roasts coffee, bakes or fries, which is why the Nobel laureate called it 'by far the most widely practiced chemical reaction in the world.'

question: Sweetened with plain white table sugar, a bread dough goes into a hot oven to brown. Some sugars leap straight into that browning, but table sugar is stubborn: it must first change before it can take part at all. What happens to the table sugar first?
answer: It splits into two simpler sugars
choices: It splits into two simpler sugars
It evaporates off as sweet steam
It soaks down into the food's interior
context: Only 'reducing' sugars like glucose and fructose join the browning directly. Ordinary table sugar (sucrose) is non-reducing: it must first split (invert) into glucose and fructose before it can take part. Source: https://byjus.com/chemistry/maillard-reaction/

question: Soft pretzels come out of a German baker's oven with a shiny, dark-mahogany skin and a flavor no plain bread roll on the same rack ever gets. The secret is one quick dip the raw pretzel takes just before baking, which drives its browning hard and fast. What does the baker do to the raw pretzel first?
answer: Dip it in a lye bath
choices: Dip it in a lye bath
Dip it in a vinegar bath
Dip it in a sugar syrup
Dip it in a salt brine
context: Pretzels get their glossy dark-brown skin from an alkaline dip before baking, traditionally a food-grade lye (sodium hydroxide) bath, which bakers handle with care, or baking soda at home. Alkaline conditions make the surface proteins far more reactive, so the Maillard reaction runs hard and fast in the oven, the same pH trick that speeds caramelized onions.

question: A hungry guest took his seat at the long feast table in a medieval lord's great hall, and servants brought out roast venison, pigeon pies and gravy-drenched stews. In front of him lay no plate or dish at all. What did he pile his meat and dripping sauce onto?
answer: A thick slab of days-old bread
choices: A thick slab of days-old bread
A shallow bowl of baked clay
context: This edible 'plate' was called a trencher — a thick round or square slab cut from a days-old loaf that soaked up the sauces and juices from the food piled on top of it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trencher_(tableware)

question: At a great medieval feast, one prized seasoning sat in a costly dish beside the host's right hand, and every guest's place was measured from it. Honored guests sat close beside it; lesser folk sat far down the table. Which seasoning marked a guest's rank?
context: Salt. The great salt cellar was a costly showpiece of pewter, silver or gold, set at the host's right hand — honoured guests sat 'above the salt' near him, while lesser folk sat 'below the salt' down the table. Your rank even decided how fine and white your salt was; commoners got coarse, dark 'bay salt.' Sources: https://www.medievalists.net/2014/05/lets-eat-banquets-middle-ages/ ; https://www.phrases.org.uk/meanings/below-the-salt.html

question: Each diner at a medieval feast ate his meat off a trencher, and by the last course it was soaked through with juices and sauce. No diner ever ate his own soggy trencher. When the feast was over, what became of them?
answer: They were collected and given to the poor at the gates
choices: They were collected and given to the poor at the gates
They were thrown to the hunting hounds under the table
They were tossed on the fire to sweeten the smoke
They were dried and kept for the servants' breakfast
context: The Almoner gathered up the gravy-soaked trenchers along with the leftover 'broken meats' and handed them out as alms to the poor waiting at the gates. Source: http://www.medievalcookery.com/notes/trenchers.html

question: At the grandest medieval Christmas feast, servants carried in a whole roasted boar's head on a gilded platter, led by trumpeters and dressed with sprigs of rosemary and bay. One final touch was wedged between its open jaws as it entered the hall. What was it?
context: An apple (sometimes a lemon) was set in the boar's mouth. The boar's head was the ceremonial Christmas centerpiece, and its entrance is still marked by the Boar's Head Carol, first printed in 1521, whose Latin refrain 'Caput apri defero' means 'the boar's head I bear.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boar%27s_Head_Carol

question: A medieval cook roasted a peacock for the high table. But first he did something painstaking, so the cooked bird could be carried in looking magnificently alive, with beak and feet gilded. What clever trick made the roasted bird look alive?
answer: He re-dressed it in its own feathered skin
choices: He re-dressed it in its own feathered skin
He propped it upright on a hidden wooden frame
He painted the bare roasted bird in lifelike colours
He perched a live peacock beside the roasted meat
context: The cook skinned the peacock with its plumage kept whole, roasted the body, then re-dressed it in its own skin and feathers so it looked alive — beak and feet gilded gold, sometimes with a golden comb and chain added. Sources: https://murreyandblue.co.uk/2025/03/01/royal-feasts-of-the-past-swan-and-peacock-in-medieval-recipes/ ; https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/year-8/medieval-food/

question: Bent on astonishing a feast's guests, a medieval cook stitched the front half of one animal onto the back half of another, roasted the whole hybrid and sent it out looking like a beast from a nightmare. Which two creatures were most famously sewn together for this dish?
context: The dish was called a 'cockentrice' — cooks sewed the front half of a piglet to the rear of a capon (a young rooster), or the reverse, and roasted the hybrid to astound the guests. Source: https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/year-8/medieval-food/

question: Servants carried a swan to a medieval lord's table crowned and garlanded, the costliest showpiece bird he could serve. Beside it came a thick sauce called chaudron, dark and almost black. What was that sauce made from?
answer: Blood and innards from the bird itself, spiced
choices: Blood and innards from the bird itself, spiced
Mashed liver boiled down with red wine
Squid ink stirred into a thick dark broth
Blackberries crushed with clove and honey
context: 'Chaudron' was a black sauce made from the swan's own blood and offal, sharpened with vinegar and spices. The swan itself was re-dressed in its cured feathered skin, its head held erect by a skewer through the mouth and neck. Source: https://murreyandblue.co.uk/2025/03/01/royal-feasts-of-the-past-swan-and-peacock-in-medieval-recipes/

question: Martino da Como, an Italian cook, set down a trick in his cookbook of around 1465 for making a roasted peacock seem to breathe real fire as it was carried in. What did he tuck into the bird's beak and set alight?
answer: Cotton wool soaked in camphor and wine
choices: Cotton wool soaked in camphor and wine
A twist of gunpowder and dried straw
A lump of pine pitch and beeswax
A rag dipped in whale oil and pepper
context: Martino da Como's Liber de arte coquinaria (c.1465) says to put a quarter-ounce of camphor wrapped in cotton wool in the beak with a little aqua vitae or strong wine, then light it as the bird is served — 'it will spew fire for a good bit.' It is a real period recipe, even though it sounds like a tall tale. Source: https://askthepast.net/how-to-serve-flaming-bird-c-1465/

question: Cooks preparing a banquet in 1343 for Pope Clement VI sent out a subtlety between the courses, a showpiece for the guests to marvel at. They built it from roasted birds and re-dressed deer, boar, goats and hares, all arranged into one huge model. What was the scene modelled as?
context: The showpieces were called 'subtleties' (sotelties) — edible sculptures of sugar, marzipan and jelly, often shaped like whole castles. At the 1343 feast for Pope Clement VI, one castle had walls built of roasted birds and was peopled with re-dressed deer, boar, goat and hare. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entremet

question: A young nobleman in a great medieval household served as carving esquire before he earned his knight's spurs, and he carved the roast birds at the table as a gentleman's art. One slip was a public embarrassment. What fussy rule did a skilled carver have to master?
answer: A different bird called for a different carving verb
choices: A different bird called for a different carving verb
The bird had to be carved without touching it by hand
Each slice had to be thinner than the one before
The carving had to be finished before the music stopped
context: 'The Boke of Kervynge' (printed by Wynkyn de Worde, 1508) gave a special verb for every bird: you 'lift that swan,' 'disfigure that peacock,' 'dismember that heron,' 'unbrace that mallard' and 'display that crane.' Mangling the wrong bird the wrong way was a real social disgrace. Sources: https://www.openculture.com/2023/07/a-creative-list-of-meat-carving-terms-from-the-middle-ages.html ; https://www.thefield.co.uk/food/how-to-carve-meat-history-carving-knives-22350

question: Guests at a medieval feast often applauded the gilded peacock, the glittering showpiece of the whole hall, instead of carving into it for a slice. As it turned out, leaving the bird barely eaten was no great loss to the diners. Why not?
answer: The meat underneath was tough, dry and tasteless
choices: The meat underneath was tough, dry and tasteless
The bird had been cooked days earlier and gone cold
The gold gilding had made the meat poisonous
Church law forbade actually eating the showpiece
context: Cooks re-dressed the peacock so magnificently that guests often applauded instead of eating — which was just as well, since the meat underneath was famously tough and dry. At these feasts, the spectacle mattered more than the meal. Source: https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/year-8/medieval-food/

question: A landlord may seal a deal in law with a token rent, a coin or a rose a year. The name for such a rent goes back to the Middle Ages, when one spice was counted out to pay rents. Which spice names it?
context: Black pepper was so valuable in the Middle Ages that it was accepted like money — paid as rent, dowries and taxes — and the phrase 'a peppercorn rent' survives today to mean a tiny, token payment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_pepper

question: A rich medieval cook seasons a meat dish with cinnamon, ginger and saffron, then unlocks the spice chest for one more costly seasoning that his kitchen counts as an exotic spice. What does he add?
context: To the rich medieval palate, sweet, sour and spicy mixed on one plate — cinnamon, ginger, saffron and sugar could all season the same meat dish, because sugar itself was treated as an exotic spice, before the savory/sweet split. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_cuisine

question: Poor villagers in southern Italy and Greece lived in the 1950s on the food that doctors now praise as the Mediterranean diet: bread, vegetables, a little fish, and one fat they used with almost every meal. Which fat was it?
context: Olive oil was the villagers' everyday fat -- used for cooking in place of butter and poured over vegetables, bread and beans. It is the signature of the whole pattern, which was low in red meat and sugar. Source: sevencountriesstudy.com/mediterranean-dietary-patterns; MDPI Rev Cardiovasc Med review (PMC12027923).

question: Heaps of vegetables filled the plates of villagers in 1950s Greece and southern Italy, along with one cheap, filling food eaten at almost every meal. It is the plainest part of the Mediterranean diet and the one its modern fans forget. Which food was it?
context: Beans and other legumes were a quiet pillar of the pattern -- cheap, filling protein the villagers ate constantly, alongside their vegetables. Modern fans remember the olive oil and the fish but skip the beans. Source: sevencountriesstudy.com/mediterranean-dietary-patterns; MDPI review (PMC12027923).

question: Comparing poor Mediterranean villagers, who ate simple food with little red meat, with well-fed Americans who ate far more meat, Ancel Keys, an American scientist, reached a surprising result that launched a whole new field of nutrition. What did he find?
answer: The poor villagers had far less heart disease
choices: The rich Americans had far less heart disease
The poor villagers had far less heart disease
Both groups suffered heart disease equally
Neither group had much heart disease
context: It was a real detective story: the simple-eating villagers had far healthier hearts than the steak-and-butter Americans. That backwards-seeming clue -- poor people healthier than rich ones -- is what set Keys hunting for the reason. Source: aboutoliveoil.org/ancel-keys-mediterranean-diet; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancel_Keys.

question: The men of one Greek island ate peasant food and touched meat only on rare feast days. In Ancel Keys's huge Seven Countries Study, which tracked thousands of middle-aged men from America to Japan, they had the healthiest hearts of any group. Which island was it?
context: Cretan men had the lowest heart-disease rate of any group in the study -- the pattern's poster child. Their fat was olive oil, their plates piled with wild greens, beans, bread and fruit, with meat only a rare treat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancel_Keys; sevencountriesstudy.com/mediterranean-dietary-patterns.

question: North Karelia's farmers, in eastern Finland, stood at the far end of Ancel Keys's study, with a heart-attack death rate among the worst ever measured. They cooked with, and ate, huge amounts of one fat. Which one?
context: North Karelia recorded one of the highest coronary death rates ever measured (reported around 700 per 100,000). Its dairy-farming men lived on butter and fatty meat -- the mirror image of the Cretans' olive oil and vegetables. Source: North Karelia / Seven Countries data via bluezones.com; sevencountriesstudy.com.

question: Ancel Keys's findings led him and others to a sweeping claim, that saturated fat itself brings on heart disease, and the idea steered half a century of low-fat advice. His study, though, showed a link, not proof. How do many researchers judge that claim today?
answer: The pattern still looks healthy, but the blanket 'saturated fat causes heart disease' verdict is now disputed
choices: It is settled beyond doubt -- saturated fat is proven to be the single cause of heart disease
The pattern still looks healthy, but the blanket 'saturated fat causes heart disease' verdict is now disputed
Keys faked his numbers, so the whole Mediterranean diet is a myth
Saturated fat is now proven harmless, and the low-fat era was a deliberate hoax
context: Steel-man both sides: the Mediterranean PATTERN still holds up well in research, but the leap to 'saturated fat is the villain' has been heavily re-examined -- partly because high-fat, low-heart-disease countries like France weren't in the study (the 'French paradox'). The opposite charge -- that Keys was a fraud who cherry-picked countries -- is also disputed: that 22-country chart came from a 1953 talk BEFORE the Seven Countries Study began, and the real study gathered fresh data on nearly 13,000 men. Source: MDPI Rev Cardiovasc Med review (PMC12027923); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancel_Keys; PubMed 29134858; True Health Initiative Seven Countries white paper.

question: Tabbouleh from a supermarket tub looks like a wheat salad, pale grain with a few green flecks. Real Levantine tabbouleh flips that: it is mostly one finely chopped green herb, with only a spoonful of bulgur wheat for texture. Which herb makes up most of it?
context: Traditional tabbouleh is overwhelmingly parsley — one Palestinian chef calls it '80 percent parsley' — with bulgur wheat playing only a bit part. Western store versions flip the ratio and pile in the wheat, which is why they look so grain-heavy. Tabbouleh is a national dish of Lebanon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabbouleh

question: A Levantine cook sets out to make baba ganoush, the eggplant dip prized for its deep, smoky flavor, and adds no smoky spice at all. The smoke comes from one dramatic thing the cook does to the whole eggplant before scooping out its soft insides. What does the cook do to it?
answer: Blacken its skin whole over an open flame
choices: Blacken its skin whole over an open flame
Smoke it for hours in a smokehouse
Brush it with liquid smoke, then bake
Grill it sealed in a foil packet
context: You char the whole eggplant black — held over a gas burner or grill for about 20 minutes — until the skin is completely blistered and the flesh inside collapses to a soft, smoky pulp. Then you scoop it out and mash it with tahini, lemon, garlic and olive oil. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baba_ghanoush; themediterraneandish.com/baba-ganoush-recipe

question: Across the Levant, cooks spread labneh, a soft white cheese, over a plate and top it with olive oil and dried mint. It takes no rennet and no aging, because it is only one everyday dairy food with its liquid strained out. Which food is it made from?
context: Labneh is strained yogurt: you hang plain yogurt in a cloth bag for hours until the watery whey drips away and it thickens into a spreadable cheese. Rolled into little balls and packed in olive oil (labneh bil zeit), it seals out the air and keeps for over a year without a fridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strained_yogurt

question: Little dolma parcels of seasoned rice and herbs come to the table each wrapped in a leaf that has been simmered soft. Nobody peels the wrapper off: it is eaten right along with the filling. Which leaf wraps a classic dolma?
context: Dolma's Arabic name is warak enab — literally 'grape leaves.' The tender vine leaf is simmered soft and eaten with the rice filling, not unwrapped. 'Dolma' comes from Turkish 'dolmak,' to be stuffed or filled; in Turkish, 'sarma' means the rolled-in-leaves kind and 'dolma' the stuffed-vegetable kind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolma

question: Cooks in Aleppo, in northern Syria, roast sweet red peppers over a fire until the skins blacken, then blend them into a brick-red dip called muhammara. Its rich, thick body and its gentle crunch come from one ground nut stirred into the mix. Which nut is it?
context: Muhammara means 'reddened' in Arabic. Ground walnuts give it body and crunch; roasted red peppers and Aleppo pepper bring the color and warmth, pomegranate molasses the sweet-tart tang, and breadcrumbs the thickness. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammara

question: Baba ganoush tastes as old as the Mediterranean, yet the ancient Greeks and Romans never had a word for its eggplant, because they had never laid eyes on one. The plant came from South Asia and had reached Spain by the 8th century. Who carried it west across the Mediterranean?
context: The eggplant comes from South Asia (India). Medieval Arab traders spread it west across the Mediterranean world, and it reached Spain — then Al-Andalus — in the 8th century. The tell that it was a newcomer: the ancient Greeks and Romans had no name for a plant they had never seen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggplant

question: Levantine cooks drizzle one thick, dark, tangy syrup into salad dressings and stir it into dips for a sweet-sour kick. They make it by simmering a single fruit's juice down until a whole potful cooks away to a small syrupy pool. Which fruit's juice becomes this syrup?
context: This is pomegranate molasses — pomegranate juice boiled down until it reduces to a dark, tart syrup. It's the sweet-sour backbone of Levantine dressings and the tang hidden inside dips like muhammara. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate_molasses

question: A steaming bowl of spicy stew gets its burn from chili peppers. Every chili pepper on Earth traces back to wild plants that grew in just one part of the world, until sailors carried them everywhere else. Where did chili peppers first come from?
context: Chili peppers grew wild only in the Americas and were unknown across Africa and Asia before Columbus sailed in 1492. From the late 1490s, Portuguese merchants carried Brazilian-grown chilies to West and North Africa, where the heat quickly became a signature of local cooking. Source: Wikipedia, 'Columbian exchange.'

question: West African cooks turn cassava, a starchy root from Brazil, into fufu and garri, two everyday staples. Raw cassava is naturally poisonous, though. Before it is safe to eat, what must the cooks first do to the roots?
answer: Soak the roots in water to ferment
choices: Soak the roots in water to ferment
Boil the roots once in salted water
Peel the tough skin off the roots
context: Cassava (manioc) is native to west-central Brazil and was brought to Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century, where it became a top staple. Raw cassava root is naturally toxic; West Africans make it safe by soaking the roots in water for about three days to ferment before drying or cooking, or by grating and lightly frying it in palm oil into garri. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cassava.'

question: Jollof rice, a one-pot dish stained deep red with tomatoes and tomato paste, sets cooks in Ghana and Nigeria arguing endlessly over whose pot is best. Portuguese ships landed the tomato in Africa about 500 years ago. Roughly how old is the tomato-rich jollof that West Africans cook today?
context: A crop's arrival and a dish's birth are two different dates. The tomato is the red heart of jollof rice, but tomatoes, tomato paste and capsicum (chili) peppers are all New World crops that reached Africa only after Columbus — and the modern tomato-based jollof dates only to about the 19th century, roughly three centuries after the tomato itself landed. Jollof takes its name from the Wolof people of Senegal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jollof rice.'

question: Cooks in Italy's sunny south, in Naples, Sicily and Puglia, reach for olive oil almost every time. In the cool north near the Alps, around Milan and Turin, dairy cows graze green meadows, and cooks fry and finish their dishes with a different fat. Which fat leads the northern kitchen?
context: Broadly, the north of Italy — Emilia-Romagna and the Alpine belt — cooks with butter (and cream) from its cattle pastures, while central and southern Italy reach for olive oil. It's a tendency, not a hard border. Source: Wikipedia, 'Italian cuisine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_cuisine).

question: Southern Italian families in Sicily, Puglia and Naples ate dried pasta every day, and it kept for months on a shelf without spoiling, a huge help in a poor home with no fridge. The north stuck to fresh pasta that had to be eaten the same day. What let the south make pasta that kept when the north could not?
answer: Hot, dry winds that air-dried the pasta while the humid north stayed too damp
choices: Hot, dry winds that air-dried the pasta while the humid north stayed too damp
Wealthy nobles who paid to stockpile food that poorer northerners could not
A shortage of fresh eggs that forced southern cooks to dry their dough
Ancient Roman laws that reserved fresh pasta for the northern cities
context: Durum ('hard') wheat thrives in the hot, dry south, and Sicily's hot, dry winds were ideal for air-drying pasta so it keeps; the cooler, wetter, humid north grew soft wheat and was too damp to air-dry pasta, so it ate fresh pasta the same day. Source: The Thinking Traveller, 'Pasta traditions in Sicily and Puglia'.

question: Poor farming families in the mountains of Piemonte and Veneto, in northern Italy, lived for generations on almost one dish, polenta. Every day the iron pot went on the fire, and a wife or grandmother stirred the thick, hot porridge for hours, made from the ground meal of one crop from their steep hillside plots. Which crop fed them?
context: Polenta — slow-cooked ground corn (maize) — has been a peasant staple of northern Italy for centuries, standard across Piemonte, Lombardia, Veneto and Friuli. The north's other non-pasta starch is risotto: creamy short-grain rice grown on the Po Valley plains, watered by Alpine snowmelt. Source: La Cucina Italiana, 'Polenta'.

question: Olive oil had cooked meals in the sunny hills of southern Italy since the days of ancient Rome, but one turn of medieval history tightened its grip on the southern kitchen for good. What gave olive oil that extra boost across the south in the Middle Ages?
answer: Lenten fasting rules banned animal fats like butter, and oil broke no rule
choices: Lenten fasting rules banned animal fats like butter, and oil broke no rule
Arab traders brought the first olive presses across the sea to Sicily
A cattle plague wiped out the south's dairy herds for a generation
Roman emperors taxed butter heavily as a foreign northern luxury
context: During Lent the Catholic Church banned animal fats such as butter and lard, and the south already had olive oil on hand — a fat that fit the rule — which reinforced oil's grip on southern cooking (a contributing factor, told as culinary history). Source: Mortadella Head, 'Butter vs olive oil'.

question: Sliced in half from top to bottom, a yellow onion shows neat rings on its cut face, one nested inside the next, all joined at the flat root plate at the bottom. The onion is really a short underground stem. What are those rings made of?
context: An onion is a bulb: a short, squat, compressed underground stem wrapped in concentric fleshy 'scale' leaves. Every ring you slice through is one of those swollen storage leaves seen end-on — the onion is a stack of fat leaf-bases, not a solid root. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion)

question: The papery brown skin of an onion peels away in crackly, whispering sheets, nothing like the moist, springy flesh underneath. To the onion plant itself, what is that brown skin?
answer: a set of outer layers, dried brittle with age
choices: a set of outer layers, dried brittle with age
a waxy rind that seals in the bulb's water
a papery husk left behind by the flower
a crust of soil baked hard onto the bulb
context: The dry, papery skin on an onion is just its outermost leaves — the same storage leaves as the juicy rings, but the outer ones dried out and went brittle as the bulb matured, forming a protective wrapper. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion)

question: A head of garlic breaks apart into a cluster of cloves, each wrapped in its own papery jacket. A gardener wanting more garlic simply pushes one single clove down into the soil. What grows up from that one clove?
context: A garlic bulb (a 'head') splits into 10-20 cloves, and each clove is itself a tiny complete storage bud wrapped in a papery leaf — plant just one clove and it grows an entire new plant. Garlic mostly copies itself this way instead of making seeds. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic)

question: A whole, unbroken clove of garlic held under the nose smells of almost nothing but faint paper. Crushed flat under the side of a knife, the same clove fills the whole kitchen with a fierce garlic punch the instant it breaks open. Where does that sudden smell come from?
answer: from a chemical reaction that builds it on the spot
choices: from a chemical reaction that builds it on the spot
from oily droplets that burst under the knife
from the papery skin as it splits open
from juice squeezed out of the broken cells
context: Whole, unbroken garlic barely smells. The sharp garlic punch only appears the instant you crush or chop it: that breaks the cells and lets the enzyme alliinase convert odorless 'alliin' into pungent 'allicin' — the smell is literally manufactured on the spot by the damage. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allicin)

question: Bitten raw, a clove of garlic is fierce: it burns and stings the tongue. Then a cook roasts a whole head slowly in the oven until it turns soft, and something happens to that fierce bite. What becomes of it?
answer: it mellows into something mild and sweet
choices: it mellows into something mild and sweet
it sharpens into something even fiercer
it sours into something harsh and metallic
it fades but stays just as sharp
context: Heat tames the alliums. Cooking breaks down the sharp compound (allicin), so raw garlic bites hard but roasted garlic turns mild, sweet, brown and jammy. The enzyme that makes the pungent compound is also destroyed by heat, so cooked garlic can't keep generating its own sharpness. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allicin)

question: Sacks of cloves, pepper and cinnamon traveled overland across Asia toward Europe long before any ship sailed around Africa, carried in slow trains of pack animals. Which animals made up those spice caravans?
context: Long before sea routes, spices moved by land: great camel caravans crossed Asia's deserts loaded with pepper, cinnamon and cloves, hauling them thousands of miles toward the Mediterranean. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com, corroborated by Wikipedia 'Spice trade' and Grokipedia 'Spice trade'.

question: One Italian port took in almost every peppercorn, cinnamon stick and clove that reached Europe for some 700 years of the Middle Ages, landing them on its stone docks, and the city grew rich as Europe's spice gateway to the East. Which city was it?
context: From roughly the 8th to the 15th century the Italian maritime republics — above all Venice — held a near-monopoly on European trade with the East, so almost every Eastern spice entered Europe through Venetian docks. Source: Wikipedia 'Spice trade', corroborated by Smithsonian Magazine.

question: A medieval merchant who unlocked a chest of cinnamon bark, carried all the way from Sri Lanka, could set it on one side of a balance scale and one metal on the other and call it a fair swap: pound for pound, the two were worth about the same. Which metal?
context: Cinnamon was so precious that a single kilogram of it cost about as much as a kilogram of silver — gold was dearer still, which is why it makes the tempting wrong guess. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com.

question: A sack of black pepper bought for a handful of coins on India's coast was worth about thirty times as much by the time it reached Europe, its price climbing at every stop as it passed from one set of merchant hands to the next. Which two groups of middlemen guarded most of that fortune?
context: Pepper bought for a handful of coins on India's Malabar Coast sold for about TEN times as much once Arab merchants had carried it west to the Mediterranean, and roughly THIRTY times its starting price by the time Venetian merchants shipped it on to Venice — so it was that relay of Arab and then Venetian middlemen, not the Ottomans who later seized the crossroads, the Portuguese who wanted in, or Venice's Genoese rivals, who guarded the spice fortune. Escaping exactly that markup is what later sent European captains hunting for a sea route of their own. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com, markup stages corroborated by mexicohistorico.com.

question: The Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople, a crossroads on the overland spice road, in 1453, and cooks across Europe braced for pepper to price itself out of their kitchens. It never did: for the next forty-five years pepper prices barely moved, because the merchants of Europe's great spice port quietly kept their own supply open. Who were they buying from?
context: The 1453 fall of Constantinople was a SQUEEZE, not a total blockade: historian A.H. Lybyer showed in 1915 that European pepper prices did not jump sharply between 1453 and 1498, because Venice kept buying through a treaty with the Mamluks of Alexandria (who charged about a 33% export tariff). The real crack came in 1498, when Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast by sea and carried pepper home the direct way — that flood of cheaper spice roughly halved Venice's pepper prices and broke the centuries-old monopoly. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com; Wikipedia 'Fall of Constantinople'; Lybyer 1915 via gertitashkomd.com.

question: Spanish and Portuguese missionaries who met a flowering vine in South America in the 1500s named its flower and fruit for the Passion. They meant something far darker than romance: to them the Passion was one particular ordeal from their faith. Which was it?
context: The word 'passion' comes from the Latin passio, meaning suffering, so 'the Passion' is the suffering and death of Jesus on the cross. Spanish and Portuguese missionaries in the Americas in the 1500s and 1600s saw the story of Christ's death in the strange flower and named it for that; it has nothing to do with romantic love. (Sources: University of Dayton Marian Library, 'Passion Flower'; Wikipedia, 'Passiflora'.)

question: Brazilian cooks whip the tart, musky pulp of the passion fruit, which grows on the same vine as the passion flower, into a fluffy mousse and spoon it over cakes. What do Brazilians call this fruit?
context: In Brazil the fruit is maracujá, from the Tupi word murukuia. Its tart pulp — wrapped around roughly 250 seeds — flavors juice, mousse, and desserts, and passion-fruit mousse is a classic Brazilian sweet. The vine, Passiflora edulis, is native to southern Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Passiflora edulis'.)

question: Missionaries who met the passion flower in South America read Christ's suffering into it part by part. To them the feature at the very heart of the bloom, the first thing to catch the eye, took one role from the story of the Crucifixion. What did they say it stood for?
context: The frilly fringe is called the corona, and in some species it is a ring of 70 to 100 or more colored threads. To the missionaries it stood for the crown of thorns pressed onto Christ's head, and it is the flower's most striking feature. (Sources: University of Dayton Marian Library, 'Passion Flower'; Wikipedia, 'Passiflora'.)  (Legend.)

question: A bowl of mixed nuts holds cashews, almonds, pecans and peanuts, but botanists say the peanut is no nut at all: it is a cousin of some very familiar garden plants. Which family does it belong to?
context: Botanists file the peanut in Fabaceae, the legume family — the same clan as beans, peas, and lentils. Its seeds grow inside a pod, exactly like peas in a pea pod, which is why it breaks every rule for a true 'nut.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: Boiled peanuts at a county fair and roasted peanuts at a ballgame feel deeply Southern, yet the plant is not native to North America at all. Spanish and Portuguese ships first carried it out of its true homeland. Where did the peanut grow wild?
answer: east of the Andes, in South America
choices: east of the Andes, in South America
in the river valleys of India
across the islands of Southeast Asia
context: The peanut grew wild east of the Andes — around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil. Spanish and Portuguese traders carried it to Africa, and it returned to North America on slave ships. That African detour marked our language: the Southern word 'goober' comes from 'nguba,' the Kongo word for the plant. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut; npr.org/sections/codeswitch (2014-04-20)

question: A peanut plant blooms with small yellow flowers up in the open air, yet no peanut ever hangs from its stems above the ground. Once one of those flowers has been pollinated, what does the plant do to turn it into a peanut?
answer: A stalk grows from the flower and pushes the young pod down into the soil.
choices: A stalk grows from the flower and pushes the young pod down into the soil.
The flower's petals harden into a shell around the seeds on the stem.
The whole plant leans over until its flowers touch the ground.
The wind scatters the seeds, and new pods sprout where they land.
context: That downward-growing stalk is called the 'peg' (a gynophore, growing from the base of the flower's ovary). It drives the fertilized pod straight into the ground, where the peanuts ripen in the dark — shielded from animals and weather. Botanists call this rare trick geocarpy, 'fruit in the earth.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: Each small yellow flower on a peanut plant opens for a single day, then wilts and closes for good, and if it is not pollinated in that time no peanut will ever form. Yet farmers plant huge fields of peanuts and reliably get a crop. How does each flower get pollinated in its one short day?
answer: It pollinates itself, needing no other flower.
choices: It pollinates itself, needing no other flower.
It draws in a single kind of bee that visits only peanuts.
It relies on ants to carry pollen up its stem.
It casts its pollen on the wind to reach other blooms.
context: The peanut's yellow flower is self-pollinating and lasts only about a day. Once pollinated, it withers and its peg begins the long push down into the soil to ripen the pod underground. Source: biologyinsights.com/are-peanuts-roots-the-science-behind-underground-pods

question: A field planted with cotton year after year goes dead, the crop stripping something vital from the dirt. A farmer sows peanuts there for one season, and next spring's corn comes up thick and tall with no fertilizer at all. What are the peanut's roots doing down in the soil?
answer: Pulling nitrogen out of the air and locking it into the soil.
choices: Pulling nitrogen out of the air and locking it into the soil.
Rotting fallen leaves into a rich compost around their roots.
Drawing deep buried minerals up toward the topsoil.
Feeding the soil's earthworms with sugars from their roots.
context: Because it's a legume, the peanut houses symbiotic bacteria (rhizobia) in nodules on its roots. They pull nitrogen straight from the air and fix it into the ground, refilling land that crops like cotton and corn drain — which is why peanuts are prized in crop rotation. The payoff is measurable: in Texas, peanuts grown in a three-year rotation with corn yield about 50% more than peanuts grown on the same land every year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: George Washington Carver, born into slavery and later a scientist at Tuskegee, urged Southern farmers to plant peanuts where cotton had worn the land out. It worked too well, and farmers were soon buried in peanuts nobody would buy. What did Carver do about it, in the work that made his name?
answer: Invent hundreds of new peanut products, from flour to glue to shaving cream.
choices: Invent hundreds of new peanut products, from flour to glue to shaving cream.
Build the South's first factory for turning peanuts into peanut butter.
Ship the leftover peanuts across the ocean to sell them in Europe.
Breed a bigger, sweeter peanut that shoppers would pay more for.
context: The Carver Museum at Tuskegee credited George Washington Carver with roughly 300 peanut uses (it counted 287) — milk, flour, dyes, paints, cosmetics, glue, even shaving cream. In 1921 he testified before Congress's House Ways and Means Committee, unpacking product after product; congressmen who came to mock him kept extending his time to hear more. One thing he did NOT do was invent peanut butter — a Canadian pharmacist, Marcellus Gilmore Edson, patented a peanut paste in 1884 (twelve years before Carver reached Tuskegee), and peanut pastes go back to the Aztecs. Carver was the peanut's great promoter and popularizer, not the inventor of its most famous product. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Carver

question: A medieval English baker sealed a hunk of meat inside a thick, rock-hard shell of flour and water to hold it together in the oven, for the first pies were not sweet at all. What did such bakers call that stiff crust?
context: The word was 'coffyn,' and it simply meant a basket or box — nothing to do with burial. It named the crust's shape, not a graveyard. These early coffins were savory: a shell of rye flour and water baked several inches thick around the meat, made to survive hours in the oven. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pie'; Matador Network, 'Coffin-Inspired History of Pie Crust.'

question: Baked inside a stiff shell of flour and water, a medieval English meat pie could ride in a saddlebag for weeks and still be safe to eat, long before anyone had a fridge. The crust was the reason. How did that thick shell keep the meat from spoiling?
answer: it locked the air away from the meat
choices: it locked the air away from the meat
it drew the moisture out of the meat
it packed salt tight against the meat
it baked the meat sterile in the oven
context: With no air reaching it, the trapped meat and its juices couldn't spoil, so a sealed pie kept for weeks — historians have nicknamed the coffin crust 'medieval Tupperware.' Bakers sometimes poured melted fat through a hole in the top crust to plug out the last of the air. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'Who Made the First Pie?'; Matador Network, 'Coffin-Inspired History of Pie Crust.'

question: A traditional English pork pie stands up on its own, with no tin and no dish, its thick pastry walls holding a heavy, juicy filling. The secret is the dough, which is made unlike any ordinary pastry. What is it made with?
choices: beaten eggs stirred into soft flour
yeast dough left to rise overnight
olive oil worked into fine semolina
context: This is 'hot-water crust.' Melting fat into boiling water and beating in the flour makes a hot, pliable paste a baker can 'hand-raise' into free-standing walls; as it bakes and cools it sets firm enough to hold a wet, heavy filling. A Melton Mowbray pork pie is shaped by hand around a wooden mould and baked with no tin at all, which is why it bulges into its famous bowed shape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hot water crust pastry'; National Geographic, 'Melton Mowbray pork pies.'

question: A baker pre-bakes an empty pie crust so a wet filling won't leave it soggy, but an empty crust puffs up and slumps in the heat. The old fix is to line it with paper and fill it with something heavy, removed again before the filling is added. What do bakers traditionally weigh an empty crust down with?
context: This is called 'blind baking' — pre-baking a crust empty. Bakers line it with parchment and pour in dried beans, rice, or ceramic 'pie weights' to stop the pastry from bubbling up or slumping, then lift them out before adding the filling. A quicker fix is 'docking': pricking the raw crust all over with a fork so trapped steam escapes through the holes instead of doming the base. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blind-baking.'

question: 'As American as apple pie,' the saying goes, yet the apple came from the Old World, carried across the Atlantic by settlers; only sour little crab apples grew wild in North America before they came. One classic pie is filled with a crop truly native to the Americas, grown by Indigenous farmers for thousands of years. Which pie is it?
context: Apple pie is actually medieval English, not American: the oldest known recipe, 'For to make Tartys in Applis,' appears in 'The Forme of Cury' (about 1381), written by King Richard II's cooks — and it tells you to bake the apples in a 'cofyn,' the very same coffin crust. The apple's wild ancestor still grows in the mountains of Kazakhstan and rode the Silk Road toward Europe long before reaching America. Pumpkin, though, is a true New World squash domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago — one of the 'Three Sisters' grown with corn and beans. Source: Wikipedia, 'Apple' & 'Pumpkin'; Tasting History, 'Medieval Apple Pie'; The Forme of Cury (c.1381).

question: A shopper in the nut aisle finds almonds, walnuts and peanuts sold in their shells to crack open at home, but every cashew comes loose and already shelled, never in a shell to crack. What is the trouble with a raw cashew shell?
answer: It's coated in a caustic oil that blisters skin.
choices: It's coated in a caustic oil that blisters skin.
It's so hard that no home nutcracker can open it.
It gives off a smell that spoils the nut inside.
It hides a bitter second seed that tastes soapy.
context: The raw cashew shell is coated in a caustic oil, chemically related to poison ivy's, that blisters and burns bare skin. That's why cashews are always shelled and heat-treated at the factory before you ever see them — you never buy a cashew in its shell. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew'; Scientific American, 'What Do Cashews, Mangoes and Poison Ivy Have in Common?'

question: Some people who bite into an unpeeled mango break out in an itchy rash around the mouth, from an oily irritant, urushiol, in the fruit's skin and sap. It is a milder version of what a certain woodland plant does to hikers who brush against it. The mango is a close cousin of which North American plant?
context: A mango's skin, sap and leaves carry urushiol — the very same rash-causing oil as poison ivy — because the two plants are close cousins in the cashew family. So an itchy mouth from unpeeled mango is a real, mild poison-ivy reaction; peeling the fruit removes the irritant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mango'; Scientific American, 'What Do Cashews, Mangoes and Poison Ivy Have in Common?'

question: A health-food store sells bags labeled 'raw cashews,' but they are not quite what they claim. Every commercial cashew has already been treated to destroy the oil in its shell. What is done to each and every one?
answer: It's roasted at high heat to burn off the shell oil.
choices: It's roasted at high heat to burn off the shell oil.
It's soaked in vinegar to dissolve the shell oil.
It's bathed in limewater to neutralize the shell oil.
It's boiled in plain water to rinse the shell oil away.
context: 'Raw' cashews are a bit of a myth — every commercial cashew is steamed or drum-roasted to destroy the caustic oil in its shell, a step that also makes the tough shell brittle enough to crack open. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew'; cashew-processing industry guides.

question: Middle Eastern cooks sprinkle sumac, a sour, lemony spice, over their dishes and stir it into za'atar. It grows on a shrub of the cashew family, and a toxic cousin of that shrub, poison sumac, must never be eaten. How does a forager tell the edible shrub from the poisonous one in the wild?
answer: The edible one has red berries; poison sumac has white.
choices: The edible one has red berries; poison sumac has white.
The edible one has thorns; poison sumac has none.
The edible one smells of lemon; poison sumac is odorless.
The edible one has broad leaves; poison sumac has needles.
context: Culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) grows clusters of red berries and is a safe, tangy spice; poison sumac is a different, toxic cousin, told apart by its white berries. Both belong to the same family as cashews and mangoes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sumac'.

question: Cashew factories do not throw away the oil they squeeze from the empty shells. They press it out by the ton and sell it as an industrial raw material, and one everyday product is built partly from it. Which one?
context: Cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL) is a real industrial raw material — its tough resin goes into brake linings and friction materials, plus varnishes, resins and paints. The same seed gives us a snack food and a car part. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew' and 'Cashew nutshell liquid'.

question: A farmer pulls a potato plant up by its leafy top, and fat potatoes come up hanging on short white shoots, full of the starch the plant stored all summer. Each is a swollen piece of one plant organ. Which one?
context: Botanists call a potato a 'stem tuber.' Tubers form at the swelling tips of long, thin underground stems called stolons, which the plant stuffs with starch to store energy - so a potato is a swollen stem, not a root. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: A forgotten potato pushes pale shoots out of the little dimples set in a spiral over its skin, the spots gardeners call its eyes. What is each eye, in plant terms?
context: Each 'eye' is a bud, exactly like the buds spaced along an above-ground stem - more evidence that a potato is really a stem. A bud is a dormant growth point that can wake up and push out a new shoot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: Irish champ, German dumplings and British chips make the potato seem the soul of European cooking, yet it reached Europe only about 500 years ago. Which cold mountain range gave the world the potato?
context: Farmers first domesticated the potato in the Andes of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, roughly 7,000-10,000 years ago - thousands of years before it reached Europe after Columbus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: A carrot patch starts from a fine scatter of seeds, but a potato farmer walks out each spring with a sack on his shoulder that holds no seeds at all. From what he plants, whole new potato plants rise. What does he drop into each hole?
context: Growers plant 'seed potatoes' - whole tubers or cut pieces, each carrying at least one eye (bud) - not true seeds. The new plants are clones of the parent. That is why people say you grow potatoes from potatoes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: A shopper at a market in the Peruvian highlands finds potatoes far stranger than the few types in a Western supermarket; those highlands still grow over four thousand native kinds. Their most surprising feature is color. Which colors do they come in?
context: More than 4,000 varieties of native potato still grow in the Andean highlands (about 3,000 in Peru alone), in reds, purples, blues and golds. The International Potato Center in Lima keeps the world's largest collection, with over 7,000 samples. Source: cipotato.org/potato/native-potato-varieties/

question: Farmers high on a freezing mountain plateau turned potatoes into chuño, a dried food that keeps for decades and once fed Inca armies on the march. Each night the potatoes froze solid, and by day, under a strong sun, the farmers forced the water out. How did they squeeze it out?
answer: they trod on them with their feet
choices: they trod on them with their feet
they pressed them under heavy stones
they wrung them out in cloth
they scraped them with sharp knives
context: This freeze-dried potato is called 'chuño.' On the high plateau (above 3,800 m) the potatoes freeze in the roughly -5C night, then people tread the water out under the day's sun. Chuño keeps for decades and fed Inca soldiers on the march. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuño

question: A cook setting a sweet potato beside an ordinary one might take it for a sweeter kind of potato, yet the two plants come from different families. The ordinary potato is a nightshade; the sweet potato is a close cousin of a familiar garden flower. Which flower?
context: A sweet potato is the swollen storage ROOT of Ipomoea batatas, in the morning-glory family (Convolvulaceae). A true potato is a stem tuber in the nightshade family - so despite the shared name, the two are different organs of barely-related plants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato

question: A gardener who lets a potato plant bloom and grow on finds something few people ever see: small, round green fruits full of seeds, hanging above the ground. They look uncannily like a tiny version of another garden favorite. What do they resemble?
context: A potato plant does flower and set fruit: small green berries that look like tiny green tomatoes - no coincidence, since potato and tomato are both nightshades. Each berry holds about 300 true seeds, but the fruits are toxic and are never eaten. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: Pulling a green-tinged potato from the bag, a cook is right to be wary of it, but like most people he takes the green itself for the poison. Food scientists say that common idea is wrong. What is the green tinge on a potato, really?
context: The green is chlorophyll - harmless in itself - made as the potato sits in light. But that same light exposure signals the tuber has built up solanine, a natural toxin the nightshade family makes. Because 30-80% of the solanine sits in and just under the skin, cutting the green away or peeling removes most of it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanine

question: The potato arrived in Europe a feared foreigner, and many people flatly refused to eat it. It grew hidden in the dark soil, it belonged to the poisonous nightshade family, and the Bible named it nowhere, so wary folk decided it must be unclean. What nickname did they pin on it?
context: Because the potato was an unfamiliar nightshade that grew hidden underground and went unmentioned in the Bible, wary Europeans nicknamed it the 'devil's apples' and shunned it as unclean before it slowly became a staple. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_potato  (Legend.)

question: Suspicious peasants across one European kingdom got orders in 1756 to plant potatoes, from a ruler sure the crop could end famine. Grateful admirers are said to leave potatoes on his grave to this day. Which ruler gave the order?
context: Frederick the Great of Prussia issued his 'potato order' in 1756 to guard against famine, earning the nickname 'Kartoffelkönig' - the potato king. Admirers still leave potatoes on his grave, a custom that lives on today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_potato  (Legend.)

question: Farmers in the Andean highlands still grow more than four thousand native kinds of potato, while a modern supermarket sells maybe five. First-time visitors to those villages are startled by one thing about them. What surprises them most?
answer: They come in bright reds, purples, and blues
choices: They come in bright reds, purples, and blues
They grow as large as ripe watermelons
They ripen into sweet red berries like fruit
They climb overhead on tall leafy vines
context: More than 4,000 varieties of native potato still grow in the Andean highlands of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador - a rainbow of shapes and colors bred over centuries to survive at 3,500-4,200 meters (about 11,000-14,000 feet). Source: cipotato.org/potato/native-potato-varieties/.

question: From Ireland to Poland, farmers across Europe's poor countryside began plowing up their grain after 1750 and planting a strange new tuber from the Americas instead, and the switch spread field by field within about one lifetime. What could the potato do for a hungry family that wheat and rye could not?
answer: Feed far more people from the same ground
choices: Feed far more people from the same ground
Ripen a second full crop every autumn
Keep for years in a dry sack indoors
Grow well in salty soil beside the sea
context: An acre of potatoes yields far more food energy than an acre of grain - about 95 gigajoules per hectare versus wheat's 31 (it beats maize's 78 and rice's 77 too). Those cheap, dense calories are the main reason Europe's poor took it up, and it became a major field crop after 1750. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato.

question: Europeans eyed the newly arrived potato warily, and they had a reason: it belongs to the nightshade family, along with deadly nightshade, a famous woodland poison that has killed unlucky travelers for centuries. Two vegetables from ordinary dinner tables are close cousins in the same family. Which pair?
context: The potato is a nightshade (family Solanaceae) - the same plant family as deadly nightshade, the tomato, and the eggplant. The tuber is a safe, everyday food; the family reputation comes from wild relatives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato.

question: The French sneered at the potato as food fit only for pigs, and in 1748 their government went further and banned the crop outright, sure it spread a dreaded disease. Which disease were potatoes wrongly blamed for?
context: France dismissed the potato as pig food and, in 1748, actually banned it - blaming it for causing leprosy. The ban stood until 1772, when the Paris Faculty of Medicine finally declared potatoes fit to eat. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/potato-history-france-western-europe.

question: Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian, two economists, added up the numbers on the potato's cheap calories and found that the humble spud drove roughly a quarter of the Old World's growth between 1700 and 1900. That growth showed up in two things at once. Which pair did the potato help swell?
context: Economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian calculated that the potato was responsible for about a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanization between 1700 and 1900 - one imported vegetable helped build modern Europe's cities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato (citing Nunn & Qian, Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(2), 2011, pp. 593-650).

question: Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, who served the French army as a pharmacist, planted potatoes on a field granted by King Louis XVI, set on making his countrymen want a crop they still refused to eat. As the story goes, how did he get villagers planting potatoes in their own gardens?
answer: He posted armed guards by day, then let thieves take the crop at night
choices: He posted armed guards by day, then let thieves take the crop at night
He sold seed potatoes so cheaply that poor farmers would plant them
He handed out free tubers so that every village would grow its own
He served potato dishes at court so the fashion would reach the poor
context: As the famous story goes, to make the potato fashionable Antoine-Augustin Parmentier planted a field on land granted by Louis XVI and posted armed guards over it by day - then pulled them off at night so curious locals would sneak in and steal the 'valuable' crop for their own gardens. Parmentier had first eaten potatoes as a French army pharmacist held prisoner by the Prussians during the Seven Years' War - the food the French fed only to hogs kept him alive, and he became its champion. He later threw banquets of about twenty potato dishes for guests including Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, and handed potato blossoms to the royals - Louis XVI wore one in his lapel, Marie Antoinette wore them in her hair. His name lives on in 'hachis Parmentier,' the French cottage pie made with mashed potato. Sources: atlasobscura.com/articles/history-of-potatoes-parmentier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine-Augustin_Parmentier.  (Legend.)

question: Servants in a wealthy Roman's house brought out roast meats, bowls of olives and jugs of watered wine for the guests. The strangest thing to modern eyes was not the food but the way every guest ate. What posture did a Roman hold all through the meal?
context: Romans reclined on couches set around a low table, treating a long, leisurely meal as a mark of the civilized life; slaves brought each course to the diners. Source: Smith's Dictionary of Greek & Roman Antiquities, 'Triclinium' (LacusCurtius); Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: A Roman family's formal dining room held wide couches set in a U around a central table, with the open side kept free for servants to bring the food. Those couches gave the room its name. What was it called?
context: Triclinium literally means 'three couches': three broad couches held nine diners, three to a couch, with the open fourth side kept clear for serving. Source: Wikipedia, 'Triclinium'; UNRV, 'Triclinium.'

question: Wealthy Romans stuffed from a feast, the popular story goes, would stagger off to a special room called a vomitorium to throw up and then eat more. The truth is far less disgusting. What was a vomitorium really?
answer: A passageway that funnels crowds out of an arena
choices: A passageway that funnels crowds out of an arena
A side kitchen for preparing extra courses
A fountain room where guests rinsed their hands
A cellar where wine was chilled before serving
context: The word comes from Latin vomere, 'to spew forth' — describing how a packed amphitheatre 'spewed' its crowd out through the exits, not diners purging. No ancient source uses it for post-meal vomiting; the Colosseum had 80 such passages, emptying tens of thousands of spectators in minutes. Source: The Conversation, 'Mythbusting Ancient Rome — the truth about the vomitorium'; Wikipedia, 'Vomitorium.'

question: Every diner at a formal Roman banquet leaned onto his left elbow on a padded couch, three guests to a couch, and kept that arm pinned beneath him through course after course of roast meat, bread and fruit. Why did every diner tie up his left arm like that?
answer: It freed the right hand to reach for food
choices: It freed the right hand to reach for food
It turned the face toward the host of honor
It was believed to settle the stomach
It kept the fine dinner robes from creasing
context: With most people right-handed, lying on the left elbow left the stronger right hand free to take food from the low central table. Source: Smith's Dictionary of Greek & Roman Antiquities, 'Triclinium'; Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: Guests at a formal Roman dinner ate it in three acts, like a play: eggs and salty little bites to begin, then the main tables of roast meat and stew, and last the secunda mensa, the 'second table', a sweet closing course. What did the Romans serve at that last table?
context: So reliably did a meal run from an egg course to a fruit finish that the poet Horace summed up a whole dinner as 'ab ovo usque ad mala' — 'from egg to apples.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Ab ovo'; Wikipedia, 'Food in ancient Rome.'

question: Greek philosophers such as Plato held drinking parties called symposia, where only men reclined on the couches and wives and daughters were kept out of the room entirely. The Romans borrowed the custom of dining on couches but changed one rule about who lay on them. What did Romans do that Greeks would have found scandalous?
answer: Respectable women reclined right beside the men
choices: Respectable women reclined right beside the men
Guests reclined in strict order of wealth
Children reclined once they turned seven
Slaves reclined for the meal's final toast
context: At a Greek symposium the couches were male-only — the only women present were entertainers and servants. Roman wives and daughters dining openly beside men became a hallmark of the Roman banquet. Source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Roman Banquet'; Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: Trimalchio, the vulgar rich host of Petronius's satirical novel the Satyricon, loved dishes that startled his guests. A whole roast hog was carried in, and he flew into a fake fury that the cook had forgotten to gut it, so the cook slit it open right at the table. What tumbled out?
answer: Cooked sausages and blood puddings, like its own innards
choices: Cooked sausages and blood puddings, like its own innards
Live thrushes, which burst free and flap off
Pastry eggs, hidden in a nest of straw
Hot spiced wine, gushing like a fountain
context: The Satyricon's feast is comic fiction, mocking a host who spends wildly to show off. Trimalchio pretends the cook forgot to gut the pig, then the belly is slit and sausages and blood puddings tumble out — one of several 'trick dishes' built purely to fool and delight the diners. Source: Petronius, Satyricon (Trimalchio's Feast), Fordham Ancient History Sourcebook.

question: One prized appetizer at a rich Roman's banquet in the age of the Caesars was no ordinary cut of meat but a whole roasted dormouse, a fat little rodent about the size of a hamster, fattened until it was plump and tender. It was a luxury meant to show off the host's wealth. How was the dormouse dressed up on the plate?
answer: Glazed in honey and rolled in poppy seeds
choices: Glazed in honey and rolled in poppy seeds
Stuffed with figs and wrapped in vine leaves
Simmered in fish sauce and dusted with pepper
Split, salted, and dried hard as a biscuit
context: The honey-and-poppy-seed dormouse appears as an hors d'oeuvre in Petronius's Satyricon. Romans thought dormice such decadent luxuries that a censor once passed a law banning them from the table, alongside shellfish and imported birds. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Dormouse-Fattening Jars of Ancient Rome'; Petronius, Satyricon.

question: A Roman farmer fattened dormice for the table in the dark, inside a special pierced earthenware pot ribbed inside with little ramps and stuffed with acorns and chestnuts, until the sleepy rodents grew plump. What was that pot called?
context: Glirarium comes from glis, the Latin for dormouse. The dark, cramped jar mimicked a burrow so the dormice fattened fast; the cookbook of Apicius even preserves a recipe for stuffing them with pork, pepper, and pine nuts before roasting. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Dormouse-Fattening Jars of Ancient Rome'; Sarah E. Bond, 'Pass the Dormice.'

question: A cook shaking salt over a pot is adding what looks like one simple ingredient, yet every tiny crystal is two different elements bonded together, and a food label tracks only one of them. Which two make up table salt?
context: Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl. By weight it's about 40% sodium and 60% chloride, and it's only the sodium half that the whole health debate is about, which is why a food label says 'sodium,' not 'salt.' One teaspoon of table salt carries roughly 2,300 mg of sodium. Source: cdc.gov, 'About Sodium and Health.'

question: A doctor tells a salt-sensitive patient to cut back on salt, because too much sodium raises blood pressure, and the warning rests on simple physics. Once extra sodium is in the blood, what does it physically do to push the pressure up?
answer: It pulls water into the bloodstream, swelling the blood's volume.
choices: It pulls water into the bloodstream, swelling the blood's volume.
It stiffens the artery walls so they can no longer flex.
It signals the heart to beat faster and harder than normal.
It thickens the blood into a slower, stickier fluid.
context: This is the reduction side's strongest case. Sodium draws water with it, so more sodium in the blood means more blood volume and higher pressure, hitting salt-sensitive and hypertensive people hardest. The American Heart Association pushes an even stricter 1,500 mg ideal; as the AHA's Dr. Frank Sacks put it, 'Most Americans are consuming more sodium than their body needs. Lowering sodium intake lowers blood pressure, which can save lives.' Source: nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu, 'Salt and Sodium'; tctmd.com.

question: Andrew Mente led the PURE (Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology) study, which tracked about 94,000 people across 18 countries for years and weighed their sodium against their heart risk. Health advice had long held that the less sodium, the better. What did the data suggest about people who kept their sodium extremely low?
answer: Their risk crept back up, as if too little salt were harmful too.
choices: Their risk crept back up, as if too little salt were harmful too.
Their risk kept dropping in a steady line, the lowest of all.
Their risk stayed flat, unchanged no matter how low they went.
Their risk fell by roughly half compared with heavy salters.
context: The PURE data traced a J-SHAPED curve: heart risk climbed clearly only above roughly 5 grams of sodium a day, but below a healthy middle the curve bent back UP. Lead author Andrew Mente concluded 'about 3 to 5 grams per day appears to be the optimal level associated with lowest risk,' so the honest takeaway is 'there's a healthy middle,' not 'less is always better.' Big caveat: this comes from observational data and is contested. The AHA's Frank Sacks argues sick people may already eat less salt (reverse causation) and that a single urine sample is a shaky measure, and population-reduction bodies hold that lowering everyone's salt still saves lives. Read it as 'evidence suggests a middle range,' not settled fact. Source: The Lancet (Mente, O'Donnell, Yusuf et al., 2018); tctmd.com.  (Legend.)

question: Set on eating less sodium, a home cook puts the salt shaker away. A dietitian says that barely moves the needle: for the average American, only a small slice of the day's sodium comes from the shaker, and around 70 percent is already in the food before it reaches the kitchen. Which foods hide most of it?
answer: Packaged and restaurant food — breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soup.
choices: Packaged and restaurant food — breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soup.
Naturally salty whole foods — celery, beets, and fresh shellfish.
Fresh fruit — bananas, oranges, ripe melons, and berries.
Raw meats and seafood — fresh chicken, beef, and white fish.
context: The CDC and FDA estimate that roughly 70% (surveys run 70-77%) of Americans' sodium is built into processed, packaged, and restaurant food: breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soups. The sneaky part is that many of them, like bread and cookies, don't even taste salty. So salting your own whole-food cooking from scratch is a small slice of the total, and it's the slice a cook can actually control. Source: fda.gov, 'Sodium Reduction in the Food Supply.'

question: Two slices of bread close over a filling, and the word sandwich seems to describe just that, yet the naming ran the other way: Sandwich belonged to a person long before it was ever a lunch. Who was the sandwich named after?
context: The food is named for John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718-1792), an English aristocrat and politician. Curiously, it took his aristocratic TITLE, not his family name (Montagu) -- otherwise we might be ordering a 'montagu' for lunch. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; Wikipedia, 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich.'

question: John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich in 18th-century England, did not invent the odd name of his title; it came down to him from his ancestors. Long before Sandwich ever named a lunch between two slices of bread, it was something else in England. What was it?
answer: an old seaport town in Kent
choices: an old seaport town in Kent
a card game played at court
an old English word for bread
context: The earldom was created in 1660 for the naval commander Edward Montagu, the 1st Earl, who chose 'Sandwich' as a compliment to the town in Kent his fleet lay off when it sailed to bring Charles II back to England. So the food is named after a man, who was named after a town. Source: Wikipedia, 'Earl of Sandwich.'

question: As the legend goes, John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, grew so absorbed at the gaming table around 1762 that he refused to leave it even to eat. He had a servant bring him meat tucked between two slices of bread. What did he gain by eating it that way?
answer: he could eat one-handed and keep the cards free of grease
choices: he could eat one-handed and keep the cards free of grease
he could tuck it away and nibble between hands
he could hand the same meal to his fellow players
he could eat without the servants noticing
context: The gambling-table tale traces to a gossipy French travel writer, Pierre-Jean Grosley, in 'A Tour to London' (early 1770s). Other gamblers supposedly began ordering 'the same as Sandwich,' and the name stuck. Tellingly, Grosley never actually named the Earl of Sandwich -- readers just assumed it was him. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; historyhit.com, 'Did the 4th Earl of Sandwich Really Invent the Sandwich?'  (Legend.)

question: Rodger, who wrote the life of John Montagu, notes that the earl spent three terms as First Lord of the Admiralty, running Britain's navy, buried in duties day and night. Historians now suspect the first sandwich was eaten not over cards but somewhere else. Where?
choices: on the deck of a warship at sea
at a grand banquet in London
at a roadside inn while travelling
context: The earliest written use of 'sandwich' is in historian Edward Gibbon's 1762 diary, describing gentlemen at the Cocoa Tree coffeehouse supping 'upon a bit of cold meat, or a Sandwich' -- and it says nothing about gambling. Biographer N.A.M. Rodger argues a quick one-handed meal at the busy official's desk fits far better than a 24-hour card binge. Source: historyhit.com, 'Did the 4th Earl of Sandwich Really Invent the Sandwich?'; wordorigins.org; Wikipedia, 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich.'

question: A Jewish sage folded Passover lamb and bitter herbs inside flatbread some 1,800 years ahead of the Earl of Sandwich, who lent the food his name, and Jews still eat that mouthful at the Seder today. Who was the sage?
context: Around the 1st century BC, Hillel the Elder combined the Passover lamb, matzah, and bitter herbs in one bite. Jews still eat it at the Seder as the 'Korech,' or 'Hillel sandwich' -- and 'Korech' comes from a root meaning to wrap or embrace, a literal description of a sandwich centuries before the English word existed. So the Earl gave the world the name, not the invention. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; Chabad.org; thejc.com, 'Karich.'

question: Butter, lard, and cheese sit as firm blocks on the counter, while olive oil and corn oil pour like water. That habit of staying solid at room temperature is a rough clue that a fat is mostly which kind?
context: Butter, lard, beef tallow, and cheese are all high in saturated fat and stay solid or semi-solid at room temperature, while the liquid cooking oils — olive, corn, soybean — are mostly unsaturated and stay liquid. The 'solid vs liquid at room temp' test is a rough sort for saturated vs unsaturated fat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat.'

question: Four fats sit side by side in a cook's pantry: butter from a dairy cow, lard rendered from a pig, tallow from a steer and olive oil pressed from Mediterranean olives. Traditional cooks have used all four for centuries. Which of them holds the biggest share of saturated fat?
context: About two-thirds of butter's fat (~63%) is saturated, and cheese is similar (~64%). By contrast, pork lard is about 39% saturated and beef tallow about 41% — so those greasy animal fats are actually LESS saturated than the butter on your toast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat' fat-composition table.

question: Ancel Keys, an American researcher, set out in 1958 to prove that saturated fat was clogging people's arteries. He launched a huge, long-running project that tracked the diets and heart health of thousands of middle-aged men, and it became the scientific backbone of the anti-fat era. What is that study remembered as today?
context: The idea traces to Ancel Keys and his 'diet-heart hypothesis' from the early 1950s: he argued saturated fat raised blood cholesterol, which caused heart disease. In 1958 he launched the Seven Countries Study, tracking middle-aged men across the USA, Finland, the Netherlands, Italy, Yugoslavia, Greece, and Japan. Source: Seven Countries Study (sevencountriesstudy.com); Wikipedia, 'Ancel Keys.'

question: Researchers sorting the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in people's blood, the kind called 'bad,' saw that it travels as particles of different sizes and densities. A diet high in saturated fat, they found, nudges a person's LDL toward one particular kind. Which kind does saturated fat tend to produce?
context: Later research added nuance the old story missed: saturated fat also raises HDL (the 'good' cholesterol), and it tends to shift LDL toward larger, buoyant particles rather than the small, dense ones more strongly tied to heart risk. It's the same LDL number telling a more complicated story. Source: Krauss/LDL particle-size research; PLOS One 2017, 'Effects of a very high saturated fat diet on LDL particles.'

question: Patty Siri-Tarino, a nutrition researcher, and her team pooled 21 separate studies covering nearly 348,000 people in 2010, the biggest test yet of whether saturated fat drives heart disease. Decades of official U.S. dietary advice, warning people off butter and red meat, all hung on what the numbers said. What did the analysis report?
answer: no clear link between saturated fat and heart disease
choices: no clear link between saturated fat and heart disease
a strong link between saturated fat and heart disease
a clear link between saturated fat and stroke alone
a link only among people who also ate lots of sugar
context: The 2010 turning point: Siri-Tarino's pooled analysis in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition combined 21 studies and 347,747 people (11,006 of whom developed heart disease or stroke) and found saturated fat intake was NOT associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, or cardiovascular disease. Source: Siri-Tarino PW et al. 2010, Am J Clin Nutr 91:535-546 (PubMed 20071648). The honest bottom line, though: those big analyses weakened the direct saturated-fat-to-heart-disease link, so guidelines eased — but Harvard's nutrition experts called the 'fat type doesn't matter' takeaway misleading. The fair verdict is 'the simple artery-clogging story was OVERSTATED,' NOT 'saturated fat is proven harmless' — the LDL rise is still real; it's the hard disease OUTCOME that's contested. Today WHO, AHA, and NHS still suggest keeping saturated fat under about 10% of daily calories. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source critique; Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat and cardiovascular disease.'
