context: The rule took effect on January 1, 1998: 140 micrograms of folic acid per 100 g of enriched cereal grain. Neural-tube-defect-affected pregnancies fell from about 4,000 a year in 1995-96 to about 3,000 in 1999-2000. Adding a dust to flour prevents birth defects -- in babies whose mothers never knew they needed it. Sources: CDC MMWR (cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6401a2.htm; mm5931a2.htm); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folic_acid.

question: A shopper picks up a bag of white flour with 'Enriched' printed across the front, its label listing iron and B vitamins that the whole-wheat bag beside it does not even advertise. Enriched white flour sounds like the healthier choice, yet nutritionists say a loaf of it still falls short of whole wheat. Why not?
answer: Enrichment puts back about five nutrients; milling stripped out dozens of them.
choices: Enrichment puts back about five nutrients; milling stripped out dozens of them.
Enrichment puts back about five nutrients; the doses are a tenth of the kernel's.
Enrichment puts back about five nutrients; bleaching then destroys most of them.
Enrichment puts back about five nutrients; the oven's heat drives most of them off.
context: The Whole Grains Council puts it plainly: enrichment 'adds back fewer than a half dozen of the many missing nutrients, and does so in proportions different than they originally existed.' Refining removes about a quarter of a grain's protein and half to two-thirds or more of a score of nutrients; fiber and vitamin E are never added back at all. Enrichment was real and it worked -- US regulations mandated it in 1941, and it took the chemist Benjamin R. Jacobs documenting the losses in the 1920s and the first synthesis of thiamine in 1936 to make it possible. But 'enriched' has never meant 'whole'. Sources: wholegrainscouncil.org/whole-grains-101/whats-whole-grain-refined-grain; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_flour.

question: Food finishes its journey in the colon, the tail end of the large intestine, home to nearly all of the body's bacteria, about 38 trillion of them. Suppose you could watch them at work: far from making you sick, they are welcome guests. What are they doing for you?
answer: Finishing digestion of food your own gut couldn't
choices: Finishing digestion of food your own gut couldn't
Soaking up every drop of water from your food
Killing all the germs that enter your mouth
Turning leftover food straight into body fat
context: Roughly 38 trillion bacteria live in your colon — outnumbering the cells of every other organ by at least a hundredfold — and they finish breaking down the leftovers your own digestion can't handle. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology.

question: Suppose you grew up reading biology textbooks that said your body carried ten bacteria for every one of your own cells, so that you were barely more human than microbe. Nobody had actually counted until a team of Israeli scientists did in 2016. What did their count show?
answer: About one microbe for each cell of yours
choices: About one microbe for each cell of yours
About three microbes for each cell of yours
About one microbe for every three cells of yours
About ten microbes for each cell of yours
context: The 10-to-1 figure was a 1972 back-of-the-envelope guess by Thomas Luckey that got repeated for decades. The 2016 recount put it near 38 trillion bacterial cells to 30 trillion human cells — about 1.3 to 1 — so you're roughly a one-to-one mix of you and them. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology.

question: Trillions of bacteria living in a person's colon pay a kind of rent for their room and board. They build a supply of nutrients, and those nutrients are absorbed into the blood and put to work. What do the bacteria make?
context: Your gut bacteria synthesize biotin and folate and are an important source of vitamin K and vitamin B12 — nutrients your own body makes little or none of on its own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gut microbiota'.

question: More than 10,000 people mailed stool samples and food diaries to the American Gut Project, one of the largest gut studies ever run. The people whose guts held the richest, most varied mix of microbes all shared one weekly habit. What did their weekly menus hold?
answer: the widest variety of different plants
choices: the widest variety of different plants
the widest variety of different meats
the widest variety of dairy foods
the widest variety of raw, uncooked foods
context: This was the American Gut Project (published 2018, led by Daniel McDonald and Rob Knight). People who ate 30 or more different plants a week had significantly more diverse gut microbiomes than those eating 10 or fewer — and the variety of plants mattered more than any diet label. Source: The Microsetta Initiative, UC San Diego.

question: Israeli scientists who counted the body's bacteria in 2016 found about 38 trillion of them, and the same careful count weighed them too. Thirty-eight trillion living creatures sounds as if it ought to weigh a great deal, a whole hidden organ's worth. Piled on a kitchen scale, about how much would one person's gut microbes weigh?
context: Weighed all together, your gut microbes come to only about half a pound (roughly 0.2 kg). The popular claim that you carry '2 to 3 pounds of gut bacteria' is an overestimate that the careful 2016 recount trimmed way down. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology.

question: Cooks across Asia prized gleaming polished white rice over plain brown for centuries. When whole villages came to live on little else, a crippling disease spread through them: weak, numb legs, swollen ankles and, in its worst form, a failing heart. What was the disease called?
context: Beriberi struck wherever polished white rice became the main food. It comes in two forms: 'wet' beriberi floods the heart and blood vessels — racing heart, breathlessness, swollen legs — while 'dry' beriberi attacks the nerves, numbing the hands and feet and buckling the legs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiamine_deficiency

question: Rice mills across Asia buffed every grain white in the 1800s, scraping off its brown outer coat, the bran and the germ, to feed whole cities and navies. People who ate little else grew weak and numb in the hands and feet, and some ended up paralyzed. Which nutrient had the polishing thrown away?
context: Thiamine, vitamin B1, lets the body turn food into energy for nerves and muscle. It rides in the bran and germ, the very layers milling strips off — which is why brown rice, keeping its coat, holds the thiamine that polished white rice loses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiamine_deficiency

question: Christiaan Eijkman, a Dutch doctor on Java, watched his laboratory chickens fall into a leg paralysis in 1897 after eating leftover polished white rice from a military hospital. Then they got better just as fast, once they were back on cheap unpolished rice. Why had their feed been switched?
answer: A new cook refused to waste valuable military rice on mere civilian chickens
choices: A new cook refused to waste valuable military rice on mere civilian chickens
The hospital's supply of white rice had simply run out that week
A brown-rice glut had made unpolished grain the cheapest feed around
Eijkman deliberately switched them, testing a hunch about the white rice
context: The switch was dumb luck. Within days the birds recovered, and Eijkman grasped that the polished rice was missing something the bran held — the sickness came from an ABSENCE, not from a germ infecting the chickens, as everyone then assumed. He and Frederick Hopkins later shared the 1929 Nobel Prize for the discovery of vitamins. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christiaan_Eijkman  (Legend.)

question: Casimir Funk, a Polish chemist, had by 1912 given a brand-new name to the tiny life-or-death factors in food whose absence, not a germ, could make a person sick. He built the name by fusing two words. Which two?
answer: 'vital' and 'amine' (a chemical group he thought they contained)
choices: 'vital' and 'amine' (a chemical group he thought they contained)
'ferment' and 'vigor' (the spark thought to drive digestion)
context: Funk's word 'vitamine' was later shortened to 'vitamin' once scientists found that not all of these factors are amines. His name gave the whole idea a banner to march under: whole classes of tiny nutrients whose absence, not their presence, makes you sick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casimir_Funk

question: Robert Williams, an American chemist, chased the vitamin in rice bran for decades, at first wringing it from the bran itself, but a whole ton of bran gave only about a third of an ounce, far too little to protect millions. He cracked the problem in 1936. What did his breakthrough let food makers do?
answer: Make thiamine in a factory and add it back into milled white rice and flour
choices: Make thiamine in a factory and add it back into milled white rice and flour
Breed a new rice that grew its thiamine deep inside the white grain
Leave a thin band of bran on each grain so it stayed white but kept its vitamin
Coat white rice in a vitamin glaze pressed from fresh green vegetables
context: Williams isolated thiamine as pure crystals in 1933 and synthesized it in 1936. Because factory-made thiamine was cheap, mills could 'enrich' white rice and white flour — dusting back the very vitamin the polishing removed. It is why a bag of white bread or rice today so often reads 'enriched.' Source: invent.org/inductees/robert-r-williams and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Williams

question: A French cook pours milk into béchamel, pale stock into velouté and brown stock into espagnole, three of the five mother sauces and three different liquids. Yet all three begin the same way, with the same two things heated in the pan before any liquid goes in. What is in that pan?
answer: Flour and butter, cooked together into a roux
choices: Flour and butter, cooked together into a roux
Egg yolks and butter, whisked into a hollandaise
Onions and carrots, softened into a mirepoix
Wine and herbs, reduced into a bearnaise
context: A roux is just flour pre-coated in fat — classically equal parts flour and fat by weight — cooked together before any liquid goes in, so the fat wraps each flour grain and they thicken evenly instead of clumping. It's the base of three of the five French 'mother sauces': bechamel (white roux + milk), veloute (blond roux + stock), and espagnole (brown roux + brown stock). Source: Wikipedia, 'Roux.'

question: Two identical steaks cook for the same time at the same 400 degrees Fahrenheit, one in a cast-iron skillet on the stove and one in the oven. One comes out dark and crusty and the other pale. Why doesn't the same temperature give the same result?
answer: The heat reaches the meat by a different route in each
choices: The heat reaches the meat by a different route in each
A steak always shrinks more inside a closed oven
Heat can only ever move through solid metal
Browning happens only where meat touches liquid
context: Physicists count just three ways heat can move: conduction (direct touch), convection (a moving hot fluid — any gas or liquid), and radiation (waves across space). A pan, an oven, and a grill each lean on a different one, so the 'same' temperature cooks three different steaks — and most cooking methods actually mix more than one at once. Source: scienceofcooking.com/how-is-heat-transferred-in-cooking; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_transfer.

question: Fat smokes in a screaming-hot cast-iron skillet as a raw steak goes in, and a dark, crackling crust forms within seconds where the meat presses flat against the iron. Which kind of heat transfer is the skillet mainly using?
context: Conduction is heat passing particle-to-particle from the hot metal straight into whatever touches it. Cast iron dumps enormous heat at every point of contact, and that tight metal-to-food touch is why a skillet delivers the hardest, fastest sear of the three methods. Source: scienceofcooking.com/how-is-heat-transferred-in-cooking; 123foodscience.com/cooking-science/heat-transfer-methods.

question: A chicken turns golden in the oven, wrapped in gentle, even heat that reaches it from every side at once, fine for roasting and baking but useless for a fast, hard sear. Which kind of heat transfer is the oven mostly using?
context: In physics a 'fluid' means any gas or liquid — so the hot air swirling around an oven is a fluid carrying heat by convection. It reaches the food gently from all sides at once, which is why an oven is built for roasting and baking rather than an instant sear. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection_oven; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_transfer.

question: A cook baking in one kind of oven turns the dial about 20 degrees Celsius (36 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than she would for an ordinary one, because it browns more evenly and cooks faster. From the outside the two look almost identical. What single part inside makes the difference?
answer: A fan that drives the hot air around
choices: A fan that drives the hot air around
A second heating element in the floor
A sealed door that traps steam inside
A thicker metal wall that holds heat
context: The fan drives the hot air around faster — physicists call fan-pushed flow 'forced convection,' versus the 'natural convection' of a still oven, where warm air merely rises on its own. That natural rising leaves a still oven hotter near the top and cooler at the bottom; the fan evens it out and cooks a bit quicker, so cooks drop the temperature about 20°C (36°F). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection_oven; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_transfer.

question: A backyard cook drops a raw steak onto the grate above a bed of glowing red charcoal, and within seconds its underside starts to char. Most of that fierce heat streams up off the coals and strikes the meat straight through the open air. Which kind of heat transfer is the grill leaning on most?
context: A grill or broiler cooks largely by radiation — invisible infrared waves thrown from glowing coals or a red-hot element; Wikipedia says grill heat travels 'primarily through thermal radiation.' It's the same warmth the Sun sends to your face, and radiation is the only method that needs nothing in between — it even crosses the empty vacuum of space, which is how the Sun reaches Earth. That's why you feel a grill's heat before you ever touch it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grilling; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_transfer.

question: A steak comes off a backyard grill with dark charred stripes running in parallel bands across it and paler meat in between, though its whole underside sat over the very same fire. Why did only the stripe lines come out branded dark?
answer: The hot metal bars pressed directly on the meat there
choices: The hot metal bars pressed directly on the meat there
Seasoning pooled along those lines and burned dark
Dripping fat flared into flames just beneath them
Smoke settled into the stripes and stained them
context: The dark stripes are where the hot metal bars touched the meat directly — that's conduction — so those lines brown fast and hard, while the gaps between the bars got only the gentler radiant heat and stayed pale. One grilled steak shows two heat modes at once: radiation over the gaps, conduction on the stripes. (When that same radiant heat is aimed DOWN from above instead of up from below, cooks call it broiling.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grilling.

question: A cook sniffs a single dry cumin seed from the jar and smells almost nothing. She tips a spoonful into a hot, dry pan and shakes it for a minute, and a warm, earthy smell fills the kitchen. Where was that flavor hiding in the seed?
answer: In tiny droplets of oil locked inside it
choices: In tiny droplets of oil locked inside it
In pockets of trapped air inside it
In grains of plant sugar inside it
In threads of tough fiber inside it
context: A spice's smell and taste come from volatile essential oils — aromatic compounds locked inside the cell walls of the seed, bark, or berry. Until heat or grinding cracks those walls open, most of the flavor stays sealed away, which is why a raw whole spice smells so faint. These oils are called 'volatile' because they turn to vapor and fly off the instant they warm — exactly why a spice 'wakes up' and fills the kitchen the moment it hits a hot pan. Source: RawSpiceBar, 'How to Toast Spices for Maximum Flavor'; The Spice Trader, 'Toasting vs Blooming Spices.'

question: Whole coriander seeds rattle in a dry, hot pan for a minute or two, until the little brown balls turn a shade darker and smell warmly nutty. The heat might seem to be cooking the flavor away, yet the toasted seeds taste far better in the finished curry. How does the browning improve the flavor?
answer: It cooks up brand-new flavor molecules in the seed
choices: It cooks up brand-new flavor molecules in the seed
It just reheats the flavors already in the seed
It melts the oils so they pour out of the seed
It hardens the shell to trap flavor in the seed
context: Toasting doesn't cook flavor out — it lightly browns the spice through the Maillard reaction, the same chemistry that browns toast and a seared steak. That browning builds brand-new nutty, earthy flavor molecules that don't exist in the raw seed at all, while the heat also concentrates the spice's oils right at the surface. Toasting whole spices before grinding can boost a blend's flavor by roughly a quarter compared with raw ground spice. Source: MasalaBear, 'The Science of Spice Blooming'; Tasting Table, 'How Heat Affects the Flavor Release of Spices.'

question: An Indian cook warms oil in the pan and fries ground cumin and coriander in it for a minute before any tomatoes, water or other watery liquid goes in. Cooks call it blooming the spices, and the oil pulls far more flavor out of the powders than water could. Why does oil beat water?
answer: Their flavor oils dissolve into fat, not into water
choices: Their flavor oils dissolve into fat, not into water
Water boils away before it can pull out the flavor
Hot oil scrubs the flavor off the outside of the spice
Oil simply holds far more flavor than water can hold
context: Most spice flavor molecules — the terpenes and essential oils — are fat-soluble, not water-soluble, so 'blooming' spices in hot oil or butter loads the fat with flavor, and the fat then carries it evenly through the whole dish, something plain water simply cannot do. America's Test Kitchen measured it in the lab: thyme bloomed in oil released about 10 times more of its main flavor compound, thymol, than thyme simmered in water, and red pepper flakes gave oil more than double the capsaicin (the heat compound) that water pulled out. Source: America's Test Kitchen, 'Blooming in Oil for Flavor'; MasalaBear, 'The Science of Spice Blooming.'

question: A jar of whole peppercorns stays sharp on the spice shelf for years, and a cook can crack one a decade later and still get a proper bite. Ground into fine black powder, the same pepper starts to fade within a few months. What is grinding doing that drains the flavor away so fast?
answer: It opens the oils to the air, so they evaporate and spoil
choices: It opens the oils to the air, so they evaporate and spoil
It packs the oils in tighter, so they smother each other
It heats the oils up, so they cook themselves away
It soaks the oils in water, so they dilute themselves
context: Grinding shatters the seed and floods air across a huge new surface, so the delicate volatile oils immediately begin evaporating and oxidizing. That's why whole spices keep their punch for years — whole peppercorns stay potent 3 years or more — while pre-ground spice can lose about half its volatile oils within six months. The lesson cooks live by: buy whole, and grind fresh right when you need it, because a spice ground the moment you use it is far more powerful than the same spice ground months ago. Source: The Spice Trader, 'Why Whole Spices Are Better Than Ground.'

question: Garam masala begins with cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and cloves, but an Indian cook does not simply stir them together in a bowl. She first roasts the whole spices together in a dry pan over the heat, and only then grinds them. What does that shared time in the pan do that plain mixing cannot?
answer: It marries their oils into one blended flavor
choices: It marries their oils into one blended flavor
It kills any germs living on the whole spices
It softens the spices so they grind more easily
It strips the bitter husks off each whole spice
context: Garam masala means 'warming spices' (in Hindi, garam = hot/warm, masala = blend). Toasting the whole spices together before grinding lets their freshly released oils mingle and meld, marrying separate spices into a single, unified blend — the same toast-then-grind trick that builds Chinese five-spice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Garam masala'; MasterClass, 'What Is Garam Masala.'

question: Drug-makers scrambled for shikimic acid, the rare starting material of the flu pill Tamiflu, whenever a flu pandemic loomed. They found a rich supply hiding in the spice rack, in one of the spices ground into Chinese five-spice powder. Which spice is packed with it?
context: Chinese five-spice's showpiece is star anise — the star-shaped fruit (usually eight points) of Illicium verum, an evergreen tree native to South China and Vietnam, whose bold licorice flavor comes from a compound called anethole. That same little star is packed with shikimic acid, the starting material used to manufacture Tamiflu (oseltamivir) — so the spice in your five-spice jar has genuinely helped fight flu pandemics. Source: Britannica, 'star anise'; Wikipedia, 'Illicium verum'; Tilda, 'A Guide to Star Anise.'

question: Chinese cooks have made tofu for over 2,000 years, and it starts with a dried bean. They soak it, grind it with water and boil the mash into a creamy white milk. Which bean is tofu made from?
context: Tofu is made from the soybean and originated in China, where it has been eaten for over 2,000 years — since the Han dynasty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu.

question: A tofu maker turns a pot of creamy soy milk into a firm block by stirring in a setter that curdles its proteins, so they clump and set into a solid. A dairy maker does the very same thing to cow's milk to make which food?
context: Tofu's coagulants work just like cheesemaking: they curdle the milk's protein into soft curds and leave watery whey behind — the same idea, but starting from a plant 'milk' instead of a dairy one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11545762.

question: Nigari begins as a salty natural water: its makers pull out the table salt, let the rest dry and keep the bitter mineral that remains. A tofu maker stirs it into warm soy milk to firm it into a block. Which salty water is nigari harvested from?
context: Nigari is produced from seawater: once the sodium chloride (ordinary table salt) is removed and the water evaporated, the bitter, magnesium-rich residue left behind is nigari, which coagulates the soy milk into tofu. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu; scienceinsights.org 'What Is Nigari: Tofu Coagulant.'

question: A cook simmers soy milk gently in a wide, shallow pan and lifts something off the top with chopsticks; in Japan it is dried into golden sheets called yuba and eaten as a delicacy. The same thing forms on a mug of hot cocoa, where most people push it aside. What is that layer on the surface?
context: Heated to about 80–90°C in an open pan, soy milk forms a thin film of soy protein and oil on its surface. Skimmed off and dried, it is called yuba (湯葉) in Japanese and doufu pi (豆腐皮) in Chinese, and prized as a delicacy in its own right. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu_skin.

question: Two identical pots of soy milk curdle side by side in a tofu shop. One block comes out silky and custard-soft, so tender it slumps on the spoon; the other comes out firm enough to cube, skewer and grill. Which single step, done harder to the firm block, made the difference?
context: Firmness comes down to pressing. Silken and soft tofu is barely pressed — or not at all — so it keeps its custardy, whey-rich texture; pressing under heavier weights squeezes out more whey to make the firm and extra-firm blocks that hold up to cubing, frying, and grilling. Source: ift.org 2016 'How Tofu Is Processed.'

question: Liu An, a Han-dynasty prince who lived some 2,000 years ago, is named in Chinese tradition as the inventor of tofu: his cooks, the legend says, curdled soy milk with a mineral salt and stumbled on the creamy white block. Historians call the story a legend rather than settled fact, for one telling reason. What is that reason?
answer: No record survives from Liu An's own lifetime that mentions tofu.
choices: No record survives from Liu An's own lifetime that mentions tofu.
Soybeans had not yet spread to China during Liu An's lifetime.
Liu An himself was a character invented by much later storytellers.
Tombs far older than Liu An's have turned up tofu-pressing tools.
context: Liu An (c. 179–122 BC), Prince of Huainan and grandson of the Han founder Liu Bang, is the traditional inventor of tofu — but no reliable source from his era records it; the attribution first appears far later, about a thousand years on, in the Ming-dynasty Bencao Gangmu. One colorful telling even says his alchemists, chasing an elixir of immortality, mixed soybeans, spring water, and gypsum and made tofu by accident. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_An; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu.  (Legend.)

question: A ribeye and a chuck roast are cut from the very same cow, yet the chuck costs a fraction of the price and needs hours of slow braising to soften. What decides which cut turns out tender and which turns out tough?
answer: How hard that muscle worked while the animal was alive
choices: How hard that muscle worked while the animal was alive
How much fat the animal built up before slaughter
How long the butcher aged the meat afterward
How quickly the meat was chilled after slaughter
context: Same animal, wildly different cuts: the muscles that work hardest in life turn tough and cheap, while the ones that barely move stay tender and pricey. Workload -- not fat, breed, or aging -- sets a cut's baseline texture. Source: Iowa State University Extension AnswerLine, 'Tender vs Less Tender Cuts of Meat.'

question: Filet mignon, the priciest cut on many steakhouse menus, carries a French name that promises tenderness rather than flavor. It comes from the tenderloin, a strip of muscle that barely works on a cow. What does filet mignon mean?
context: 'Mignon' means dainty or cute, so filet mignon is the 'dainty little fillet' -- a name that promises tenderness, not flavor. Source: MasterClass, 'Beef Tenderloin vs. Filet Mignon.'  (Legend.)

question: A butcher breaking down a steer of well over 1,200 pounds takes hundreds of pounds of beef from it, yet only about a single pound of filet mignon, cut from the prized tenderloin. That scarcity helps restaurants charge so much for one small steak. Why does such a huge animal give so little?
answer: The tenderloin is just two slim muscles, among the smallest on the steer
choices: The tenderloin is just two slim muscles, among the smallest on the steer
Most of the tenderloin is trimmed away as fat and waste
The tenderloin shrinks by half the instant it hits heat
Butchers grind most of the tenderloin into cheap mince
context: Every steer has only two tenderloins -- together barely 1% of the whole carcass, about a pound of usable filet mignon. That scarcity, on top of the tenderness, is why it is the priciest everyday cut. Source: MasterClass, 'Beef Tenderloin vs. Filet Mignon'; TruBeef.  (Legend.)

question: A chuck roast stays chewy unless a cook braises it for hours, while a ribeye grills up soft in minutes, and two cuts can carry the same amount of fat and still differ in toughness. Meat scientists point to one tough, ropy protein that a hard-working muscle builds up far more of than a barely used one. Which protein is it?
context: Collagen is the tough connective protein that sheathes each muscle fiber and bundles fibers into the 'grain' you can see. The harder a muscle works, the more -- and thicker -- collagen it lays down, so workload, not fat, sets how tough a cut starts out. Source: Bailey & Light, ScienceDirect, 'The role of epimysial, perimysial and endomysial collagen...'; Frontiers in Physiology.

question: A cook braises cross-cut veal shank, a cut from a calf's lower leg so tough it is almost inedible grilled, low and slow for hours until it turns meltingly tender. Which classic Italian dish comes out of the pot?
context: Osso buco -- Italian for 'bone with a hole' -- is braised cross-cut veal or beef shank. Hours of gentle, moist heat break the shank's heavy connective tissue down, turning a rock-tough cut into silky, spoon-tender meat. Source: Nourish Food Club; S.R. Cooper Meats, 'Shin of Beef.'

question: A cow standing in a field has no collarbone, so no bone braces the front of its body. One hard-working cut carries roughly 60 percent of its weight instead, every moment it stands and walks, which is why that cut starts out among the toughest on the steer. Which cut is it?
context: With no collarbone, a cow's front end rests on its brisket -- the breast and pectoral muscles -- which bear about 60% of its standing weight. Holding that load takes huge amounts of connective tissue, so brisket is brutally tough raw and needs many hours of low, slow smoking to give in. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisket.'  (Legend.)

question: A steakhouse chef wraps a filet mignon in a strip of bacon, or drowns it in a rich peppercorn sauce, though it is the tenderest steak money can buy. Its muscle, the tenderloin, barely moves in the animal's life. What does that habit quietly admit about the filet?
answer: On its own it tastes surprisingly mild
choices: On its own it tastes surprisingly mild
On its own it is too lean to stay juicy
On its own it is dangerously easy to overcook
On its own it is simply too pricey to serve plain
context: The tenderloin barely works in life, so it develops little of the deep, beefy flavor that hard-used muscles build. It is tender but famously mild -- which is why chefs lend it flavor with bacon, butter, or sauce. Tender is not the same as tasty. Source: Wikipedia, 'Filet mignon.'

question: Chuck and shank, cuts from hard-working endurance muscles, look a deeper red than a pale, lean tenderloin and taste far beefier. Both the color and the flavor trace back to one protein packed into hard-working muscle. Which protein is it?
context: Muscles built for steady, enduring work rely on slow-twitch fibers loaded with myoglobin, the deep-red protein that stores oxygen -- and carries rich, beefy flavor. Lean, barely-worked muscle like the tenderloin holds little of it, so it looks pale and tastes flat by comparison. Source: Mason's Meats cow-anatomy guide.

question: Asked for the most flavorful bite of beef on the whole steer, many butchers skip the famous, pricey tenderloin. They point instead to a thin, heavily marbled strip of steak that does little work, nicknamed the lifter. Which prized cut is it?
context: That strip is the spinalis dorsi, better known as the ribeye cap -- the fatty crescent wrapped around the lean 'eye' of a ribeye. It rides high on the back and works little, yet carries far more marbling than the eye, making it both more tender and more flavorful than the eye -- which is why many chefs call it the tastiest single muscle on the steer. Source: MeatIdentifier/ButcherIQ; Mason's Meats cow-anatomy guide.  (Legend.)

question: Meat scientists ran a bite-force machine down the whole length of one long back muscle, rib by rib: the muscle that gives both the ribeye and the New York strip, cut only a few ribs apart and cooked by steakhouses exactly the same way. What did their map show?
answer: Tenderness rose and fell in patches down its length
choices: Tenderness rose and fell in patches down its length
Tenderness measured the same at every point down its length
Tenderness climbed steadily toward the tail end
Tenderness climbed steadily toward the shoulder end
context: Sliding a shear-force test down the muscle, researchers found distinct tender and tougher zones from one rib position to the next -- proof that even one muscle isn't uniform, because different sections flex by different amounts in life. (Which end is tenderer varies study to study, so there is no single fixed pattern.) Source: ScienceDirect, 'A mapping method for the description of Warner-Bratzler shear force gradients in beef Longissimus...'

question: Families in the mid-1900s were told to give up butter and spread margarine instead: doctors said butter carried a villain that clogged the arteries. Margarine went from cheap knock-off to the heart-healthy pick. Which part of butter did the doctors blame?
context: Butter is roughly two-thirds saturated fat, and mid-1900s heart research pinned saturated fat as the artery-clogging culprit — the verdict that transformed margarine from budget spread into a 'health food.' It is exactly that verdict the trans-fat story would later overturn. Source: medicalnewstoday.com/articles/304283.

question: A margarine factory starts with runny vegetable oil, the kind poured from a bottle, and turns it into a soft, solid fat that cooks scoop from a tub. It bubbles one particular gas through the oil under high heat and pressure until the oil sets. Which gas does it use?
context: Bubbling hydrogen through hot oil is called hydrogenation; German chemist Wilhelm Normann worked it out around 1901. Stop partway — 'partial hydrogenation' — and the oil turns semi-solid and spreadable. That very process is what creates trans fat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_fat; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8452362/.

question: A can of snow-white shortening reached American grocery shelves in June 1911: cottonseed oil made solid by Procter & Gamble, the soap company, and the first all-vegetable shortening in America. The company taught cooks to reach for it when they fried or baked, and it is still sold today. What did Procter & Gamble name it?
context: They named it Crisco — a word widely said to squeeze together 'CRYStallized Cottonseed Oil,' since it was made from cottonseed oil hardened into a solid shortening. It was the first shortening built entirely from vegetable oil, and it stormed American kitchens. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisco; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8452362/.

question: Procter & Gamble sold its new vegetable shortening by giving away free cookbooks where every recipe called for it. A whole generation learned to reach for the can instead of the old animal fat their grandmothers had baked and fried with. Which fat did the shortening push out?
context: For generations, lard — rendered pig fat — was the workhorse of American baking and frying. Crisco's free-cookbook blitz toppled it, a key moment in how industrial vegetable fat elbowed traditional animal fats out of the American kitchen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisco; smithsonianmag.com/innovation/how-crisco-made-americans-believers-industrial-food-180973845/.

question: Doctors measured what butter's fat does to the blood: it lifts the 'bad' cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), a little, and leaves the 'good' high-density lipoprotein (HDL) alone. Old margarine was made from trans fat, an artificial fat that food scientists eventually admitted was far worse for the heart than butter. What did that trans fat do to LDL and HDL?
answer: Raises bad LDL and lowers good HDL
choices: Raises bad LDL and lowers good HDL
Raises bad LDL and raises good HDL
Lowers bad LDL and lowers good HDL
Lowers bad LDL and raises good HDL
context: Trans fat is the only common fat that does both harmful things at once — raising LDL while lowering HDL — which makes it worse for your heart than the very butter it replaced. The clean proof came from a 1990 Dutch study (Mensink & Katan, NEJM): a trans-fat diet cut good HDL about 12% and raised bad LDL about 14%. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8452362/; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2374566/.

question: A shopper would expect one grocery-store ingredient to account for only a tiny sliver of a nation's heart attacks. Yet by 2006, researchers estimated that the artificial trans fat hidden in fried and packaged food was behind a large share of America's. Roughly what fraction?
context: Roughly one in five — up to about 250,000 heart attacks and 50,000 deaths a year in the U.S. were blamed on artificial trans fat (a 1994 estimate had already put it near 20,000 deaths a year). A cheap ingredient in cookies and fries was quietly among the deadliest things on the shelf. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8452362/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_fat.

question: Food companies packed fried fast food, microwave popcorn and boxed cookies with factory-hardened vegetable oil, and their reasons were honest: it was cheap, it stayed solid at room temperature, and it gave crackers a crisp snap. It also beat butter at a fourth thing the companies cared about. What was that advantage?
answer: It kept the food fresh for many months
choices: It kept the food fresh for many months
It added protein to the food
It made the food cook much faster
It kept the food from ever crumbling
context: The fourth virtue was a long shelf life: partially hydrogenated oil resisted going rancid, so cookies, crackers, and pie crust could sit for months without spoiling. Cheap, shelf-stable, and crisp, it replaced pricier lard and butter and got baked into the American diet — the trade-off that spread it everywhere before the science caught up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_fat; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8452362/.

question: A boy helping his mother with the groceries sorts them into two bins on the kitchen counter, one for food barely changed from the farm and one for food built in a factory from refined ingredients a farmer would not recognize. Which item goes in the factory bin?
choices: A fresh apple from the crate
A carton of plain whole milk
A scoop of plain rolled oats
context: This is the NOVA system, which sorts food by how much it's been industrially processed rather than by its nutrients. Group 1 is minimally processed — a fresh apple, an egg, milk, plain yogurt, oats; the top Group 4 is 'ultra-processed,' like soda, a snack cake, or a neon breakfast cereal. Source: NOVA classification (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_classification).

question: Carlos Monteiro and his colleagues in Brazil built a food-grouping system called NOVA in 2009. Under NOVA, a home-cooked beef stew and a sugary breakfast cereal fall into different groups, even when a lab finds the same sugar, fat and calories in each. What difference does NOVA care about?
answer: How much a factory reworked the food
choices: How much a factory reworked the food
How the food tastes to most people
How long the food lasts on a shelf
How much the food costs at the store
context: NOVA groups food by degree of processing, not grams of sugar or fat — which is why a plain home-cooked stew or a real loaf of bread counts only as 'processed' (Group 3), and the line into ultra-processed is crossed only by adding industrial substances a home cook would never reach for. The system was created by Brazilian researcher Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of Sao Paulo in 2009. Source: NOVA classification (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_classification).

question: Twenty adults lived on a hospital ward for a month in 2019 while Kevin Hall, of the National Institutes of Health, fed them two weeks of ultra-processed meals and two weeks of whole foods. The diets were matched for calories, sugar, fat, fiber and salt, and the volunteers could eat as much or as little as they liked. On the ultra-processed weeks, how did their eating and weight change?
answer: They ate about 500 more calories a day and gained weight
choices: They ate about 500 more calories a day and gained weight
They ate about 500 fewer calories a day and lost weight
They ate about the same and their weight held steady
They ate a little more but their weight held steady
context: Kevin Hall's team found people ate 508 more calories a day on the ultra-processed diet and gained about 2 pounds, while on the whole-food diet they lost about 2 pounds — even though both diets were rated equally tasty and matched on paper. Hall: 'This is the first study to demonstrate causality, that ultra-processed foods cause people to eat too many calories and gain weight.' Source: Hall et al. 2019, Cell Metabolism (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7946062/).

question: Cameras rolled at every meal on Kevin Hall's hospital ward at the National Institutes of Health, where volunteers ate whole foods for two weeks and ultra-processed food for two. The ultra-processed meals were soft, easy to chew and calorie-dense, and the volunteers ate them measurably faster. How could eating that fast push a person to eat more?
answer: The meal was gone before the gut's 'full' signal reached the brain
choices: The meal was gone before the gut's 'full' signal reached the brain
The fast chewing burned fewer calories, so more got stored
The quick meals emptied the stomach faster, sparking hunger
The speed sped up digestion, so calories absorbed faster
context: People ate the ultra-processed food about 17 calories per minute faster, finishing before the gut's fullness signals could catch up. Their appetite hormones shifted with the food, too: on the whole-food diet they made more of the fullness hormone PYY and less of the hunger hormone ghrelin, so the real food told the brain to stop sooner. Source: Hall et al. 2019, Cell Metabolism (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7946062/).

question: Kevin Hall and his team at the National Institutes of Health priced out the two menus from their hospital-ward study: a week of ultra-processed meals against a week of whole foods, each at 2,000 calories a day. What did they find about the ultra-processed week?
answer: It was the cheaper diet, about $45 less a week
choices: It was the cheaper diet, about $45 less a week
It was the pricier diet, about $45 more a week
It cost almost exactly the same as the whole-food diet
It was cheaper, but only by a dollar or two
context: A week of ultra-processed meals cost about $106, versus about $151 for the whole-food meals — so the food that caused weight gain was also the cheaper one. Hall noted that 'it takes more time and more money to prepare less-processed foods.' Source: Hall et al. 2019, Cell Metabolism (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7946062/).

question: Dariush Mozaffarian and Mike Gibney, two critics of the NOVA system, point to a blind spot in its 'ultra-processed' label: it files a can of soda in the same group as plain whole-grain bread and plain yogurt. They argue it sorts food by the wrong thing, not by its real health value. By what, in their view?
choices: Its calorie count and fat content
context: Critics including Mike Gibney and Dariush Mozaffarian argue that NOVA judges food by its ingredient list and formulation rather than its actual health value, which is why the blunt category can lump soda together with plain whole-grain bread and plain yogurt. The fair takeaway: the 500-calorie result is strong evidence that heavy processing can drive overeating, but 'ultra-processed' is a useful-but-imperfect guide, not a law that every packaged food is poison. Source: NOVA critique review, Cambridge (cambridge.org) + Hall et al. 2019, Cell Metabolism.

question: A diner sips dashi and tastes a deep, mouth-filling savoriness that is neither sweet, sour, salty nor bitter. Aged parmesan and cured ham share it, and cooks count it a fifth basic taste. What is it called?
context: That fifth taste is umami, a Japanese word. Sweet, sour, salty, and bitter had been the accepted list for centuries before umami joined them — the savory taste that makes food rich and 'meaty' even with no meat in it, as in a ripe tomato or a mushroom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami

question: A cook tastes a ripe tomato beside a crumb of aged parmesan. The tomato holds only a few hundred milligrams of glutamate, the savory molecule, against the cheese's thousands, yet one old method drives a tomato's several times higher. How are those tomatoes prepared?
context: Sun-drying pulls the water out of a tomato and concentrates its free glutamate several times over — the same fruit, far more savory. Aged parmesan holds well over a thousand milligrams of free glutamate per 100 g and kelp even more, while a fresh tomato holds only a couple hundred; time, drying, and aging are how cooks build umami. Source: info.newbiotic.com (glutamate content in foods); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami

question: A Japanese cook simmers kelp in water and gets a faintly savory broth; she steeps dried bonito flakes alone and gets something mild. Together the two make dashi, which tastes far more savory than either can explain on its own. What is behind the leap?
answer: The kelp's savory molecule and the fish's multiply each other's power.
choices: The kelp's savory molecule and the fish's multiply each other's power.
Long simmering boils off water and concentrates the broth.
Sea salt carried in the kelp sharpens the fish's flavor.
Fat from the fish coats the tongue and makes it linger.
context: The kelp gives glutamate; the bonito brings a SECOND savory molecule, inosinate (found in dried bonito by Ikeda's student Shintaro Kodama in 1913; a third, guanylate, was later found in dried shiitake). Together they don't just add -- the umami MULTIPLIES, so the combined broth tastes many times more savory than either ingredient alone. That multiplication is exactly why the kombu-plus-bonito pairing became the timeless classic. Source: PMC 'Umami the Fifth Basic Taste'; ramenchemistry.com 'Umami Synergy'.  (Legend.)

question: Glutamate-rich kelp and dried bonito, which brings a second savory molecule, inosinate, make the classic pair of Japanese dashi. Long before anyone knew the chemistry, cooks far from Japan hit on the same kind of pairing by taste. Which everyday Western plate marries the two?
context: A cheeseburger is a glutamate-plus-nucleotide bomb — glutamate-rich cheese meets inosinate-rich beef, and together they taste far bigger than either alone, the same synergy as kelp-and-bonito dashi, parmesan over tomato, or soy sauce on meat. Great cuisines found these pairings by taste, long before the chemistry was known. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami

question: The man who started the scare over monosodium glutamate (MSG) wrote one letter in 1968, to a medical journal, blaming it for headaches after Chinese meals and coining the phrase 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome.' Decades of fear followed. What did he later admit about his famous claim?
answer: He had no scientific evidence for it
choices: He had no scientific evidence for it
He had tested only a single patient
He had confused MSG with plain salt
He had been paid by a rival company
context: The 1968 New England Journal of Medicine letter's author admitted he had 'no scientific evidence' for the syndrome. Decades of controlled studies never substantiated it, and the U.S. FDA classifies MSG as 'generally recognized as safe' — the same category as salt and sugar. Source: sciencehistory.org (the rotten science behind the MSG scare)

question: A diner tastes beef broth and soy sauce and finds in both a deep, meaty richness that is not sweet, sour, salty or bitter. Kikunae Ikeda named that fifth taste in 1908 with a word he made up: umami. What does the word mean?
context: Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda coined 'umami' from 'umai' (delicious); it means 'deliciousness' or a pleasant savory taste — the deep note you meet in broth, aged parmesan, and a ripe tomato. Source: Wikipedia, 'Umami.'

question: Sipping a plain Japanese broth simmered from one ingredient, Kikunae Ikeda kept tasting a savory something that was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter, the same savoriness he had noticed in tomatoes and cheese while studying in Germany. He boiled down huge amounts of that ingredient to pull out the molecule behind its kick. Which ingredient was it?
context: Ikeda traced the savory taste of kombu (kelp) dashi broth to glutamic acid, glutamate, and in 1908 named the taste umami, Japanese for 'pleasant savory deliciousness.' Kelp, not the other ingredient in the stock, was his source. A year later he co-founded Ajinomoto and sold purified glutamate as MSG, and a spoon of miso or a splash of soy sauce delivers that same glutamate. (Wikipedia: 'Umami'; Umami Information Center)

question: Kikunae Ikeda named umami in 1908, but for most of the 20th century some scientists shrugged it off as just a blend of the other four tastes, sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Around 2000, more than 90 years after Ikeda, researchers showed it stands as a basic taste of its own. What did they find?
answer: a taste receptor tuned to umami alone
choices: a taste receptor tuned to umami alone
a taste bud shaped for umami alone
a nerve fiber wired for umami alone
a brain region firing for umami alone
context: Around 2000 — over 90 years after Ikeda — researchers confirmed a dedicated umami receptor on the tongue (the TAS1R1+TAS1R3 pair), proving umami is a genuine basic taste, not a blend of the other four. Source: Wikipedia, 'Umami.'

question: Left to ripen red on the vine, a rock-hard green tomato that was barely savory turns deeply savory, just as a cheese or a cured ham does as it ages for months. What change inside the food ramps up its umami as it ripens or ages?
answer: its proteins break apart into free glutamate
choices: its proteins break apart into free glutamate
its sugars rearrange into free glutamate
its fats split apart into free glutamate
its fibers dissolve into free glutamate
context: As foods ripen or age, their proteins break down into free glutamate — the umami compound. In a tomato, the amino acid GABA dominates when green, but free glutamate climbs steeply as the fruit reddens. Source: Wikipedia, 'Umami'; PubMed 19876714.

question: A food scientist measures free glutamate, the natural substance behind umami's deep savory taste, in one milk after another. Most milks taste gentle and mildly sweet, not savory, yet one kind turns out to be a natural umami bomb, carrying roughly ten times the free glutamate of any of the others. Which milk is it?
context: Human breast milk carries about 22 mg of free glutamate per 100 g — roughly ten times cow's milk — and glutamate makes up about half of its free amino acids, so a baby's very first taste of food is umami. Source: Wikipedia, 'Glutamic acid (flavor)'; umamiinfo.com.

question: An Italian grandmother wants her pot of minestrone to taste rich, deep and almost meaty without a scrap of meat. She reaches for a trick Italian home cooks have used for centuries: the hard leftover rind of a famous aged Italian cheese, saved in the freezer for this, dropped into the simmering pot to melt slowly and release its savory umami. Which cheese's rind is the traditional choice?
context: Aged parmesan is loaded with free glutamate, so a simmered rind lends deep, meaty umami to a meatless soup — the same trick as a splash of fish sauce. Source: Wikipedia, 'Umami.'

question: A cook pairs a food full of glutamate with one rich in nucleotides, and the savoriness multiplies far beyond what either brings alone, a hidden umami synergy. Plenty of savory duos look as if they should pull off the same trick. Which pairing truly does?
context: Tomato-and-parmesan, mushroom-and-meat, and ham-and-eggs each team a glutamate-rich food with a nucleotide-rich one, so the savoriness multiplies. Source: Wikipedia, 'Umami.'

question: Vanilla for ice cream and birthday cake comes from a cured seed pod, which growers like to call a bean although it is nothing of the sort. It grows on a tropical climbing vine, the only member of an enormous flower family raised as a food crop. What kind of flower is it?
context: Vanilla is the world's only orchid grown for food - of tens of thousands of orchid species, it's the single one whose fruit we eat, and one species, Vanilla planifolia, yields about 98% of it. That fragrant 'bean' is really its cured seed pod. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vanilla'; Rodelle Kitchen vanilla facts.  (Legend.)

question: Vanilla growers tend every flower and pick every pod one at a time, which makes vanilla one of the costliest spices on Earth. Only one spice costs more, gram for gram. Which spice takes the top spot?
context: Saffron is the only spice pricier than vanilla; both are back-breaking, hand-worked crops, which is why every vanilla pod has to be pollinated and picked one flower at a time. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vanilla.'  (Legend.)

question: Totonac farmers in Mexico were the first to grow vanilla, and the Aztecs who conquered them prized the black pods too, grinding them into their most treasured drink. What did the Aztecs stir vanilla into?
context: The Aztecs called vanilla 'tlilxochitl,' meaning 'black flower,' and stirred it into their cacao drink - vanilla and chocolate were partners centuries before Europe tasted either. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; Mexicolore, 'Aztec vanilla.'

question: Colonists carried vanilla vines to tropical colonies in Asia and Africa after Spanish ships brought the pods to Europe in the 1500s. For three centuries the vines climbed and bloomed there, but not one ever made a pod, for the vine's partner in pollination lived only in Mexico. What was it?
context: Only in its Mexican homeland did the wild vanilla orchid have its natural pollinator - traditionally said to be a stingless Melipona bee, though modern researchers now suspect orchid bees and treat the exact species as unsettled. The bee wasn't extinct, just local; with no pollinator abroad, the transplanted vines flowered but never fruited. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vanilla'; PLOS ONE (2024) Yucatan study.  (Legend.)

question: A worker on a vanilla plantation pollinates the flowers one at a time, racing to reach each bloom before it shuts, because a flower she misses is a pod lost for the whole year. Once a vanilla flower opens, how long does it stay open?
context: A vanilla flower opens in the morning and closes for good by that afternoon. Miss that window and the bloom is lost, so on a big plantation every single flower must be hand-pollinated the very day it opens. Source: Danwatch; American Orchid Society, 'Pollinating the Vanilla Flower.'  (Legend.)

question: Vanilla vines outside Mexico had bloomed for three centuries without setting a pod when, in 1841 on the island of Réunion, someone cracked the problem with a splinter and a thumb. Growers still use that method on every vanilla flower today. Who worked it out?
context: The boy was Edmond Albius, just twelve years old, enslaved on Reunion. His enslaver, Ferreol Bellier-Beaumont, had taught him about plants, and Edmond's quick splinter-and-thumb method - lifting the flap called the rostellum, then pressing the pollen home - is still the exact gesture used on every vanilla bean grown today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Edmond Albius'; Linnean Society.  (Legend.)

question: A baker reaches for a bottle labeled Bourbon vanilla, the fancy kind said to be the finest in the world. It has nothing to do with Kentucky whiskey: it grows on tropical plantations far out at sea, and the name honors where it is grown. What is Bourbon vanilla named after?
context: 'Bourbon vanilla' is named after Ile Bourbon, the old name of Reunion island - the same island where Edmond Albius cracked hand-pollination. Today only vanilla from Reunion, Madagascar, the Comoros, Mauritius, and the Seychelles may carry the label. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vanilla'; indian-ocean.com.

question: A visitor walks through a vanilla plantation in Madagascar, where the flowering vines climb wooden posts in the shade of taller trees. A farmer snaps a plump pod, still green, from the vine and hands it over for a good long sniff. First-time visitors are always astonished by what they smell, or don't smell. What is a fresh, uncured vanilla pod like?
context: A fresh green pod has almost no aroma at all. The famous flavor is built afterward during curing - weeks of blanching the pods in hot water, sweating them wrapped in blankets and boxes, then slowly drying them, which lets the pod's own enzymes create the flavor molecule vanillin. Source: Ndali, 'Vanilla Curing'; Wikipedia, 'Vanilla.'  (Legend.)

question: A poor harvest and a wave of thieves on the vines hit Madagascar, where most of the world's vanilla grows, in 2018, and top-grade beans climbed to around $600 a pound. Gram for gram, that made cured vanilla worth more than which precious material?
context: In 2018, a poor harvest and a wave of theft from the vines in Madagascar - the source of most of the world's vanilla - pushed top-grade beans to around $600 a pound, worth more gram for gram than silver. Source: Marketplace (2018); Tasting Table, 'Why Madagascar Vanilla Is So Expensive.'  (Legend.)

question: An ice-cream maker flavoring a cheap tub of vanilla almost never touches a real pod: it buys lab-made vanillin instead. Much of that vanillin starts from petrochemicals, but a large share is squeezed from a surprising leftover of another industry. Which waste product?
context: Around 95-99% of vanilla flavoring is synthetic vanillin - roughly 85% built from the petrochemical guaiacol and about 15% from lignin, the leftover wood-pulp waste of paper mills. Real vanilla-pod flavor is under 1% of the market, because the orchid is so costly. Source: Scientific American, 'The Problem With Vanilla'; Wikipedia, 'Vanillin.'  (Legend.)

question: Suppose you pick up a magazine that crowns this year's miracle food, salmon one year and blueberries the next, and promises it gives your body every nutrient you need. A nutrition professor at the Harvard School of Public Health says flatly that the promise can never be kept. Why does every miracle food fall short of it?
answer: No single food supplies all the many nutrients your body needs
choices: No single food supplies all the many nutrients your body needs
Your body can only absorb one vitamin at a time
Cooking destroys the nutrients in almost every food
Fresh food loses all its nutrients within a day of harvest
context: 'Superfood' is a marketing word, not a scientific one -- it fills ads and magazine covers but never appears in medical literature, and no country (US, UK, or EU) regulates what it means. The promise fails for one simple reason: no single food supplies all the dozens of nutrients the body needs, so every 'hero food' leaves a gap. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source, 'Superfoods or Superhype?' (nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/superfoods).

question: Oberon Sinclair, a New York publicist, took on a bitter leafy green as a client in the early 2010s, when most American shoppers walked past it and restaurants used it mainly as a plate garnish. A clever ad campaign rebranded it, and almost overnight the vegetable became the poster child of the superfood craze. Which green was it?
context: Kale was an obscure vegetable until a marketer branded it a 'superfood.' It really is nutritious -- but so is any leafy green, and like all of them it is high in some nutrients (vitamins A, C, K, fiber) and low in others. No lone ingredient is complete. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source, 'Superfoods or Superhype?' (nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/superfoods).

question: A cook peels a pile of deep-orange carrots and sweet potatoes. Each color in a fruit or vegetable is a different helpful plant chemical, and the orange one turns into a vitamin once it is inside the body. Which vitamin does it become?
context: Different colors deliberately deliver different nutrients: red tomatoes carry lycopene, purple and blue berries carry anthocyanins, and deep-green spinach carries folate, vitamin K, and lutein. The orange beta-carotene in carrots and sweet potatoes is the one the body turns into vitamin A. Sources: Harvard Health, 'Phytonutrients: Paint your plate with the colors of the rainbow'; Clemson HGIC, 'Phytonutrients: Why We Should Eat the Rainbow.'

question: Marketers crowned their superfoods with a lab score for antioxidants, the Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity (ORAC) score, and a bigger score meant more hype. Then in 2012 the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), which had made the ORAC list, quietly pulled it down. What reason did the agency give?
answer: The scores had no proven health value and were being misused to sell products
choices: The scores had no proven health value and were being misused to sell products
A measurement error had quietly inflated the antioxidant numbers for years
A private company had bought the exclusive rights to the whole database
Newer, trendier foods had made the old antioxidant rankings out of date
context: Superfoods really are nutritious -- the error was never the food, it was the shortcut claim. Marketers leaned on an 'antioxidant score' called ORAC to rank foods, but in 2012 the USDA withdrew the entire ORAC database, finding the values had 'no relevance' to health and had been 'routinely misused' by companies to sell products. Whole-food variety, not one hero ingredient or a pill, is what actually works. Sources: Nutraceuticals World, 'ORAC Database Withdrawn'; Wikipedia, 'Oxygen radical absorbance capacity.'

question: A peppercorn bound for a European table passed through many traders' hands on its long road from the East, and each pair of hands raised the price until it cost a small fortune. What did that price make Europeans dream of doing?
answer: Sailing directly to the spice lands themselves
choices: Sailing directly to the spice lands themselves
Forcing Venice to lower its prices by law
Growing their own pepper vines at home
Swapping pepper for cheaper local herbs
context: Each middleman — Arab caravan traders, then Venetian merchants at Alexandria — marked the price up, so a peppercorn could cost a small fortune by the time it reached a European table. That markup is exactly why Europeans dreamed of sailing straight to the source and cutting the middlemen out. Source: Wikipedia, 'Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India.'

question: Vasco da Gama of Portugal led the first European fleet ever to sail straight to the source of black pepper. In 1498, after ten more months at sea past Africa's southern tip, his ships dropped anchor at last. Where did they arrive?
answer: Calicut, on the southwest coast of India
choices: Calicut, on the southwest coast of India
Alexandria, on the coast of Egypt
context: Da Gama's fleet rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut (Kozhikode) on India's southwest coast on 20 May 1498 — the first sea route ever opened from Europe straight to the pepper source. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vasco da Gama'; missedhistory.com.

question: Storm-beaten Portuguese ships crept back into Lisbon harbor under Vasco da Gama in 1499, two years after setting out, with half his crew lost to scurvy and shipwreck on the voyage around Africa and back. The cargo in his holds was worth about 60 times what the whole expedition had cost. What was packed in those holds?
context: The pepper and cinnamon packed into da Gama's holds was reportedly worth about 60 times the whole cost of the voyage — the payoff that proved the sea road to India was worth chasing. Source: missedhistory.com; Wikipedia, 'Vasco da Gama.'

question: The Zamorin, ruler of the great pepper port Vasco da Gama's men had crossed the ocean to find, asked them in 1498 what had drawn them so far. They were the first Europeans ever to sail there, and their blunt reply named the two things they were after. What were they?
context: Asked at the Zamorin's court what they wanted, the Portuguese answered that they had come 'in search of Christians and spices' — the spice motive said right out loud. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vasco da Gama.'

question: Tiny Portugal muscled into the rich Indian Ocean spice trade after Vasco da Gama came home in 1499, and rivals from every direction, Muslim traders, the Mughals, the Dutch and later the English, wanted a share of the pepper route. How did the Portuguese hold their grip on the Indian Ocean for decades?
answer: By ringing its shores with forts and trading posts
choices: By ringing its shores with forts and trading posts
By marrying into the local royal families
By paying the Zamorin a yearly tribute
By keeping their route a secret from all rivals
context: That one voyage let tiny Portugal grab the spice trade, then ring the Indian Ocean with forts and trading posts to guard the pepper route — locking in a pepper monopoly by about 1504. Source: Wikipedia, 'Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India.'

question: Venice had grown rich for hundreds of years as Europe's main gate for spices, marking up the spices that reached it through Cairo and Alexandria before selling them on. Then Portuguese ships began landing pepper straight at Lisbon in the early 1500s, for a fraction of the price. What happened to Venice's spice empire?
answer: Its grip on the spice trade was broken for good
choices: Its grip on the spice trade was broken for good
Its merchants seized the new sea route for themselves
It struck a deal with Portugal to split the trade
It switched to selling cheaper local herbs
context: With cheap pepper arriving at Lisbon by ship, 'the fall of the Venetian monopoly on the spice trade in Europe was inevitable' — the caravan price could not compete, and Europe's whole spice map flipped. Source: Wikipedia, 'Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India'; 'Spice trade.'

question: Louis XIV, the Sun King, sat down to supper around ten each night at Versailles, his enormous palace outside Paris, in a ceremony called the grand couvert, the great table setting. What was the strange custom at the heart of it?
answer: A crowd of courtiers stood and watched the king eat.
choices: A crowd of courtiers stood and watched the king eat.
The king ate blindfolded behind a silk screen.
Servants set each dish alight before serving it.
The king shared every course with his hunting dogs.
context: The grand couvert was the king's public supper: Louis XIV (with the queen on his left) sat in a high-backed armchair while courtiers stood around and watched. Only his children and grandchildren shared the table, and he kept up this daily performance of power his whole life -- unlike the kings who came after him. Source: Chateau de Versailles, 'Royal tables'; Shannon Selin, 'Watching French Royals Eat: The Grand Couvert.'

question: Ordinary travelers passing through Versailles in the late 1600s, nobles or not, could be led into the room during Louis XIV's ten o'clock supper, the grand couvert. What was the one thing an outsider needed to get in the door?
choices: To pay a silver coin at the gate.
To have been born in France.
context: As long as you were decently dressed, you could join the crowd -- led in one door and out another, filing single-file past the king's table, though you were not allowed to stare directly at him. Source: Shannon Selin, 'Watching French Royals Eat: The Grand Couvert'; 'This is Versailles' blog, 'Dining with Royalty.'

question: Elisabeth Charlotte, Louis XIV's sister-in-law, wrote home of one supper in the 1690s at which the Sun King plowed through four plates of soup, a whole pheasant, a partridge, a big salad, ham and mutton with garlic. What did he polish off at the very end, after even the pastry and fruit?
context: The grand couvert showed off the king's famous appetite. The Princess Palatine (Elisabeth Charlotte) recorded seeing him eat four plates of soup, a whole pheasant, a partridge, a big salad, two slices of ham, mutton with jus and garlic, a plate of pastry, then fruit and hard-boiled eggs -- all at one sitting. Framed here as her eyewitness testimony. Source: Princess Palatine, quoted in Picturesque Voyages, 'Dining at Versailles.'  (Legend.)

question: Servants sprinted through Versailles with silver-covered dishes for Louis XIV's ten o'clock supper, yet the food kept reaching his table cold or lukewarm, however fast they ran. What was the built-in reason the royal kitchens could never serve the king a hot meal?
answer: The kitchens stood nearly a quarter-mile from his table.
choices: The kitchens stood nearly a quarter-mile from his table.
Each course was cooked many hours ahead of time.
The heavy silver platters drew the heat from the food.
The dishes were carried up freezing outdoor stairs.
context: The kitchens sat roughly a quarter-mile (nearly a kilometre) from the table, so covered dishes made a long, cooling procession. To fight it, the best goldsmiths were set to designing dish shapes that held heat longer, and later reigns used a rechauffoir (warming room) to reheat food just before it reached the royal table. Source: 'This is Versailles' blog, 'The Kitchens - Feeding the Court'; Picturesque Voyages, 'Dining at Versailles'; Chateau de Versailles, 'Royal tables.'

question: Jean-Baptiste de La Quintinie, Louis XIV's kitchen gardener, put asparagus and strawberries on the king's table in the dead of winter by sneaking warmth to his garden beds. Where did he get the heat to trick the plants into thinking it was spring?
answer: Fresh manure from the royal stables.
choices: Fresh manure from the royal stables.
Bonfires kept burning through the night.
Hot stones hauled up from the kitchens.
Buried pipes of warm spring water.
context: La Quintinie, director of the royal fruit and vegetable gardens, ran the Potager du Roi (built 1678-1683, about 25 acres). Besides the heat of fresh stable manure, he trapped warmth with glass bell-jars (cloches) set over plants, trained fruit trees flat as espaliers along sun-facing walls, and built a heated fig-house -- coaxing strawberries by late March and asparagus in December. Source: Wikipedia, 'Potager du roi, Versailles'; La Route des Gourmets, 'The King's Kitchen Garden.'

question: Courtiers at Versailles could not stop eating one fashionable vegetable in 1696: one court lady's letter says some, after supping at the king's own table, went home to eat more before bed, at the risk of indigestion; she called it a fashion and a passion. Which vegetable?
context: These were petits pois, the newly fashionable luxury vegetable at Versailles. A court lady's letter of 1696 -- attributed sometimes to Madame de Maintenon, sometimes to Madame de Sevigne -- wrote that 'the impatience to eat them, the pleasure of having eaten them, and the joy of eating them again' had become 'a fashion, indeed a passion.' Framed as the letter's testimony. Source: histoiresroyales.fr; Monsieur de France, 'Peas: the delight of King Louis XIV.'  (Legend.)

question: A cook in Goa, where vindaloo was born on India's west coast, will say chili is not the dish's real trademark, whatever its Western fame as one of the fieriest curries on the menu. Which taste sets a real vindaloo apart from every other curry?
context: Authentic Goan vindaloo is only moderately hot — the West rebranded it as a heat challenge, but its true signature is a sharp vinegar tang. That sourness is what makes it stand out on any curry menu. Source: grubdaily.com, 'Vindaloo: the most misunderstood curry in the West.'

question: English speakers slurred the name of a Portuguese sailors' dish, carne de vinha d'alhos, into vindaloo, a word that sounds Indian but is not. The old name lists the two things the sailors' dish was soaked in. What does it mean?
context: 'Carne de vinha d'alhos' means 'meat in wine and garlic.' English speakers slurred those Portuguese words into 'vindaloo,' which is how a Portuguese recipe ended up wearing an Indian-sounding name. Source: en.wikipedia.org, 'Vindaloo.'

question: Portuguese colonists who settled Goa, on India's west coast, in the 1500s built the first vindaloo around the meat they loved most back home. In Goa that meat set the new Christian community apart, since the Hindus and Muslims around them did not eat it. Which meat sits at the heart of a real vindaloo?
context: The original is pork. That mattered in Goa: newly converted Goan Christians could eat pork freely — a meat their Hindu and Muslim neighbours avoided — so a pork vindaloo became a distinctive badge of their community. Source: en.wikipedia.org, 'Vindaloo.'

question: Goan cooks making the Portuguese colonists' marinade found the grape wine it called for almost impossible to get, though the wine was what gave the old Portuguese recipe its bite. So they fermented a local ingredient into a tangy vinegar instead. What did they ferment?
answer: the sap of the coconut palm
choices: the sap of the coconut palm
context: Short of European wine, Goan cooks fermented the sap of the coconut palm — called 'toddy' — into a sharp local vinegar. (Historian Lizzie Collingham notes they also reached for sour tamarind.) That swap is exactly why vindaloo turned out so tangy. Source: en.wikipedia.org, 'Vindaloo,' quoting Collingham, 'Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors.'

question: A diner ordering vindaloo hears the ending of its name, aloo, which is Hindi for potato, and pictures a bowl loaded with chunks of it. Plenty of diners around the world do the same. In a classic Goan vindaloo, how much potato is there?
context: None — despite the name. The '-aloo' isn't the Hindi 'aloo' (potato) at all; it's the Portuguese 'alhos,' meaning garlic, worn smooth by English mouths. The twist runs deeper: potatoes really did reach India aboard the same Portuguese ships in the 1500s, yet they were never part of vindaloo. The potato in some modern versions was added later, by cooks who took the name literally. Source: en.wikipedia.org, 'Vindaloo'; tasteoflisboa.com.

question: A glass of wine left out on the counter for a few days draws tiny airborne microbes, which settle on its surface and feed on the alcohol, changing it one more chemical step. Soon nobody wants to drink it, because it has turned into vinegar. What has the alcohol in it become?
context: That sharp taste is acetic acid. Table vinegar is only about 4-8% acid mixed with water, which is why it's safe to splash on your food — vinegar is really just alcohol that fermented one step past the drink. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vinegar'.

question: A French cook who leaves wine standing open too long ends up with vin aigre, the two words English borrowed whole as vinegar. Vin means wine. What does aigre mean?
context: 'Vin aigre' means 'sour wine.' The name records precisely what vinegar is — wine gone tart. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vinegar'.  (Legend.)

question: A vinegar maker relies on a relay of two tiny crews. Yeast eats the fruit's sugar first and makes the alcohol of wine or cider, then hits its limit and stops. What kind of organism carries the alcohol the rest of the way into vinegar?
context: Yeast can make alcohol but not vinegar. A different microbe — acetic-acid bacteria — takes the alcohol the final step into acid. That's why wine becomes wine vinegar and cider becomes cider vinegar: the drink you start with decides the vinegar you get. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vinegar'.

question: Babylonian cooks brewed vinegar from dates, figs and beer some five thousand years ago and loved its sharp taste. It was useful at the table in another way too. What could food soaked in vinegar do?
choices: take on a smoky, grilled flavor
harden into a firm, crisp shell
context: The Babylonians used vinegar three ways at once — to flavor food, as a medicine, and, because its acid holds off rot, to preserve food. Soaking food in vinegar to make it last is the origin of pickling. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vinegar'.

question: The microbes souring a barrel of wine into vinegar do not sink and spread through the liquid the way most microbes in a ferment do. They crowd upward and gather in a living layer at the very top of the barrel. What can they get only up there?
context: This is what makes vinegar the oddball of the ferment world. Bread, wine, and sauerkraut are anaerobic — they want no air — but acetic-acid bacteria are aerobic and can only turn alcohol into acid in the presence of oxygen. Vinegar is the one ferment that has to breathe. Source: Wikipedia, 'Acetobacter'.

question: A rubbery, jelly-like raft floats on top of a barrel of wine as it turns to vinegar, woven by the microbes doing the work. It looks revolting yet is completely harmless, and old-time cooks gave it a surprising name. What do they call it?
context: The floating raft is the 'mother of vinegar' — a jelly of cellulose and living bacteria. It looks unappetizing but is harmless, and you can scoop it into a fresh bottle of wine or cider to start a whole new batch, the way bakers hand down sourdough. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mother of vinegar'.

question: In the back of the eye, the retina turns vitamin A into rhodopsin, a pigment that catches even tiny amounts of light. When a person runs low on vitamin A for months, the eyes feel it first, and one kind of sight starts to fail before the rest. Which kind of vision goes first?
answer: Seeing in dim light and darkness
choices: Seeing in dim light and darkness
context: Vitamin A is the raw material your retina turns into rhodopsin, the pigment that lets you see in near-darkness — so the first sign of running short is night blindness. Untreated, deficiency can progress to xerophthalmia, a blinding dry-eye disease and still a leading cause of childhood blindness worldwide. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source, Vitamin A; Chemistry LibreTexts, rhodopsin.

question: A cook wants to load her family's plates with vitamin A. The body cannot make it on its own, but it can build it from beta-carotene, a bright orange pigment plants make in their leaves and roots, and some vegetables are packed with it while others carry almost none. Which group of vegetables is richest in beta-carotene?
answer: Orange and dark-green ones — carrots, spinach, kale
choices: Orange and dark-green ones — carrots, spinach, kale
Pale and white ones — cauliflower, onion, potato
Red and purple ones — beetroot, red cabbage, radish
context: Carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach and kale don't hold vitamin A directly — they supply beta-carotene, which the body converts. The swap is inefficient: it takes roughly 12 micrograms of food beta-carotene to make just 1 microgram of retinol. Source: Harvard Nutrition Source, Vitamin A; Biology Insights, Beta-Carotene conversion.

question: British officials in World War II spread word that their night-flying pilots shot down enemy planes in the dark because they ate so many carrots, and kids have heard the story ever since. Suppose you grew up on it. Carrots really are rich in vitamin A, which the eye does need to see in dim light. What is the honest truth about the carrot claim?
answer: Half-true: carrots restore night vision only if you were low on vitamin A — never past normal
choices: Half-true: carrots restore night vision only if you were low on vitamin A — never past normal
Fully true: the more carrots you eat, the sharper your night vision grows, past normal
Totally false: carrots do nothing at all for your eyesight, day or night
Half-true: carrots aid only daytime color vision and do nothing for night sight
context: The 'carrots give super night vision' claim is only half-true: if you were vitamin-A deficient, carrots restore your NORMAL night sight — but once you have enough, extra carrots grant no superpower and won't beat normal human vision. Source: American Optometric Association, 'Of retinol, ruses and root veggies'; Smithsonian Magazine.
