question: John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham, a Royal Air Force night-fighter pilot, was downing German bombers in total darkness in 1940; 19 of his 20 kills came at night. British officials told the newspapers that his secret was a carrot-heavy diet sharpening his night vision. What were they really covering up with that carrot story?
answer: A secret new airborne radar that spotted enemy planes in the dark
choices: A secret new airborne radar that spotted enemy planes in the dark
A batch of experimental night-vision goggles issued to top aces
The fact that ground spotters, not the pilots, aimed the guns
A new engine that let his fighter climb above the bombers
context: It was WWII British propaganda. In 1940 RAF night-fighter ace John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham was racking up night kills, and the government credited his carrot-heavy diet to hide the real reason: secret onboard Airborne Interception (A.I.) radar. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Carrots Can't Help You See in the Dark'; explorethearchive.com.

question: Suppose you ate huge helpings of carrots and sweet potatoes, far more than anyone needs. Their orange beta-carotene will never overdose anyone on vitamin A, yet one harmless, reversible thing would happen to you. What would it be?
answer: Your skin takes on a yellow-orange tint
choices: Your skin takes on a yellow-orange tint
The whites of your eyes turn yellow
Your tears and sweat run faintly orange
Your fingertips go numb for a day
context: This harmless, reversible tint is called carotenemia — leftover orange pigment building up in the skin. Because plant beta-carotene is self-limiting, you can't actually overdose on vitamin A from veg. Unlike jaundice, carotenemia does NOT color the whites of the eyes. Source: Cleveland Clinic; DermNet NZ, carotenoderma.

question: Arctic explorers learned the hard way that the ready-made vitamin A in animal liver has no safety cap: polar bear and seal livers are so packed with it that a single meal can poison an adult. First come pounding headaches and heavy sleepiness. Then, most alarming of all, what happens to the victims?
answer: Their skin peels off in sheets
choices: Their skin peels off in sheets
Their teeth loosen and fall out
context: Animal vitamin A (retinol) isn't self-capped the way plant beta-carotene is, so certain Arctic livers are simply too rich to eat — an estimated 500 g of polar-bear liver is an acutely toxic dose. Source: Wikipedia, Hypervitaminosis A; McGill OSS, polar bear liver.

question: Gerrit de Veer, a Dutch explorer iced in for the winter of 1597, wrote that his men fell gravely ill after eating polar-bear liver, so loaded with vitamin A that about a pound can poison a person. One northern people had shunned polar-bear liver, and bearded-seal liver too, for countless generations. Which people had known to avoid it all along?
context: The danger of Arctic liver was ancient knowledge to the Inuit, who refuse the liver of polar bears and bearded seals. Gerrit de Veer, wintering on Nova Zembla in 1597, wrote that during his men's recovery their skin peeled off dramatically. Source: Wikipedia, Hypervitaminosis A (de Veer, 1597); Science History Institute, 'Death by Nutrition'.

question: A polar bear spends its whole life gorging on seal, rich in vitamin A, and carries inside itself a liver so loaded with the vitamin that a few hundred grams of it could kill a grown person. Yet the bear itself stays unharmed. How does it get away with it?
answer: Its liver cells evolved to tolerate huge retinol loads
choices: Its liver cells evolved to tolerate huge retinol loads
It sheds the extra vitamin A through its dense fur
Its stomach breaks the vitamin down before it's absorbed
It fasts through summer to let its body clear the excess
context: Polar bears have evolved liver cells that tolerate enormous retinol loads — a side effect of their extremely high-fat seal diet. The very trait that makes their liver deadly to a starving explorer leaves the bear unharmed. Source: McGill OSS, polar bear liver; A-Z Animals, 'The Toxic Vitamin Inside Polar Bear Livers'.

question: Salt beef and dry biscuit fed sailors for months at sea, and on that diet a strange rot called scurvy set in. Gums swelled, blackened and bled until teeth dropped out, and wounds healed years before tore open again. One cheap food reliably cured it. Which food?
context: The disease is scurvy, and its eeriest sign is real: without the missing nutrient the body can't hold old scars together, so long-healed wounds and even old bone fractures split open again. The cure was ordinary fresh citrus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind.

question: A cook slices an orange, the fruit most people think of first for vitamin C, the nutrient scurvy patients lack. Ounce for ounce, though, one everyday raw vegetable carries more than twice as much. Which vegetable beats the orange?
context: A raw red bell pepper holds about 128 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, more than double an orange's 53. Broccoli (about 90 mg) and blackcurrants (about 200 mg, the richest common source) also beat citrus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C.

question: The Royal Navy issued its sailors a daily ration from 1795 on, and scurvy nearly disappeared from British ships. Rival crews mocked the habit with a nickname that stuck to British seamen for good. What did they call a British sailor?
context: 'Limey' is short for 'lime-juicer.' From 1795 the Navy issued a daily citrus-juice ration — lemon first — after HMS Suffolk reached India in four months with no scurvy; later the juice was lime, and 'limey' stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limey; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy.

question: Sailors on long voyages lost their teeth and bled from the gums as scurvy took hold, for lack of one substance found in fresh food. Chemists who isolated it in the 1930s named it ascorbic acid, building the word from Latin. What does ascorbic mean?
choices: for the surgeon who found it
from the ships that carried it
context: 'Ascorbic' comes from a- ('no' or 'against') plus the Latin scorbutus ('scurvy'), so ascorbic acid literally means 'anti-scurvy.' The vitamin is named after the very disease it defeats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C.

question: James Lind, surgeon of HMS Salisbury, tested six remedies on twelve sailors sick with scurvy in 1747, a rot that otherwise took months to kill. He tried cider, vinegar, seawater, a spiced paste and a mouthful of acid, and gave one pair fresh fruit every day. How fast did the fruit work?
answer: one man was back on duty in six days
choices: one man was back on duty within a day
one man was back on duty in six days
one man was back on duty in six weeks
one man was back on duty after six months
context: The two men given two oranges and a lemon a day recovered — one of them fit for duty within six days, against a disease that otherwise took months to kill. By comparing remedies side by side on matched patients, Lind had run one of medicine's first controlled clinical trials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind.

question: Mediterranean lemons went into the British sailor's daily rum ration until scurvy all but vanished from the Royal Navy. Then the Navy switched to cheaper limes from its West Indian colonies, sure it was the same cure by another name, and slowly scurvy crept back. What was wrong with the lime?
answer: it held only half a lemon's vitamin C
choices: it held only half a lemon's vitamin C
it held its vitamin C in the rind, not the juice
it held a form of vitamin C the body ignored
it held vitamin C that faded within days of picking
context: West Indian limes carry only about half the vitamin C of Mediterranean lemons — and pumping the juice through copper tubing and leaving it open to the air destroyed much of what little remained. The Navy had quietly gutted its own cure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limey.

question: The crew of an old wooden sailing ship and the ship's dog ate the same salted pork and hardtack for months at sea, without a scrap of fresh fruit. The sailors started losing teeth and bleeding from the gums, the signs of scurvy, a lack of vitamin C, while the dog stayed perfectly healthy. Why did the dog need no fruit?
answer: its liver makes its own vitamin C
choices: its liver makes its own vitamin C
its thick fur locks vitamin C in
it draws vitamin C from seawater
it needs no vitamin C to live
context: Most mammals build their own vitamin C in the liver, but humans — along with other primates and guinea pigs — carry a broken copy of the final gene (called GULO), so we must eat it or sicken. A dog or cat simply makes its own. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-gulonolactone_oxidase.

question: Fresh fruit rotted on long voyages, so James Lind, sure that it beat scurvy, strained the juice, boiled it down to a thick syrup he called rob and sealed it in casks for the fleet. To his bafflement, the rob barely worked. Which step had wrecked his cure?
answer: boiling the juice down destroyed its vitamin C
choices: boiling the juice down destroyed its vitamin C
straining the juice left the vitamin C in the pulp
sealing the casks let the vitamin C settle out
months at sea drained the vitamin C from the casks
context: Lind never knew vitamin C existed — it wasn't isolated until long after his death. He only knew citrus worked, and vitamin C is fragile to heat, so boiling the juice into 'rob' wrecked the very thing that made it work, which helped his cure fall into doubt for years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind.

question: Albert Szent-Györgyi, a Hungarian scientist, pinned down the substance in fresh food that defeats scurvy between 1928 and 1933, nearly two centuries after Lind's shipboard trial. Vitamin C then claimed a first that no other vitamin could match. Which first?
answer: the first vitamin ever made in a lab
choices: the first vitamin ever made in a lab
the first vitamin ever found in fruit
the first vitamin ever proven to cure a disease
the first vitamin ever sold as a pill
context: The scientist was Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, who isolated vitamin C between 1928 and 1933 — the first vitamin ever to be chemically produced in a lab. He won the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine partly for the discovery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C.

question: A child who plays outside in strong summer sun makes vitamin D without eating a bite of it, the only vitamin the body can make on its own. That is why doctors call it the sunshine vitamin. Which part of the body makes it?
context: Vitamin D is the 'sunshine vitamin' because your skin manufactures it when UVB sunlight strikes it — the one vitamin your body can make itself, so unlike every other vitamin you don't strictly need it from food. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_D); PMC9919777.

question: A cook shopping on a short, cloudy winter day, when the sun is too weak for the body to make much vitamin D, wants to put some on the plate instead. Most breakfasts hold almost none. Which everyday food is by far the richest natural source?
answer: Oily fish like salmon and mackerel
choices: Oily fish like salmon and mackerel
Leafy greens like spinach and kale
Citrus fruits like oranges and lemons
Whole grains like oats and brown rice
context: The best natural food sources of vitamin D are fatty fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines and herring. A single serving of salmon carries roughly 570-800 IU, more than a full day's supply. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_D); Wikipedia (sockeye salmon ~570 IU per 3 oz).

question: Mothers in Britain and America lined their children up each morning for one dreaded, smelly spoonful, well into the 1950s. Doctors said it kept young bones strong and warded off rickets, a disease of vitamin D shortage. What did the spoon hold?
choices: A spoon of honey and vinegar
context: Cod liver oil — pressed from fish livers and loaded with vitamin D (and vitamin A) — is one of the richest sources known, about 10,000 IU per 100 g (~450 IU per teaspoon), and children were dosed with it well into the 1950s. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_D); Wikipedia.

question: American health officials had extra vitamin D added in the 1930s to one drink that most children already had every single day. Within a few years rickets, the soft-bone disease, dropped steeply, even in the cold cities of the north where winter sun was scarce. Which everyday drink was it?
context: Vitamin D is so scarce in ordinary food that milk is deliberately fortified with it — roughly 100-120 IU per cup — and milk fortification in the 1930s all but wiped out rickets in industrial nations within a few years. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_D); PMC9919777.

question: A doctor watching a toddler learn to walk could once spot rickets at a glance, the disease of children short of vitamin D, whose bones never harden properly. One classic deformity gave it away. What does rickets do to the legs?
answer: Bows them outward into curved legs
choices: Bows them outward into curved legs
Twists the feet to point backward
Leaves one far shorter than the other
context: Too little vitamin D in childhood causes rickets: without it the body can't absorb the calcium needed to harden bone, so the soft bones bow outward under the child's own weight — the classic bowed legs. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Vitamin_D); Medscape (985510-overview).

question: In the crowded factory cities of 1800s Britain, so many slum kids came down with rickets that people called it 'the English disease.' Kids on country farms were spared. What about city life kept these kids from getting vitamin D?
answer: Coal smoke and packed tenements blocked out the sun
choices: Coal smoke and packed tenements blocked out the sun
Filthy slum water spread the disease between them
The factory diet gave them no fish or milk
Endless work shifts left them too weak to grow
context: Rickets exploded in the smoky, sunless industrial cities of 1800s Britain — coal smog and tall tenements kept sunlight off slum children, so their bodies could not make vitamin D. So common in the UK, it became known as 'the English disease,' and is often called the first childhood disease caused by environmental pollution. Source: PMC5133108 ('English Disease: Historical Notes on Rickets'); Physiological Society.

question: Through months of Arctic winter the sun sat too low for the Inuit to make vitamin D from it, yet, bundled in fur through the long darkness, they never got rickets. Where did their vitamin D come from?
answer: From fatty fish, seal and whale blubber
choices: From fatty fish, seal and whale blubber
From berries gathered in the short summer
From roots and greens stored for winter
From grain and dairy traded from the south
context: Traditional Arctic Inuit beat the no-sun problem with food, not sunlight — vitamin D from fatty fish, seal liver, fish-egg yolks, and seal, walrus and whale blubber. Seal fat alone packs about 75 mcg (~3,000 IU) of vitamin D per 100 g. Source: The Globe and Mail (Arctic Inuit diet); PMC9573337 ('Vitamin D Scarcity: Arctic and Tropical Peoples').

question: Four dishes sit on a supper table, and one is loaded with vitamin K1, a vitamin plants make: about 530 micrograms in a half-cup, several times what a body needs in a day. The other three carry almost none. Which dish is the K1 giant?
answer: A pot of braised collard greens
choices: A pot of braised collard greens
A bowl of steamed white rice
A plate of grilled chicken breast
A dish of sliced red apple
context: The everyday form is vitamin K1, called phylloquinone, and it is manufactured in the leaves' photosynthetic tissue — the same green machinery that turns sunlight into sugar. So the vitamin rides along with the leaf pile: cooked collard greens pack about 530 micrograms per half-cup, boiled spinach about 445, and kale is right behind; broccoli is loaded too. Eat a salad or a pot of braised greens and you are eating the plant's solar panels, vitamin included. There is a second form, K2, and it comes from a completely different kind of food. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K

question: Henrik Dam, a Danish biochemist, tracked down a new vitamin in the 1930s. By then vitamins A, B, C, D and E had their letters, given roughly in the order they were found, but Dam jumped ahead to K. He chose the letter not for its place in the alphabet but for the vitamin's job, spelled the Danish way. What is the job?
answer: Clotting blood so a cut stops bleeding
choices: Clotting blood so a cut stops bleeding
Carrying oxygen around in red blood cells
context: Dam's clue came from his chickens: fed a fat-free diet, they developed hemorrhages and bled uncontrollably, and feeding them purified cholesterol did not fix it — something hidden was missing. His key paper appeared in 1935, and a German journal labeled the new substance 'Koagulationsvitamin' — koagulation being the Danish and German spelling of coagulation, i.e. blood clotting. So the letter names the JOB, not the sequence. Without vitamin K, blood cannot form the clots that stop bleeding. Dam shared the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with American biochemist Edward Adelbert Doisy, who worked independently in St. Louis and figured out vitamin K's chemical structure. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Dam ; https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1943/summary/

question: Bacteria at work inside one traditional Japanese dish, eaten for about a thousand years, pack it with vitamin K2. Most fermented and animal foods carry only a modest dose of this form of the vitamin, but this dish holds roughly 1,100 micrograms per 100 grams, ten times more than any other common food. Which dish is it?
context: Natto is sticky and stringy — pull a spoonful and it trails threads. About 90% of its K2 is the long-lasting MK-7 form, and the bacterium Bacillus subtilis (natto) manufactures it during fermentation. The traditional method is a beautiful trick: wrap boiled soybeans in rice straw and leave them warm — the straw itself already carries the bacteria that ferment the beans. MK-7 also sticks around in the body far longer than the K1 you get from greens: studies show roughly 2.5x higher availability over 24 hours and up to about 6x over 96 hours, thanks to a much longer half-life. The other K2 foods are real but smaller: aged cheese, egg yolk (~32 mcg per 100g), butter, goose and organ meat. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16232939/ ; https://nattomk7.com/about-vitamin-k/what-is-natto/

question: Dutch researchers followed about 4,800 adults over 55 for roughly a decade. Those who ate the most vitamin K2, the form in fermented and animal foods, were far less likely to die of heart disease, while K1, the form from plant foods, showed no such link. The researchers stress it is an association, not proof: promising, not settled. What do they propose K2 does with calcium?
answer: Switches on proteins that lock calcium into bone and keep it out of artery walls
choices: Switches on proteins that lock calcium into bone and keep it out of artery walls
Switches on proteins that pull calcium out of artery walls and back into the blood
Switches on proteins that push extra calcium into urine and out of the body
Switches on proteins that catch calcium in the gut and pass it out in stool
context: The proposed mechanism makes K2 a kind of traffic cop for calcium: it switches on osteocalcin, which locks calcium into bone and teeth, and matrix Gla protein, which keeps calcium OUT of artery walls — steering the same mineral toward one destination and away from the other. The study is the Rotterdam Study (Geleijnse et al., Journal of Nutrition, 2004): the highest dietary K2/menaquinone intake was associated with roughly 50% less severe aortic calcification and coronary-heart-disease death, and about 25% lower all-cause mortality, while K1 showed no such link — which is what suggests the effect is K2-specific. Be careful with it: this is observational, emerging science. It shows an association in a population, not proof of cause in you. It is one honest reason traditional fermented and animal foods get defended, not a settled verdict. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K ; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022316623028961

question: Fancy steakhouses toss the word 'wagyu' around as if it named some exotic recipe. Split in two, 'wa' and 'gyu', it turns out to be a plain description of the animal the beef comes from. What does the name actually say?
context: 'Wa' means Japanese and 'gyu' means cattle, so wagyu is simply 'Japanese cattle.' It's a group name covering four Japanese breeds — but one, the Japanese Black, does nearly all the heavy marbling and makes up over 90% of Japan's wagyu. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagyu

question: Ordinary steak fat stays solid at room temperature and needs a hot pan to melt, but wagyu fat gives way at a startlingly low warmth. Suppose you warm a slice of each: about how warm must the wagyu get before its fat starts to melt?
answer: roughly the warmth of your own body
choices: roughly the warmth of your own body
roughly the chill of a spring morning
roughly the warmth of a summer room
roughly the heat of a very hot bath
context: It's real, not just hype: wagyu's intramuscular fat can begin softening below 37°C — human body temperature — which is why a slice really can seem to 'melt in your mouth,' while ordinary beef fat stays firm until far hotter. Scientists even showed the low melt is inherited: in one sire study, which bull fathered a calf decided whether its fat melted this low. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagyu; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29201894/

question: A butcher sets a slab of wagyu beside an ordinary steak, and their fats are built from different molecules. Ordinary beef fat is packed with the hard, saturated kind, but wagyu's fat is dominated by a softer one, the same molecule that makes up most of one common kitchen oil. Which oil?
context: The soft fat is called monounsaturated fat, and its main ingredient — oleic acid — is the very same fat that keeps olive oil liquid. Wagyu fat is roughly 45–55% oleic acid, versus about 30% in ordinary beef, which also gives it that buttery, faintly sweet richness. Soft fats like this melt at lower temperatures than the hard, saturated fat in normal beef. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagyu; secondcityprime.com

question: A burger bar far from Japan sells pricey 'Kobe' sliders. In Japan the word is fiercely protected by law: a carcass earns it only after strict inspection and a chrysanthemum stamp, and just a few thousand cattle a year pass. Legally, what does calling beef 'Kobe' certify above all?
answer: that it came from one specific region of Japan
choices: that it came from one specific region of Japan
that it reached the very highest marbling grade
that the cattle were massaged and fed beer
that it was aged to a set standard of tenderness
context: 'Kobe' is a protected place-name, like Champagne — not a quality grade. To be sold legally as Kobe, beef must come from the Tajima bloodline of Japanese Black cattle, born and raised in Japan's Hyogo prefecture, and pass strict marbling and texture tests, certified with a chrysanthemum stamp. Only about 3,000 cattle a year qualify, and true Kobe wasn't even exported from Japan until 2012 — so most 'Kobe beef' abroad is really just 'Kobe-style.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobe_beef; kobe-niku.jp

question: Suppose you are making dinner: you rinse some rice, pet the dog, cut up a slippery uncooked chicken breast, then slice tomatoes for a salad nobody will cook. Any of these might send you to the sink, but food-safety experts call one moment the most important. Which moment?
answer: Right after the raw chicken, just before the tomatoes
choices: Right after the raw chicken, just before the tomatoes
Right after petting the dog, before touching food
The moment you first walk into the kitchen
Once dinner is over and you start the dishes
context: Raw meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs can spread germs to food that won't be cooked again to kill them, and your hands are the ferry that carries them. So the most critical wash is right after handling the raw chicken and before you touch the ready-to-eat salad. Source: CDC 'Handwashing Facts' / Clean Hands.

question: A cook cuts up a raw chicken breast on her cutting board, and afterward her hands look completely clean: no blood, no smell, nothing to see. Yet the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention still tells her to scrub with soap and water before she touches anything else. What can raw poultry leave on her fingers even when they look spotless?
answer: Traces of the bird's own feces
choices: Traces of the bird's own feces
Traces of the bird's egg white
Traces of the bird's feather dust
Traces of the bird's bone powder
context: Raw meat and poultry can carry invisible amounts of animal feces, so germs end up on your hands even when they look clean, which is exactly why the CDC says to wash after handling uncooked meat, chicken, seafood, flour, or eggs. Source: CDC 'Handwashing Facts' / Clean Hands.

question: Suppose you keep hand sanitizer and plain soap by the kitchen sink. Sanitizer kills germs on the skin; soap barely kills a thing, yet experts want you to use the soap. What does the soap mainly do to the germs on your hands?
answer: Lifts them off your skin so the rinse carries them away
choices: Lifts them off your skin so the rinse carries them away
Smothers them in foam so the bubbles carry them away
Cracks their shells so the rinse flushes them away
Slicks your skin so the germs slide off in the rinse
context: Soap's real job isn't killing. Its surfactants 'lift soil and microbes from skin,' in the CDC's own words, and then the water rinses them away. That is why washing works even against germs sanitizer can't kill. Source: CDC 'Handwashing Facts' / Clean Hands.

question: A cook splashes plain water on greasy hands and it just beads off, since oil and water will not mix. Add soap, and the water suddenly rinses the grease away cleanly, along with the germs trapped in it. How does a single soap molecule pull that off?
answer: It grabs the grease with one end and water with the other
choices: It grabs the grease with one end and water with the other
It heats the grease until it melts into the water
It chops the grease into bits too small to see
It turns the grease into a gas that floats away
context: A soap molecule is two-ended: a water-repelling tail that buries into grease and germs, and a water-loving head that faces the water. The tail grabs the grease, the head grabs the rinse, and the whole clump washes off your skin. Source: Northeastern Global News (chemistry professor Thomas Gilbert); Soaps & Scents 'Science of Lathering'.

question: Suppose you wash your hands for the full 20 seconds the rule asks, humming 'Happy Birthday' twice through, instead of a quick two-second splash. The splash still coats your hands in soap, yet it barely dents the germs. What is it about the longer wash that gets hands clean?
answer: The scrubbing friction is what pries the germs loose
choices: The scrubbing friction is what pries the germs loose
The soap has to soak deep into your skin first
The water has to heat up enough to kill the germs
The bubbles must dry before they can trap anything
context: Those seconds do two jobs: the soap needs time to surround the grease into tiny rinse-away spheres, and your scrubbing friction physically pries the germs loose. A 2-second splash simply can't remove as many, and the CDC notes people also scrub more thoroughly when they use soap. Source: CDC 'Handwashing Facts'; Northeastern Global News.

question: Stomach flu sweeps through a cruise ship, and the germ behind it shrugs off the alcohol in hand sanitizer, so only soap and water reliably get it off a passenger's hands. That is one reason the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention calls sanitizer only a backup for a good wash. Which germ is it?
context: Norovirus is 'non-enveloped': it has no fragile fatty coat, just a tough protein shell that alcohol can't break through, so sanitizer fails. Soap and water win because they physically wash the virus away instead of trying to kill it (the same is true for the germs Cryptosporidium and C. difficile). That is also why sanitizer is only a backup, it doesn't remove grease, dirt, or germs it can't kill, so use it only when soap and water aren't available. Source: CDC 'Hand Sanitizer Facts'; Infection Control Today.

question: Weston Price, an American dentist, traveled the world in the 1930s seeking peoples whose teeth stayed healthy without modern dental care. In the Lötschental valley of the Swiss Alps he met children who had never held a toothbrush, yet he found almost no cavities among them. Besides dark rye sourdough, what was at the heart of their diet?
answer: Raw milk, cheese, and yellow butter
choices: Raw milk, cheese, and yellow butter
Goat cheese, dried mutton, and lard
context: In the Loetschental Valley, families lived on dark rye sourdough, raw milk and cheese, and thick deep-yellow butter from cows grazing spring alpine grass — and Price recorded only about 0.3 cavities per person, despite the children never brushing. Price studied other healthy peoples too, each thriving on its own native foods: Scotland's Gaelic islanders on oatcakes and seafood, Africa's cattle-herding Masai on milk, meat, and blood, and the Arctic Eskimos on fish, seal meat, and whale blubber. Source: Weston A. Price Foundation, 'A Visit to Switzerland's Loetschental.'  (Legend.)

question: Deep golden-yellow butter caught Weston Price's eye, but he noticed it was not golden all year. Its color, and the nutrient Price valued in it, could swing as much as fiftyfold with what the cows ate. Which pasture gave the richest, most golden butter?
choices: Lush clover pasture of high summer
Fresh green regrowth of autumn rain
Damp shaded grass of valley floors
context: The golden color was the tell. Price found the level of his mystery nutrient in butterfat varied up to fifty-fold with how fast the grass was growing and how mineral-rich the soil was — the richest, most golden butter came from cows on rapidly growing green spring pasture. Source: Weston A. Price Foundation, 'On the Trail of the Elusive X-Factor.'

question: In nearly every healthy people he visited, Weston Price met the same custom: a few foods were held almost sacred and kept back for expectant mothers and growing children. He measured them as carrying up to ten times the nutrients of everyday food. What sort of foods were they?
answer: Organ meats, fish eggs, and shellfish
choices: Organ meats, fish eggs, and shellfish
Lean muscle meat, tallow, and gelatin
Fresh blood, bone marrow, and tripe
Aged cheese, dried fish, and lard
context: The 'sacred foods' were animal foods rich in fat-soluble vitamins — organ meats, fish eggs (roe), shellfish, fish liver oils, and rich butter from grass-fed cows; it was those fat-soluble vitamins that Price measured at up to ten times the level of everyday food. Many groups set them aside deliberately for pregnant and nursing mothers and for young couples before marriage — a kind of 'pre-conception nutrition,' generations before science named the vitamins involved. Source: Weston A. Price Foundation, 'Weston A. Price, DDS.'

question: Gaelic islanders on Scotland's storm-battered Isle of Lewis kept famously strong teeth on a diet of oatcakes and seafood, cod and other fish pulled from the cold Atlantic. One unusual dish was saved as a special food to help their children grow. What was it?
context: On the Isle of Lewis, fish heads stuffed with oats were considered a prized dish for growing children — pairing oats with the fat-soluble vitamins concentrated in the fish. When bakeries and shops brought in white bread and jam, the islanders' famously good teeth began to rot. Source: Weston A. Price Foundation, 'Weston A. Price, DDS.'

question: Weston Price could never say what the mystery factor in his golden butter was, so he named it 'Activator X,' and for more than sixty years no one else could say either. In 2007 Chris Masterjohn, writing for the Weston A. Price Foundation, concluded he had found it, though that answer is the Foundation's, not settled science. Which vitamin did he name?
context: Writing for the Weston A. Price Foundation in 2007, researcher Chris Masterjohn concluded that Activator X was vitamin K2 — specifically the animal form MK-4 — in an article titled 'On the Trail of the Elusive X-Factor: A Sixty-Two-Year-Old Mystery Finally Solved.' K2 works alongside vitamins A and D, switching on proteins that steer calcium into bones and teeth and away from the arteries. This identification is the Foundation's, and is not universally settled science. Source: Weston A. Price Foundation, 'On the Trail of the Elusive X-Factor.'  (Legend.)

question: Sally Fallon wrote a bestselling cookbook, Nourishing Traditions, and with it and the Weston A. Price Foundation, today's traditional-foods movement was launched in 1999 on the strength of Price's findings. What style of eating does the movement champion?
answer: Whole-fat dairy, bone broth, and fermented foods
choices: Whole-fat dairy, bone broth, and fermented foods
Cured meats, sourdough bread, and olive oil
Grass-fed steak, tallow, and pickled eggs
Raw juices, sprouted nuts, and sea vegetables
context: In 1999 Sally Fallon Morell and nutritionist Mary Enig founded the Weston A. Price Foundation. Fallon's cookbook 'Nourishing Traditions' (1996, over 750,000 copies sold) champions whole-fat dairy, bone broth, organ meats, and lacto-fermented foods like sauerkraut, natto, and yogurt — plus grains that are soaked or soured before cooking, the way Price's healthy peoples prepared them. How solid is the science underneath it? Price's own evidence was observational travel fieldwork from short visits, not controlled trials: a 1981 review by William Jarvis in Nutrition Today called it a classic 'myth of the healthy savage,' and a JAMA review judged Price 'observant but not wholly unbiased' and 'evangelistic rather than scientific.' Yet his core insight — that whole traditional foods beat a diet of white flour and sugar — is widely accepted today. The broader disease claims remain debated, and no standardized 'Weston Price diet' has ever been tested in a randomized trial. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Weston A. Price Foundation'; Wikipedia, 'Weston A. Price.'

question: A boy bakes a cake but leaves one everyday ingredient out, and the oven gives him a dry heap that crumbles at a touch. That ingredient is the batter's glue: it firms up in the heat and holds everything together. Which ingredient is it?
context: Raw egg proteins are tightly coiled chains; in the oven's heat they unwind (denature) and link into a three-dimensional web that traps water and sets firm. That coagulated protein net is what locks the loose flour, sugar and butter together, so a cake holds its shape instead of crumbling apart. Source: Baking Sense — baking-sense.com/baking-school/baking-science/ingredients/eggs/

question: Eggs crack into a bowl for a pound cake: mostly clear, runny white around a small golden yolk, which holds nearly all of the egg's fat. The baker beats a batch of yolks into the batter. What does all their fat do to the crumb?
answer: Coats the flour and holds in moisture, so the crumb turns tender and rich.
choices: Coats the flour and holds in moisture, so the crumb turns tender and rich.
Weighs the batter down, so the crumb turns dense and gummy.
Coats the flour and blocks moisture, so the crumb turns dry and crumbly.
Toughens the batter, so the crumb turns firm and chewy.
context: The yolk is the fatty half of the egg — about a third of the whole egg's weight, and by composition roughly half water, a third fat and the rest protein, so nearly a third of the yolk is pure fat. That fat coats the flour and holds in moisture, giving a tender, rich crumb — which is why yolk-heavy bakes like pound cake and custard taste so much richer than a white-only cake. Source: Baking Sense; yolk composition per PMC — pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9114219/

question: A pound cake comes out of the oven with a crumb that glows gold, a color that comes straight from the egg yolks in the batter. Yet the hen that laid each egg cannot make that yellow herself. Where does the yolk's rich gold come from?
answer: Pigments in the corn and marigold she eats.
choices: Pigments in the corn and marigold she eats.
The particular breed of hen that laid it.
How fresh the egg is when it is cracked.
Sunlight warming the shell in the nest.
context: A yolk's golden color comes from carotenoid pigments — the xanthophylls lutein and zeaxanthin. A hen can't make them herself; she absorbs them from feed like corn, alfalfa and marigold and stores them in the yolk, and those pigments carry straight into the batter to give a rich yellow-gold crumb. Source: ScienceDirect — egg-yolk-color; EW Nutrition — natural pigmentation.

question: Harry Baker, an insurance salesman in Los Angeles, baked his chiffon cake for Hollywood stars at the Brown Derby and told no one his method for twenty years. Then, in the 1940s, he sold the recipe to General Mills. His trick, for a cake lighter and moister than any butter cake, was to swap the butter for something cakes had never used. What did he use instead?
context: Harry Baker invented the chiffon cake in 1927 and guarded the recipe for two decades before selling it to General Mills, which released it as a Betty Crocker recipe in 1948. His breakthrough was swapping butter for vegetable oil, which stays liquid even when cold, giving a cake that is both airy and moist. Source: What's Cooking America — whatscookingamerica.net chiffon-cake history; Seattle Times.

question: In a hot pan, a plain beaten egg scrambles firm almost at once. A pastry cook stirs the same egg into milk and sugar for a custard, and now it refuses to thicken until it is heated far hotter and more slowly, which keeps the baked custard silky instead of rubbery. Which ingredient makes the egg set at a higher temperature?
context: Sugar raises the temperature an egg needs to set, while acid lowers it. A plain egg white coagulates at about 144-149°F, but an egg-milk-sugar custard won't thicken until roughly 176-185°F — hotter than a plain egg. Bakers use this to keep custards tender and smooth rather than rubbery. Source: American Egg Board — coagulation/thickening; opentextbc.ca modern pastry.

question: A baker follows a cake recipe's fussiest instruction: she cracks each egg over two bowls, the yolk into one and the white into the other. She beats the two apart and only then folds them back together, though whole eggs would be far easier. Why does she bother splitting each egg in two?
answer: The white and yolk do opposite jobs, so beating them apart captures both airy lift and rich fat.
choices: The white and yolk do opposite jobs, so beating them apart captures both airy lift and rich fat.
The white and yolk clash in flavor, so beating them apart keeps the cake from tasting too eggy.
The white and yolk cook at different speeds, so beating them apart bakes the crumb more evenly.
The white and yolk each weigh the same, so beating them apart makes the batter easier to measure.
context: Whites and yolks pull in opposite directions: the white is nearly fat-free structure that whips into an airy foam for lift, while the yolk is fat, richness and moisture. Split them and a baker gets both at once — airy whipped whites folded into rich yolk batter — which is exactly why a chiffon or sponge recipe tells you to 'separate the eggs.' Source: Baking Sense — baking-sense.com/baking-school/baking-science/ingredients/eggs/

question: A cook tips fresh vegetables into a pot of boiling water for dinner. Of all the vitamins in them, one is the delicate one, the first to break down in the heat. Which vitamin does cooking wreck most easily?
context: Vitamin C is the single most heat-sensitive vitamin in food, and it takes a double hit: heat breaks it apart, and because it dissolves in water it also drains out of the vegetable into the cooking water. A University of California, Davis review found home cooking typically destroys 15% to 55% of a vegetable's vitamin C, depending on the method. Source: AFC Urgent Care, 'Ask Well: Does Boiling or Baking Vegetables Destroy Their Vitamins?' (citing a UC Davis review) — https://www.afcurgentcare.com/denver-university-hills/blog/ask-well-does-boiling-or-baking-vegetables-destroy-their-vitamins/

question: A cook boils one batch of broccoli and loses more than half of a fragile vitamin in it. She cooks a second batch a different way and keeps nearly all of it. Which cooking method protects the vegetable's vitamins best?
context: Steaming beats boiling by a landslide because the vegetable never sits in the water that carries the vitamins away. In one comparison, steaming lost only 14.3% of broccoli's vitamin C while boiling the same broccoli lost 54.6% (boiling was nearly as brutal on spinach, 50.5%, and lettuce, 40.4%). Boiling greens has been measured to pull about 60% of their vitamin C straight out into the pot water. Source: ResearchGate, 'Effects of different cooking methods on the vitamin C content of selected vegetables' — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263613203_Effects_of_different_cooking_methods_on_the_vitamin_C_content_of_selected_vegetables

question: A cook who fears for her vegetables' vitamins shuns one common kitchen appliance, sure it zaps them out of food even worse than a long boil in a pot of water. Food scientists who have measured it say she has it backward: it is among the very best at saving them. Which appliance is the surprise vitamin-saver?
context: Microwaving is one of the best ways to keep vitamins, not the worst, because it uses barely any water and a short cooking time. Cornell scientists found spinach cooked in a microwave kept almost all of its folate and held on to over 90% of its vitamin C, while boiling the same spinach in water lost nearly 80% of that folate. Source: Have A Plant / Produce for Better Health Foundation (Cornell finding on microwaved vs. boiled spinach) — https://fruitsandveggies.org/blog/about-the-buzz-microwaving-fruits-vegetables-kills-all-their-essential-nutrientss/

question: A pot of vegetables simmers on the stove, and most of their vitamins slowly break down in the heat. A few are genuinely rugged, though, and barely notice the temperature, coming through the cooking almost intact. Which vitamin is one of those tough survivors?
context: Here's the rule that explains it all. Water-soluble vitamins — vitamin C and the whole B group — dissolve into the cooking water AND break down in heat, so boiling is a double loss. The fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — don't dissolve in water and shrug off heat far better; they're only lost in fat that gets drained away. Vitamin K is especially tough and holds up well through cooking. Source: Food Safety Institute, 'Functions and Applications of Water-Soluble Vitamins,' and Farm Forum, 'Cooking methods and vitamin loss' — https://foodsafety.institute/food-fundamentals-chemistry/functions-applications-water-soluble-vitamins/

question: A Southern cook simmers a huge batch of collard greens for hours, and she never pours away the dark broth left in the pot: she sips it from a cup like tea or sops it up with cornbread. What do Southern cooks call that broth?
context: In the American South this leftover green-cooking water is called 'pot liquor' (or 'pot likker'), traditionally sipped like tea or sopped up with cornbread — and it's the smart move, because it's loaded with what leached out of the greens: boiling releases roughly 50% of their flavonoids and 60% of their vitamin C into that liquid. Source: NPR, The Salt, 'Pot Liquor: A Southern Tip To Save Nutritious Broth From Greens' — https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2013/08/06/209543044/pot-liquor-a-southern-tip-to-save-nutritious-broth-from-greens

question: A shopper picks up produce wearing the green Organic seal of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. People argue over what it promises, yet it rests on one kind of rule. What does the seal certify?
choices: How many vitamins the food contains
How fresh the food is at the store
How many calories the food has
context: The USDA Organic seal certifies HOW produce is grown — without synthetic pesticides, without synthetic fertilizers, and without GMOs (genetic engineering is expressly prohibited). It makes no promise at all about vitamins or nutrition. Source: USDA, 'Organic 101: What the USDA Organic Label Means' / USDA AMS Organic Basics (ams.usda.gov).

question: One farmer has sprayed synthetic pesticides and fertilizers on his fields for years. He decides to switch, and this autumn he slaps the organic seal of the U.S. Department of Agriculture on his harvest, but an inspector stops him cold: the crop is not the only thing that has to qualify. What else must meet the standard first?
answer: The soil, kept free of prohibited chemicals for three years
choices: The soil, kept free of prohibited chemicals for three years
The seeds, bought from a government-run seed bank
The water, lab-tested for minerals every week
The workers, trained at a licensed farming school
context: To sell a crop as USDA organic, the soil must have had no prohibited substances (most synthetic pesticides and fertilizers) applied for the three years before harvest — a farm can't just switch overnight. USDA-accredited inspectors then visit certified farms every year to confirm they still meet the standard. Source: USDA AMS Organic Basics; USDA, 'Understanding the USDA Organic Label' (usda.gov).

question: Researchers at Stanford University pooled 237 separate studies in 2012 to test the benefits shoppers hope for when they pay almost twice as much for organic food: tastier, safer, more nutritious. Just one claim came out clearly backed up. Which claim did the pooled evidence support?
choices: It stays fresh on the shelf far longer
It tastes noticeably richer and sweeter
It grows to a noticeably larger size
context: The best-supported reason to choose organic is lower pesticide exposure. A large 2012 Stanford meta-analysis of 237 studies found organic produce carried a roughly 30% lower risk of detectable pesticide residue than conventional fruit and vegetables; a 2014 review of 343 studies found detectable residues about four times more often on conventional crops. Both, though, stayed within legal safety limits. Source: Smith-Spangler, Bravata et al. 2012, Annals of Internal Medicine; Baranski et al. 2014, British Journal of Nutrition.

question: Side by side in a big Stanford review of 237 studies in 2012, organic and ordinary fruit and vegetables came out almost even on nutrition. Yet the review did find organic winning more clearly in one place, and it was not produce at all. Where did organic come out ahead?
answer: Organic chicken and pork — fewer antibiotic-resistant bacteria
choices: Organic chicken and pork — fewer antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Organic beef and lamb — fewer product recalls
Organic eggs and milk — a much longer shelf life
Organic fish and shellfish — far lower mercury levels
context: Hunting for a nutritional edge, the 2012 Stanford review of 237 studies came up nearly empty on produce — only phosphorus edged higher, which the authors judged clinically unimportant, and lead author Crystal Smith-Spangler said the team was 'a little surprised.' The one clearer win beyond fruit and vegetables: organic chicken and pork carried a lower risk of antibiotic-resistant bacteria — though the authors cautioned its real-world health significance is unclear. (A 2014 British review did find organic crops modestly higher in antioxidants, which is why 'organic is more nutritious' stays contested.) Source: Smith-Spangler, Bravata et al. 2012, Annals of Internal Medicine; Stanford Medicine news release; Baranski et al. 2014, British Journal of Nutrition.

question: An organic grower walks his rows with a sprayer, because 'organic' does not mean pesticide-free: he may use approved natural bug-killers. One popular one, pyrethrin, is pressed straight from the petals of a common garden flower. Which flower?
context: 'Organic' does not mean pesticide-free. Organic growers spray approved NATURAL pesticides — pyrethrin, pressed from chrysanthemum flowers; neem oil, from the seeds of the neem tree; and Bt, made by a soil bacterium. The Stanford researchers noted organic foods are 'not necessarily 100 percent free of pesticides' — the residues are simply lower. Source: Rodale Institute, 'Wait, Organic Farmers Use Pesticides?' (rodaleinstitute.org); Stanford Medicine news release, 2012.

question: On his organic fields, a farmer fighting a plant disease may reach for copper sulfate, but only as a documented last resort, because copper builds up in the soil and in the body. On the U.S. Department of Agriculture's official list of what organic farms may use, how is copper sulfate itself classified?
answer: As a synthetic chemical, made in a factory
choices: As a synthetic chemical, made in a factory
As a natural mineral, dug from the ground
As a plant extract, pressed from seeds
As a living microbe, grown in soil
context: Copper builds up in soil and the body and never breaks down, so organic rules let farmers use copper-based fungicides only with a documented need, after other options fail — proof that 'natural' doesn't automatically mean safer. The real twist: copper sulfate is technically SYNTHETIC, yet the USDA's National List specifically permits it — one of about 25 synthetic substances allowed in organic crop production — because no natural alternative controls the same plant diseases as well. Source: USDA National List of Allowed and Prohibited Substances; Rodale Institute; AGDAILY, 'The list of organic pesticides approved by the USDA' (agdaily.com).

question: A cook cracks open a coconut and finds four very different parts: a fibrous brown husk, a hard woody shell, watery juice sloshing inside and a pale, solid lining pressed against the shell. Around a thousand coconuts go into just a few bottles of coconut oil, all of it from one part. Which part is pressed?
context: Coconut oil comes from the white flesh, or 'meat,' of the coconut, the flesh of a fruit rather than a seed, which puts it in the same family as olive and avocado oil. Below about 25C (77F) it sits as a solid white fat and melts to a clear liquid just above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coconut oil'.

question: A grandmother keeps a coffee can of lard on the back of the stove for her flaky pie crusts, refried beans and biscuits. Lard is rendered, slowly melted out and strained, from the thick fatty layers of one farm animal raised for its meat and fat since ancient times. Which animal is it?
context: Lard is pork fat. The same gentle melting-out process gives tallow from beef or mutton, and schmaltz from chicken or goose fat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rendering (animal products)'.

question: A cook keeps two kinds of sesame oil: a pale one for frying, and a dark, aromatic one she only ever drizzles on at the very end, because heat scorches it bitter. The dark oil gets its color and punch from one thing done to the seeds before pressing. What was done to them?
choices: the seeds were soaked in brine
the seeds were left to sprout
context: Sesame seeds are toasted before pressing to make dark, amber, intensely aromatic toasted sesame oil, a finishing oil since frying with it scorches it bitter. Raw, untoasted seeds instead make pale 'light' sesame oil that's fine for frying. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sesame oil'.

question: Canadian plant scientists took a wild weed in the 1970s and spent years cross-breeding it to strip out a bitter oil compound that upset stomachs, until a mild, safe cooking oil was left. They named the new crop canola, joining 'Canadian oil' to two words for the trait they had bred in. What were those two words?
context: 'Canola' is short for 'CANadian Oil, Low Acid.' Scientists bred rapeseed to strip out its bitter, once-toxic erucic acid; to be sold as food, canola must contain less than 2% of it. The crushed seed left after pressing becomes animal feed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Canola oil'.

question: On a shop shelf, a bottle of olive oil stamped 'First Cold Pressed' costs half again as much as the plain extra virgin oil beside it. A working olive miller would say the word 'first' on that fancy label is worth nothing. Why is it an empty boast?
answer: the olives are never pressed a second time
choices: the olives are never pressed a second time
the second pressing makes the finer oil
the first pressing is mostly olive water
the mill blends the pressings together
context: 'First press' is really just marketing; there is no genuine 'second press' of virgin oil. 'Cold pressed' does mean something: the oil was squeezed below about 27C (80F) so heat can't cook off its flavor. 'Extra virgin' is the top grade: cold mechanical pressing only, no chemicals, no taste defects, and very low acidity (no more than 0.8%). Plain 'virgin' allows more acidity and minor faults, while 'refined' oils were cleaned up with heat or solvents. Source: Wikipedia, 'Olive oil'.

question: A trained dog noses along a wooded hillside in northern Italy and stops over a white Alba truffle buried in the soil. It is one of the costliest foods on Earth, sold by the gram like a jewel, sometimes for thousands of dollars a pound. What kind of living thing is a truffle?
choices: A root vegetable, like a potato
context: A truffle is the fruiting body of a fungus in the genus Tuber; the white Alba truffle's scientific name is Tuber magnatum. Unlike the mushrooms you know that push up into the air, a truffle ripens its whole life underground and never breaks the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_magnatum

question: Truffle hunters return to the same wooded hillsides of northern Italy year after year to dig up the white Alba truffle, which spends its whole life hidden in the soil and grows in only one very particular place. Where does a white truffle actually grow?
answer: On the roots of living trees
choices: On the roots of living trees
In the dung of forest animals
context: The truffle wraps its fine threads around the roots of oaks, hazels, poplars, and beeches in a partnership called mycorrhiza: the fungus feeds the tree water and minerals gathered from the soil, and the tree feeds the fungus sugars it makes in its leaves. The truffle never shows above ground, which is exactly what makes it so hard to find. Sources: geographical.co.uk 'Unravelling the mystery of the white truffle'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_magnatum

question: Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin, the French food writer, praised the truffle in his famous book The Physiology of Taste in 1825. He gave it a glittering nickname that still clings to the white Alba truffle today. What did he call it?
context: Brillat-Savarin wrote the line in The Physiology of Taste in 1825, and 'the diamond of the kitchen' has stuck to the white Alba truffle ever since. Source: Brillat-Savarin, The Physiology of Taste (1825), via thedailymeal.com

question: A truffle hunter of old walked the woods with a pig, whose keen nose can sniff out a truffle buried nearly a metre deep. The pig had one serious flaw as a hunting partner, and today hunters work with trained dogs instead. What was the trouble with the pig?
answer: It ate the truffle before the hunter could grab it
choices: It ate the truffle before the hunter could grab it
It tired out on the steep hillsides and stopped
It dozed off in the warm soil and would not work
It kept leading the hunter to the wrong tree
context: A sow can smell a truffle nearly a metre down, but her rooting tore up the ground and she often ate the prize first. Italy banned pigs from truffle hunting in 1985 because the digging damages the fungus and slows the patch's recovery. Today Italy's specialist truffle dog, the Lagotto Romagnolo, points to the spot and lets the hunter dig it up gently. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truffle_hog; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagotto_Romagnolo

question: Stanley Ho, a casino billionaire from Macau, paid US$330,000 in December 2007 for a single white truffle dug up near Pisa, one of the biggest found in decades and worth far more than its weight in gold. A truffle that dear is rare for one particular reason. Why does a fine white truffle command such a price?
answer: It has defied every attempt to farm it
choices: It has defied every attempt to farm it
It rots almost as soon as it is dug up
It grows only in the deepest old forests
It must be eaten the very day it is found
context: For more than a century the white truffle beat every attempt to farm it, even after growers planted hundreds of thousands of seedlings laced with its spores. Only in 2021 did French scientists (INRAE, with the ROBIN nursery) harvest the first few cultivated white truffles, so it remains, for now, essentially a wild treasure. Stanley Ho's 1.5-kilogram truffle sold for about US$330,000. Sources: inrae.fr; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_magnatum

question: A chef in an Italian restaurant unwraps a knobby white truffle worth more per gram than gold. Over a plate of hot buttered pasta he shaves it into paper-thin, see-through slices that fall raw onto the steaming noodles, and it never goes near a hot pan or an oven. Why does he refuse to cook such a costly ingredient?
answer: Heat destroys its delicate aroma in seconds
choices: Heat destroys its delicate aroma in seconds
Cooking turns its flesh bitter and hard
The slices are too thin to survive a pan
Heat makes it shrink away to nothing
context: The white truffle's scent is so fragile that a flame destroys it, so it is never cooked. Shaved raw in almost transparent slices, it lands on hot buttered pasta, risotto, or fried eggs, and the warmth of the dish, not a fire, coaxes out its powerful garlic-and-cheese aroma. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_magnatum; geographical.co.uk 'Unravelling the mystery of the white truffle'

question: Suppose you eat carrots and sweet potatoes every day for years: you will never be poisoned by vitamin A, yet a megadose vitamin A pill from a supplement bottle can poison you. Nutritionists say a clever built-in switch keeps the carrots safe. What is that switch?
answer: Your body slows its conversion of beta-carotene once vitamin A stores are full.
choices: Your body slows its conversion of beta-carotene once vitamin A stores are full.
Your stomach destroys any beta-carotene beyond the first serving.
Carrots carry only trace amounts, far too little to ever build up.
Your kidneys flush the surplus vitamin A out within hours.
context: From food, the body throttles its own beta-carotene-to-vitamin-A conversion once levels are high enough, so you cannot overdose on vitamin A by eating vegetables — a built-in brake. A fixed high-dose pill bypasses that brake. Source: Cleveland Clinic (health.clevelandclinic.org/beta-carotene).

question: Researchers running a big American trial in the 1990s gave tens of thousands of smokers a daily high-dose pill of beta-carotene, the orange pigment of carrots and sweet potatoes, hoping it would guard them against cancer. The results grew so alarming that the trial was stopped early. What had the pills done to the smokers?
answer: Given them more lung cancer, not less.
choices: Given them more lung cancer, not less.
Turned their skin a permanent bright orange.
Triggered dangerous bleeding by thinning their blood.
Ruined their night vision within a year.
context: Two big trials tested the bet that a beta-carotene pill would prevent lung cancer. In Finland's ATBC trial (NEJM 1994), 29,133 male smokers on 20 mg/day got about 18% MORE lung cancer and an 8% higher death rate. The U.S. CARET trial (Omenn et al., JNCI/NEJM 1996) gave smokers and asbestos-exposed workers 30 mg beta-carotene plus vitamin A and was halted in January 1996 after 28% more lung cancers and 17% more deaths. ACCURACY RAIL: this harm appeared only in SMOKERS taking a high-dose isolated pill — it does NOT mean carrots are dangerous or that 'vitamins cause cancer.' Whole-food beta-carotene never showed this harm. Sources: NEJM 1994 (ATBC); Omenn et al., PubMed 8901853 (CARET).

question: James Lind, a naval surgeon, ran one of history's first controlled experiments in 1747 on sailors dying of scurvy, the disease of rotting gums and old wounds splitting open. Scurvy once killed more of Britain's seamen than enemy cannon fire ever did, and Lind found the cure sitting in the ship's own stores. What brought the dying men back?
context: James Lind's 1747 trial is remembered as one of the first controlled experiments: the sailors given citrus recovered fastest. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C — though that vitamin was not identified until the 20th century, long after Lind. Scurvy is estimated to have killed more British sailors than all their naval battles combined. Source: Wikipedia, James Lind.

question: A carrot and a pill of the beta-carotene pulled from it read the same on a label, yet they behave very differently in the body. Smokers given beta-carotene pills at high doses every day in trials of the 1990s were harmed, though eating carrots had never shown such harm. What do scientists see as the leading reason?
answer: In the whole carrot it arrives bundled with fiber and hundreds of interacting compounds.
choices: In the whole carrot it arrives bundled with fiber and hundreds of interacting compounds.
The extraction process quietly destroys most of the pill's beta-carotene.
Supplement beta-carotene is synthetic and the body simply cannot absorb it.
Cooking always strips a carrot's beta-carotene out before you eat it.
context: Nutrition scientists call this the 'food matrix' or food synergy: in a whole food a nutrient arrives packaged with fiber and hundreds of other compounds that regulate and interact with it, so the whole is greater than any single nutrient pulled out and megadosed. The carrot is not the pill. Source: Jacobs et al., 'Food synergy,' Am J Clin Nutr (PMC2731586).

question: A woman who takes one ordinary vitamin around the time she conceives cuts her baby's risk of neural-tube birth defects like spina bifida by up to 70 percent. It is the clearest case of a supplement that fills a genuine gap, an honest exception to eating the food rather than the pill. Which vitamin is it?
context: Folic acid is a supplement that clearly works because it fills a real gap: about 400 micrograms daily around conception can cut neural-tube defects like spina bifida by up to roughly 70%. It is the honest counterweight to 'food first' — other fair uses of a pill include vitamin D in high-latitude winters (when UVB is too weak for skin to make any) and vitamin B12 for long-term vegans (B12 is found almost only in animal foods). The fair rule is 'food first, pills to fix a real gap,' not 'all supplements are useless.' Sources: CDC (cdc.gov/folic-acid); Rashid et al., Eur J Haematol 2021 (vegan B12); UK winter vitamin D review (PMC6121420).

question: A baker who buys white flour gets none of the wheat germ: the miller stripped it out, and with it went the richest natural source known of one vitamin. One tablespoon of the germ's oil carries about a whole day's supply. Which vitamin goes out with the germ?
context: Wheat germ oil is the richest natural source of vitamin E known — roughly a full day's worth in a single tablespoon. When millers discard the germ to make white flour, that vitamin E goes out with it. (Healthline, 'Foods High in Vitamin E'; Darwin Nutrition, 'Wheat germ')

question: A miller pours a sack of whole wheat kernels into his mill and grinds them into snow-white flour. When he weighs the fiber left in that pale flour, it is only about a fifth of what the whole grain carried in. The rest went out with the tough brown flakes he sifts away. Which part of the kernel is that?
context: Nearly all of a wheat grain's fiber sits in the bran, its tough outer coat. Milling strips the bran off to make white flour, so refined flour keeps only about a fifth — roughly 22% — of the whole grain's fiber; the rest leaves with the bran. (Wikipedia, 'Refined grains'; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, The Nutrition Source, 'Whole Grains')

question: A miller splits a wheat kernel and points to a tiny speck inside it, the only living part of it. In warm, wet soil that speck would sprout into a whole new plant, and the rest of the kernel is its stored food. What is the speck called?
context: That living sprout-to-be is the germ (as in 'germinate'). It is the smallest part of the grain but is rich in vitamins and healthy oils. The other two parts are the fibrous bran on the outside and the big starchy core in the middle; brown rice and whole-wheat flour keep all three. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal_germ

question: White flour leaves the mill as nearly one part of the wheat grain and nothing else. The mill strips away the grain's nutritious outer layers and keeps only the big, pale, starchy core, the food the seed packed away for the plant it would become. What is that core called?
context: The starchy core is the endosperm — the seed's own energy store. White flour and white rice are mostly pure endosperm, because milling scrapes off the fiber-rich bran and the vitamin-rich germ and keeps the bland, long-lasting starch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal_germ

question: Families across Asia who lived on rice fell ill with beriberi in the late 1800s, a crippling disease of the nerves and heart that brought numb legs, racing hearts and sometimes sudden death. What simple change to the rice cured it?
choices: switching to whiter, more polished rice
rinsing the rice in clean water
context: By the late 1800s, new steam-powered mills were polishing rice pearly white on a massive scale — and the disease spread right alongside the shiny grain. The missing nutrient was thiamine (vitamin B1), which had been living in the bran the mills polished off. Brown rice keeps its bran, so simply switching back to unpolished rice cured the disease — the healing 'medicine' had never been in the white grain at all. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'How Killer Rice Crippled Tokyo and the Japanese Navy'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiamine_deficiency

question: A sealed bag of white flour sits in a warehouse for a year and still bakes up fine. It keeps so long largely because the mill took out each grain's tiny living sprout-to-be, the very part that would otherwise turn the flour bad. What is it about that part that would spoil the flour?
answer: it is packed with delicate oils that go rancid
choices: it is packed with delicate oils that go rancid
it is packed with live yeasts that ferment
it is packed with trapped water that molds
it is packed with sweet sugars that draw bugs
context: The germ is rich in delicate polyunsaturated oils that oxidize and turn rancid over time. Here is the twist: that same germ is where much of the grain's goodness lives — so the good part and the perishable part are the very same part. Stripping it out is exactly what lets white flour keep for months. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal_germ

question: A baker reads the word 'enriched' on a bag of white flour: the mill has sprayed a handful of nutrients back into the refined grain, after whole regions fell ill living on stripped white rice and flour. But one thing milling strips out has never been put back. What can enriched flour never return?
context: Since the 1940s (the U.S. Army required enriched flour in 1942), mills add back thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, folic acid, and iron. But the fiber lived in the bran that milling throws away, and no one sprays fiber back on — it is the one thing refining takes that fortification cannot return. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_flour

question: A Japanese Navy training ship limped home in 1883 from a nine-month voyage. Fed on nothing but polished white rice, 169 of its 376 sailors had come down with beriberi and 25 were dead. Takaki Kanehiro, the navy's doctor, suspected the diet, and the following year he sent another ship on the identical route with the meals overhauled. Not one man died of beriberi. Besides rice, what had he added?
context: Most doctors then blamed an invisible germ, but Takaki Kanehiro had shown it was the food: polished white rice was stripped of thiamine (vitamin B1), and the added barley, meat, and milk restored it. His two-voyage test — same route, different diet — was decades ahead of its time, and it traced the sickness back to the bran the mills polished away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takaki_Kanehiro

question: A chef sears a thick steak brown outside, leaves it pink and rare in the middle, and serves it safely. A hamburger patty ground from the same cow's beef is held to a different rule. To be safe, how must the patty be cooked?
answer: All the way through, until no pink is left
choices: All the way through, until no pink is left
Rare in the center, just like the steak
Seared outside, still red in the middle
Barely warmed, so it stays soft
context: This is the whole puzzle in one bite: same beef, opposite rules. A whole steak is treated as safe cooked rare, but a burger made of ground beef is not. The reason has nothing to do with ground beef being somehow dirtier; it is entirely about WHERE the bacteria sit. Source: Tasting Table, 'A Rare Steak Is Safer To Eat Than A Rare Burger. Here's Why' (tastingtable.com/1236087).

question: A chef pulls a whole, uncut ribeye from the fridge. Any harmful bacteria on it cling only to the surface, where air and hands have touched the meat, and the red middle stays essentially germ-free, which is why a steak can be served rare. What keeps those surface germs out of the center?
answer: The dense, unbroken muscle blocks them
choices: The dense, unbroken muscle blocks them
The cold of the fridge freezes them out
The salt naturally in beef kills them
The red juices wash them back out
context: The interior of an intact cut is essentially sterile because tightly packed, unbroken muscle fibers act as a barrier. Butchering only smears micro-organisms onto the exterior, and pathogens almost never migrate below the surface of an unbroken piece of muscle. That is exactly why a hard sear on the outside is enough to make a rare steak safe. Sources: USDA National Agricultural Library, 'Examination of the Microbiological Safety of Rare Steak'; Beef Research 'Non-Intact Beef' fact sheet.

question: A butcher sells a whole beef steak to be eaten rare, pink in the middle, and food-safety experts agree it is fine. Fed through a meat grinder and shaped into a hamburger patty, the same beef loses that freedom under the food-safety rules. What does the spinning grinder do to the beef that makes the difference?
answer: It spreads the outside bacteria all through the meat
choices: It spreads the outside bacteria all through the meat
It adds new bacteria from the machine's blades
It warms the beef up into the danger zone
It squeezes the natural juices out of the beef
context: This is the key reveal: the grinder churns the outer surface, and any bacteria on it, all the way through the whole mass of meat. The germs are no longer just on the outside; they are mixed everywhere inside, so the entire patty must reach a safe temperature. In big plants the blending is enormous, and a single mass-produced patty can contain trimmings from around 100 (by some estimates over 1,000) different cattle, so one dirty animal's surface bacteria can be spread through a huge batch. Sources: USDA FSIS, 'Ground Beef and Food Safety'; Washington Post (2015).

question: A shopper picks up a supermarket steak in ordinary packaging, looking just like the rest of the case. Food-safety experts warn that this kind of steak should be treated like a ground-beef burger, never served rare. What has been done to it at the meat plant?
answer: It has been blade-tenderized with rows of needles
choices: It has been blade-tenderized with rows of needles
It has been dry-aged on a rack for weeks
It has been flash-frozen and then thawed
It has been marinated in vinegar and garlic
context: Blade- or needle-tenderizing drives rows of thin blades through a steak to soften it, and they drag surface bacteria down into the middle, exactly like grinding does. These steaks have caused real outbreaks: in 2009, 21 people across 16 states were infected with E. coli O157 traced to blade-tenderized steaks; 9 were hospitalized and one developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a kind of kidney failure. The CDC has linked at least six such outbreaks since 2000. USDA advises cooking these to 145F with a 3-minute rest, and some experts say treat them like a burger. Sources: USDA FSIS 'Mechanically Tenderized Beef'; PBS NewsHour; Northeastern University News (2024).

question: Undercooked hamburgers from a fast-food chain sickened more than 700 people across the western United States in 1992 and 1993 and killed four children. The disaster was so severe that U.S. regulators took a drastic step for hamburger meat. What did they do?
answer: Outlawed selling ground beef contaminated with the germ
choices: Outlawed selling ground beef contaminated with the germ
Outlawed serving hamburgers at all fast-food chains
Required every burger patty to be sold frozen
Required all beef cattle to be inspected weekly
context: The culprit is E. coli O157:H7, which lives harmlessly in cattle intestines and gets smeared onto meat during slaughter; its infectious dose is frighteningly low, as few as 10 to 100 organisms. After the Jack in the Box outbreak, the USDA declared the strain an 'adulterant' in ground beef, meaning it is now illegal to sell ground beef containing it in any amount. Sources: CDC MMWR, 'Multistate Outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers, Western United States, 1992-1993'; Wikipedia, '1992-1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak'.

question: A lean, active ten-year-old weighs about half as much as his big, desk-bound dad, yet pound for pound the boy needs more protein each day than his father does. Why does the smaller one need more?
answer: He's adding brand-new body tissue every single year as he grows.
choices: He's adding brand-new body tissue every single year as he grows.
He burns off protein for fuel while he runs and plays all day.
His small stomach can't store protein, so he must eat it often.
His young gut digests protein less efficiently than a grown-up's.
context: Protein is the raw building material of the body -- muscle, bone, organs, skin, and hair are all made from it. A growing child is literally adding new body every year, so per pound of bodyweight he needs MORE protein than a sit-still adult who is only maintaining what he already has. Source: UC Davis Nutrition Health Info Sheet, 'Protein Requirements.'

question: A high-school lifter finishes a hard set of squats, and his coach shoves a chicken sandwich into his hands. Coaches push protein right after a hard workout, because a muscle only grows bigger once the training has first changed it in some way. What does hard lifting do to the muscle in the moment?
answer: It tears tiny fibers, which then rebuild thicker and stronger than before.
choices: It tears tiny fibers, which then rebuild thicker and stronger than before.
It stretches the fibers, which then set at that new, greater length.
It floods the fibers with blood, which then stays locked in as bulk.
It drains the fibers of fuel, which the body then refills to overflow.
context: Hard training -- lifting, sprinting -- tears tiny muscle fibers, and the damage is worst on the lowering (eccentric) half of a lift, like slowly lowering a curl. The body then rebuilds each fiber thicker and stronger, but only if protein is on hand to do the rebuilding -- which is the whole reason for the 'eat protein after your workout' rule. The repair stays switched on for up to about 48 hours afterward. Source: House of Hypertrophy, 'Do Microtears in the Muscle Cause Growth?'; NASM, 'The Power of Protein.'

question: A pregnant woman sits down to dinner with her big husband, yet she needs more protein each day than he does. Nutritionists' tables show her daily need jumping well above a normal grown adult's. What is her body doing through those nine months that runs up such a protein bill?
answer: Growing a whole second person -- its placenta and extra blood as well.
choices: Growing a whole second person -- its placenta and extra blood as well.
Storing a protein reserve to get her through the hard work of labor.
Replacing the protein she loses to months of morning-sickness nausea.
Padding on fat stores that the baby will draw down after it is born.
context: A pregnant mother's protein target climbs from about 0.8 up to roughly 1.1 grams per kilogram of bodyweight a day, because the baby, its placenta, and her own extra blood are all newly built tissue. A nursing mother needs even more -- about 25 extra grams a day -- because she is making milk out of her own body. Source: WeNatal, 'The Hidden Protein Needs of Pregnancy'; PMC5104202, 'Nutrition Recommendations in Pregnancy and Lactation.'

question: A toddler in a West African famine is fed bowl after bowl of starchy cassava porridge, mostly carbohydrate and almost no protein. Doctors call his illness kwashiorkor, and its strangest sign is his belly, which swells up round so that he looks puffy and well fed even as he starves. What makes the belly swell?
answer: His blood turns too thin to hold its water, so fluid pools in his belly.
choices: His blood turns too thin to hold its water, so fluid pools in his belly.
The bulky porridge slowly stretches his stomach out wider and wider.
Starch he cannot fully digest ferments into gas that swells him up.
The all-carbohydrate porridge packs fat straight onto his middle.
context: This is kwashiorkor -- the malnutrition that proves enough calories is not the same as enough protein. It strikes children filled up on starchy food like maize, cassava, or rice porridge but given almost no protein. With too little protein in the blood, the body's fluid balance breaks down (doctors measure it as low albumin), so watery fluid pools and the child looks 'fed' and even puffy while actually starving; the liver also swells with fat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kwashiorkor'; ScienceDirect kwashiorkor overview.

question: Small children in parts of Ghana sometimes fall ill with a swollen belly, thinning hair and pale skin, the signs of severe protein starvation. The Ga people of Ghana have their own name for the illness, kwashiorkor, and the doctor Cicely Williams brought it into medicine in 1935. The word names no symptom but the family moment that brings the illness on. What does it mean?
answer: The sickness the older child gets when a new baby arrives
choices: The sickness the older child gets when a new baby arrives
The sickness the whole family gets when the harvest fails
The sickness the youngest gets when the mother stops eating
The sickness a child gets when he is sent off to relatives
context: The Ga name means roughly 'the disease of the deposed child.' It pinpoints exactly when the illness hits: a toddler is weaned off protein-rich breast milk to make room for a new baby and switched to starchy porridge, losing his main protein source just when he still needs it to grow.
